text:
XLoader loads a copy of NTDLL to evade hooks from security monitoring tools on this library. XLoader can add the path of its executable to the Microsoft Defender exclusion list.
XLoader can create scheduled tasks for persistence.
XLoader has exploited Office vulnerabilities during local execution such as CVE-2017-11882 and CVE-2018-0798.
XLoader uses various packers, including CyaX, to obfuscate malicious executables.

text:
Metamorfo has a command to launch a keylogger and capture keystrokes on the victim’s machine.
Metamorfo has a function to hijack data from the clipboard by monitoring the contents of the clipboard and replacing the cryptocurrency wallet with the attacker's.
Metamorfo collects a list of installed antivirus software from the victim’s system.
Metamorfo has a function that can watch the contents of the system clipboard for valid bitcoin addresses, which it then overwrites with the attacker's address.
Metamorfo has used VMProtect to pack and protect files.
Metamorfo had used AutoIt to load and execute the DLL payload.
Metamorfo has used MsiExec.exe to automatically execute files.

text:
reGeorg is a Python-based web shell.
reGeorg can establish an HTTP or SOCKS proxy to tunnel data in and out of a network.
title: xl7dev. (2016). reGeorg-master. Retrieved December 3, 2024.

text:
SocGholish can use `whoami` to obtain the username from a compromised host.
SocGholish can exfiltrate data directly to its C2 domain via HTTP.
SocGholish has the ability to enumerate system information including the victim computer name.
SocGholish can download additional malware to infected hosts.
The SocGholish JavaScript payload has been delivered within a compressed ZIP archive.
The SocGholish payload is executed as JavaScript.
SocGholish has the ability to enumerate the domain name of a victim, as well as if the host is a member of an Active Directory domain.
SocGholish can send output from `whoami` to a local temp file using the naming convention `rad<5-hex-chars>.tmp`.
SocGholish can profile compromised systems to identify domain trust relationships.

text:
Meteor execution begins from a scheduled task named `Microsoft\Windows\Power Efficiency Diagnostics\AnalyzeAll` and it creates a separate scheduled task called `mstask` to run the wiper only once at 23:55:00.
Meteor has the ability to discover the hostname of a compromised host.
Meteor has been disguised as the Windows Power Efficiency Diagnostics report tool.
Meteor can disconnect all network adapters on a compromised host using `powershell -Command "Get-WmiObject -class Win32_NetworkAdapter | ForEach { If ($.NetEnabled) { $.Disable() } }" > NUL`.
Meteor can use Wevtutil to remove Security, System and Application Event Viewer logs.
Meteor can change both the desktop wallpaper and the lock screen image to a custom image.
Meteor can use `bcdedit` to delete different boot identifiers on a compromised host; it can also use `vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet` and `C:\\Windows\\system32\\wbem\\wmic.exe shadowcopy delete`.
Meteor can check if a specific process is running, such as Kaspersky's `avp.exe`.
Meteor can use group policy to push a scheduled task from the AD to all network machines.
Meteor can attempt to uninstall Kaspersky Antivirus or remove the Kaspersky license; it can also add all files and folders related to the attack to the Windows Defender exclusion list.
Meteor will delete the folder containing malicious scripts if it detects the hostname as `PIS-APP`, `PIS-MOB`, `WSUSPROXY`, or `PIS-DB`.
Meteor can hide its console window upon execution to decrease its visibility to a victim.
Meteor has the ability to search for Kaspersky Antivirus on a victim's machine.
Meteor can use `wmic.exe` as part of its effort to delete shadow copies.
Meteor can fill a victim's files and directories with zero-bytes in replacement of real content before deleting them.
Meteor can use `WinAPI` to remove a victim machine from an Active Directory domain.
Meteor has the ability to download additional files for execution on the victim's machine.
Meteor can run `set.bat`, `update.bat`, `cache.bat`, `bcd.bat`, `msrun.bat`, and similar scripts.
Meteor has the ability to change the password of local users on compromised hosts and can log off users.
Meteor can use PowerShell commands to disable the network adapters on a victim machines.
title: Check Point Research Team. (2021, August 14). Indra - Hackers Behind Recent Attacks on Iran. Retrieved February 17, 2022.

text:
jRAT’s Java payload is encrypted with AES. Additionally, backdoor files are encrypted using DES as a stream cipher. Later variants of jRAT also incorporated AV evasion methods such as Java bytecode obfuscation via the commercial Allatori obfuscation tool.
jRAT has a function to delete files from the victim’s machine.
jRAT uses WMIC to identify anti-virus products installed on the victim’s machine and to obtain firewall details.
title: Sharma, R. (2018, August 15). Revamped jRAT Uses New Anti-Parsing Techniques. Retrieved September 21, 2018.

text:
IOCONTROL has removed the malware binary and associated log file (i.e., `/tmp/iocontrol.log`) from a system upon command.
IOCONTROL has used the `date` and `timezone` commands to gather the system date and time information.
IOCONTROL has used the `uname -v` and `uname –r` commands to obtain kernel version and release information as well as the `hostname` command to obtain the hostname of the system.
IOCONTROL has used an RC script (`/etc/rc3.d/S93InitSystemd.sh`) to establish persistence on a system across restarts.
IOCONTROL has removed malware persistence from a system upon command.
IOCONTROL has used the `whoami` command to get the current user on the system.

text: Crutch has exfiltrated stolen data to Dropbox. Crutch has used a hardcoded GitHub repository as a fallback channel. Crutch has the ability to persist using scheduled tasks. Crutch has conducted C2 communications with a Dropbox account using the HTTP API. Crutch has automatically exfiltrated stolen files to Dropbox. Crutch can use Dropbox to receive commands and upload stolen data. Crutch can automatically monitor removable drives in a loop and copy interesting files. Crutch can persist via DLL search order hijacking on Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, or Microsoft OneDrive. Crutch can monitor removable drives and exfiltrate files matching a given extension list. Crutch can exfiltrate data over the primary C2 channel (Dropbox HTTP API). Crutch has established persistence with a scheduled task impersonating the Outlook item finder. Crutch has used the WinRAR utility to compress and encrypt stolen files. Crutch can monitor for removable drives being plugged into the compromised machine. Crutch can exfiltrate files from compromised systems. Crutch has staged stolen files in the C:\AMD\Temp directory.
title: Faou, M. (2020, December 2). Turla Crutch: Keeping the “back door” open. Retrieved December 4, 2020.

text:
MiniDuke can download additional encrypted backdoors onto the victim via GIF files.
MiniDuke uses Google Search to identify C2 servers if its primary C2 method via Twitter is not working.
Some MiniDuke components use Twitter to initially obtain the address of a C2 server or as a backup if no hard-coded C2 server responds.

text: PLAINTEE encodes C2 beacons using XOR. PLAINTEE uses reg add to add a Registry Run key for persistence. PLAINTEE uses cmd.exe to execute commands on the victim’s machine. PLAINTEE gains persistence by adding the Registry key HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce. PLAINTEE performs the tasklist command to list running processes. DDKONG uses Rundll32 to ensure only a single instance of itself is running at once. DDKONG downloads and uploads files on the victim’s machine. PLAINTEE has downloaded and executed additional plugins. PLAINTEE collects general system enumeration data about the infected machine and checks the OS version. DDKONG decodes an embedded configuration using XOR. PLAINTEE uses the ipconfig /all command to gather the victim’s IP address. An older variant of PLAINTEE performs UAC bypass. DDKONG lists files on the victim’s machine.
title: Ash, B., et al. (2018, June 26). RANCOR: Targeted Attacks in South East Asia Using PLAINTEE and DDKONG Malware Families. Retrieved July 2, 2018.

QuietSieve can collect files from a compromised host.
PowerPunch can download payloads from adversary infrastructure.
PowerPunch can use the volume serial number from a target host to generate a unique XOR key for the next stage payload.
QuietSieve can check C2 connectivity with a `ping` to 8.8.8.8 (Google public DNS).
Pteranodon has used various API calls.
QuietSieve can identify and search removable drives for specific file name extensions.
Pteranodon can use a dynamic Windows hashing algorithm to map API components.
PowerPunch has the ability to execute through PowerShell.
QuietSieve has the ability to execute payloads in a hidden window.
QuietSieve can use HTTPS in C2 communications.
QuietSieve can download and execute payloads on a target host.
Pteranodon can decrypt encrypted data strings prior to using them.
PowerPunch can use Base64-encoded scripts.
QuietSieve can identify and search networked drives for specific file name extensions.
QuietSieve can search files on the target host by extension, including doc, docx, xls, rtf, odt, txt, jpg, pdf, rar, zip, and 7z.
title: Microsoft Threat Intelligence Center. (2022, February 4). ACTINIUM targets Ukrainian organizations. Retrieved February 18, 2022.

text:
The discovery modules used with Duqu can collect information on process details.
Modules can be pushed to and executed by Duqu that copy data to a staging area, compress it, and XOR encrypt it.
Duqu uses a custom command and control protocol that communicates over commonly used ports, and is frequently encapsulated by application layer protocols.
The reconnaissance modules used with Duqu can collect information on network configuration.
Adversaries can instruct Duqu to spread laterally by copying itself to shares it has enumerated and for which it has obtained legitimate credentials (via keylogging or other means). The remote host is then infected by using the compromised credentials to schedule a task on remote machines that executes the malware.
Duqu can track key presses with a keylogger module.
Duqu can be configured to have commands relayed over a peer-to-peer network of infected hosts if some of the hosts do not have Internet access.
Duqu creates a new service that loads a malicious driver when the system starts. When Duqu is active, the operating system believes that the driver is legitimate, as it has been signed with a valid private key.
Duqu will inject itself into different processes to evade detection. The selection of the target process is influenced by the security software that is installed on the system (Duqu will inject into different processes depending on which security suite is installed on the infected host).
Duqu is capable of loading executable code via process hollowing.
The discovery modules used with Duqu can collect information on open windows.
The Duqu command and control protocol's data stream can be encrypted with AES-CBC.
The discovery modules used with Duqu can collect information on network connections.
The discovery modules used with Duqu can collect information on accounts and permissions.
When the Duqu command and control is operating over HTTP or HTTPS, Duqu uploads data to its controller by appending it to a blank JPG file.
title: Symantec Security Response. (2011, November). W32.Duqu: The precursor to the next Stuxnet. Retrieved September 17, 2015.

text:
XCSSET's `dfhsebxzod` module searches for `.xcodeproj` directories within the user’s home folder and subdirectories. For each match, it locates the corresponding `project.pbxproj` file and embeds an encoded payload into a build rule, target configuration, or project setting. The payload is later executed during the build process.
For several modules, XCSSET attempts to access or list the contents of user folders such as Desktop, Downloads, and Documents. If the folder does not exist or access is denied, it enters a loop where it resets the TCC database and retries access.
Using AppleScript, XCSSET adds it's executable to the user's `~/.zshrc_aliases` file (`"echo " & payload & " > ~/zshrc_aliases"`), it then adds a line to the .zshrc file to source the `.zshrc_aliases` file (`[ -f $HOME/.zshrc_aliases ] && . $HOME/.zshrc_aliases`). Each time the user starts a new `zsh` terminal session, the `.zshrc` file executes the `.zshrc_aliases` file.
Older XCSSET variants use `xxd` to encode modules. Later versions pass an `xxd` or `base64` encoded blob through multiple decoding stages to reconstruct the module name, AppleScript, or shell command. For example, the initial network request uses three layers of hex decoding before executing a curl command in a shell.
title: Microsoft Threat Intelligence. (2025, March 11). New XCSSET malware adds new obfuscation, persistence techniques to infect Xcode projects. Retrieved April 2, 2025.

text: Nidiran can create a new service named msamger (Microsoft Security Accounts Manager), which mimics the legitimate Microsoft database by the same name.
title: Microsoft. (2006, October 30). How to use the SysKey utility to secure the Windows Security Accounts Manager database. Retrieved August 3, 2016.

text:
LOWBALL command and control occurs via HTTPS over port 443.
LOWBALL uses the Dropbox cloud storage service for command and control.
BUBBLEWRAP can communicate using HTTP or HTTPS.
BUBBLEWRAP collects system information, including the operating system version and hostname.
LOWBALL uses the Dropbox API to request two files, one of which is the same file as the one dropped by the malicious email attachment. This is most likely meant to be a mechanism to update the compromised host with a new version of the LOWBALL malware.
BUBBLEWRAP can communicate using SOCKS.
title: FireEye Threat Intelligence. (2015, December 1). China-based Cyber Threat Group Uses Dropbox for Malware Communications and Targets Hong Kong Media Outlets. Retrieved December 4, 2015.

text:
Regin appears to have functionality to modify remote Registry information.
Regin contains a keylogger.
Regin appears to have functionality to sniff for credentials passed over HTTP, SMTP, and SMB.
Regin leveraged several compromised universities as proxies to obscure its origin.
Regin stage 1 modules for 64-bit systems have been found to be signed with fake certificates masquerading as originating from Microsoft Corporation and Broadcom Corporation.
The Regin malware platform supports many standard protocols, including HTTP and HTTPS.
Regin has used a hidden file system to store some of its components.
The Regin malware platform can use ICMP to communicate between infected computers.
The Regin malware platform supports many standard protocols, including SMB.
The Regin malware platform can use Windows admin shares to move laterally.
The Regin malware platform uses Extended Attributes to store encrypted executables.
title: Kaspersky Lab's Global Research and Analysis Team. (2014, November 24). THE REGIN PLATFORM NATION-STATE OWNAGE OF GSM NETWORKS. Retrieved December 1, 2014.

text: Epic has overwritten the function pointer in the extra window memory of Explorer's Shell_TrayWnd in order to execute malicious code in the context of the explorer.exe process.
title: Boutin, J. and Faou, M. (2018). Visiting the snake nest. Retrieved May 7, 2019.

text: TrickBot has the ability to capture RDP credentials by capturing the CredEnumerateA API TrickBot has attempted to get users to launch malicious documents to deliver its payload. TrickBot can obtain passwords stored in files from several applications such as Outlook, Filezilla, OpenSSH, OpenVPN and WinSCP. Additionally, it searches for the ".vnc.lnk" affix to steal VNC credentials. TrickBot has used macros in Excel documents to download and deploy the malware on the user’s machine. TrickBot has used an email with an Excel sheet containing a malicious macro to deploy the malware TrickBot has retrieved PuTTY credentials by querying the Software\SimonTatham\Putty\Sessions registry key
title: Llimos, N., Pascual, C.. (2019, February 12). Trickbot Adds Remote Application Credential-Grabbing Capabilities to Its Repertoire. Retrieved March 12, 2019.

text:
Briba installs a service pointing to a malicious DLL dropped to disk.
Briba downloads files onto infected hosts.
Briba uses rundll32 within Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder entries to execute malicious DLLs.
Briba creates run key Registry entries pointing to malicious DLLs dropped to disk.
title: Ladley, F. (2012, May 15). Backdoor.Briba. Retrieved February 21, 2018.

text:
FunnyDream can upload files from victims' machines.
FunnyDream can collect information about hosts on the victim network.
title: Global Research and Analysis Team. (2020, April 30). APT trends report Q1 2020. Retrieved September 19, 2022.

text:
HermeticWiper has the ability to overwrite its own file with random bites.
HermeticWiper can decompress and copy driver files using `LZCopy`.
HermeticWiper can disable pop-up information about folders and desktop items and delete Registry keys to hide malicious services.
HermeticWiper has the ability to corrupt disk partitions and obtain raw disk access to destroy data.
HermeticWiper can load drivers by creating a new service using the `CreateServiceW` API.
HermeticWiper has the ability to receive a command parameter to sleep prior to carrying out destructive actions on a targeted host.
title: Thomas, W. et al. (2022, February 25). CrowdStrike Falcon Protects from New Wiper Malware Used in Ukraine Cyberattacks. Retrieved March 25, 2022.

text:
Avaddon has used encrypted strings.
Avaddon has collected information about running processes.
Avaddon deletes backups and shadow copies using native system tools.
Avaddon looks for and attempts to stop database processes.
Avaddon has enumerated shared folders and mapped volumes.
Avaddon uses registry run keys for persistence.
Avaddon has searched for specific files prior to encryption.
Avaddon modifies several registry keys for persistence and UAC bypass.
Avaddon has decrypted encrypted strings.
Avaddon encrypts the victim system using a combination of AES256 and RSA encryption schemes.
Avaddon checks for specific keyboard layouts and OS languages to avoid targeting Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) entities.
Avaddon bypasses UAC using the CMSTPLUA COM interface.
Avaddon looks for and attempts to stop anti-malware solutions.

text: Clop has used the sleep command to avoid sandbox detection. Clop can kill several processes and services related to backups and security solutions. Clop can encrypt files using AES, RSA, and RC4 and will add the ".clop" extension to encrypted files. Clop can use code signing to evade detection.
title: Santos, D. (2021, April 13). Threat Assessment: Clop Ransomware. Retrieved July 30, 2021.

text:
BUSHWALK is a web shell that has the ability to execute arbitrary commands or write files.
FRAMESTING uses a cookie named `DSID` to mimic the name of a cookie used by Ivanti Connect Secure appliances for maintaining VPN sessions.
LIGHTWIRE can imbed itself into the legitimate `compcheckresult.cgi` component of Ivanti Connect Secure VPNs to enable command execution.
BUSHWALK can encrypt the resulting data generated from C2 commands with RC4.
LIGHTWIRE can RC4 encrypt C2 commands.
FRAMESTING can decompress data received within `POST` requests.
WARPWIRE can send captured credentials to C2 via HTTP `GET` or `POST` requests.
FRAMESTING can retrieve C2 commands from values stored in the `DSID` cookie from the current HTTP request or from decompressed zlib data within the request's `POST` data.
ZIPLINE can create a proxy server on compromised hosts.
ZIPLINE can use AES-128-CBC to encrypt data for both upload and download.
ZIPLINE can download files to be saved on the compromised system.
FRAMESTING is a Python web shell that can embed in the Ivanti Connect Secure CAV Python package.
FRAMESTING is a web shell capable of enabling arbitrary command execution on compromised Ivanti Connect Secure VPNs.
LIGHTWIRE can RC4 decrypt and Base64 decode C2 commands.
ZIPLINE can communicate with C2 using a custom binary protocol.
LIGHTWIRE can use HTTP for C2 communications.
FRAMESTING can send and receive zlib compressed data within `POST` requests.
FRAMESTING can embed itself in the CAV Python package of an Ivanti Connect Secure VPN located in `/home/venv3/lib/python3.6/site-packages/cav-0.1-py3.6.egg/cav/api/resources/category.py.`
LIGHTWIRE is a web shell capable of command execution and establishing persistence on compromised Ivanti Secure Connect VPNs.

text: KGH_SPY can collect credentials from the Windows Credential Manager. KGH_SPY has the ability to set a Registry key to run a cmd.exe command. KGH_SPY has been spread through Word documents containing malicious macros. KGH_SPY can decrypt encrypted strings and write them to a newly created folder. KGH_SPY has the ability to steal data from the Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Thunderbird, and Opera browsers. KGH_SPY can execute PowerShell commands on the victim's machine. KGH_SPY has the ability to download and execute code from remote servers. KGH_SPY has masqueraded as a legitimate Windows tool. KGH_SPY can perform keylogging by polling the GetAsyncKeyState() function. KGH_SPY can save collected system information to a file named "info" before exfiltration. KGH_SPY can collect drive information from a compromised host. KGH_SPY can enumerate files and directories on a compromised host. KGH_SPY has used encrypted strings in its installer. KGH_SPY can harvest data from mail clients. KGH_SPY can collect information on installed applications. KGH_SPY can send data to C2 with HTTP POST requests. KGH_SPY can send a file containing victim system information to C2. KGH_SPY can exfiltrate collected information from the host to the C2 server. KGH_SPY can collect credentials from WINSCP. KGH_SPY has the ability to set the HKCU\Environment\UserInitMprLogonScript Registry key to execute logon scripts.
title: Dahan, A. et al. (2020, November 2). Back to the Future: Inside the Kimsuky KGH Spyware Suite. Retrieved November 6, 2020.

text: Misdat has used Windows APIs, including `ExitWindowsEx` and `GetKeyboardType`. The ZLib backdoor compresses communications using the standard Zlib compression library. Mis-Type network traffic can communicate over a raw socket. S-Type has run tests to determine the privilege level of the compromised user. Mis-Type first attempts to use a Base64-encoded network protocol over a raw TCP socket for C2, and if that method fails, falls back to a secondary HTTP-based protocol to communicate to an alternate C2 server. Misdat network traffic is Base64-encoded plaintext. Misdat is capable of deleting the backdoor file. S-Type may create the file %HOMEPATH%\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\Realtek {Unique Identifier}.lnk, which points to the malicious `msdtc.exe` file already created in the `%CommonFiles%` directory. S-Type may save itself as a file named `msdtc.exe`, which is also the name of the legitimate Microsoft Distributed Transaction Coordinator service binary. S-Type can download additional files onto a compromised host. ZLib has the ability to enumerate files and drives. ZLib has sent data and files from a compromised host to its C2 servers. S-Type has run the command `net user` on a victim. ZLib has the ability to discover and manipulate Windows services. S-Type has used `ipconfig /all` on a compromised host. Misdat is capable of providing shell functionality to the attacker to execute commands. Mis-Type runs tests to determine the privilege level of the compromised user. Mis-Type saves itself as a file named `msdtc.exe`, which is also the name of the legitimate Microsoft Distributed Transaction Coordinator service binary. ZLib has the ability to download files. S-Type may create a .lnk file to itself that is saved in the Start menu folder. It may also create the Registry key HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\ IMJPMIJ8.1{3 characters of Unique Identifier}. ZLib mimics the resource version information of legitimate Realtek Semiconductor, Nvidia, or Synaptics modules. S-Type may create a temporary user on the system named `Lost_{Unique Identifier}` with the password `pond~!@6”{Unique Identifier}`. Misdat has collected files and data from a compromised host. S-Type uses Base64 encoding for C2 traffic. S-Type has deleted accounts it has created. Mis-Type may create a file containing the results of the command cmd.exe /c ipconfig /all. Mis-Type has been injected directly into a running process, including `explorer.exe`. Misdat network traffic communicates over a raw socket. Misdat saves itself as a file named `msdtc.exe`, which is also the name of the legitimate Microsoft Distributed Transaction Coordinator service binary. Misdat has uploaded files and data to its C2 servers. ZLib creates Registry keys to allow itself to run as various services. ZLib has the ability to execute shell commands. Misdat is capable of deleting Registry keys used for persistence. Mis-Type has used `cmd.exe` to run commands on a compromised host. Misdat was typically packed using UPX. Many Misdat samples were programmed using Borland Delphi, which will mangle the default PE compile timestamp of a file. S-Type has deleted files it has created on a compromised host. Some S-Type samples have been packed with UPX. Mis-Type has downloaded additional malware and files onto a compromised host. Misdat has created registry keys for persistence, including `HKCU\Software\dnimtsoleht\StubPath`, `HKCU\Software\snimtsOleht\StubPath`, `HKCU\Software\Backtsaleht\StubPath`, `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Active Setup\Installed. Components\{3bf41072-b2b1-21c8-b5c1-bd56d32fbda7}`, and `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Active Setup\Installed Components\{3ef41072-a2f1-21c8-c5c1-70c2c3bc7905}`. S-Type has provided the ability to execute shell commands on a compromised host. Misdat is capable of running commands to obtain a list of files and directories, as well as enumerating logical drives. ZLib has the ability to enumerate system information. ZLib has the ability to obtain screenshots of the compromised system. Mis-Type has used Windows API calls, including `NetUserAdd` and `NetUserDel`. Mis-Type has collected files and data from a compromised host. Mis-Type has transmitted collected files and data to its C2 server. S-Type uses HTTP for C2. ZLib communicates over HTTP for C2. Mis-Type uses Base64 encoding for C2 traffic. S-Type has attempted to determine if a compromised system was using a Japanese keyboard via the `GetKeyboardType` API call. Mis-Type has temporarily stored collected information to the files `“%AppData%\{Unique Identifier}\HOSTRURKLSR”` and `“%AppData%\{Unique Identifier}\NEWERSSEMP”`. Mis-Type may create a file containing the results of the command cmd.exe /c net user {Username}. The initial beacon packet for Misdat contains the operating system version of the victim. Mis-Type may create a temporary user on the system named `Lost_{Unique Identifier}`. Misdat is capable of downloading files from the C2. Mis-Type network traffic can communicate over HTTP. Misdat has attempted to detect if a compromised host had a Japanese keyboard via the Windows API call `GetKeyboardType`. S-Type has used Windows APIs, including `GetKeyboardType`, `NetUserAdd`, and `NetUserDel`. The initial beacon packet for Mis-Type contains the operating system version and file system of the victim. S-Type runs the command net start on a victim. The initial beacon packet for S-Type contains the operating system version and file system of the victim. S-Type primarily uses port 80 for C2, but falls back to ports 443 or 8080 if initial communication fails. Mis-Type has created registry keys for persistence, including `HKCU\Software\bkfouerioyou`, `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Active Setup\Installed Components\{6afa8072-b2b1-31a8-b5c1-{Unique Identifier}`, and `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Active Setup\Installed Components\{3BF41072-B2B1-31A8-B5C1-{Unique Identifier}`. S-Type has uploaded data and files from a compromised host to its C2 servers.
title: Gross, J. (2016, February 23). Operation Dust Storm. Retrieved December 22, 2021.

text: LoudMiner has set the attributes of the VirtualBox directory and VBoxVmService parent directory to "hidden". LoudMiner is typically bundled with pirated copies of Virtual Studio Technology (VST) for Windows and macOS. LoudMiner launched the QEMU services in the /Library/LaunchDaemons/ folder using launchctl. It also uses launchctl to unload all Launch Daemons when updating to a newer version of LoudMiner. LoudMiner used shell scripts to launch various services and to start/stop the QEMU virtualization. LoudMiner harvested system resources to mine cryptocurrency, using XMRig to mine Monero. LoudMiner can automatically launch a Linux virtual machine as a service at startup if the AutoStart option is enabled in the VBoxVmService configuration file. LoudMiner has used QEMU and VirtualBox to run a Tiny Core Linux virtual machine, which runs XMRig and makes connections to the C2 server for updates. LoudMiner used SCP to update the miner from the C2. LoudMiner deleted installation files after completion. LoudMiner used the ps command to monitor the running processes on the system. LoudMiner used a script to gather the IP address of the infected machine before sending to the C2. LoudMiner has obfuscated various scripts. LoudMiner has monitored CPU usage. LoudMiner started the cryptomining virtual machine as a service on the infected machine. LoudMiner adds plist files with the naming format com.[random_name].plist in the /Library/LaunchDaemons folder with the RunAtLoad and KeepAlive keys set to true. LoudMiner has encrypted DMG files. LoudMiner used an MSI installer to install the virtualization software. LoudMiner used a batch script to run the Linux virtual machine as a service.

Qilin has been delivered to victims through spearphishing emails with malicious attachments.

text:

text: SUNBURST communicated via HTTP GET or HTTP POST requests to third party servers for C2. SUNBURST masqueraded its network traffic as the Orion Improvement Program (OIP) protocol. SUNBURST delivered different payloads, including TEARDROP in at least one instance. SUNBURST used DNS for C2 traffic designed to mimic normal SolarWinds API communications. SUNBURST was digitally signed by SolarWinds from March - May 2020. SUNBURST collected information from a compromised host. SUNBURST obfuscated collected system information using a FNV-1a + XOR algorithm. SUNBURST collected device `UPTIME`. SUNBURST collected the username from a compromised host. SUNBURST remained dormant after initial access for a period of up to two weeks. SUNBURST collected a list of process names that were hashed using a FNV-1a + XOR algorithm to check against similarly-hashed hardcoded blocklists. SUNBURST had commands that allow an attacker to write or delete registry keys, and was observed stopping services by setting their HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\services\\[service_name]\\Start registry entries to value 4. It also deleted previously-created Image File Execution Options (IFEO) Debugger registry values and registry keys related to HTTP proxy to clean up traces of its activity. SUNBURST used the WMI query Select * From Win32_SystemDriver to retrieve a driver listing. SUNBURST collected hostname and OS version. TEARDROP files had names that resembled legitimate Window file and directory names. TEARDROP checked that HKU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\CTF existed before decoding its embedded payload. SUNBURST collected the registry value HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Cryptography\MachineGuid from compromised hosts. SUNBURST had a command to delete files. SUNBURST dynamically resolved C2 infrastructure for randomly-generated subdomains within a parent domain. SUNBURST used Base64 encoding in its C2 traffic. SUNBURST collected a list of service names that were hashed using a FNV-1a + XOR algorithm to check against similarly-hashed hardcoded blocklists. SUNBURST had commands to enumerate files and directories. SUNBURST collected all network interface MAC addresses that are up and not loopback devices, as well as IP address, DHCP configuration, and domain information. SUNBURST added junk bytes to its C2 over HTTP. SUNBURST encrypted C2 traffic using a single-byte-XOR cipher.
title: FireEye. (2020, December 13). Highly Evasive Attacker Leverages SolarWinds Supply Chain to Compromise Multiple Global Victims With SUNBURST Backdoor. Retrieved January 4, 2021.

text: OSInfo specifically looks for Domain Admins and power users within the domain. RemoteCMD copies a file over to the remote system before execution. OSInfo enumerates local and domain users OSInfo performs a connection test to discover remote systems in the network RemoteCMD can execute commands remotely by creating a new schedule task on the remote system OSInfo has enumerated the local administrators group. OSInfo discovers the current domain information. OSInfo discovers shares on the network RemoteCMD can execute commands remotely by creating a new service on the remote system. OSInfo queries the registry to look for information about Terminal Services. OSInfo enumerates the current network connections similar to net use . OSInfo discovers information about the infected machine.

text: BADNEWS is sometimes signed with an invalid Authenticode certificate in an apparent effort to make it look more legitimate. BADNEWS has a command to download an .exe and execute it via CreateProcess API. It can also run with ShellExecute. NDiskMonitor uses AES to encrypt certain information sent over its C2 channel. BADNEWS encodes C2 traffic with base64. BADNEWS has a command to download an .exe and use process hollowing to inject it into a new process. NDiskMonitor can download and execute a file from given URL. Socksbot creates a suspended svchost process and injects its DLL into it. BADNEWS collects C2 information via a dead drop resolver. BADNEWS is capable of executing commands via cmd.exe. BADNEWS encrypts C2 data with a ROR by 3 and an XOR by 0x23. Socksbot can write and execute PowerShell scripts. Socksbot can start SOCKS proxy threads. Socksbot can take screenshots. When it first starts, BADNEWS spawns a new thread to log keystrokes. NDiskMonitor obtains the victim computer name and encrypts the information to send over its C2 channel. BADNEWS monitors USB devices and copies files with certain extensions to a predefined directory. BADNEWS copies files with certain extensions from USB devices to a predefined directory. Socksbot can list all running processes. NDiskMonitor can obtain a list of all files and directories as well as logical drives. BADNEWS can use multiple C2 channels, including RSS feeds, Github, forums, and blogs. NDiskMonitor obtains the victim username and encrypts the information to send over its C2 channel. BADNEWS checks for new hard drives on the victim, such as USB devices, by listening for the WM_DEVICECHANGE window message. BADNEWS identifies files with certain extensions from USB devices, then copies them to a predefined directory. BADNEWS is capable of downloading additional files through C2 channels, including a new version of itself. BADNEWS copies documents under 15MB found on the victim system to is the user's %temp%\SMB\ folder. It also copies files from USB devices to a predefined directory.

text:
BPFDoor creates a zero byte PID file at `/var/run/haldrund.pid`. BPFDoor uses this file to determine if it is already running on a system to ensure only one instance is executing at a time.
BPFDoor can create a reverse shell and supports vt100 emulator formatting.
BPFDoor starts a shell on a high TCP port starting at 42391 up to 43391, then changes the local `iptables` rules to redirect all packets from the attacker to the shell port.
After initial setup, BPFDoor's original execution process deletes the dropped binary and exits.
BPFDoor uses the `utimes()` function to change the executable's timestamp.
After initial execution, BPFDoor forks itself and runs the fork with the `--init` flag, which allows it to execute secondary clean up operations. The parent process terminates leaving the forked process to be inherited by the legitimate process init.
BPFDoor clears the file location `/proc/<PID>/environ` removing all environment variables for the process.
BPFDoor uses BPF bytecode to attach a filter to a network socket to view ICMP, UDP, or TCP packets coming through ports 22 (ssh), 80 (http), and 443 (https). When BPFDoor finds a packet containing its “magic” bytes, it parses out two fields and forks itself. The parent process continues to monitor filtered traffic while the child process executes the instructions from the parsed fields.
BPFDoor overwrites the `argv[0]` value used by the Linux `/proc` filesystem to determine the command line and command name to display for each process. BPFDoor selects a name from 10 hardcoded names that resemble Linux system daemons, such as; `/sbin/udevd -d`, `dbus-daemon --system`, `avahi-daemon: chroot helper`, `/sbin/auditd -n`, and `/usr/lib/systemd/systemd-journald`.
BPFDoor can require a password to activate the backdoor and uses RC4 encryption or static library encryption `libtomcrypt`.
BPFDoor sets the `MYSQL_HISTFILE` and `HISTFILE` to `/dev/null` preventing the shell and MySQL from logging history in `/proc/<PID>/environ`.
title: The Sandfly Security Team. (2022, May 11). BPFDoor - An Evasive Linux Backdoor Technical Analysis. Retrieved September 29, 2023.

text: If running with root permissions, OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D can create a persistence file in the folder /Library/LaunchDaemons. OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D sets the main loader file’s attributes to hidden. OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D can create a persistence file in the folder /Library/LaunchAgents. OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D collects processor information, memory information, computer name, hardware UUID, serial number, and operating system version. OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D has used the ioreg command to gather some of this information. OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D encrypts its strings in RSA256 and encodes them in a custom base64 scheme and XOR. OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D has a command to download and execute a file on the victim’s machine. OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D has a command to delete a file from the system. OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D deletes the app bundle and dropper after execution. OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D uses Word macros for execution. OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D uses PowerShell scripts. OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D scrambles and encrypts data using AES256 before sending it to the C2 server. OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D can collect the network interface MAC address on the infected host.

text: HOPLIGHT has connected outbound over TCP port 443 with a FakeTLS method. HOPLIGHT can launch cmd.exe to execute commands on the system. A variant of HOPLIGHT hooks lsass.exe, and lsass.exe then checks the Registry for the data value 'rdpproto' under the key SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa Name. HOPLIGHT can use WMI event subscriptions to create persistence. HOPLIGHT has been observed enumerating system drives and partitions. HOPLIGHT has the ability to connect to a remote host in order to upload and download files. HOPLIGHT has multiple C2 channels in place in case one fails. HOPLIGHT has injected into running processes.

text: Zeus Panda can hook GetClipboardData function to watch for clipboard pastes to collect. Zeus Panda checks for running processes on the victim’s machine. Zeus Panda searches for specific directories on the victim’s machine. Zeus Panda can perform keylogging on the victim’s machine by hooking the functions TranslateMessage and WM_KEYDOWN. Zeus Panda has a command to delete a file. It also can uninstall scripts and delete files to cover its track. Zeus Panda modifies several Registry keys under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Internet Explorer\ PhishingFilter\ to disable phishing filters. text:
GlassWorm has the ability to check the OS of the victim host. GlassWorm has checked whether the OS platform value includes `darwin` prior to execution of macOS specific scripts.
GlassWorm has collected data from macOS devices through the gathering of Apple Notes related files by targeting `/Library/Group Containers/group.com.apple.notes/NoteStore.sqlite`, `/Library/Group Containers/group.com.apple.notes/NoteStore.sqlite-wal`, and `/Library/Group Containers/group.com.apple.notes/NoteStore.sqlite-shm`.
GlassWorm has leveraged AES-256-CBC encryption to obfuscate its malicious JavaScript payload. GlassWorm has also utilized Base64 encoding to obfuscate the C2 details stored in the Solana memo field.
GlassWorm has leveraged blockchain-based C2 infrastructure to include Solana blockchain that contains additional C2 details within the memo field. GlassWorm has also leveraged Google Calendar to host encoded data.
GlassWorm has leveraged JavaScript to execute its malicious code to include its hidden Unicode characters using the `eval` call. GlassWorm has also utilized encrypted payloads compiled in JavaScript.
GlassWorm has leveraged geofencing logic to detect whether it is operating in a Russian associated time zone to determine whether it continues to execute.
GlassWorm has staged collected data in a working directory within a temp folder to include `/tmp/ijewf`.
GlassWorm has identified the system language settings by checking for `ru_RU`, `ru-RU`, `ru`, and `Russian` to prevent execution in a Russian associated device.
GlassWorm has archived collected files within a zip file prior to exfiltration to include `/tmp/out.zip`.
GlassWorm has spread through Visual Studio extensions. GlassWorm has also spread through JavaScript projects hosted on Github.
GlassWorm has established persistence on macOS via a LaunchAgent by writing a plist under `/library/LaunchAgents`.
GlassWorm has the ability to check the system’s time zone on the victim device.
GlassWorm has gathered credentials stored in Mozilla FireFox and Chromium-based Browsers.
GlassWorm has gathered data pertaining to VPN configurations. GlassWorm has also targeted locally stored data on macOS located in `/Library/Application Support/Fortinet/FortiClient/conf/vpn.plist`.
GlassWorm has harvested Safari cookies stored within `/Library/Containers/com.apple.Safari/Data/Library/Cookies/ Cookies.binarycookies`. GlassWorm has also stolen cookies within Chromium and Firefox browsers.
GlassWorm has downloaded additional payloads from C2.

LiteDuke has the ability to discover the proxy configuration of Firefox and/or Opera. RegDuke can use control-flow flattening or the commercially available .NET Reactor for obfuscation. text: In older versions, XCSSET uses the plutil command to modify the LSUIElement, DFBundleDisplayName, and CFBundleIdentifier keys in the /Contents/Info.plist file to change how XCSSET is visible on the system. In later versions, XCSSET leverages a third-party notarized `dockutil` tool to modify the `.plist` file responsible for presenting applications to the user in the Dock and LaunchPad to point to a malicious application. XCSSET uses scp to access the ~/Library/Cookies/Cookies.binarycookies file. XCSSET uses ps aux with the grep command to enumerate common browsers and system processes potentially impacting XCSSET's exfiltration capabilities. XCSSET loads a system level launchdaemon using the launchctl load -w command from /System/Librarby/LaunchDaemons/ssh.plist. XCSSET prompts the user to input credentials using a native macOS dialog box leveraging the system process /Applications/Safari.app/Contents/MacOS/SafariForWebKitDevelopment. XCSSET uses a shell script to execute Mach-o files and osacompile commands such as, osacompile -x -o xcode.app main.applescript. XCSSET uses the ssh launchdaemon to elevate privileges, bypass system controls, and enable remote access to the victim. XCSSET uses AppleScript to check the host's language and location with the command user locale of (get system info). XCSSET installs malicious application bundles that mimic native macOS apps, such as Safari, by using the legitimate app’s icon and customizing the `Info.plist` to match expected metadata. XCSSET collects contacts and application data from files in Desktop, Documents, Downloads, Dropbox, and WeChat folders. XCSSET identifies the macOS version and uses ioreg to determine serial number. XCSSET adds malicious code to a host's Xcode projects by enumerating CocoaPods target_integrator.rb files under the /Library/Ruby/Gems folder or enumerates all .xcodeproj folders under a given directory. XCSSET then downloads a script and Mach-O file into the Xcode project folder. XCSSET performs AES-CBC encryption on files under ~/Documents, ~/Downloads, and ~/Desktop with a fixed key and renames files to give them a .enc extension. Only files with sizes less than 500MB are encrypted. XCSSET uses a hidden folder named .xcassets and .git to embed itself in Xcode. XCSSET uses a malicious browser application to replace the legitimate browser in order to continuously capture credentials, monitor web traffic, and download additional modules. XCSSET searches firewall configuration files located in /Library/Preferences/ and uses csrutil status to determine if System Integrity Protection is enabled. XCSSET adds malicious file paths to the DYLD_FRAMEWORK_PATH and DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH environment variables to execute malicious code. XCSSET retrieves files that match the pattern defined in the INAME_QUERY variable within the user's home directory, such as `*test.txt`, and are below a specific size limit. It then archives the files and exfiltrates the data over its C2 channel. XCSSET downloads browser specific AppleScript modules using a constructed URL with the curl command, https://" & domain & "/agent/scripts/" & moduleName & ".applescript. XCSSET attempts to discover accounts from various locations such as a user's Evernote, AppleID, Telegram, Skype, and WeChat data. XCSSET will create an ssh key if necessary with the ssh-keygen -t rsa -f $HOME/.ssh/id_rsa -P command. XCSSET will upload a private key file to the server to remotely access the host without a password. Using the machine's local time, XCSSET waits 43200 seconds (12 hours) from the initial creation timestamp of a specific file, .report. After the elapsed time, XCSSET executes additional modules. XCSSET saves a screen capture of the victim's system with a numbered filename and .jpg extension. Screen captures are taken at specified intervals based on the system. XCSSET uses RC4 encryption over TCP to communicate with its C2 server. XCSSET will compress entire ~/Desktop folders excluding all .git folders, but only if the total data size is under 200MB. XCSSET has used a zero-day exploit in the ssh launchdaemon to elevate privileges and bypass SIP.
title: Mac Threat Response, Mobile Research Team. (2020, August 13). The XCSSET Malware: Inserts Malicious Code Into Xcode Projects, Performs UXSS Backdoor Planting in Safari, and Leverages Two Zero-day Exploits. Retrieved October 5, 2021.
