Valak can use a .NET compiled module named exchgrabber to enumerate credentials from the Credential Manager. Valak can determine the Windows version and computer name on a compromised host. Valak has the ability to modify the Registry key HKCU\Software\ApplicationContainer\Appsw64 to store information regarding the C2 server and downloads. Valak has used packed DLL payloads. Valak has used scheduled tasks to execute additional payloads and to gain persistence on a compromised host. Valak can download a module to search for and build a report of harvested credential data. Valak has the ability save and execute files as alternate data streams (ADS). Valak has the ability to store information regarding the C2 server and downloads in the Registry key HKCU\Software\ApplicationContainer\Appsw64. Valak has the ability to exfiltrate data over the C2 channel. Valak has the ability to base64 encode and XOR encrypt strings. Valak has been executed via Microsoft Word documents containing malicious macros. Valak can execute tasks via OLE. Valak can use the clientgrabber module to steal e-mail credentials from the Registry.
title: Reaves, J. and Platt, J. (2020, June). Valak Malware and the Connection to Gozi Loader ConfCrew. Retrieved August 31, 2020.

text:
PoisonIvy creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can open a command-line interface.
PoisonIvy creates a Registry subkey that registers a new service. PoisonIvy also creates a Registry entry modifying the Logical Disk Manager service to point to a malicious DLL dropped to disk.
PoisonIvy creates run key Registry entries pointing to a malicious executable dropped to disk.
PoisonIvy creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can steal system information.
PoisonIvy stages collected data in a text file.
PoisonIvy creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can upload files.
PoisonIvy starts a rootkit from a malicious file dropped to disk.
PoisonIvy creates a Registry subkey that registers a new system device.
PoisonIvy captures window titles.
PoisonIvy hides any strings related to its own indicators of compromise.
title: Hayashi, K. (2005, August 18). Backdoor.Darkmoon. Retrieved February 23, 2018.

text:
HexEval Loader has masqueraded and typosquatted as legitimate code repository packages and projects.
HexEval Loader has encoded module names and C2 URLs as hexadecimal strings in attempts to evade analysis.
HexEval Loader has executed malicious JavaScript code.
HexEval Loader has exfiltrated victim data using HTTPS POST requests to its C2 servers.
title: Kirill Boychenko. (2025, April 4). Lazarus Expands Malicious npm Campaign: 11 New Packages Add Malware Loaders and Bitbucket Payloads. Retrieved October 20, 2025.

text:
Lokibot has obfuscated strings with base64 encoding.
Lokibot has stolen credentials from multiple applications and data sources including Windows OS credentials, email clients, FTP, and SFTP clients.
Lokibot has used several packing methods for obfuscation.
Lokibot has the ability to copy itself to a hidden file and directory.
Lokibot has demonstrated the ability to steal credentials from multiple applications and data sources including Safari and the Chromium and Mozilla Firefox-based web browsers.
title: Hoang, M. (2019, January 31). Malicious Activity Report: Elements of  Lokibot Infostealer. Retrieved May 15, 2020.

text:
The C2 server response to a beacon sent by a variant of Emissary contains a 36-character GUID value that is used as an encryption key for subsequent network communications. Some variants of Emissary use various XOR operations to encrypt C2 data.
Emissary has the capability to create a remote shell and execute specified commands.
Variants of Emissary encrypt payloads using various XOR ciphers, as well as a custom algorithm that uses the "srand" and "rand" functions.
Emissary injects its DLL file into a newly spawned Internet Explorer process.
Emissary has the capability to download files from the C2 server.
Emissary uses HTTP or HTTPS for C2.
title: Falcone, R. and Miller-Osborn, J.. (2015, December 18). Attack on French Diplomat Linked to Operation Lotus Blossom. Retrieved February 15, 2016.

text: Emotet has maintained persistence through a scheduled task, e.g. though a .dll file in the Registry.
title: Office of Information Security, Health Sector Cybersecurity Coordination Center. (2023, November 16). Emotet Malware: The Enduring and Persistent Threat to the Health Sector. Retrieved June 19, 2024.

text:
H1N1 uses a custom packing algorithm.
H1N1 uses multiple techniques to obfuscate strings, including XOR.
title: Reynolds, J.. (2016, September 13). H1N1: Technical analysis reveals new capabilities. Retrieved September 26, 2016.

text:
TrickBot used COM to setup scheduled task for persistence.
TrickBot utilizes EternalBlue and EternalRomance exploits for lateral movement in the modules wormwinDll, wormDll, mwormDll, nwormDll, tabDll.
TrickBot establishes persistence in the Startup folder.
title: Boutin, J. (2020, October 12). ESET takes part in global operation to disrupt Trickbot. Retrieved March 15, 2021.

text:
PUBLOAD has renamed malicious files to mimic legitimate file names such as adobe_wf.exe.
TONESHELL has used RC4 encryption in C2 communications. TONESHELL variants used a randomly generated variable length (0x20 - 0x200 bytes) rolling XOR key to encrypt and decrypt network packets.
TONESHELL has renamed malicious files to mimic legitimate file names and file extensions. TONESHELL has also masqueraded as legitimate file names to include LogMeIn.dll.
TONESHELL has obtained the username from an infected host.
TONESHELL has checked the process name and process path to ensure it matches the expected one prior to triggering a custom exception handler. TONESHELL has also searched for running antivirus processes to include ESET’s antivirus associated executables ekrn.exe and egui.exe.
TONESHELL has utilized a magic value in C2 communications and only executes in memory when response packets match specific values.
TONESHELL has leveraged `GetForegroundWindow` to detect virtualization or sandboxes by calling the API twice and comparing each window handle.
PUBLOAD has used `tasklist` to gather running processes on victim host. PUBLOAD has also leveraged the `OpenEventA` Windows API function to check whether the same process was already running.
TONESHELL has leveraged custom exception handlers to hide code flow and stop execution of a debugger.
TONESHELL has utilized TCP-based reverse shells.
TONESHELL has used `GetForegroundWindow` to detect virtualization or sandboxes by calling the API twice and comparing each window handle.
title: Nick Dai, Vickie Su, Sunny Lu. (2022, November 18). Earth Preta Spear-Phishing Governments Worldwide. Retrieved August 4, 2025.

text:
CaddyWiper can work alphabetically through drives on a compromised system to take ownership of and overwrite all files.
CaddyWiper has the ability to dynamically resolve and use APIs, including `SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege`.
CaddyWiper can modify ACL entries to take ownership of files.
CaddyWiper has the ability to destroy information about a physical drive's partitions including the MBR, GPT, and partition entries.
title: Malhotra, A. (2022, March 15). Threat Advisory: CaddyWiper. Retrieved March 23, 2022.

text: Nebulae has the ability to use CreateProcess to execute a process. RainyDay can use TCP in C2 communications. RainyDay can use a file exfiltration tool to collect recently changed files on a compromised host. Nebulae can use CMD to execute a process. RainyDay has the ability to switch between TCP and HTTP for C2 if one method is not working. The file collection tool used by RainyDay can utilize native API including ReadDirectoryChangeW for folder monitoring. Nebulae has the ability to delete files and directories. RainyDay can use scheduled tasks to achieve persistence. RainyDay can use a file exfiltration tool to upload specific files to Dropbox. Nebulae can achieve persistence through a Registry Run key. Nebulae can list files and directories on a compromised host. Nebulae has the capability to upload collected files to C2. Nebulae can use RC4 and XOR to encrypt C2 communications. Nebulae has created a service named "Windows Update Agent1" to appear legitimate. Nebulae can use DLL side-loading to gain execution. RainyDay can enumerate processes on a target system. RainyDay can use a file exfiltration tool to collect recently changed files with specific extensions. RainyDay can use RC4 to encrypt C2 communications. RainyDay can decrypt its payload via a XOR key. RainyDay has the ability to capture screenshots. RainyDay can use a file exfiltration tool to copy files to C:\ProgramData\Adobe\temp prior to exfiltration. RainyDay can download files to a compromised host. RainyDay can use the Windows Command Shell for execution. RainyDay can use HTTP in C2 communications. RainyDay has used names to mimic legitimate software including "vmtoolsd.exe" to spoof Vmtools. Nebulae can discover logical drive information including the drive type, free space, and volume information. RainyDay can use proxy tools including boost_proxy_client for reverse proxy functionality. RainyDay can create and register a service for execution. RainyDay has named services and scheduled tasks to appear benign including "ChromeCheck" and "googleupdate." RainyDay can use services to establish persistence. RainyDay has the ability to uninstall itself by deleting its service and files. Nebulae can use TCP in C2 communications. Nebulae can download files from C2. RainyDay can use the QuarksPwDump tool to obtain local passwords and domain cached credentials. Nebulae uses functions named StartUserModeBrowserInjection and StopUserModeBrowserInjection indicating that it's trying to imitate chrome_frame_helper.dll. Nebulae can create a service to establish persistence. RainyDay can use tools to collect credentials from web browsers. Nebulae can enumerate processes on a target system. RainyDay can use side-loading to run malicious executables. RainyDay has downloaded as a XOR-encrypted payload.
title: Vrabie, V. (2021, April 23). NAIKON – Traces from a Military Cyber-Espionage Operation. Retrieved June 29, 2021.

text:
Vidar has been distributed through emails that include malicious links that redirect to fake download pages for Adobe Illustrator.
Vidar has obfuscated stack strings within executable files.
Vidar has used `icacls` to modify file permissions.
Vidar has loaded and executed common Windows DLLs during execution.
Vidar has been distributed through emails that include malicious attachments, such as an ISO file, often masquerading as legitimate software, such as Adobe Photoshop or Microsoft Teams.
Vidar has collected data using automated scripts within malicious executables.
Vidar has attempted to collect browser information.
An AES-encrypted version of Vidar has been embedded into an inflated executable named Setup.exe, bypassing defensive tools.
Vidar has injected itself into a legitimate Windows process.
title: Quorum Cyber. (n.d.). Malware Analysis Report Vidar - Stealerware. Retrieved August 28, 2026.

text:
Vidar has also used control flow flattening to slow down static analysis.
Vidar has extracted session cookies.
Vidar has signed its DLL using fake certificates githab[.]com and grow[.]com. Vidar has also signed its files with an expired digital certificate.
Vidar has been distributed via a malicious link that redirects to a filesharing website.
Vidar has been executed as a file named msedge_elf.dll through sideloading.
title: Intrinsec. (2026, April). "Chaos is a ladder": Vidar's recent rise to the top. Retrieved April 27, 2026.

text:
Pysa has used RSA and AES-CBC encryption algorithm to encrypt a list of targeted file extensions.
Pysa can stop services and processes.
Pysa has used PsExec to copy and execute the ransomware.
Pysa has deleted batch files after execution.
Pysa has extracted credentials from the password database before encrypting the files.
Pysa has modified the registry key “SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System” and added the ransom note.
Pysa has used brute force attempts against a central management console, as well as some Active Directory accounts.
Pysa has executed a malicious executable by naming it svchost.exe.
Pysa has the capability to stop antivirus services and disable Windows Defender.
Pysa has the functionality to delete shadow copies.
Pysa can perform network reconnaissance using the Advanced IP Scanner tool.
Pysa has laterally moved using RDP connections.
Pysa has used Powershell scripts to deploy its ransomware.
Pysa can perform OS credential dumping using Mimikatz.
Pysa can perform network reconnaissance using the Advanced Port Scanner tool.
Pysa has used Python scripts to deploy ransomware.
title: CERT-FR. (2020, April 1). ATTACKS INVOLVING THE MESPINOZA/PYSA RANSOMWARE. Retrieved March 1, 2021.

text: Emotet can download follow-on payloads and items via malicious `url` parameters in obfuscated PowerShell code.
title: Süleyman Özarslan, PhD; Pincus Security Inc.. (2020, July 14). An Analysis of Emotet Malware: PowerShell Unobfuscation. Retrieved November 25, 2024.

text: Clambling has the ability to communicate over HTTP. Clambling can record screen content in AVI format. RCSession can use HTTP in C2 communications. Clambling can identify the username on a compromised host. RCSession can write its configuration file to the Registry. RCSession has the ability to modify a Registry Run key to establish persistence. Clambling can enumerate processes on a targeted system. Clambling has gained execution through luring victims into opening malicious files. Clambling can send files from a victim's machine to Dropbox. Clambling has the ability to enumerate network shares. Clambling has the ability to use TCP and UDP for communication. HyperBro can unpack and decrypt its payload prior to execution. RCSession can collect data from a compromised host. RCSession can compress and obfuscate its strings to evade detection on a compromised host. RCSession can use `cmd.exe` for execution on compromised hosts. RCSession has the ability to capture keystrokes on a compromised host. Clambling can set and delete Registry keys. The Clambling dropper can use PowerShell to download the malware. Clambling can browse directories on a compromised host. Clambling can determine the current time. Clambling has the ability to capture screenshots. RCSession has used a file named English.rtf to appear benign on victim hosts. Clambling can deobfuscate its payload prior to execution. Clambling has the ability to capture and store clipboard data. RCSession can bypass UAC to escalate privileges. Clambling can use Dropbox to download malicious payloads, send commands, and receive information. Clambling can enumerate the IP address of a compromised machine. Clambling can capture keystrokes on a compromised host. Clambling has the ability to enumerate Registry keys, including KEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Bitcoin\Bitcoin-Qt\strDataDir to search for a bitcoin wallet. Clambling can wait 30 minutes before initiating contact with C2. RCSession can be installed via DLL side-loading. Clambling has the ability to use Telnet for communication. The Clambling executable has been obfuscated when dropped on a compromised host. Clambling can create and start services on a compromised host. RCSession has the ability to use TCP and UDP in C2 communications. PlugX can use API hashing and modify the names of strings to evade detection. RCSession can store its obfuscated configuration file in the Registry under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Plus` or `HKCU\SOFTWARE\Plus`. Clambling has the ability to bypass UAC using a `passuac.dll` file. Clambling can collect information from a compromised host. Clambling can discover the hostname, computer name, and Windows version of a targeted machine. Clambling can inject into the `svchost.exe` process for execution. RCSession can launch itself from a hollowed svchost.exe process. Clambling has been delivered to victim's machines through malicious e-mail attachments. Clambling has the ability to set its file attributes to hidden. Clambling can execute binaries through process hollowing. Clambling can establish persistence by adding a Registry run key. HyperBro can be delivered encrypted to a compromised host. Clambling can use cmd.exe for command execution. Clambling can store a file named `mpsvc.dll`, which opens a malicious `mpsvc.mui` file, in the same folder as the legitimate Microsoft executable `MsMpEng.exe` to gain execution.
title: Lunghi, D. et al. (2020, February). Uncovering DRBControl. Retrieved November 12, 2021.

text:
BeaverTail has obfuscated strings of code with Base64 encoding within the JavaScript version of the malware. BeaverTail has also utilized the open-source tool JavaScript-Obfuscator to obfuscate strings and functions.
BeaverTail has been hosted on code repositories and disseminated to victims through NPM packages.
BeaverTail has been executed through lures involving malicious JavaScript projects or trojanized remote conferencing software such as MicroTalk or FreeConference. BeaverTail has also been executed through macOS and Windows installers disguised as chat applications.
BeaverTail has executed malicious JavaScript code. BeaverTail has also been compiled with the Qt framework to execute in both Windows and macOS.
InvisibleFerret has identified specific directories and files for exfiltration using the `ssh_upload` command which contains subcommands of `.sdira`, `sdir`, `sfile`, `sfinda`, `sfindr`, `sfind`. InvisibleFerret also has the capability to scan and upload files of interest from multiple OS systems through the use of scripts that check file names, file extensions, and avoids certain path names. InvisibleFerret has utilized the `findstr` on Windows or the macOS `find` commands to search for files of interest.
BeaverTail has searched the victim device for browser extensions commonly associated with cryptocurrency wallets.
BeaverTail has communicated with C2 IP addresses over ports 1224 or 1244.
BeaverTail has masqueraded as MiroTalk installation packages: “MiroTalk.dmg” for macOS and “MiroTalk.msi” for Windows, and has included login GUIs with MiroTalk themes.
title: Unit42. (2024, October 9). Contagious Interview: DPRK Threat Actors Lure Tech Industry Job Seekers to Install New Variants of BeaverTail and InvisibleFerret Malware. Retrieved October 17, 2025.

text: Cuba has used several built-in API functions for discovery like GetIpNetTable and NetShareEnum. Cuba can enumerate processes running on a victim's machine. Cuba can enumerate local drives, disk type, and disk free space. Cuba can retrieve the ARP cache from the local system by using GetIpNetTable. Cuba has a hardcoded list of services and processes to terminate. Cuba can discover shared resources using the NetShareEnum API call. Cuba can use the command cmd.exe /c del to delete its artifacts from the system. Cuba can check if Russian language is installed on the infected machine by using the function GetKeyboardLayoutList. Cuba can download files from its C2 server. Cuba has used cmd.exe /c and batch files for execution. Cuba has executed hidden PowerShell windows. Cuba can modify services by using the OpenService and ChangeServiceConfig functions. Cuba has used SeDebugPrivilege and AdjustTokenPrivileges to elevate privileges. Cuba can use the function GetIpNetTable to recover the last connections to the victim's machine. Cuba can enumerate files by using a variety of functions. Cuba can query service status using QueryServiceStatusEx function. Cuba logs keystrokes via polling by using GetKeyState and VkKeyScan functions. Cuba has been dropped onto systems and used for lateral movement via obfuscated PowerShell scripts. Cuba has the ability to encrypt system data and add the ".cuba" extension to encrypted files. Cuba has been disguised as legitimate 360 Total Security Antivirus and OpenVPN programs. Cuba has a packed payload when delivered. Cuba loaded the payload into memory using PowerShell. Cuba has used multiple layers of obfuscation to avoid analysis, including its Base64 encoded payload.
title: Roccio, T., et al. (2021, April). Technical Analysis of Cuba Ransomware. Retrieved June 18, 2021.

text: NETWIRE has the ability to search for files on the compromised host.
title: Proofpoint. (2020, December 2). Geofenced NetWire Campaigns. Retrieved January 7, 2021.

text: ZxShell can delete files from the system. ZxShell can query the netsvc group value data located in the svchost group Registry key. ZxShell has a command to open a file manager and explorer on the system. ZxShell has used rundll32.exe to execute other DLLs and named pipes. ZxShell can create a new service using the service parser function ProcessScCommand. ZxShell has been dropped through exploitation of CVE-2011-2462, CVE-2013-3163, and CVE-2014-0322. ZxShell hooks several API functions to spawn system threads. ZxShell can check the services on the system. ZxShell can collect the local hostname, operating system details, CPU speed, and total physical memory. ZxShell can disable the firewall by modifying the registry key HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\SharedAccess\Parameters\FirewallPolicy\StandardProfile. ZxShell supports functionality for VNC sessions. ZxShell has a command to perform video device spying. ZxShell can create a new service for execution. ZxShell can transfer files from a compromised host. ZxShell can kill AV products' processes. ZxShell has remote desktop functionality. ZxShell can collect the owner and organization information from the target workstation. ZxShell can launch a reverse command shell. ZxShell has a command, ps, to obtain a listing of processes on the system. ZxShell has used FTP for C2 connections. ZxShell can create Registry entries to enable services to run. ZxShell has a feature to capture a remote computer's keystrokes using a keylogger. ZxShell has a command called RunAs, which creates a new process as another user or process context. ZxShell has a feature to perform SYN flood attack on a host. ZxShell can launch port scans. ZxShell has a feature to create local user accounts. ZxShell is injected into a shared SVCHOST process. ZxShell can set up an HTTP or SOCKS proxy. ZxShell has a command to clear system event logs. ZxShell has a command to transfer files from a remote host. ZxShell has used HTTP for C2 connections. ZxShell can use ports 1985 and 1986 in HTTP/S communication.
title: Allievi, A., et al. (2014, October 28). Threat Spotlight: Group 72, Opening the ZxShell. Retrieved September 24, 2019.

text:
WellMess can use junk data in the Base64 string for additional obfuscation.
WellMess has used Base64 encoding to uniquely identify communication to and from the C2.
WellMess can identify the IP address and user domain on the target machine.
WellMess can encrypt HTTP POST data using RC6 and a dynamically generated AES key encrypted with a hard coded RSA public key.
WellMess can send files from the victim machine to C2.
WellMess can use HTTP and HTTPS in C2 communications.
WellMess can decode and decrypt data received from C2.
WellMess can communicate to C2 with mutual TLS where client and server mutually check certificates.
WellMess can identify domain group membership for the current user.
WellMess can write files to a compromised host.
WellMess can identify the computer name of a compromised host.
WellMess can execute PowerShell scripts received from C2.
WellMess can collect the username on the victim machine to send to C2.
title: CISA. (2020, July 16). MAR-10296782-2.v1 – WELLMESS. Retrieved September 24, 2020.

text: Hacking Team UEFI Rootkit is a UEFI BIOS rootkit developed by the company Hacking Team to persist remote access software on some targeted systems.
title: Lin, P. (2015, July 13). Hacking Team Uses UEFI BIOS Rootkit to Keep RCS 9 Agent in Target Systems. Retrieved December 11, 2015.

text:
IcedID has modified legitimate .dll files to include malicious code.
IcedID has embedded malicious functionality in a legitimate DLL file.
IcedID has cloned legitimate websites/applications to distribute the malware.
IcedID has manipulated Keitaro Traffic Direction System to filter researcher and sandbox traffic.
title: Kenefick , I. (2022, December 23). IcedID Botnet Distributors Abuse Google PPC to Distribute Malware. Retrieved July 24, 2024.

text:
Carberp has exfiltrated data via HTTP to already established C2 servers.
Carberp has created a hidden file in the Startup folder of the current user.
Carberp can download and execute new plugins from the C2 server.
Carberp has captured credentials when a user performs login through a SSL session.
Carberp has connected to C2 servers via HTTP.
Carberp has used the NtQueryDirectoryFile and ZwQueryDirectoryFile functions to hide files and directories.
Carberp has masqueraded as Windows system file names, as well as "chkntfs.exe" and "syscron.exe".
Carberp has collected a list of running processes.
title: Trusteer Fraud Prevention Center. (2010, October 7). Carberp Under the Hood of Carberp: Malware & Configuration Analysis. Retrieved July 15, 2020.

text:
PUBLOAD has communicated via `curl` over HTTP to identify device IP data. PUBLOAD has also utilized HTTP for a command-and-control protocol through HTTP POST. PUBLOAD has also leveraged HTTPS for C2.
PUBLOAD has checked supported languages on the compromised system.
PUBLOAD has utilized a magic value in C2 communications and only executes in memory when response packets match specific values of 17 03 03. PUBLOAD has also used magic bytes consisting of 46 77 4d.
PUBLOAD has used valid legitimate digital signatures and certificates to evade detection.
TONESHELL has been initiated using LNK files that were programmed to display a PDF icon to entice the victim to click on the file to execute an office.exe binary.
TONESHELL has utilized HTTP for a C2 protocol through HTTP POST. TONESHELL has also utilized HTTPS for C2.
TONESHELL has used valid legitimate digital signatures and certificates to evade detection.
TONESHELL has abused legitimate executables to side-load malicious DLLs. TONESHELL has also been loaded via DLL side-loading, using legitimate, signed executables to include: FastVD.exe, Bandizip.exe and gpgconf.exe.
title: CSIRT CTI. (2024, January 23). Stately Taurus Targets Myanmar Amidst Concerns over Military Junta’s Handling of Rebel Attacks. Retrieved August 4, 2025.

text: Taidoor can upload data and files from a victim's machine. Taidoor has been delivered through spearphishing emails. Taidoor can perform DLL loading. Taidoor has modified the HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run key for persistence. Taidoor has downloaded additional files onto a compromised host. Taidoor has collected the MAC address of a compromised host; it can also use GetAdaptersInfo to identify network adapters. Taidoor has relied upon a victim to click on a malicious email attachment. Taidoor has used HTTP GET and POST requests for C2. Taidoor uses RC4 to encrypt the message body of HTTP content. Taidoor has the ability to use native APIs for execution including GetProcessHeap, GetProcAddress, and LoadLibrary.
title: Trend Micro. (2012). The Taidoor Campaign. Retrieved November 12, 2014.

text:
Troll Stealer is dropped as a DLL file and executed via `rundll32.exe` by its installer.
Troll Stealer has been delivered as a VMProtect-packed binary.
Troll Stealer, along with its associated dropper, utilizes legitimate, stolen code signing certificates.
title: AhnLab ASEC. (2024, February 16). TrollAgent That Infects Systems Upon Security Program Installation Process (Kimsuky Group). Retrieved January 17, 2025.

text: Hancitor has used verclsid.exe to download and execute a malicious script.
title: Haag, M., Levan, K. (2017, April 6). Old Phishing Attacks Deploy a New Methodology: Verclsid.exe. Retrieved August 10, 2020.

text:
Cheerscrypt has the ability to terminate VM processes on compromised hosts through execution of `esxcli vm process kill`.
Cheerscrypt has leveraged `esxcli` in order to terminate running virtual machines.
Cheerscrypt can search for log and VMware-related files with .log, .vmdk, .vmem, .vswp, and .vmsn extensions.
Cheerscrypt has leveraged `esxcli vm process list` in order to gather a list of running virtual machines to terminate them.
title: Dela Cruz, A. et al. (2022, May 25). New Linux-Based Ransomware Cheerscrypt Targeting ESXi Devices Linked to Leaked Babuk Source Code. Retrieved December 19, 2023.

text: ThiefQuest exfiltrates targeted file extensions in the /Users/ folder to the command and control server via unencrypted HTTP. Network packets contain a string with two pieces of information: a file path and the contents of the file in a base64 encoded string. ThiefQuest uploads files via unencrypted HTTP. ThiefQuest prepends a copy of itself to the beginning of an executable file while maintaining the name of the executable. ThiefQuest searches through the /Users/ folder looking for executable files. For each executable, ThiefQuest prepends a copy of itself to the beginning of the file. When the file is executed, the ThiefQuest code is executed first. ThiefQuest creates a hidden file, copies the original target executable to the file, then executes the new hidden file to maintain the appearance of normal behavior.
title: Thomas Reed. (2020, July 7). Mac ThiefQuest malware may not be ransomware after all. Retrieved March 22, 2021.

text:
Agent Tesla has used HTTP for C2 communications.
Agent Tesla can collect account information from the victim’s machine.
Agent Tesla can collect the timestamp from the victim’s machine.
title: The DigiTrust Group. (2017, January 12). The Rise of Agent Tesla. Retrieved November 5, 2018.

text:
JumbledPath has the ability to perform packet capture on remote devices via actor-defined jump-hosts.
JumbledPath can compress and encrypt exfiltrated packet captures from targeted devices.
JumbledPath can clear logs on all devices used along its connection path to compromised network infrastructure.
JumbledPath can impair logging on all devices used along its connection path to compromised hosts.
JumbledPath can communicate over a unique series of connections to send and retrieve data from exploited devices.
JumbledPath can use a chain of jump hosts to communicate with compromised devices to obscure actor infrastructure.
title: Cisco Talos. (2025, February 20). Weathering the storm: In the midst of a Typhoon. Retrieved February 24, 2025.

text: DarkGate uses a malicious Windows Batch script to run the Windows code utility to retrieve follow-on script payloads. DarkGate has also used `cmd.exe` to create a remote shell. DarkGate has stolen `sitemanager.xml` and `recentservers.xml` from `%APPDATA%\FileZilla\` if present. DarkGate has used WMI to execute files over the network and to obtain information about the domain. DarkGate has deleted all files in the Mozilla directory using the following command: `/c del /q /f /s C:\Users\User\AppData\Roaming\Mozilla\firefox*`. DarkGate has deleted its staging directories. DarkGate attempts to steal Opera cookies, if present, after terminating the related process. DarkGate has used the `shutdown`command to shut down and/or restart the victim system. DarkGate has used PowerShell to create a remote shell.
title: McGraw, T. (2024, December 4). Black Basta Ransomware Campaign Drops Zbot, DarkGate, and Custom Malware. Retrieved December 9, 2024.

text:
Bumblebee can achieve persistence by copying its DLL to a subdirectory of %APPDATA% and creating a Visual Basic Script that will load the DLL via a scheduled task.
The Bumblebee loader can support the `Dij` command which gives it the ability to inject DLLs into the memory of other processes.
Bumblebee has used `rundll32` for execution of the loader component.
Bumblebee can create a Visual Basic script to enable persistence.
title: Kamble, V. (2022, June 28). Bumblebee: New Loader Rapidly Assuming Central Position in Cyber-crime Ecosystem. Retrieved August 24, 2022.

text:
Dyre has a command to download and executes additional files.
Dyre injects into other processes to load modules.
Dyre uses HTTPS for C2 communications.
Dyre decrypts resources needed for targeting the victim.
Dyre can detect sandbox analysis environments by inspecting the process list and Registry.
Dyre registers itself as a service by adding several Registry keys.
title: Symantec Security Response. (2015, June 23). Dyre: Emerging threat on financial fraud landscape. Retrieved August 23, 2018.

text: Some InnaputRAT variants create a new Windows service to establish persistence. InnaputRAT gathers volume drive information. InnaputRAT uses the API call ShellExecuteW for execution. InnaputRAT enumerates directories and obtains file attributes on a system. InnaputRAT variants have attempted to appear legitimate by using the file names SafeApp.exe and NeutralApp.exe. InnaputRAT uses an 8-byte XOR key to obfuscate API names and other strings contained in the payload. InnaputRAT has a command to delete files. InnaputRAT launches a shell to execute commands on the victim’s machine. InnaputRAT variants have attempted to appear legitimate by adding a new service named OfficeUpdateService. Some InnaputRAT variants establish persistence by modifying the Registry key HKU\\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run:%appdata%\NeutralApp\NeutralApp.exe. InnaputRAT gathers system information.
title: ASERT Team. (2018, April 04). Innaput Actors Utilize Remote Access Trojan Since 2016, Presumably Targeting Victim Files. Retrieved July 9, 2018.

text:
Amadey has used a variety of Windows API calls, including `GetComputerNameA`, `GetUserNameA`, and `CreateProcessA`.
Amadey has checked for a variety of antivirus products.
Amadey has collected the user name from a compromised host using `GetUserNameA`.
Amadey has changed the Startup folder to the one containing its executable by overwriting the registry keys.
Amadey has collected the computer name and OS version from a compromised machine.
Amadey has sent victim data to its C2 servers.
Amadey has obfuscated strings such as antivirus vendor names, domains, files, and others.
Amadey does not run any tasks or install additional malware if the victim machine is based in Russia.
Amadey can download and execute files to further infect a host machine with additional malware.
Amadey has overwritten registry keys for persistence.
Amadey has used HTTP for C2 communications.
Amadey can collect information from a compromised host.
Amadey can identify the IP address of a victim machine.
title: Kasuya, M. (2020, January 8). Threat Spotlight: Amadey Bot Targets Non-Russian Users. Retrieved July 14, 2022.

text: Grandoreiro has added BMP images to the resources section of its Portable Executable (PE) file increasing each binary to at least 300MB in size. Grandoreiro can collect the computer name and OS version from a compromised host. Grandoreiro can log keystrokes on the victim's machine. Grandoreiro can detect VMWare via its I/O port and Virtual PC via the vpcext instruction. Grandoreiro can decrypt its encrypted internal strings. Grandoreiro can bypass UAC by registering as the default handler for .MSC files. Grandoreiro can modify the Registry to store its configuration at `HKCU\Software\` under frequently changing names including %USERNAME% and ToolTech-RM. Grandoreiro can determine the IP and physical location of the compromised host via IPinfo. Grandoreiro can execute through the WinExec API. Grandoreiro can modify the binary ACL to prevent security tools from running. Grandoreiro can identify installed security tools based on process names. Grandoreiro can list installed security products including the Trusteer and Diebold Warsaw GAS Tecnologia online banking protections. Grandoreiro can parse Outlook .pst files to extract e-mail addresses. Grandoreiro can determine the time on the victim machine via IPinfo. Grandoreiro can delete .LNK files created in the Startup folder. Grandoreiro can hook APIs, kill processes, break file system paths, and change ACLs to prevent security tools from running. Grandoreiro can block the Deibold Warsaw GAS Tecnologia security tool at the firewall level. Grandoreiro can collect the username from the victim's machine. Grandoreiro can identify installed security tools based on window names. Grandoreiro can store its configuration in the Registry at `HKCU\Software\` under frequently changing names including %USERNAME% and ToolTech-RM. Grandoreiro can send data it retrieves to the C2 server.
title: ESET. (2020, April 28). Grandoreiro: How engorged can an EXE get?. Retrieved November 13, 2020.

text:
Ursnif has used a 30 minute delay after execution to evade sandbox monitoring tools.
Ursnif has copied itself to and infected removable drives for propagation.
Ursnif has copied itself to and infected files in network drives for propagation.
title: Caragay, R. (2014, December 11). Info-Stealing File Infector Hits US, UK. Retrieved June 5, 2019.

text:
More_eggs's payload has been encrypted with a key that has the hostname and processor family information appended to the end.
EVILNUM can run a remote scriptlet that drops a file and executes it via regsvr32.exe.
title: Porolli, M. (2020, July 9). More evil: A deep look at Evilnum and its toolset. Retrieved January 22, 2021.

text:
Wingbird performs multiple process injections to hijack system processes and execute malicious code.
Wingbird checks the victim OS version after executing to determine where to drop files based on whether the victim is 32-bit or 64-bit.
Wingbird uses services.exe to register a new autostart service named "Audit Service" using a copy of the local lsass.exe file.
Wingbird exploits CVE-2016-4117 to allow an executable to gain escalated privileges.
Wingbird side loads a malicious file, sspisrv.dll, in part of a spoofed lssas.exe service.
Wingbird deletes its payload along with the payload's parent process after it finishes copying files.
Wingbird drops a malicious file (sspisrv.dll) alongside a copy of lsass.exe, which is used to register a service that loads sspisrv.dll as a driver. The payload of the malicious driver (located in its entry-point function) is executed when loaded by lsass.exe before the spoofed service becomes unstable and crashes.
Wingbird checks for the presence of Bitdefender security software.
title: Anthe, C. et al. (2016, December 14). Microsoft Security Intelligence Report Volume 21. Retrieved November 27, 2017.

text: PoetRAT has the ability to copy files and download/upload files into C2 channels using FTP and HTTPS. PoetRAT was delivered with documents using DDE to execute malicious code. PoetRAT checked the size of the hard drive to determine if it was being run in a sandbox environment. In the event of sandbox detection, it would delete itself by overwriting the malware scripts with the contents of "License.txt" and exiting. PoetRAT has used a Python tool named Browdec.exe to steal browser credentials. PoetRAT used TLS to encrypt communications over port 143 PoetRAT has added a registry key in the hive for persistence. PoetRAT has used a .NET tool named dog.exe to exiltrate information over an e-mail account. PoetRAT has used a custom encryption scheme for communication between scripts. PoetRAT has the ability to hide and unhide files. PoetRAT has used Word documents with VBScripts to execute malicious activities. PoetRAT has used a Python tool named Bewmac to record the webcam on compromised hosts. PoetRAT has the ability to take screen captures. PoetRAT has used ftp for exfiltration. PoetRAT has made registry modifications to alter its behavior upon execution. PoetRAT was distributed via malicious Word documents. PoetRAT has used spearphishing attachments to infect victims. PoetRAT sent username, computer name, and the previously generated UUID in reply to a "who" command from C2. PoetRAT has the ability to list all running processes. PoetRAT has the ability to list files upon receiving the ls command from C2. PoetRAT has the ability to gather information about the compromised host. PoetRAT has used a Python tool named klog.exe for keylogging. PoetRAT was executed with a Python script and worked in conjunction with additional Python-based post-exploitation tools. PoetRAT used voStro.exe, a compiled pypykatz (Python version of Mimikatz), to steal credentials. PoetRAT used file system monitoring to track modification and enable automatic exfiltration. PoetRAT has the ability to overwrite scripts and delete itself if a sandbox environment is detected. PoetRAT used Nmap for remote system discovery. PoetRAT used TLS to encrypt command and control (C2) communications. PoetRAT has the ability to compress files with zip.
title: Mercer, W, et al. (2020, April 16). PoetRAT: Python RAT uses COVID-19 lures to target Azerbaijan public and private sectors. Retrieved April 27, 2020.

text:
ROKRAT can extract clipboard data from a compromised host.
ROKRAT relies on a specific victim hostname to execute and decrypt important strings.
title: Cash, D., Grunzweig, J., Adair, S., Lancaster, T. (2021, August 25). North Korean BLUELIGHT Special: InkySquid Deploys RokRAT. Retrieved October 1, 2021.

text: Ryuk can create .dll files that actually contain a Rich Text File format document. Ryuk can use stolen domain admin accounts to move laterally within a victim domain. Ryuk can remotely create a scheduled task to execute itself on a system. Ryuk can launch icacls /grant Everyone:F /T /C /Q to delete every access-based restrictions on files and directories.
title: ANSSI. (2021, February 25). RYUK RANSOMWARE. Retrieved March 29, 2021.

text:
Downdelph uses search order hijacking of the Windows executable sysprep.exe to escalate privileges.
HIDEDRV is a rootkit that hides certain operating system artifacts.
After downloading its main config file, Downdelph downloads multiple payloads from C2 servers.
HIDEDRV injects a DLL for Downdelph into the explorer.exe process.
Downdelph uses RC4 to encrypt C2 responses.
Downdelph inserts pseudo-random characters between each original character during encoding of C2 network requests, making it difficult to write signatures on them.
Downdelph bypasses UAC to escalate privileges by using a custom “RedirectEXE” shim database.
title: ESET. (2016, October). En Route with Sednit - Part 3: A Mysterious Downloader. Retrieved November 21, 2016.

text:
Lumma Stealer has used SmartAssembly to obfuscate .NET payloads.
Lumma Stealer has used reflective loading techniques to load content into memory during execution.
Lumma Stealer has checked for debugger strings by invoking `GetForegroundWindow` and looks for strings containing “x32dbg”, “x64dbg”, “windbg”, “ollydbg”, “dnspy”, “immunity debugger”, “hyperdbg”, “debug”, “debugger”, “cheat engine”, “cheatengine” and “ida”.
Lumma Stealer has queried system resources on the victim device to identify if it is executing in a sandbox or virtualized environments, checking usernames, conducting WMI queries for system details, checking for files commonly found in virtualized environments, searching system services, and inspecting process names. Lumma Stealer has checked system GPU configurations for sandbox detection.
Lumma Stealer has used HTTPS for command and control purposes.
Lumma Stealer has utilized the .NET `ProcessStartInfo` class features to prevent the process from creating a visible window through setting the `CreateNoWindow` setting to “True,” which allows the executed command or script to run without displaying a command prompt window.
title: Cara Lin, Fortinet. (2024, January 8). Deceptive Cracked Software Spreads Lumma Variant on YouTube. Retrieved March 22, 2025.

text:
ComRAT has injected its orchestrator DLL into explorer.exe. ComRAT has also injected its communications module into the victim's default browser to make C2 connections appear less suspicious as all network connections will be initiated by the browser process.
ComRAT has encrypted its virtual file system using AES-256 in XTS mode.
ComRAT has checked the victim system's date and time to perform tasks during business hours (9 to 5, Monday to Friday).
ComRAT has the ability to use the Gmail web UI to receive commands and exfiltrate information.
ComRAT has modified Registry values to store encrypted orchestrator code and payloads.
ComRAT has used PowerShell to load itself every time a user logs in to the system. ComRAT can execute PowerShell scripts loaded into memory or from the file system.
ComRAT has stored encrypted orchestrator code and payloads in the Registry.
ComRAT can use SSL/TLS encryption for its HTTP-based C2 channel. ComRAT has used public key cryptography with RSA and AES encrypted email attachments for its Gmail C2 channel.
ComRAT has embedded a XOR encrypted communications module inside the orchestrator module.
ComRAT has used encryption and base64 to obfuscate its orchestrator code in the Registry. ComRAT has also used encoded PowerShell scripts.
ComRAT has used unique per machine passwords to decrypt the orchestrator payload and a hardcoded XOR key to decrypt its communications module. ComRAT has also used a unique password to decrypt the file used for its hidden file system.
ComRAT has used a scheduled task to launch its PowerShell loader.
title: CISA. (2020, October 29). Malware Analysis Report (AR20-303A). Retrieved December 9, 2020.

text: njRAT is capable of logging keystrokes. njRAT has used a fast flux DNS for C2 IP resolution. njRAT can create, delete, or modify a specified Registry key or value. njRAT can search a list of running processes for Tr.exe. njRAT has modified the Windows firewall to allow itself to communicate through the firewall. njRAT can capture screenshots of the victim’s machines. njRAT is capable of deleting files. njRAT has included a base64 encoded executable. njRAT has added persistence via the Registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\CurrentVersion\Run\ and dropped a shortcut in %STARTUP%. njRAT has a module that steals passwords saved in victim web browsers. njRAT is capable of manipulating and deleting registry keys, including those used for persistence. njRAT has used the ShellExecute() function within a script. njRAT has used C2 infrastructure to receive stolen information from the infected machine including screenshots and other system information. njRAT has used AutoIt to compile the payload and main script into a single executable after delivery. njRAT has used port 1177 for HTTP C2 communications. njRAT will attempt to detect if the victim system has a camera during the initial infection. njRAT can also detect any removable drives connected to the system. njRAT can download files to the victim’s machine. APT-C-36 has used modified versions of njRAT to enable the download of .NET assemblies. njRAT can read specific registry values. njRAT can be configured to spread via removable drives. njRAT has used HTTP for C2 communications. njRAT has executed PowerShell commands via auto-run registry key persistence.
title: Pascual, C. (2018, November 27). AutoIt-Compiled Worm Affecting Removable Media Delivers Fileless Version of BLADABINDI/njRAT Backdoor. Retrieved June 4, 2019.

text:
Dridex has encrypted traffic with RSA.
Dridex has encrypted traffic with RC4.
title: Slepogin, N. (2017, May 25). Dridex: A History of Evolution. Retrieved May 31, 2019.

text: Bandook contains keylogging capabilities.
title: Galperin, E., Et al.. (2016, August 4). When Governments Attack: State Sponsored Malware Attacks Against Activists, Lawyers, and Journalists. Retrieved May 23, 2018.

text:
Naid creates a new service to establish.
Naid collects the domain name from a compromised host.
Naid collects a unique identifier (UID) from a compromised host.
Naid creates Registry entries that store information about a created service and point to a malicious DLL dropped to disk.
title: Neville, A. (2012, June 15). Trojan.Naid. Retrieved February 22, 2018.

text:
Daserf uses file and folder names related to legitimate programs in order to blend in, such as HP, Intel, Adobe, and perflogs.
Daserf leverages Mimikatz and Windows Credential Editor to steal credentials.
Some Daserf samples were signed with a stolen digital certificate.
Daserf hides collected data in password-protected .rar archives.
title: DiMaggio, J. (2016, April 28). Tick cyberespionage group zeros in on Japan. Retrieved July 16, 2018.

text: Derusbi variants have been seen that use Registry persistence to proxy execution through regsvr32.exe.
title: Fidelis Threat Research Team. (2016, May 2). Turbo Twist: Two 64-bit Derusbi Strains Converge. Retrieved August 16, 2018.

text: StrelaStealer variants have used packers to obfuscate payloads and make analysis more difficult.
title: Benjamin Chang, Goutam Tripathy, Pranay Kumar Chhaparwal, Anmol Maurya & Vishwa Thothathri, Palo Alto Networks. (2024, March 22). Large-Scale StrelaStealer Campaign in Early 2024. Retrieved December 31, 2024.

text:
LockerGoga installation has been immediately preceded by a "task kill" command in order to disable anti-virus.
LockerGoga has been observed shutting down infected systems.
LockerGoga has been signed with stolen certificates in order to make it look more legitimate.
title: Greenberg, A. (2019, March 25). A Guide to LockerGoga, the Ransomware Crippling Industrial Firms. Retrieved July 17, 2019.

text:
Hydraq uses svchost.exe to execute a malicious DLL included in a new service group.
Hydraq creates new services to establish persistence.
title: Fitzgerald, P. (2010, January 26). How Trojan.Hydraq Stays On Your Computer. Retrieved February 22, 2018.

text: EKANS uses encoded strings in its process kill list.
title: Zafra, D., et al. (2020, February 24). Ransomware Against the Machine: How Adversaries are Learning to Disrupt Industrial Production by Targeting IT and OT. Retrieved March 2, 2021.

text:
InvisiMole has a command to disable routing and the Firewall on the victim’s machine.
InvisiMole gathers information on the IP forwarding table, MAC address, configured proxy, and network SSID.
InvisiMole can can remove all system restore points.
InvisiMole can list information about files in a directory and recently opened or used documents. InvisiMole can also search for specific files by supplied file mask.
InvisiMole has a command to list account information on the victim’s machine.
InvisiMole can be launched by using DLL search order hijacking in which the wrapper DLL is placed in the same folder as explorer.exe and loaded during startup into the Windows Explorer process instead of the legitimate library.
InvisiMole InvisiMole can identify proxy servers used by the victim and use them for C2 communication.
InvisiMole can upload files to the victim's machine for operations.
InvisiMole can use zlib to compress and decompress data.
InvisiMole uses variations of a simple XOR encryption routine for C&C communications.
InvisiMole can function as a proxy to create a server that relays communication between the client and C&C server, or between two clients.
InvisiMole lists local users and session information.
InvisiMole can collect data from the system, and can monitor changes in specified directories.
InvisiMole can launch a remote shell to execute commands.
InvisiMole can enumerate Registry values, keys, and data.
InvisiMole can mimic HTTP protocol with custom HTTP “verbs” HIDE, ZVVP, and NOP.
InvisiMole can capture screenshots of not only the entire screen, but of each separate window open, in case they are overlapping.
InvisiMole can collect information about installed software used by specific users, software executed on user login, and software executed by each system.
InvisiMole can remotely activate the victim’s webcam to capture content.
InvisiMole can decrypt, unpack and load a DLL from its resources, or from blobs encrypted with Data Protection API, two-key triple DES, and variations of the XOR cipher.
InvisiMole gathers the local system time from the victim’s machine.
InvisiMole can gather information on the mapped drives and system volume serial number.
InvisiMole has been configured with several servers available for alternate C2 communications.
InvisiMole can enumerate windows and child windows on a compromised host.
InvisiMole uses WinRAR to compress data that is intended to be exfiltrated.
InvisiMole can obtain running services on the victim.
InvisiMole has disguised its droppers as legitimate software or documents, matching their original names and locations, and saved its files as mpr.dll in the Windows folder.
InvisiMole can record sound using input audio devices.
InvisiMole uses HTTP for C2 communications.
InvisiMole can use fileless UAC bypass and create an elevated COM object to escalate privileges.
InvisiMole has a command to create, set, copy, or delete a specified Registry key or value.
InvisiMole uses a variation of the XOR cipher to encrypt files before exfiltration.
InvisiMole has deleted files and directories including XML and files successfully uploaded to C2 servers.
InvisiMole can obtain a list of running processes.
InvisiMole can disconnect previously connected remote drives.
InvisiMole can sort and collect specific documents as well as generate a list of all files on a newly inserted drive and store them in an encrypted file.
InvisiMole can gather network share information.
InvisiMole avoids analysis by encrypting all strings, internal files, configuration data and by using a custom executable format.
InvisiMole samples were timestomped by the authors by setting the PE timestamps to all zero values. InvisiMole also has a built-in command to modify file times.
InvisiMole determines a working directory where it stores all the gathered data about the compromised machine.
InvisiMole can gather information on the OS version, computer name, DEP policy, and memory size.
title: Hromcová, Z. (2018, June 07). InvisiMole: Surprisingly equipped spyware, undercover since 2013. Retrieved July 10, 2018.

text: Lucifer can use certutil for propagation on Windows hosts within intranets. Lucifer can identify the process that owns remote connections. Lucifer can check for existing stratum cryptomining information in HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\spreadCpuXmr – %stratum info%. Lucifer has established persistence by creating the following scheduled task schtasks /create /sc minute /mo 1 /tn QQMusic ^ /tr C:Users\%USERPROFILE%\Downloads\spread.exe /F. Lucifer can decrypt its C2 address upon execution. Lucifer can download and execute a replica of itself using certutil. Lucifer can perform a decremental-xor encryption on the initial C2 request before sending it over the wire. Lucifer can exploit multiple vulnerabilities including EternalBlue (CVE-2017-0144) and EternalRomance (CVE-2017-0144). Lucifer has attempted to brute force TCP ports 135 (RPC) and 1433 (MSSQL) with the default username or list of usernames and passwords. Lucifer has used UPX packed binaries. Lucifer can use the Stratum protocol on port 10001 for communication between the cryptojacking bot and the mining server. Lucifer can scan for open ports including TCP ports 135 and 1433. Lucifer can collect the computer name, system architecture, default language, and processor frequency of a compromised host. Lucifer can infect victims by brute forcing SMB. Lucifer can clear and remove event logs. Lucifer has the ability to identify the username on a compromised host. Lucifer can execute TCP, UDP, and HTTP denial of service (DoS) attacks. Lucifer can use system resources to mine cryptocurrency, dropping XMRig to mine Monero. Lucifer can collect the IP address of a compromised host. Lucifer can identify the IP and port numbers for all remote connections from the compromised host. Lucifer can issue shell commands to download and execute additional payloads. Lucifer can check for specific usernames, computer names, device drivers, DLL's, and virtual devices associated with sandboxed environments and can enter an infinite loop and stop itself if any are detected. Lucifer can use WMI to log into remote machines for propagation. Lucifer can persist by setting Registry key values HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\QQMusic and HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\QQMusic.
title: Hsu, K. et al. (2020, June 24). Lucifer: New Cryptojacking and DDoS Hybrid Malware Exploiting High and Critical Vulnerabilities to Infect Windows Devices. Retrieved November 16, 2020.

text:
Havoc has the ability to copy files from one location to another.
Havoc features a module capable of host enumeration.
Havoc can use `NtAllocateVirtualMemory` and `NtCreateThreadEx` to aid process injection.
Havoc can execute commands via `cmd.exe`.
The Havoc interface can display a file explorer view of the compromised host.
The Havoc SMB demon can use named pipes for communication through a parent demon.
Havoc can use an SMB listener for C2 communication.
Havoc has a module for network enumeration including determining IP addresses.
Havoc can use HTTP/S listeners to establish and maintain C2 communications.
Havoc has a module capable of token impersonation.
Havoc has the ability to route HTTP/S communications through designated proxies.
Havoc has DLL spawn and injection modules.
Havoc has the ability to upload files to infected systems.
The Havoc demon agent can be set to sleep for a specified time.
Havoc has itself injected into `C:\\Windows\\System32\\Werfault.exe` on targeted systems.
Havoc can capture screenshots.
Havoc can enumerate processes on targeted hosts.
Havoc can download files from the victim's computer.
title: Ungur, P. (n.d.). HAVOC. Retrieved August 4, 2025.

text: TrickBot uses the Windows API call, CreateProcessW(), to manage execution flow. TrickBot has also used Nt* API functions to perform Process Injection. TrickBot has used printf and file I/O loops to delay process execution as part of API hammering. TrickBot has used Nt* Native API functions to inject code into legitimate processes such as wermgr.exe.
title: Joe Security. (2020, July 13). TrickBot's new API-Hammering explained. Retrieved September 30, 2021.

text:
WannaCry uses Tor for command and control traffic.
WannaCry uses Tor for command and control traffic and routes a custom cryptographic protocol over the Tor circuit.
WannaCry will attempt to determine the local network segment it is a part of.
WannaCry scans its local network segment for remote systems to try to exploit and copy itself to.
title: Counter Threat Unit Research Team. (2017, May 18). WCry Ransomware Analysis. Retrieved March 26, 2019.

text: LightNeuron has used filenames associated with Exchange and Outlook for binary and configuration files, such as winmail.dat. LightNeuron can be configured to automatically collect files under a specified directory. LightNeuron uses AES to encrypt C2 traffic. LightNeuron has the ability to download and execute additional files. LightNeuron is capable of starting a process using CreateProcess. LightNeuron gathers the victim computer name using the Win32 API call GetComputerName. LightNeuron is capable of modifying email content, headers, and attachments during transit. LightNeuron is controlled via commands that are embedded into PDFs and JPGs using steganographic methods. LightNeuron collects Exchange emails matching rules specified in its configuration. LightNeuron exfiltrates data over its email C2 channel. LightNeuron contains a function to encrypt and store emails that it collects. LightNeuron can be configured to exfiltrate data during nighttime or working hours. LightNeuron is capable of executing commands via cmd.exe. LightNeuron can be configured to automatically exfiltrate files under a specified directory. LightNeuron has used a malicious Microsoft Exchange transport agent for persistence. LightNeuron encrypts its configuration files with AES-256. LightNeuron has used AES and XOR to decrypt configuration files and commands. LightNeuron gathers information about network adapters using the Win32 API call GetAdaptersInfo. LightNeuron uses SMTP for C2. LightNeuron can store email data in files and directories specified in its configuration, such as C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\NetworkService\appdata\Local\Temp\. LightNeuron can collect files from a local system. LightNeuron has a function to delete files.
title: Faou, M. (2019, May). Turla LightNeuron: One email away from remote code execution. Retrieved June 24, 2019.

text:
Orz can execute shell commands. Orz can execute commands with JavaScript.
NanHaiShu can gather information about the victim proxy server.
Some Orz versions have an embedded DLL known as MockDll that uses process hollowing and Regsvr32 to execute another payload.
Orz can gather victim proxy information.
NanHaiShu can change Internet Explorer settings to reduce warnings about malware activity.
NanHaiShu can download additional files from URLs.
Orz can download files onto the victim.
Orz has used Technet and Pastebin web pages for command and control.
Some Orz versions have an embedded DLL known as MockDll that uses Process Hollowing and regsvr32 to execute another payload.
Orz can gather victim drive information.
Orz can perform Registry operations.
Orz can overwrite Registry settings to reduce its visibility on the victim.
NanHaiShu can gather the victim computer name and serial number.
Orz can gather the victim's Internet Explorer version.
Orz can gather a process list from the victim.
Orz can gather the victim OS version and whether it is 64 or 32 bit.
Some Orz strings are base64 encoded, such as the embedded DLL known as MockDll.
title: Axel F, Pierre T. (2017, October 16). Leviathan: Espionage actor spearphishes maritime and defense targets. Retrieved February 15, 2018.

text: BADCALL disables the Windows firewall before binding to a port. BADCALL communicates on ports 443 and 8000 with a FakeTLS method. BADCALL collects the network adapter information. BADCALL functions as a proxy server between the victim and C2 server. BADCALL collects the computer name and host name on the compromised system. BADCALL encrypts C2 traffic using an XOR/ADD cipher. BADCALL modifies the firewall Registry key SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\SharedAccess\Parameters\FirewallPolicy\StandardProfileGloballyOpenPorts\\List.
title: US-CERT. (2018, February 06). Malware Analysis Report (MAR) - 10135536-G. Retrieved June 7, 2018.

text:
Latrodectus has been distributed through reply-chain phishing emails with malicious attachments.
Latrodectus has been executed through malicious links distributed in email campaigns.
Latrodectus has been distributed to victims through emails containing malicious links.
Latrodectus can use rundll32.exe to execute downloaded DLLs.
Latrodectus has lured users into opening malicious email attachments for execution.
Latrodectus has called `msiexec` to install remotely-hosted MSI files.
title: Abrams, L. (2024, April 30). New Latrodectus malware attacks use Microsoft, Cloudflare themes. Retrieved September 13, 2024.

text:
NanHaiShu executes additional Jscript code on the victim's machine.
NanHaiShu uses mshta.exe to load its program and files.
NanHaiShu executes additional VBScript code on the victim's machine.
NanHaiShu modifies the %regrun% Registry to point itself to an autostart mechanism.
NanHaiShu encodes files in Base64.
NanHaiShu collects the username from the victim.
NanHaiShu launches a script to delete their original decoy file to cover tracks.
NanHaiShu uses DNS for the C2 communications.
title: F-Secure Labs. (2016, July). NANHAISHU RATing the South China Sea. Retrieved July 6, 2018.

text:
Depending on the Linux distribution, RotaJakiro executes a set of commands to collect device information and sends the collected information to the C2 server.
When executing with non-root level permissions, RotaJakiro can install persistence by adding a command to the .bashrc file that executes a binary in the `${HOME}/.gvfsd/.profile/` folder.
RotaJakiro sends device and other collected data back to the C2 using the established C2 channels over TCP.
Depending on the Linux distribution and when executing with root permissions, RotaJakiro may install persistence using a `.service` file under the `/lib/systemd/system/` folder.
RotaJakiro uses ZLIB Compression to compresses data sent to the C2 server in the `payload` section network communication packet.
Depending on the Linux distribution and when executing with root permissions, RotaJakiro may install persistence using a `.conf` file in the `/etc/init/` folder.
When executing with non-root permissions, RotaJakiro uses the the `shmget API` to create shared memory between other known RotaJakiro processes. This allows processes to communicate with each other and share their PID.
When executing with user-level permissions, RotaJakiro can install persistence using a .desktop file under the `$HOME/.config/autostart/` folder.
RotaJakiro uses dynamically linked shared libraries (`.so` files) to execute additional functionality using `dlopen()` and `dlsym()`.
RotaJakiro executes a set of commands to collect device information, including `uname`. Another example is the `cat /etc/*release | uniq` command used to collect the current OS distribution.
RotaJakiro uses the AES algorithm, bit shifts in a function called `rotate`, and an XOR cipher to decrypt resources required for persistence, process guarding, and file locking. It also performs this same function on encrypted stack strings and the `head` and `key` sections in the network packet structure used for C2 communications.
RotaJakiro encrypts C2 communication using a combination of AES, XOR, ROTATE encryption, and ZLIB compression.
When executing with non-root permissions, RotaJakiro uses the the `shmget` API to create shared memory between other known RotaJakiro processes. RotaJakiro also uses the `execvp` API to help its dead process "resurrect".
RotaJakiro can monitor the `/proc/[PID]` directory of known RotaJakiro processes as a part of its persistence when executing with non-root permissions. If the process is found dead, it resurrects the process. RotaJakiro processes can be matched to an associated Advisory Lock, in the `/proc/locks` folder, to ensure it doesn't spawn more than one process.

text: Ryuk has injected itself into remote processes to encrypt files using a combination of VirtualAlloc, WriteProcessMemory, and CreateRemoteThread. Ryuk has attempted to adjust its token privileges to have the SeDebugPrivilege. Ryuk has called kill.bat for stopping services, disabling services and killing processes. Ryuk has used multiple native APIs including ShellExecuteW to run executables,GetWindowsDirectoryW to create folders, and VirtualAlloc, WriteProcessMemory, and CreateRemoteThread for process injection. Ryuk has constructed legitimate appearing installation folder paths by calling GetWindowsDirectoryW and then inserting a null byte at the fourth character of the path. For Windows Vista or higher, the path would appear as C:\Users\Public. Ryuk has been observed to query the registry key HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Nls\Language and the value InstallLanguage. If the machine has the value 0x419 (Russian), 0x422 (Ukrainian), or 0x423 (Belarusian), it stops execution. Ryuk has used a combination of symmetric (AES) and asymmetric (RSA) encryption to encrypt files. Files have been encrypted with their own AES key and given a file extension of .RYK. Encrypted directories have had a ransom note of RyukReadMe.txt written to the directory. text:
LightSpy encrypts the C2 configuration file using AES with a static key, while the module `.dylib` files use a rolling one-byte encoding for obfuscation.
To collect data on the host's Wi-Fi connection history, LightSpy reads the `/Library/Preferences/SystemConfiguration/com.apple.airport.preferences.plist file`.It also utilizes Apple's CWWiFiClient API to scan for nearby Wi-Fi networks and obtain data on the SSID, security type, and RSSI (signal strength) values.
LightSpy uses Apple's built-in AVFoundation Framework library to capture and manage audio recordings then transform them to JSON blobs for exfiltration.
LightSpy uses Apple's built-in AVFoundation Framework library to access the user's camera and screen. It uses the `AVCaptureStillImage` to take a picture using the user's camera and the `AVCaptureScreen` to take a screenshot or record the user's screen for a specified period of time.
LightSpy's configuration file is appended to the end of the binary. For example, the last `0x1d0` bytes of one sample is an AES encrypted configuration file with a static key of `3e2717e8b3873b29`.
LightSpy performs an in-memory keychain query via `SecItemCopyMatching()` then formats the retrieved data as a JSON blob for exfiltration.
LightSpy uses the `NSFileManager` to move, create and delete files. LightSpy can also use the assembly `bt` instruction to determine a file's executable permissions.
LightSpy's main executable and module `.dylib` binaries are loaded using a combination of `dlopen()` to load the library, `_objc_getClass()` to retrieve the class definition, and `_objec_msgSend()` to invoke/execute the specified method in the loaded class.
On macOS, LightSpy downloads a `.json` file from the C2 server. The `.json` file contains metadata about the plugins to be downloaded, including their URL, name, version, and MD5 hash. LightSpy retrieves the plugins specified in the `.json` file, which are compiled `.dylib` files. These `.dylib` files provide task and platform specific functionality. LightSpy also imports open-source libraries to manage socket connections.
To exfiltrate data, LightSpy configures each module to send an obfuscated JSON blob to hardcoded URL endpoints or paths aligned to the module name.
If sent the command `16001`, LightSpy uses the `NSFileManger contentsOfDirectoryAtPath()` to enumerate the Applications folder to collect the bundle name, bundle identifier, and version information from each application's `info.plist` file. The results are then converted into a JSON blob for exfiltration.
LightSpy's second stage implant uses the `DeviceInformation` class to collect system information, including CPU usage, battery statistics, memory allocations, screen size, etc.
If sent the command `16002`, LightSpy uses the `NSWorkspace runningApplications()` method to collect the process ID, path to the executable, bundle information, and the filename of the executable for all running applications.
LightSpy's C2 communication is performed over WebSockets using the open source library SocketRocket with functionality such as, heartbeat, receiving commands, and updating command status.
On macOS, LightSpy checks the existence of a process identification number (PID) file, `/Users/Shared/irc.pid`, to verify if LightSpy is currently running.
To collect data on the host's Wi-Fi connection history, LightSpy reads the `/Library/Preferences/SystemConfiguration/com.apple.airport.preferences.plist` file. It also utilizes Apple's `CWWiFiClient` API to scan for nearby Wi-Fi networks and obtain data on the SSID, security type, and RSSI (signal strength) values.
