Lumma Stealer has used payloads that resemble benign file extensions such as .mp3, .accdb, and .pub, though the files contained malicious JavaScript content.
Lumma Stealer has used Base64-encoded content during execution, decoded via PowerShell.
title: Leandro Fróes, Netskope. (2025, January 23). Lumma Stealer: Fake CAPTCHAs & New Techniques to Evade Detection. Retrieved March 22, 2025.

text:
StrelaStealer has been distributed as a malicious JavaScript object.
StrelaStealer communicates externally via HTTP POST with encrypted content.
StrelaStealer variants include functionality to identify and evade debuggers.
StrelaStealer variants have included excessive mathematical functions padding the binary and slowing execution for anti-analysis and sandbox evasion purposes.
StrelaStealer has included BAT files in some instances for installation.
StrelaStealer variants check system language settings via keyboard layout or similar mechanisms.
StrelaStealer has been delivered via JScript files in a ZIP archive.
StrelaStealer payloads have included strings encrypted via XOR. StrelaStealer JavaScript payloads utilize Base64-encoded payloads that are decoded via certutil to create a malicious DLL file.
StrelaStealer exfiltrates collected email credentials via HTTP POST to command and control servers.
StrelaStealer enumerates the registry key `HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Office\16.0\Outlook\Profiles\Outlook\9375CFF0413111d3B88A00104B2A6676\` to identify the values for "IMAP User," "IMAP Server," and "IMAP Password" associated with the Outlook email application.
StrelaStealer payloads have used control flow obfuscation techniques such as excessively long code blocks of mathematical instructions to defeat sandboxing and related analysis methods.
StrelaStealer variants only execute if the keyboard layout or language matches a set list of variables.
StrelaStealer attempts to identify and collect mail login data from Thunderbird and Outlook following execution.
StrelaStealer searches for and if found collects the contents of files such as `logins.json` and `key4.db` in the `$APPDATA%\Thunderbird\Profiles\` directory, associated with the Thunderbird email application.
StrelaStealer variants include the use of mutex values based on the victim system name to prevent reinfection.
title: Fortgale. (2023, September 18). StrelaStealer Malware Analysis. Retrieved December 31, 2024.

text: Emotet has enumerated all users connected to network shares.
title: MITRE ATT&CK software S0367

text: RAPIDPULSE is a web shell that is capable of arbitrary file read on targeted web servers to exfiltrate items of interest on the victim device. SLOWPULSE is applied in compromised environments through modifications to legitimate Pulse Secure files. RAPIDPULSE listens for specific HTTP query parameters in received communications. If specific parameters match, a hard-coded RC4 key is used to decrypt the HTTP query paremter hmacTime. This decrypts to a filename that is then open, read, encrypted with the same RC4 key, base64-encoded, written to standard out, then passed as a response to the HTTP request. RAPIDPULSE has the ability to RC4 encrypt and base64 encode decrypted files on compromised servers prior to writing them to stdout. RAPIDPULSE retrieves files from the victim system via encrypted commands sent to the web shell. RAPIDPULSE can transfer files to and from compromised hosts.
title: Perez, D. et al. (2021, May 27). Re-Checking Your Pulse: Updates on Chinese APT Actors Compromising Pulse Secure VPN Devices. Retrieved February 5, 2024.

text: QakBot can maintain persistence by creating an auto-run Registry key.
title: Trend Micro. (2020, December 17). QAKBOT: A decade-old malware still with new tricks. Retrieved November 17, 2024.

text:
RARSTONE obtains installer properties from Uninstall Registry Key entries to obtain information about installed applications and how to uninstall certain applications.
After decrypting itself in memory, RARSTONE downloads a DLL file from its C2 server and loads it in the memory space of a hidden Internet Explorer process. This “downloaded” file is actually not dropped onto the system.
title: Camba, A. (2013, February 27). BKDR_RARSTONE: New RAT to Watch Out For. Retrieved January 8, 2016.

text:
Zeus Panda uses PowerShell to download and execute the payload.
Zeus Panda queries the system's keyboard mapping to determine the language used on the system. It will terminate execution if it detects LANG_RUSSIAN, LANG_BELARUSIAN, LANG_KAZAK, or LANG_UKRAINIAN.
Zeus Panda encrypts strings with XOR. Zeus Panda also encrypts all configuration and settings in AES and RC4.
Zeus Panda decrypts strings in the code during the execution process.
Zeus Panda checks to see if anti-virus, anti-spyware, or firewall products are installed in the victim’s environment.
Zeus Panda uses HTTP for C2 communications.
Zeus Panda collects the OS version, system architecture, computer name, product ID, install date, and information on the keyboard mapping to determine the language used on the system.
Zeus Panda adds persistence by creating Registry Run keys.
Zeus Panda obfuscates the macro commands in its initial payload.
title: Brumaghin, E., et al. (2017, November 02). Poisoning the Well: Banking Trojan Targets Google Search Results. Retrieved November 5, 2018.

text: SHARPSTATS has the ability to upload and download files. POWERSTATS can retrieve screenshots from compromised hosts. POWERSTATS can use VBScript (VBE) code for execution. SHARPSTATS has the ability to identify the domain of the compromised host. POWERSTATS uses character replacement, PowerShell environment variables, and XOR encoding to obfuscate code. POWERSTATS's backdoor code is a multi-layer obfuscated, encoded, and compressed blob. POWERSTATS has used PowerShell code with custom string obfuscation SHARPSTATS has the ability to identify the IP address, machine name, and OS of the compromised host. SHARPSTATS has the ability to identify the username on the compromised host. SHARPSTATS has the ability to identify the current date and time on the compromised host. POWERSTATS has used useless code blocks to counter analysis. POWERSTATS can retrieve OS name/architecture and computer/domain name information from compromised hosts. SHARPSTATS has used base64 encoding and XOR to obfuscate PowerShell scripts. POWERSTATS uses PowerShell for obfuscation and execution. SHARPSTATS has the ability to employ a custom PowerShell script. POWERSTATS can retrieve IP, network adapter configuration information, and domain from compromised hosts. POWERSTATS has used get_tasklist to discover processes on the compromised host. POWERSTATS has the ability to identify the username on the compromised host.
title: Lunghi, D. and Horejsi, J.. (2019, June 10). MuddyWater Resurfaces, Uses Multi-Stage Backdoor POWERSTATS V3 and New Post-Exploitation Tools. Retrieved May 14, 2020.

text:
KillDisk deletes system files to make the OS unbootable. KillDisk also targets and deletes files with 35 different file extensions.
The BlackEnergy component KillDisk is capable of deleting Windows Event Logs.
KillDisk deletes Application, Security, Setup, and System Windows Event Logs.
title: Cherepanov, A.. (2016, January 3). BlackEnergy by the SSHBearDoor: attacks against Ukrainian news media and electric industry. Retrieved May 18, 2016.

text: Dridex has used the OutputDebugStringW function to avoid malware analysis as part of its anti-debugging technique. Dridex has relied upon users clicking on a malicious attachment delivered through spearphishing. Dridex has used POST requests and HTTPS for C2 communications. Dridex can use multiple layers of proxy servers to hide terminal nodes in its infrastructure. Dridex has collected a list of installed software on the system. Dridex's strings are obfuscated using RC4. Dridex has collected the computer name and OS architecture information from the system. Dridex contains a backconnect module for tunneling network traffic through a victim's computer. Infected computers become part of a P2P botnet that can relay C2 traffic to other infected peers.
title: Check Point Research. (2021, January 4). Stopping Serial Killer: Catching the Next Strike. Retrieved September 7, 2021.

text:
Neo-reGeorg can tunnel data in and out of targeted networks.
Neo-reGeorg can create multiple TCP connections for a single session.
Neo-reGeorg can use modified Base64 encoding to obfuscate communications.
Neo-reGeorg is a Python-based web shell.
Neo-reGeorg has the ability to download files to targeted systems.
Neo-reGeorg has the ability to establish a SOCKS5 proxy on a compromised web server.
reGeorg has the ability to download files to targeted systems.
Neo-reGeorg can be installed on compromised web servers to tunnel C2 connections.
Neo-reGeorg can use customized HTTP headers.
title: L-Codes. (2019). Neo-reGeorg. Retrieved December 4, 2024.

text:
EKANS uses standard encryption library functions to encrypt files.
EKANS stops database, data backup solution, antivirus, and ICS-related processes.
EKANS removes backups of Volume Shadow Copies to disable any restoration capabilities.
title: Hinchliffe, A. Santos, D. (2020, June 26). Threat Assessment: EKANS Ransomware. Retrieved February 9, 2021.

text:
LODEINFO has been distributed to targeted victims via malicious email attachments.
LODEINFO has the ability to download additional files from the C2.
LODEINFO has used control flow flattening to obfuscate code.
LODEINFO can delete files to remove traces of activity from victim systems.
LODEINFO has been executed via victims opening malicious email attachments.
LODEINFO can execute commands with WMI.
LODEINFO has inserted junk code to obstruct code analysis.
LODEINFO can identify the associated username on targeted machines.
The LODEINFO loader module contains XOR-encrypted shellcode.
LODEINFO has the ability to designate specific files and folders to encryption.
LODEINFO can capture keystrokes on targeted systems.
LODEINFO can kill a process using specific process ID.
LODEINFO can inject shellcode into the memory of compromised hosts.
LODEINFO has the ability to take screenshots.
LODEINFO can disover machine information including OS architecture, the ANSI code page (ACP) identifier, and hostname.
LODEINFO can incorporate a ransom command to encrypt specified files and folders.
LODEINFO can upload files from infected hosts to the C2.
title: ITOCHU. (2024, January 24). The Endless Struggle Against APT10: Insights from LODEINFO v0.6.6 - v0.7.3 Analysis. Retrieved April 17, 2026.

text:
Fysbis has been encrypted using XOR and RC4.
Fysbis can collect information about running processes.
Fysbis has masqueraded as the rsyncd and dbus-inotifier services.
Fysbis can use Base64 to encode its C2 traffic.
Fysbis has masqueraded as trusted software rsyncd and dbus-inotifier.
Fysbis has the ability to search for files.
Fysbis has the ability to delete files.
Fysbis has established persistence using a systemd service.
title: Doctor Web. (2014, November 21). Linux.BackDoor.Fysbis.1. Retrieved December 7, 2017.

text: IPsec Helper can identify the process it is currently running under and its number, and pass this back to a command and control node. DEADWOOD can be executed as a service using various names, such as ScDeviceEnums. DEADWOOD XORs some strings within the binary using the value 0xD5, and deobfuscates these items at runtime. Apostle writes batch scripts to disk, such as system.bat and remover.bat, that perform various anti-analysis and anti-forensic tasks, before finally deleting themselves at the end of execution. Apostle attempts to delete itself after encryption or wiping operations are complete and before shutting down the victim machine. DEADWOOD will attempt to masquerade its service execution using benign-looking names such as ScDeviceEnums. Apostle retrieves a list of all running processes on a victim host, and stops all services containing the string "sql," likely to propagate ransomware activity to database files. IPsec Helper can run arbitrary commands passed to it through cmd.exe. Apostle will attempt to delete all event logs on a victim machine following file wipe activity. DEADWOOD contains an embedded, AES-encrypted payload labeled METADATA that provides configuration information for follow-on execution. Apostle compiled code is obfuscated in an unspecified fashion prior to delivery to victims. DEADWOOD opens and writes zeroes to the first 512 bytes of each drive, deleting the MBR. DEADWOOD then sends the control code IOCTL_DISK_DELETE_DRIVE_LAYOUT to ensure the MBR is removed from the drive. IPsec Helper can delete various service traces related to persistent execution when commanded. IPsec Helper is run as a Windows service in victim environments. IPsec Helper contains an embedded XML configuration file with an encrypted list of command and control servers. These are written to an external configuration file during execution. IPsec Helper exfiltrates specific files through its command and control framework. IPsec Helper can delete itself when given the appropriate command. DEADWOOD will set a timestamp value to determine when wiping functionality starts. When the timestamp is met on the system, a trigger file is created on the operating system allowing for execution to proceed. If the timestamp is in the past, the wiper will execute immediately. IPsec Helper can identify specific files and folders for follow-on exfiltration. Apostle creates new, encrypted versions of files then deletes the originals, with the new filenames consisting of a random GUID and ".lock" for an extension. IPsec Helper will sleep for a random number of seconds, iterating 200 times over sleeps between one to three seconds, before continuing execution flow. DEADWOOD overwrites files on victim systems with random data to effectively destroy them. IPsec Helper connects to command and control servers via HTTP POST requests based on parameters hard-coded into the malware. DEADWOOD deletes files following overwriting them with random data. IPsec Helper can run arbitrary Visual Basic scripts and commands passed to it. DEADWOOD contains an embedded, AES-encrypted resource named METADATA that contains configuration information for follow-on execution. Apostle achieves persistence by creating a scheduled task, such as MicrosoftCrashHandlerUAC. Apostle's ransomware variant requires that a base64-encoded argument is passed when executed, that is used as the Public Key for subsequent encryption operations. If Apostle is executed without this argument, it automatically runs a self-delete function. IPsec Helper can delete various registry keys related to its execution and use. IPsec Helper can run arbitrary PowerShell commands passed to it. DEADWOOD changes the password for local and domain users via net.exe to a random 32 character string to prevent these accounts from logging on. Additionally, DEADWOOD will terminate the winlogon.exe process to prevent attempts to log on to the infected system. IPsec Helper can make arbitrary changes to registry keys based on provided input. Apostle reboots the victim machine following wiping and related activity. Apostle searches for files on available drives based on a list of extensions hard-coded into the sample for follow-on wipe activity. Apostle initially masqueraded as ransomware but actual functionality is a data destruction tool, supported by an internal name linked to an early version, wiper-action. Apostle writes random data to original files after an encrypted copy is created, along with resizing the original file to zero and changing time property metadata before finally deleting the original file. IPsec Helper can download additional payloads from command and control nodes and execute them.
title: Amitai Ben & Shushan Ehrlich. (2021, May). From Wiper to Ransomware: The Evolution of Agrius. Retrieved May 21, 2024.

text: Ragnar Locker has used VirtualBox and a stripped Windows XP virtual machine to run itself. The use of a shared folder specified in the configuration enables Ragnar Locker to encrypt files on the host operating system, including files on any mapped drives. Ragnar Locker has attempted to terminate/stop processes and services associated with endpoint security products. Ragnar Locker can delete volume shadow copies using vssadmin delete shadows /all /quiet. Ragnar Locker has been delivered as an unsigned MSI package that was executed with msiexec.exe. Ragnar Locker has used regsvr32.exe to execute components of VirtualBox. Ragnar Locker has used sc.exe to execute a service that it creates. Ragnar Locker has used sc.exe to create a new service for the VirtualBox driver. Ragnar Locker may attempt to connect to removable drives and mapped network drives. Ragnar Locker has used rundll32.exe to execute components of VirtualBox. Ragnar Locker has attempted to stop services associated with business applications and databases to release the lock on files used by these applications so they may be encrypted. Ragnar Locker encrypts files on the local machine and mapped drives prior to displaying a note demanding a ransom. Ragnar Locker has used cmd.exe and batch scripts to execute commands.
title: SophosLabs. (2020, May 21). Ragnar Locker ransomware deploys virtual machine to dodge security. Retrieved June 29, 2020.

text: FoggyWeb can configure custom listeners to passively monitor all incoming HTTP GET and POST requests sent to the AD FS server from the intranet/internet and intercept HTTP requests that match the custom URI patterns defined by the actor. FoggyWeb can be decrypted in memory using a Lightweight Encryption Algorithm (LEA)-128 key and decoded using a XOR key. FoggyWeb's loader can enumerate all Common Language Runtimes (CLRs) and running Application Domains in the compromised AD FS server's Microsoft.IdentityServer.ServiceHost.exe process. FoggyWeb's loader can use API functions to load the FoggyWeb backdoor into the same Application Domain within which the legitimate AD FS managed code is executed. FoggyWeb has been XOR-encoded. FoggyWeb can remotely exfiltrate sensitive information from a compromised AD FS server. FoggyWeb can allow abuse of a compromised AD FS server's SAML token. FoggyWeb has used a dynamic XOR key and custom XOR methodology for C2 communications. FoggyWeb's loader can call the load() function to load the FoggyWeb dll into an Application Domain on a compromised AD FS server. FoggyWeb can retrieve configuration data from a compromised AD FS server. FoggyWeb can masquerade the output of C2 commands as a fake, but legitimately formatted WebP file. FoggyWeb's loader has reflectively loaded .NET-based assembly/payloads into memory. FoggyWeb has the ability to communicate with C2 servers over HTTP GET/POST requests. FoggyWeb's loader can check for the FoggyWeb backdoor .pri file on a compromised AD FS server. FoggyWeb can retrieve token signing certificates and token decryption certificates from a compromised AD FS server. FoggyWeb's loader has used DLL Search Order Hijacking to load malicious code instead of the legitimate `version.dll` during the `Microsoft.IdentityServer.ServiceHost.exe` execution process. FoggyWeb can compile and execute source code sent to the compromised AD FS server via a specific HTTP POST. FoggyWeb can be disguised as a Visual Studio file such as `Windows.Data.TimeZones.zh-PH.pri` to evade detection. Also, FoggyWeb's loader can mimic a genuine `dll` file that carries out the same import functions as the legitimate Windows `version.dll` file. FoggyWeb can invoke the `Common.Compress` method to compress data with the C# GZipStream compression class. FoggyWeb can use a dynamic XOR key and a custom XOR methodology to encode data before exfiltration. Also, FoggyWeb can encode C2 command output within a legitimate WebP file. FoggyWeb can receive additional malicious components from an actor controlled C2 server and execute them on a compromised AD FS server.
title: Ramin Nafisi. (2021, September 27). FoggyWeb: Targeted NOBELIUM malware leads to persistent backdoor. Retrieved October 4, 2021.

text: Raspberry Robin uses rundll32 execution without any command line parameters to contact command and control infrastructure, such as IP addresses associated with Tor nodes. Raspberry Robin retrieves its second stage payload in a variety of ways such as through msiexec.exe abuse, or running the curl command to download the payload to the victim's %AppData% folder. Raspberry Robin uses newly-registered domains containing only a few characters for command and controll purposes, such as "v0[.]cx". Raspberry Robin uses regsvr32.exe execution without any command line parameters for command and control requests to IP addresses associated with Tor nodes. Raspberry Robin uses mixed-case letters for filenames and commands to evade detection. Raspberry Robin uses msiexec.exe for post-installation communication to command and control infrastructure. Msiexec.exe is executed referencing a remote resource for second-stage payload retrieval and execution. Raspberry Robin uses the Windows utility odbcconf.exe to execute malicious commands, using the regsvr flag to execute DLLs and bypass application control mechanisms that are not monitoring for odbcconf.exe abuse. Raspberry Robin is capable of contacting the TOR network for delivering second-stage payloads. Raspberry Robin has historically been delivered via infected USB drives containing a malicious LNK object masquerading as a legitimate folder. Raspberry Robin uses cmd.exe to read and execute a file stored on an infected USB device as part of initial installation. Raspberry Robin will communicate via HTTP over port 8080 for command and control traffic. Raspberry Robin uses outbound HTTP requests containing victim information for retrieving second stage payloads. Variants of Raspberry Robin can download archive files (such as 7-Zip files) via the victim web browser for second stage execution. Raspberry Robin has historically used infected USB media to spread to new victims. Raspberry Robin will use the legitimate Windows utility fodhelper.exe to run processes at elevated privileges without requiring a User Account Control prompt.
title: Lauren Podber and Stef Rand. (2022, May 5). Raspberry Robin gets the worm early. Retrieved May 17, 2024.

text: Kobalos can exfiltrate credentials over the network via UDP. Kobalos can write captured SSH connection credentials to a file under the /var/run directory with a .pid extension for exfiltration. Kobalos can record the IP address of the target machine. Kobalos replaced the SSH client with a trojanized SSH client to steal credentials on compromised systems. Kobalos can record the hostname and kernel version of the target machine. Kobalos can modify timestamps of replaced files, such as ssh with the added credential stealer or sshd used to deploy Kobalos. Kobalos decrypts strings right after the initial communication, but before the authentication process.
title: M.Leveille, M., Sanmillan, I. (2021, January). A WILD KOBALOS APPEARS Tricksy Linux malware goes after HPCs. Retrieved August 24, 2021.

text:
StealBit can be configured to exfiltrate specific file types.
StealBit can use HTTP to exfiltrate files to actor-controlled infrastructure.
StealBit can be configured to exfiltrate files at a specified rate to evade network detection mechanisms.
StealBit can detect it is being run in the context of a debugger.
StealBit will execute an empty infinite loop if it detects it is being run in the context of a debugger.
StealBit can upload data and files to the LockBit victim-shaming site.
StealBit can enumerate the computer name and domain membership of the compromised system.
StealBit can deobfuscate loaded modules prior to execution.
StealBit can configure processes to not display certain Windows error messages by through use of the `NtSetInformationProcess`.
StealBit can determine system location based on the default language setting and will not execute on systems located in former Soviet countries.
StealBit can use interprocess communication (IPC) to enable the designation of multiple files for exfiltration in a scalable manner.
StealBit can use native APIs including `LoadLibraryExA` for execution and `NtSetInformationProcess` for defense evasion purposes.
StealBit stores obfuscated DLL file names in its executable.
StealBit can self-delete its executable file from the compromised system.
StealBit can use the Windows Socket networking library to communicate with attacker-controlled endpoints.
title: Cybereason Global SOC Team. (n.d.). THREAT ANALYSIS REPORT: Inside the LockBit Arsenal - The StealBit Exfiltration Tool. Retrieved January 29, 2025.

text:
XLoader features encrypted functions using the RC4 algorithm and bytecode operations.
XLoader can utilize decoy command and control domains within the malware configuration to circumvent sandbox analysis.
XLoader uses process hollowing by injecting itself into the `explorer.exe` process and other files ithin the Windows `SysWOW64` directory.
title: ANY.RUN. (2023, February 28). XLoader/FormBook: Encryption Analysis and Malware Decryption . Retrieved March 11, 2025.

text:
SystemBC has collected the Windows account username on the victim machine.
SystemBC has used `cmd.exe` to execute VBS scripts, BAT scripts and CMD scripts.
SystemBC has used hidden scheduled tasks to execute PowerShell commands by adding the following: `-WindowStyle Hidden -ep bypass -file `.
SystemBC has encrypted its C2 traffic with RC4.
SystemBC has used multiple proxy layers, such as SOCKS5 and Tor, for C2 communication. SystemBC has also leveraged Tor for encrypting and concealing C2 traffic. The server component of SystemBC has used SOCKS5 for C2 communication.
SystemBC has downloaded additional files for execution on the victim’s machine. The server component of SystemBC has the ability to send additional files to victim machines.
SystemBC has utilized native Windows API functions such as `EnumWindows`and `GetVolumeInformationA` during discovery activities.
SystemBC has leveraged the Sleep functions before and after commands to ensure execution using the hexadecimal values within commands to include `Sleep(0x2710u)` that waits 10 seconds, and `Sleep(0xEA60u)` for 60 seconds.
SystemBC has executed a copy of itself as a scheduled task with the `start` command. The copy of SystemBC has random file and directory names within the ProgramData directory.
SystemBC has checked if the last characters of DNS server names end in .bit before initializing C2 communication. SystemBC has identified running processes associated with anti-virus solutions to include `a2guard.exe` to determine whether it executes or not.
SystemBC has leveraged VBScript to execute malicious code.
SystemBC has utilized the `-WindowStyle Hidden -ep bypass -file `to conceal PowerShell windows.
SystemBC has the ability to enumerate running processes.
title: Gallagher, S., Gn, S. (2020, December 16). Ransomware operators use SystemBC RAT as off-the-shelf Tor backdoor. Retrieved May 16, 2025.

text: Emotet has encrypted data before sending to the C2 server.
title: Xiaopeng Zhang. (2017, May 3). Deep Analysis of New Emotet Variant – Part 1. Retrieved April 1, 2019.

text: NotPetya can use PsExec, which interacts with the ADMIN$ network share to execute commands on remote systems. Olympic Destroyer uses PsExec to interact with the ADMIN$ network share to execute commands on remote systems.
title: Russinovich, M. (2004, June 28). PsExec. Retrieved December 17, 2015.

text:
LockBit 3.0 can attempt a CMSTP UAC bypass if it does not have administrative privileges.
LockBit 3.0 can install system services for persistence.
LockBit 3.0 can check heap memory parameters for indications of a debugger and stop the flow of events to the attached debugger in order to hinder dynamic analysis.
title: Walter, J. (2022, July 21). LockBit 3.0 Update | Unpicking the Ransomware’s Latest Anti-Analysis and Evasion Techniques. Retrieved February 5, 2025.

text: DarkComet can access the victim’s webcam to take pictures. DarkComet can disable Security Center functions like the Windows Firewall. DarkComet adds several Registry entries to enable automatic execution at every system startup. DarkComet can use HTTP for C2 communications. DarkComet adds a Registry value for its installation routine to the Registry Key HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System Enable LUA=”0” and HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\DC3_FEXEC. DarkComet can launch a remote shell to execute commands on the victim’s machine. DarkComet can disable Security Center functions like anti-virus. DarkComet can list active processes running on the victim’s machine. DarkComet can execute various types of scripts on the victim’s machine. DarkComet can load any files onto the infected machine to execute. DarkComet can steal data from the clipboard. DarkComet can listen in to victims' conversations through the system’s microphone. DarkComet can collect the computer name, RAM used, and operating system version from the victim’s machine. DarkComet has the option to compress its payload using UPX or MPRESS. DarkComet can open an active screen of the victim’s machine and take control of the mouse and keyboard.
title: Kujawa, A. (2018, March 27). You dirty RAT! Part 1: DarkComet. Retrieved November 6, 2018.

text: Bankshot generates a false TLS handshake using a public certificate to disguise C2 network communications.
title: US-CERT. (2017, December 13). Malware Analysis Report (MAR) - 10135536-B. Retrieved August 15, 2024.

text: AvosLocker has enumerated shared drives on a compromised network.
title: FBI, FinCEN, Treasury. (2022, March 17). Indicators of Compromise Associated with AvosLocker Ransomware. Retrieved January 11, 2023.

text:
Sardonic has the ability to collect data from a compromised machine to deliver to the attacker.
Sardonic can use certain ConfuserEx features for obfuscation and can be encoded in a base64 string.
Sardonic has the ability to run `cmd.exe` or other interactive processes on a compromised computer.
Sardonic can first decrypt with the RC4 algorithm using a hardcoded decryption key before decompressing.
Sardonic can use the `QueueUserAPC` API to execute shellcode on a compromised machine.
Sardonic has a plugin system that can load specially made DLLs into memory and execute their functions.
title: Symantec Threat Hunter Team. (2023, July 18). FIN8 Uses Revamped Sardonic Backdoor to Deliver Noberus Ransomware. Retrieved August 9, 2023.

text: Revenge RAT has a plugin for keylogging. Revenge RAT has a plugin for microphone interception. Revenge RAT uses cmd.exe to execute commands and run scripts on the victim's machine. Revenge RAT uses the Forfiles utility to execute commands on the system. Revenge RAT used blogpost.com as its primary command and control server during a campaign. Revenge RAT has the ability to access the webcam. Revenge RAT uses the PowerShell command Reflection.Assembly to load itself into memory to aid in execution. Revenge RAT schedules tasks to run malicious scripts at different intervals. Revenge RAT uses mshta.exe to run malicious scripts on the system.
title: Gannon, M. (2019, February 11). With Upgrades in Delivery and Support Infrastructure, Revenge RAT Malware is a Bigger Threat. Retrieved November 17, 2024.

text:
Zebrocy uses SSL and AES ECB for encrypting C2 communications.
Zebrocy uses cmd.exe to execute commands on the system.
Zebrocy has a command to delete files and directories.
Zebrocy gets the username from the system.
Zebrocy gathers the current time zone and date information from the system.
Zebrocy has exfiltrated data to the designated C2 server using HTTP POST requests.
Zebrocy has a command to create a scheduled task for persistence.
title: CISA. (2020, October 29). Malware Analysis Report (AR20-303B). Retrieved December 9, 2020.

text: SPACESHIP identifies files with certain extensions and copies them to a directory in the user's profile. SHIPSHAPE achieves persistence by creating a shortcut in the Startup folder. NETEAGLE can send process listings over the C2 channel. SPACESHIP copies staged data to removable drives when they are inserted into the system. FLASHFLOOD stages data it copies from the local system or removable drives in the "%WINDIR%\$NtUninstallKB885884$\" directory. NETEAGLE is capable of reading files over the C2 channel. NETEAGLE will decrypt resources it downloads with HTTP requests by using RC4 with the key "ScoutEagle." BACKSPACE achieves persistence by creating a shortcut to itself in the CSIDL_STARTUP directory. NETEAGLE allows adversaries to enumerate and modify the infected host's file system. It supports searching for directories, creating directories, listing directory contents, reading and writing to files, retrieving file attributes, and retrieving volume information. SPACESHIP identifies files and directories for collection by searching for specific file extensions or file modification time. Data SPACESHIP copies to the staging area is compressed with zlib. Bytes are rotated by four positions and XOR'ed with 0x23. FLASHFLOOD searches for interesting files (either a default or customized set of file extensions) on removable media and copies them to a staging area. The default file types copied would include data copied to the drive by SPACESHIP. Adversaries can direct BACKSPACE to execute from the command line on infected hosts, or have BACKSPACE create a reverse shell. BACKSPACE is capable of enumerating and making modifications to an infected system's Registry. During its initial execution, BACKSPACE extracts operating system information from the infected host. APT30 may have used the SHIPSHAPE malware to move onto air-gapped networks. SHIPSHAPE targets removable drives to spread to other systems by modifying the drive to use Autorun to execute or by hiding legitimate document files and copying an executable to the folder with the same name as the legitimate document. NETEAGLE will attempt to detect if the infected host is configured to a proxy. If so, NETEAGLE will send beacons via an HTTP POST request. NETEAGLE will also use HTTP to download resources that contain an IP address and Port Number pair to connect to for further C2. SPACESHIP achieves persistence by creating a shortcut in the current user's Startup folder. FLASHFLOOD searches for interesting files (either a default or customized set of file extensions) on the local system and removable media. BACKSPACE uses HTTP as a transport to communicate with its command server. BACKSPACE may collect information about running processes. FLASHFLOOD achieves persistence by making an entry in the Registry's Run key. The "ZJ" variant of BACKSPACE allows "ZJ link" infections with Internet access to relay traffic from "ZJ listen" to a command server. BACKSPACE allows adversaries to search for files. Newer variants of BACKSPACE will encode C2 communications with a custom system. Adversaries can direct BACKSPACE to upload files to the C2 Server. If NETEAGLE does not detect a proxy configured on the infected machine, it will send beacons via UDP/6000. Also, after retrieving a C2 IP address and Port Number, NETEAGLE will initiate a TCP connection to this socket. The ensuing connection is a plaintext C2 channel in which commands are specified by DWORDs. BACKSPACE attempts to avoid detection by checking a first stage command and control server to determine if it should connect to the second stage server, which performs "louder" interactions with the malware. NETEAGLE will attempt to detect if the infected host is configured to a proxy. If so, NETEAGLE will send beacons via an HTTP POST request; otherwise it will send beacons via UDP/6000. NETEAGLE can use HTTP to download resources that contain an IP address and port number pair to connect to for C2. The "ZR" variant of BACKSPACE will check to see if known host-based firewalls are installed on the infected systems. BACKSPACE will attempt to establish a C2 channel, then will examine open windows to identify a pop-up from the firewall software and will simulate a mouse-click to allow the connection to proceed. FLASHFLOOD searches for interesting files (either a default or customized set of file extensions) on the local system. FLASHFLOOD will scan the My Recent Documents, Desktop, Temporary Internet Files, and TEMP directories. FLASHFLOOD also collects information stored in the Windows Address Book. NETEAGLE allows adversaries to execute shell commands on the infected host. BACKSPACE is capable of deleting Registry keys, sub-keys, and values on a victim system. The "SCOUT" variant of NETEAGLE achieves persistence by adding itself to the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run Registry key. FLASHFLOOD employs the same encoding scheme as SPACESHIP for data it stages. Data is compressed with zlib, and bytes are rotated four times before being XOR'ed with 0x23.

text: Exaramel for Linux has a hardcoded location that it uses to achieve persistence if the startup system is Upstart or System V and it is running as root. P.A.S. Webshell can scan networks for open ports and listening services. Exaramel for Linux can uninstall its persistence mechanism and delete its configuration file. P.A.S. Webshell can delete scripts from a subdirectory of /tmp after they are run. Exaramel for Linux uses HTTPS for C2 communications. P.A.S. Webshell can use predefined users and passwords to execute brute force attacks against SSH, FTP, POP3, MySQL, MSSQL, and PostgreSQL services. P.A.S. Webshell has the ability to list and extract data from SQL databases. P.A.S. Webshell can gain remote access and execution on target web servers. Exaramel for Linux has a hardcoded location under systemd that it uses to achieve persistence if it is running as root. Exaramel for Linux uses crontab for persistence if it does not have root privileges. P.A.S. Webshell has the ability to create reverse shells with Perl scripts. Exaramel for Linux can decrypt its configuration file. P.A.S. Webshell has the ability to copy files on a compromised host. P.A.S. Webshell can use encryption and base64 encoding to hide strings and to enforce access control once deployed. P.A.S. Webshell can upload and download files to and from compromised hosts. Exaramel for Linux can attempt to find a new C2 server if it receives an error. P.A.S. Webshell can issue commands via HTTP POST. Exaramel for Linux can run whoami to identify the system owner. Exaramel for Linux can execute commands with high privileges via a specific binary with setuid functionality. Exaramel for Linux has a command to execute a shell command on the system. P.A.S. Webshell can display the /etc/passwd file on a compromised host. Exaramel for Linux uses RC4 for encrypting the configuration. P.A.S. Webshell has the ability to modify file permissions. P.A.S. Webshell has the ability to list files and file characteristics including extension, size, ownership, and permissions.

text: Winnti for Windows can run as a service using svchost.exe. Winnti for Windows can check for the presence of specific files prior to moving to the next phase of execution. Winnti for Windows can check if the explorer.exe process is responsible for calling its install function. Winnti for Windows can XOR encrypt C2 traffic. The Winnti for Windows dropper can decrypt and decompresses a data blob. The Winnti for Windows HTTP/S C2 mode can make use of a local proxy. Winnti for Windows can determine if the OS on a compromised host is newer than Windows XP. Winnti for Windows has the ability to encrypt and compress its payload. Winnti for Windows has the ability to use encapsulated HTTP/S in C2 communications. The Winnti for Windows dropper can place malicious payloads on targeted systems. The Winnti for Windows dropper component can verify the existence of a single command line parameter and either terminate if it is not found or later use it as a decryption key. Winnti for Windows can set the timestamps for its worker and service components to match that of cmd.exe. Winnti for Windows can communicate using custom TCP. Winnti for Windows can delete the DLLs for its various components from a compromised host. Winnti for Windows can use Native API to create a new process and to start services. Winnti for Windows can use a variant of the sysprep UAC bypass. The Winnti for Windows HTTP/S C2 mode can make use of an external proxy. Winnti for Windows can add a service named wind0ws to the Registry to achieve persistence after reboot.

Mispadu has the ability to capture screenshots on compromised hosts.

text: MegaCortex was used to kill endpoint security processes. MegaCortex has used .cmd scripts on the victim's system. MegaCortex can wipe deleted data from all drives using cipher.exe. MegaCortex has added entries to the Registry for ransom contact information. After escalating privileges, MegaCortex calls TerminateProcess(), CreateRemoteThread, and other Win32 APIs. MegaCortex has changed user account passwords and logged users off the system. MegaCortex has used code signing certificates issued to fake companies to bypass security controls. MegaCortex can parse the available drives and directories to determine which files to encrypt. MegaCortex loads injecthelper.dll into a newly created rundll32.exe process. MegaCortex can stop and disable services on the system. MegaCortex has checked the number of CPUs in the system to avoid being run in a sandbox or emulator. MegaCortex has deleted volume shadow copies using vssadmin.exe. MegaCortex can enable SeDebugPrivilege and adjust token privileges. MegaCortex has used a Base64 key to decode its components. MegaCortex has used rundll32.exe to load a DLL for file encryption.

CanisterWorm has parsed the /var/log/auth.log and /var/log/secure files for source IP addresses.

SharpStage can execute arbitrary commands with PowerShell.

Linux Rabbit attempts to gain access to the server via SSH.

Snip3 can download additional payloads from web services including Pastebin and top4top.
Snip3 can use visual basic scripts for first-stage execution.

text: BitPaymer compares file names and paths to a list of excluded names and directory names during encryption. BitPaymer can enumerate the sessions for each user logged onto the infected host. BitPaymer has copied itself to the :bin alternate data stream of a newly created file. BitPaymer can enumerate existing Windows services on the host that are configured to run as LocalSystem. BitPaymer can use the tokens of users to create processes on infected systems. BitPaymer attempts to remove the backup shadow files from the host using vssadmin.exe Delete Shadows /All /Quiet. BitPaymer can search for network shares on the domain or workgroup using net view . BitPaymer can import a hard-coded RSA 1024-bit public key, generate a 128-bit RC4 key for each file, and encrypt the file in place, appending .locked to the filename. BitPaymer can use icacls /reset and takeown /F to reset a targeted executable's permissions and then take ownership. BitPaymer can set values in the Registry to help in execution. BitPaymer can use net view to discover remote systems. BitPaymer can suppress UAC prompts by setting the HKCU\Software\Classes\ms-settings\shell\open\command registry key on Windows 10 or HKCU\Software\Classes\mscfile\shell\open\command on Windows 7 and launching the eventvwr.msc process, which launches BitPaymer with elevated privileges. BitPaymer has used dynamic API resolution to avoid identifiable strings within the binary, including RegEnumKeyW. BitPaymer has set the run key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run for persistence. BitPaymer has used RC4-encrypted strings and string hashes to avoid identifiable strings within the binary. BitPaymer can modify the timestamp of an executable so that it can be identified and restored by the decryption tool. BitPaymer can use the RegEnumKeyW to iterate through Registry keys. BitPaymer has attempted to install itself as a service to maintain persistence.
title: Frankoff, S., Hartley, B. (2018, November 14). Big Game Hunting: The Evolution of INDRIK SPIDER From Dridex Wire Fraud to BitPaymer Targeted Ransomware. Retrieved January 6, 2021.

text:
Anchor can execute payloads via shell scripting.
Anchor can support windows execution via SMB shares.
Anchor can create and execute services to load its payload.
Variants of Anchor can use DNS tunneling to communicate with C2.
Anchor can determine the hostname and linux version on a compromised host.
Anchor can install itself as a cron job.
Anchor can download additional payloads.
Anchor can determine the public IP and location of a compromised host.
title: Grange, W. (2020, July 13). Anchor_dns malware goes cross platform. Retrieved September 10, 2020.

text:
BOOKWORM has modified HTTP POST requests to resemble legitimate communications.
BOOKWORM has used various Windows API calls during execution and defense evasion. BOOKWORM has created a buffer on the heap using `HeapCreate` and `HeapAlloc` which allows for copying of shell code and then execution on the heap is initiated through callback function of legitimate API functions such as `EnumChildWindows` or `EnumSystemLanguageGroupsA`.
BOOKWORM has utilized Base64 encoding to obfuscate its payload.
TONESHELL has utilized Native Windows API functions such as `WriteProcessMemory` and `CreateRemoteThreadEx`. TONESHELL has also utilized Windows API functions for creating seed values including `CoCreateGuid` and `GetTickCount`. TONESHELL has leveraged the legitimate API function `EnumSystemLocalesA` to run its shellcode through the callback function.
BOOKWORM has modified file timestamps from the export address table (EAT) to make it difficult to discern when the module was created.
title: Robert Falcone. (2025, February 20). Stately Taurus Activity in Southeast Asia Links to Bookworm Malware. Retrieved July 21, 2025.

title: Cybereason Nocturnus. (n.d.). Triple Threat: Emotet Deploys TrickBot to Steal Data & Spread Ryuk. Retrieved November 28, 2023.

text:
Drovorub can use the WebSocket protocol and has initiated communication with C2 servers with an HTTP Upgrade request.
Drovorub has used XOR encrypted payloads in WebSocket client to server messages.
Drovorub can exfiltrate files over C2 infrastructure.
Drovorub can execute arbitrary commands as root on a compromised system.
Drovorub has used a kernel module rootkit to hide processes, files, executables, and network artifacts from user space view.
Drovorub can delete specific files from a compromised host.
Drovorub can use a port forwarding rule on its agent module to relay network traffic through the client module to a remote host on the same network.
Drovorub can use kernel modules to establish persistence.
Drovorub can use TCP to communicate between its agent and client modules.
Drovorub can transfer files from the victim machine.
Drovorub has de-obsfuscated XOR encrypted payloads in WebSocket messages.
Drovorub can download files to a compromised host.
title: NSA/FBI. (2020, August). Russian GRU 85th GTsSS Deploys Previously Undisclosed Drovorub Malware. Retrieved August 25, 2020.

text:
Tarrask may abuse the Windows schtasks command-line tool to create "hidden" scheduled tasks.
Tarrask has masqueraded as executable files such as `winupdate.exe`, `date.exe`, or `win.exe`.
Tarrask leverages token theft to obtain `lsass.exe` security permissions.
Tarrask is able to create “hidden” scheduled tasks for persistence.
Tarrask creates a scheduled task called “WinUpdate” to re-establish any dropped C2 connections.
Tarrask is able to delete the Security Descriptor (`SD`) registry subkey in order to “hide” scheduled tasks.
Tarrask is able to create “hidden” scheduled tasks by deleting the Security Descriptor (`SD`) registry value.
title: Microsoft Threat Intelligence Team & Detection and Response Team . (2022, April 12). Tarrask malware uses scheduled tasks for defense evasion. Retrieved June 1, 2022.

text:
Medusa Ransomware has leveraged the `CreatePipe` API to enable inter-process communication.
Medusa Ransomware has terminated antivirus services utilizing the gaze.exe executable. Medusa Ransomware has also terminated antivirus services utilizing PowerShell scripts.
Medusa Ransomware has decoded XOR encrypted strings prior to execution in memory.
Medusa Ransomware has searched for files within the victim environment for encryption and exfiltration. Medusa Ransomware has also identified files associated with remote management services.
Medusa Ransomware has leveraged Windows Native API functions to execute payloads.
Medusa Ransomware has leveraged an encoded list of services that it designates for termination.
Medusa Ransomware has enumerated logical drives on infected hosts.
Medusa Ransomware has launched PowerShell scripts for execution and defense evasion.
Medusa Ransomware has discovered device uptime through `GetTickCount()`.
Medusa Ransomware has used `cmd.exe` to execute command on an infected host.
Medusa Ransomware has created a new PowerShell process using the `CreateProcessA` API.
Medusa Ransomware has identified networked drives.
Medusa Ransomware has encrypted files using AES-256 encryption, which then appends the file extension “.medusa” to encrypted files and leaves a ransomware note named “!READ_ME_MEDUSA!!!.txt.”
Medusa Ransomware has avoided specified files, file extensions and folders to ensure successful execution of the payload and continued operations of the impacted device.
Medusa Ransomware has utilized an encoded list of the processes that it detects and terminates.
Medusa Ransomware has deleted recovery files such as shadow copies using `vssadmin.exe`.
Medusa Ransomware has utilized XOR encrypted strings.
Medusa Ransomware has collected data from the SMBIOS firmware table using `GetSystemFirmwareTable`.
Medusa Ransomware has the ability to delete itself after execution. Medusa Ransomware also has the ability to delete itself after execution through the command `cmd /c ping localhost -n 3 > nul & del`.
Medusa Ransomware has the capability to terminate services related to backups, security, databases, communication, filesharing and websites. Medusa Ransomware has also utilized the `taskkill /F /IM <process> /T` command to stop targeted processes and `net stop <process>` command to stop designated services.
Medusa Ransomware has utilized the `ShowWindow` function to hide current window.
title: Vlad Pasca. (2024, January 1). A Deep Dive into Medusa Ransomware. Retrieved October 15, 2025.

text:
MechaFlounder has been downloaded as a file named lsass.exe, which matches the legitimate Windows file.
MechaFlounder has the ability to use HTTP in communication with C2.
MechaFlounder has the ability to run commands on a compromised host.
MechaFlounder has the ability to send the compromised user's account name and hostname within a URL to C2.
MechaFlounder has the ability to upload and download files to and from a compromised host.
MechaFlounder uses a python-based payload.
MechaFlounder has the ability to use base16 encoded strings in C2.
MechaFlounder has the ability to identify the username and hostname on a compromised host.

The Winnti for Windows installer loads a DLL using rundll32.

Cuckoo Stealer can search for files associated with specific applications.
Cuckoo Stealer strings are XOR-encrypted.
Cuckoo Stealer can discover and send the username from a compromised host to C2.
Cuckoo Stealer has staged collected application data from Safari, Notes, and Keychain to `/var/folder`.
Cuckoo Stealer can use osascript to generate a password-stealing prompt, duplicate files and folders, and set environmental variables.

Cuckoo Stealer can capture files from a targeted user's keychain directory.
Cuckoo Stealer is a stripped binary payload.
Cuckoo Stealer can determine the geographical location of a victim host by checking the language.
Cuckoo Stealer can use `launchctl` to load a LaunchAgent for persistence.
Cuckoo Stealer can gather information about the OS version and hardware on compromised hosts.
Cuckoo Stealer can create and populate property list (plist) files to enable execution.
Cuckoo Stealer has captured passwords by prompting victims with a “macOS needs to access System Settings” GUI window.

text:
StrifeWater can use a variety of APIs for execution.
StrifeWater can collect the OS version, architecture, and machine name to create a unique token for the infected host.

StrifeWater can self delete to cover its tracks.

text:
Ryuk can use anti-disassembly and code transformation obfuscation techniques.
Bazar has been spread via emails with embedded malicious links.

text:
BADHATCH can use `net.exe group "domain admins" /domain` to identify Domain Administrators.

BADHATCH can obtain the `DATETIME` and `UPTIME` from a compromised machine.
BADHATCH can perform pass the hash on compromised machines with x64 versions.
BADHATCH can check for open ports on a computer by establishing a TCP connection.

Bandook can collect information about the drives available on the system.
Bandook has a command built in to use a raw TCP socket.
Bandook has used lure documents to convince the user to enable macros.
Bandook has used AES encryption for C2 communication.
Bandook has used the ShellExecuteW() function call.
Bandook has decoded its PowerShell script.
Bandook has used .PNG images within a zip file to build the executable.

Bandook can support commands to execute Python-based payloads.
Bandook has a command to get the public IP address from a system.

text:
ROKRAT can use HTTP and HTTPS for command and control communication.

ROKRAT can check for debugging tools.
