text: xCaon has a command to download files to the victim's machine. BoxCaon can upload files from a compromised host. BoxCaon established persistence by setting the HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows\load registry key to point to its executable. BoxCaon has used Windows API calls to obtain information about the compromised host. BoxCaon has created a working folder for collected files that it sends to the C2 server. xCaon has uploaded files from victims' machines. BoxCaon has searched for files on the system, such as documents located in the desktop folder. xCaon has communicated with the C2 server by sending POST requests over HTTP. xCaon has used the GetAdaptersInfo() API call to get the victim's MAC address. BoxCaon used the "StackStrings" obfuscation technique to hide malicious functionalities. BoxCaon can collect the victim's MAC address by using the GetAdaptersInfo API. BoxCaon has the capability to download folders' contents on the system and upload the results back to its Dropbox drive. BoxCaon uploads files and data from a compromised host over the existing C2 channel. xCaon has a command to start an interactive shell. xCaon has encrypted data sent to the C2 server using a XOR key. BoxCaon can download files. xCaon has added persistence via the Registry key HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows\load which causes the malware to run each time any user logs in. xCaon has used Base64 to encode its C2 traffic. xCaon has decoded strings from the C2 server before executing commands. BoxCaon has used DropBox for C2 communications. xCaon has checked for the existence of Kaspersky antivirus software on the system. BoxCaon can execute arbitrary commands and utilize the "ComSpec" environment variable. xCaon has leveraged native OS function calls to retrieve victim's network adapter's information using GetAdapterInfo() API.
title: CheckPoint Research. (2021, July 1). IndigoZebra APT continues to attack Central Asia with evolving tools. Retrieved September 24, 2021.

text: Pillowmint has stored a compressed payload in the Registry key HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\DRM. Pillowmint has used shellcode which reads code stored in the registry keys \REGISTRY\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\DRM using the native Windows API as well as read HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip\Parameters\Interfaces as part of its C2. Pillowmint has encrypted stolen credit card information with AES and further encoded it with Base64. Pillowmint can iterate through running processes every six seconds collecting a list of processes to capture from later. Pillowmint has used the NtQueueApcThread syscall to inject code into svchost.exe. Pillowmint has collected credit card data using native API functions. Pillowmint has used a PowerShell script to install a shim database. Pillowmint has been decompressed by included shellcode prior to being launched. Pillowmint has modified the Registry key HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\DRM to store a malicious payload. Pillowmint has used multiple native Windows APIs to execute and conduct process injections. Pillowmint has used a malicious shim database to maintain persistence. Pillowmint has been compressed and stored within a registry key. Pillowmint has obfuscated the AES key used for encryption. Pillowmint has deleted the filepath %APPDATA%\Intel\devmonsrv.exe. Pillowmint can uninstall the malicious service from an infected machine.
title: Trustwave SpiderLabs. (2020, June 22). Pillowmint: FIN7’s Monkey Thief . Retrieved July 27, 2020.

text: RATANKBA uses tasklist /svc to display running tasks. RATANKBA runs the net view /domain and net view commands. RATANKBA uses the net user command. RATANKBA uses netstat -ano to search for specific IP address ranges. RATANKBA uses the command reg query “HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\InternetSettings”. RATANKBA runs the whoami and query user commands.
title: Trend Micro. (2017, February 27). RATANKBA: Delving into Large-scale Watering Holes against Enterprises. Retrieved May 22, 2018.

text:
DnsSystem can exfiltrate collected data to its C2 server.
DnsSystem can use the Windows user name to create a unique identification for infected users and systems.
DnsSystem can upload files from infected machines after receiving a command with `uploaddd` in the string.
DnsSystem can Base64 encode data sent to C2.
DnsSystem can write itself to the Startup folder to gain persistence.
DnsSystem has lured victims into opening macro-enabled Word documents for execution.
DnsSystem can download files to compromised systems after receiving a command with the string `downloaddd`.
DnsSystem can use `cmd.exe` for execution.
DnsSystem can direct queries to custom DNS servers and return C2 commands using TXT records.
title: Shivtarkar, N. and Kumar, A. (2022, June 9). Lyceum .NET DNS Backdoor. Retrieved June 23, 2022.

text:
GeminiDuke collects information on network settings and Internet proxy settings from the victim.
CosmicDuke uses a keylogger.
PinchDuke searches for files created within a certain timeframe and whose file extension matches a predefined list.
GeminiDuke collects information on local user accounts from the victim.
PinchDuke steals credentials from compromised hosts. PinchDuke's credential stealing functionality is believed to be based on the source code of the Pinch credential stealing malware (also known as LdPinch). Credentials targeted by PinchDuke include ones associated with many sources such as The Bat!, Yahoo!, Mail.ru, Passport.Net, Google Talk, and Microsoft Outlook.
OnionDuke steals credentials from its victims.
SeaDuke uses HTTP and HTTPS for C2.
CosmicDuke attempts to exploit privilege escalation vulnerabilities CVE-2010-0232 or CVE-2010-4398.
PinchDuke steals credentials from compromised hosts. PinchDuke's credential stealing functionality is believed to be based on the source code of the Pinch credential stealing malware (also known as LdPinch). Credentials targeted by PinchDuke include ones associated with many sources such as Netscape Navigator, Mozilla Firefox, Mozilla Thunderbird, and Internet Explorer.
OnionDuke uses HTTP and HTTPS for C2.
MiniDuke uses HTTP and HTTPS for command and control.
PinchDuke steals credentials from compromised hosts. PinchDuke's credential stealing functionality is believed to be based on the source code of the Pinch credential stealing malware (also known as LdPinch). Credentials targeted by PinchDuke include ones associated many sources such as WinInet Credential Cache, and Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP).
CosmicDuke collects user credentials, including passwords, for various programs including Web browsers.
PinchDuke gathers system configuration information.
OnionDuke uses Twitter as a backup C2.
PinchDuke collects user files from the compromised host based on predefined file extensions.
CosmicDuke collects LSA secrets.
PinchDuke transfers files from the compromised host via HTTP or HTTPS to a C2 server.
CosmicDuke collects user credentials, including passwords, for various programs including popular instant messaging applications and email clients as well as WLAN keys.
GeminiDuke uses HTTP and HTTPS for command and control.
One variant of CloudDuke uses HTTP and HTTPS for C2.
GeminiDuke collects information on running processes and environment variables from the victim.
CosmicDuke collects Windows account hashes.
CloudDuke downloads and executes additional malware from either a Web address or a Microsoft OneDrive account.
GeminiDuke collects information on programs and services on the victim that are configured to automatically run at startup.
GeminiDuke collects information from the victim, including installed drivers, programs previously executed by users, programs and services configured to automatically run at startup, files and folders present in any user's home folder, files and folders present in any user's My Documents, programs installed to the Program Files folder, and recently accessed files, folders, and programs.
One variant of CloudDuke uses a Microsoft OneDrive account to exchange commands and stolen data with its operators.
title: F-Secure Labs. (2015, September 17). The Dukes: 7 years of Russian cyberespionage. Retrieved December 10, 2015.

text: Industroyer2 has the ability to cyclically enumerate running processes such as PServiceControl.exe, PService_PDD.exe, and other targets supplied through a hardcoded configuration.
title: Daniel Kapellmann Zafra, Raymond Leong, Chris Sistrunk, Ken Proska, Corey Hildebrandt, Keith Lunden, Nathan Brubaker. (2022, April 25). INDUSTROYER.V2: Old Malware Learns New Tricks. Retrieved March 30, 2023.

text:
Calisto presents an input prompt asking for the user's login and password.
Calisto has the capability to upload and download files to the victim's machine.
Calisto adds permissions and remote logins to all users.
Calisto has the capability to add its own account to the victim's machine.
title: Pantig, J. (2018, July 30). OSX.Calisto. Retrieved September 7, 2018.

text:
Lumma Stealer has created registry keys to maintain persistence using `HKCU:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run`.
Lumma Stealer has gathered credential and other information from multiple browsers.
Lumma Stealer has been delivered through phishing emails containing malicious links.
Lumma Stealer has used malicious Python scripts to execute payloads.
Lumma Stealer has installed a malicious browser extension to target Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Opera and Brave browsers for the purpose of stealing data.
Lumma Stealer has automated collection of various information including cryptocurrency wallet details.
Lumma Stealer has harvested cookies from various browsers.
Lumma Stealer has taken screenshots of victim machines.
Lumma Stealer has gained initial execution through victims opening malicious executable files embedded in zip archives, and MSI files within RAR files.
Lumma Stealer has been delivered through cracked software downloads.
Lumma Stealer has been delivered through phishing emails with malicious attachments.
Lumma Stealer has leveraged legitimate applications to then side-load malicious DLLs during execution.
Lumma Stealer has identified and gathered information from two-factor authentication extensions for multiple browsers.
Lumma Stealer has gathered various system information from victim machines.
title: Cybereaon Security Services Team. (n.d.). Your Data Is Under New Lummanagement: The Rise of LummaStealer. Retrieved March 22, 2025.

text: Carbanak stores a configuration files in the startup directory to automatically execute commands in order to persist across reboots. Carbanak can create a Windows account. Carbanak has a command to delete files. Carbanak lists running processes. Carbanak downloads an executable and injects it directly into a new process. Carbanak has a command to create a reverse shell. Carbanak exfiltrates data in compressed chunks if a message is larger than 4096 bytes . Carbanak encrypts strings to make analysis more difficult. Carbanak checks the Registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Internet Settings for proxy configurations information. Carbanak searches recursively for Outlook personal storage tables (PST) files within user directories and sends them back to the C2 server. Carbanak has a plugin for VNC and Ammyy Admin Tool. Carbanak obtains Windows logon password details. Carbanak enables concurrent Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) sessions. Carbanak performs desktop video recording and captures screenshots of the desktop and sends it to the C2 server.
title: Bennett, J., Vengerik, B. (2017, June 12). Behind the CARBANAK Backdoor. Retrieved June 11, 2018.

text: CHOPSTICK provides access to the Windows Registry, which can be used to gather information. CORESHELL C2 messages are encrypted with custom stream ciphers using six-byte or eight-byte keys. OLDBAIT can use SMTP for C2. CORESHELL contains unused machine instructions in a likely attempt to hinder analysis. CORESHELL collects the volume serial number from the victim and sends the information to its C2 server. OLDBAIT installs itself in %ALLUSERPROFILE%\\Application Data\Microsoft\MediaPlayer\updatewindws.exe; the directory name is missing a space and the file name is missing the letter "o." CORESHELL downloads another dropper from its C2 server. OLDBAIT collects credentials from Internet Explorer, Mozilla Firefox, and Eudora. CHOPSTICK may store RC4 encrypted configuration information in the Windows Registry. OLDBAIT collects credentials from several email clients. CORESHELL obfuscates strings using a custom stream cipher. CHOPSTICK checks for antivirus and forensics software. CORESHELL C2 messages are Base64-encoded. CORESHELL collects hostname and OS version data from the victim and sends the information to its C2 server. OLDBAIT obfuscates internal strings and unpacks them at startup. OLDBAIT can use HTTP for C2. CHOPSTICK includes runtime checks to identify an analysis environment and prevent execution on it.
title: FireEye. (2015). APT28: A WINDOW INTO RUSSIA’S CYBER ESPIONAGE OPERATIONS?. Retrieved August 19, 2015.

text:
Nerex creates a Registry subkey that registers a new service.
Nerex drops a signed Microsoft DLL to disk.
title: Ladley, F. (2012, May 15). Backdoor.Nerex. Retrieved February 23, 2018.

text: GRIFFON has used a reconnaissance module that can be used to retrieve the date and time of the system. GRIFFON has used PowerShell to execute the Meterpreter downloader TinyMet. GRIFFON has used a screenshot module that can be used to take a screenshot of the remote system. GRIFFON has used a reconnaissance module that can be used to retrieve Windows domain membership information. GRIFFON is written in and executed as JavaScript. GRIFFON has used a reconnaissance module that can be used to retrieve information about a victim's computer, including the resolution of the workstation . GRIFFON has used a persistence module that stores the implant inside the Registry, which executes at logon. GRIFFON has used sctasks for persistence.
title: Namestnikov, Y. and Aime, F. (2019, May 8). FIN7.5: the infamous cybercrime rig “FIN7” continues its activities. Retrieved October 11, 2019.

text:
HeartCrypt strings are encrypted via a single-byte XOR operation rotating over a hard-coded key, possibly provided by the PaaS customers.
HeartCrypt has the ability to use `NtQueueApcThread` as an alternate method for process injection.
HeartCrypt can use Windows API functions to modify the Registry and `FindResourceW`, `LoadResource`, and `LockResource` to acquire a pointer to corresponding code resources.
For .NET payloads, HeartCrypt can use process hollowing to inject into processes spawned by csc.exe or AppLaunch.exe.
HeartCrypt can append a BMP header to encoded malicious payloads to masquerade them as BMP files.
HeartCrypt can set the `CurrentVersion\Run` key to establish persistence.
HeartCrypt can use the `reg add` command via `cmd.exe` for Registry modification.
HeartCrypt can add several hundred thousand kilobytes of null padding to payloads before saving onto the file system.
HeartCrypt will attempt to load non-existent DLLs in attempt to detect sandbox creation of a dummy DLL to prevent the program from crashing.
title: Tujague, J., Bunce, D. (n.d.). Crypted Hearts: Exposing the HeartCrypt Packer-as-a-Service Operation. Retrieved April 16, 2026.

text:
VERMIN gathers the local IP address.
VERMIN can get a list of the processes and running tasks on the system.
VERMIN uses WMI to check for anti-virus software installed on the system.
VERMIN uses HTTP for C2 communications.
VERMIN can delete files on the victim’s machine.
VERMIN collects the OS name, machine name, and architecture information.
VERMIN encrypts the collected files using 3-DES.
VERMIN can perform audio capture.
VERMIN saves each collected file with the automatically generated format {0:dd-MM-yyyy}.txt .
VERMIN is initially packed.
VERMIN can perform screen captures of the victim’s machine.
VERMIN decrypts code, strings, and commands to use once it's on the victim's machine.
VERMIN can download and upload files to the victim's machine.
VERMIN collects data stored in the clipboard.
VERMIN is obfuscated using the obfuscation tool called ConfuserEx.
VERMIN gathers the username from the victim’s machine.
VERMIN collects keystrokes from the victim machine.
title: Lancaster, T., Cortes, J. (2018, January 29). VERMIN: Quasar RAT and Custom Malware Used In Ukraine. Retrieved July 5, 2018.

text:
Mango can collect the user name from a compromised system which is used to create a unique victim identifier.
Mango contains an unused capability to block endpoint security solutions from loading user-mode code hooks via a DLL in a specified process by using the `UpdateProcThreadAttribute API` to set the `PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_MITIGATION_POLICY` to `PROCESS_CREATION_MITIGATION_POLICY_BLOCK_NON_MICROSOFT_BINARIES_ALWAYS_ON` for an identified process.
Mango has the ability to use Native APIs.
Mango can receive Base64-encoded commands from C2.
Solar has the ability to delete staged files after they are uploaded to C2.
Solar can create scheduled tasks named Earth and Venus, which run every 30 and 40 seconds respectively, to support C2 and exfiltration.
Mango can create a scheduled task to run every 32 seconds to communicate with C2 and execute received commands.
Mango has been executed through a Microsoft Word document with a malicious macro.
Solar can send basic information about the infected host to C2.
Solar can Base64-encode and gzip compress C2 communications including command outputs.
Solar can send staged files to C2 for exfiltration.
Mango can use TLS to encrypt C2 communications.
Solar can automatically exfitrate files from compromised systems.
Mango can retrieve C2 commands sent in HTTP responses.
Mango can collect the machine name of a compromised system which is later used as part of a unique victim identifier.
Solar can XOR encrypt C2 communications.
Solar has the ability to download and execute files.
Mango can enumerate the contents of current working or other specified directories.
Mango can use its HTTP C2 channel for exfiltration.
Mango contains a series of base64 encoded substrings.
Mango can receive XOR-encrypted commands from C2.
title: Hromcova, Z. and Burgher, A. (2023, September 21). OilRig’s Outer Space and Juicy Mix: Same ol’ rig, new drill pipes. Retrieved November 21, 2024.

text: Mispadu can log keystrokes on the victim's machine.
title: SCILabs. (2023, May 23). Evolution of banking trojan URSA/Mispadu. Retrieved March 13, 2024.

text: TEARDROP was decoded using a custom rolling XOR algorithm to execute a customized Cobalt Strike payload. TEARDROP ran as a Windows service from the c:\windows\syswow64 folder. TEARDROP modified the Registry to create a Windows service for itself on a compromised host. TEARDROP created and read from a file with a fake JPG header, and its payload was encrypted with a simple rotating XOR cipher.
title: Check Point Research. (2020, December 22). SUNBURST, TEARDROP and the NetSec New Normal. Retrieved January 6, 2021.

text: Avenger has the ability to identify the OS architecture on a compromised host. Avenger has the ability to decrypt files downloaded from C2. ABK has the ability to download files from C2. BBK has the ability to inject shellcode into svchost.exe. BBK has the ability to download files from C2 to the infected host. build_downer can extract malware from a downloaded JPEG. BBK has the ability to use cmd to run a Portable Executable (PE) on the compromised host. down_new has the ability to identify the system volume information of a compromised host. Avenger has the ability to XOR encrypt files to be sent to C2. Avenger has the ability to browse files in directories such as Program Files and the Desktop. Avenger can identify the domain of the compromised host. ABK can extract a malicious Portable Executable (PE) from a photo. build_downer has the ability to detect if the infected host is running an anti-virus process. ABK has the ability to use HTTP in communications with C2. build_downer has the ability to send system volume information to C2. down_new has the ability to use HTTP in C2 communications. down_new has the ability to list running processes on a compromised host. down_new has the ability to gather information on installed applications. Avenger has the ability to identify the host volume ID. down_new has the ability to download files to the compromised host. Avenger has the ability to use HTTP in communication with C2. Avenger has the ability to identify installed anti-virus products on a compromised host. down_new has the ability to base64 encode C2 communications. ABK has the ability to inject shellcode into svchost.exe. ABK has the ability to identify the installed anti-virus product on the compromised host. Avenger has the ability to download files from C2 to a compromised host. ABK has the ability to use cmd to run a Portable Executable (PE) on the compromised host. build_downer has the ability to determine the local time to ensure malware installation only happens during the hours that the infected system is active. build_downer has the ability to add itself to the Registry Run key for persistence. ABK has the ability to decrypt AES encrypted payloads. BBK has the ability to use HTTP in communications with C2. Avenger can extract backdoor malware from downloaded images. BBK has the ability to decrypt AES encrypted payloads. Avenger has the ability to inject shellcode into svchost.exe. down_new has the ability to AES encrypt C2 communications. BBK has the ability to use the CreatePipe API to add a sub-process for execution via cmd. down_new has the ability to list the directories on a compromised host. down_new has the ability to detect anti-virus products and processes on a compromised host. build_downer has the ability to download files from C2 to the infected host. down_new has the ability to identify the MAC address of a compromised host. BBK can extract a malicious Portable Executable (PE) from a photo. Avenger has the ability to use Tasklist to identify running processes. build_downer has the ability to use the WinExec API to execute malware on a compromised host. build_downer has added itself to the Registry Run key as "NVIDIA" to appear legitimate.
title: Chen, J. et al. (2019, November). Operation ENDTRADE: TICK’s Multi-Stage Backdoors for Attacking Industries and Stealing Classified Data. Retrieved June 9, 2020.

text:
SharpDisco can leverage Native APIs through plugins including `GetLogicalDrives`.
NightClub has created a Windows service named `WmdmPmSp` to establish persistence.
NightClub has used a non-standard encoding in DNS tunneling removing any `=` from the result of base64 encoding, and replacing `/` characters with `-s` and `+` characters with `-p`.
Disco has achieved initial access and execution through content injection into DNS, HTTP, and SMB replies to targeted hosts that redirect them to download malicious files.
Disco can create a scheduled task to run every minute for persistence.
NightClub can modify the Creation, Access, and Write timestamps for malicious DLLs to match those of the genuine Windows DLL user32.dll.
SharpDisco can use `cmd.exe` to execute plugins and to send command output to specified SMB shares.
NightClub can obfuscate strings using the congruential generator `(LCG): staten+1 = (690069 × staten + 1) mod 232`.
NightClub can load multiple additional plugins on an infected host.
NightClub has copied captured files and keystrokes to the `%TEMP%` directory of compromised hosts.
NightClub can use emails for C2 communications.
NightClub has the ability to monitor removable drives.
Disco can download files to targeted systems via SMB.
NightClub can use a DNS tunneling plugin to exfiltrate data by adding it to the subdomain portion of a DNS request.
SharpDisco can use a plugin to enumerate system drives.
SharpDisco can create scheduled tasks to execute reverse shells that read and write data to and from specified SMB shares.
SharpDisco has the ability to transfer data between SMB shares.
NightClub has the ability to use `GetWindowThreadProcessId` to identify the process behind a specified window.
SharpDisco has dropped a plugin to monitor external drives to `C:\Users\Public\It3.exe`.
SharpDisco can identify recently opened files by using an LNK format parser to extract the original file path from LNK files found in either `%USERPROFILE%\Recent` (Windows XP) or `%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Recent` (newer Windows versions) .
SharpDisco has dropped a recent-files stealer plugin to `C:\Users\Public\WinSrcNT\It11.exe`.
NightClub can modify the Registry to set the ServiceDLL for a service created by the malware for persistence.
NightClub can use `GetForegroundWindow` to enumerate the active window.
NightClub can use multiple native APIs including `GetKeyState`, `GetForegroundWindow`, `GetWindowThreadProcessId`, and `GetKeyboardLayout`.
NightClub has created a service named `WmdmPmSp` to spoof a Windows Media service.
NightClub can load a module to leverage the LAME encoder and `mciSendStringW` to control and capture audio.
NightClub can load a module to call `CreateCompatibleDC` and `GdipSaveImageToStream` for screen capture.
Disco can use SMB to transfer files.
NightClub has chosen file names to appear legitimate including EsetUpdate-0117583943.exe for its dropper.
SharpDisco can load a plugin to exfiltrate stolen files to SMB shares also used in C2.
NightClub can use SMTP and DNS for file exfiltration and C2.
NightClub can use a file monitor to identify .lnk, .doc, .docx, .xls, .xslx, and .pdf files.
NightClub can use a file monitor to steal specific files from targeted systems.
SharpDisco can hide windows using `ProcessWindowStyle.Hidden`.
Disco has been executed through inducing user interaction with malicious .zip and .msi files.
SharpDisco has been used to download a Python interpreter to `C:\Users\Public\WinTN\WinTN.exe` as well as other plugins from external sources.
NightClub can use a plugin for keylogging.
title: Faou, M. (2023, August 10). MoustachedBouncer: Espionage against foreign diplomats in Belarus. Retrieved September 25, 2023.

text:
PUBLOAD has acted as a stager that can download the next-stage payload from its C2 server. PUBLOAD has also delivered FDMTP as a secondary control tool and PTSOCKET for exfiltration to some infected systems.
PUBLOAD has used various Windows API calls during execution, when establishing persistence and defense evasion. PUBLOAD stager leveraged Windows API functions with callback including `GrayStringW`, `EnumDateFormatsA`, and `LineDDA` to bypass anti-virus monitoring. PUBLOAD has also utilized other native windows API functions with callback functions such as `EnumChildWindows` and `EnumSystemLanguageGroupsA`.
PUBLOAD has been delivered as compressed files within ZIP files to victims.
PUBLOAD has modified HTTP POST requests to resemble legitimate communications. PUBLOAD used FakeTLS headers in network packets to impersonate various versions of TLS protocols to blend in with legitimate network traffic. PUBLOAD has utilized FakeTLS headers with the bytes 17 03 03.
title: Dex. (n.d.). New Mustang Panda’s campaing against Australia. Retrieved August 4, 2025.

text:
Kapeka utilizes WinAPI calls and registry queries to gather system information.
Kapeka utilizes HTTP for command and control.
Kapeka persists via scheduled tasks.
Kapeka queries registry values for stored configuration information.
Kapeka utilizes AES-256 (CBC mode), XOR, and RSA-2048 encryption schemas for various configuration and other objects.
Kapeka allows for arbitrary Windows command execution.
Kapeka can identify system proxy settings via `WinHttpGetIEProxyConfigForCurrentUser()` during initialization and utilize these settings for subsequent command and control operations.
Kapeka utilizes obfuscated JSON structures for various data storage and configuration management items.
Kapeka utilizes JSON objects to send and receive information from command and control nodes.
Kapeka writes persistent configuration information to the victim host registry.
Kapeka masquerades as a Microsoft Word Add-In file, with the extension `.wll`, but is a malicious DLL file.
Kapeka will clear registry values used for persistent configuration storage when uninstalled.
Kapeka utilizes WinAPI calls to gather victim system information.
Kapeka is a Windows DLL file executed via ordinal by `rundll32.exe`.
title: Mohammad Kazem Hassan Nejad, WithSecure. (2024, April 17). KAPEKA A novel backdoor spotted in Eastern Europe. Retrieved January 6, 2025.

text: PlugX can use the Windows API functions `GetProcAddress`, `LoadLibrary`, and `CreateProcess` to execute another process.
title: Vasilenko, R. (2013, December 17). An Analysis of PlugX Malware. Retrieved November 24, 2015.

text:
Qilin has the ability to delay execution.
Qilin can use WinSCP for the secure file transfer of the Linux ransomware binary to a targeted system.
Qilin can use the Splashtop remote management service (SRManager.exe) to execute the Linux ransomware binary directly on Windows systems.
Qilin can detect whether a system is running FreeBSD, VMkernel (ESXi), Nutanix AHV, or a standard Linux distribution to enable platform-specific encryption behaviors.
title: Trend Micro. (2025, October 23). Agenda Ransomware Deploys Linux Variant on Windows Systems Through Remote Management Tools and BYOVD Techniques. Retrieved March 26, 2026.

text:
MiniBrowse has sent JSON files to a named pipe.
MiniJunk has leveraged legitimate digital signatures from SSL[.]com to appear legitimate.
MiniBrowse has obfuscated code leveraging junk code insertion, control-flow obfuscation, opaque predicates, obfuscated function calls, and encrypted strings to hinder analysis.
MiniJunk has been executed using the auto-run registry key `HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\MigAutoPlay` that executes the benign windows executable `MigAutoPlay`.
MiniJunk has listed all hard drives or has listed files within a specified directory.
MiniJunk has been compiled through several obfuscation techniques to include junk code insertion.
MiniJunk has obfuscated code that utilized junk code insertion, control-flow obfuscation, opaque predicates, obfuscated function calls, and encrypted strings to hinder analysis.
MiniBrowse has utilized HTTP POST requests for communications with C2.
MiniJunk has utilized Windows API calls to make HTTPs requests to C2.
MiniJunk has been delivered within a malicious zip file.
MiniBrowse has leveraged JSON to exfiltrate data.
MiniBrowse has encrypted strings that obfuscate code.
MiniJunk has the ability to load a DLL from the C2.
MiniJunk has the ability to validate running processes.
MiniBrowse has the ability to gather the username associated with the victim host.
MiniBrowse has stolen credentials from Chrome and Edge browsers.
MiniBrowse has collected the domain associated with the victim system.
MiniJunk has the ability to gather the computer name.
MiniJunk has encoded network data by converting strings into bytes, then reversing the bytes and the entire strings. MiniJunk has also encrypted strings to obfuscate code.
MiniBrowse has the ability to upload stolen data over C2 communications.
MiniBrowse has gathered browser data to include Edge login data.
MiniBrowse contains obfuscated code leveraging junk code insertion.
MiniJunk has the ability to move or rename files.
MiniJunk has a command that is capable of deleting a file.
MiniJunk has collected the domain name with username.
MiniJunk has leveraged HTTPS calls to the C2.
title: Check Point. (2025, September 22). Nimbus Manticore Deploys New Malware Targeting Europe. Retrieved September 24, 2026.

text: Industroyer has a data wiper component that enumerates keys in the Registry HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services. Industroyer has used a Trojanized version of the Windows Notepad application for an additional backdoor persistence mechanism. Industroyer uses a custom DoS tool that leverages CVE-2015-5374 and targets hardcoded IP addresses of Siemens SIPROTEC devices. Industroyer sends information about hardware profiles and previously-received commands back to the C2 server in a POST-request. Industroyer downloads a shellcode payload from a remote C2 server and loads it into memory. Industroyer decrypts code to connect to a remote C2 server. Industroyer’s 61850 payload component enumerates connected network adapters and their corresponding IP addresses. Industroyer’s data wiper component enumerates specific files on all the Windows drives. Industroyer can use supplied user credentials to execute processes and stop services. Industroyer uses heavily obfuscated code in its Windows Notepad backdoor. Industroyer uses a custom port scanner to map out a network. Industroyer’s main backdoor connected to a remote C2 server using HTTPS. Industroyer can enumerate remote computers in the compromised network.
title: Anton Cherepanov. (2017, June 12). Win32/Industroyer: A new threat for industrial controls systems. Retrieved December 18, 2020.

text: Pony has used scripts to delete itself after execution. Pony can download additional files onto the infected system. Pony has sent collected information to the C2 via HTTP POST request. Pony has collected the Service Pack, language, and region information to send to the C2. Pony has used several Windows functions for various purposes. Pony attachments have been delivered via compressed archive files. Pony obfuscates memory flow by adding junk instructions when executing to make analysis more difficult. Pony has used batch scripts to delete itself after execution. Pony has been delivered via spearphishing emails which contained malicious links. Pony has used the NetUserEnum function to enumerate local accounts. Pony has attempted to lure targets into downloading an attached executable (ZIP, RAR, or CAB archives) or document (PDF or other MS Office format). Pony has used a small dictionary of common passwords against a collected list of local accounts. Pony has been delivered via spearphishing attachments. Pony has used the Adobe Reader icon for the downloaded file to look more trustworthy. Pony has attempted to lure targets into clicking links in spoofed emails from legitimate banks. Pony has delayed execution using a built-in function to avoid detection and analysis.
title: hasherezade. (2016, April 11). No money, but Pony! From a mail to a trojan horse. Retrieved May 21, 2020.

text:
Latrodectus has used multiple Windows API post exploitation including `GetAdaptersInfo`, `CreateToolhelp32Snapshot`, and `CreateProcessW`.
Latrodectus can collect desktop filenames.
Latrodectus can create scheduled tasks for persistence.
Latrodectus has the ability to delete itself.
Latrodectus can send registration information to C2 via HTTP `POST`.
Latrodectus can download and execute PEs, DLLs, and shellcode from C2.
Latrodectus can send RC4 encrypted data over C2 channels.
Latrodectus can discover the IP and MAC address of a targeted host.
Latrodectus can run `C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe /c nltest /domain_trusts` to discover domain trusts.
Latrodectus has used WMI in malicious email infection chains to facilitate the installation of remotely-hosted files.
Latrodectus can identify domain groups through `cmd.exe /c net group "Domain Admins" /domain`.
The Latrodectus command handler can use `cmdexe` to run multiple discovery commands.
Latrodectus can use the Windows Component Object Model (COM) to set scheduled tasks.
Latrodectus can determine if it is running in a virtualized environment by checking the OS version, checking the number of running processes, ensuring a 64-bit application is running on a 64-bit host, and checking if the host has a valid MAC address.
Latrodectus can exfiltrate encrypted system information to the C2 server.
Latrodectus can collect data from a compromised host using a stealer module.
Latrodectus can run `C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe /c net view /all` to discover network shares.
Latrodectus has the ability to deobfuscate encrypted strings.
Latrodectus can enumerate running processes including process grandchildren on targeted hosts.
Latrodectus can gather operating system information.
Latrodectus has used a pseudo random number generator (PRNG) algorithm and a rolling XOR key to obfuscate strings.
Latrodectus has the ability to identify installed antivirus products.
title: Batista, J. (2024, June 17). Latrodectus, are you coming back?. Retrieved September 13, 2024.

text:
BACKUPOSINT v9.0 APEX PREDATOR has a module that gathered Cloud Secrets Management Stores from password vaults within Microsoft Azure, Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Google Cloud Platform (GCP).
BACKUPOSINT v9.0 APEX PREDATOR has the ability to leverage `sudo` for executing commands.
BACKUPOSINT v9.0 APEX PREDATOR can interact with and execute Docker and Kerberos commands.
BACKUPOSINT v9.0 APEX PREDATOR has a module that is capable of gathering Cloud Instance Metadata to include AWS, Google Cloud Platform, and Azure.
BACKUPOSINT v9.0 APEX PREDATOR has the ability to identify NFS and SMB shares within the victim environment.
BACKUPOSINT v9.0 APEX PREDATOR has the ability to steal application tokens for CI/CD services to include Bamboo, Github, and Jenkins.
BACKUPOSINT v9.0 APEX PREDATOR has the ability to abuse Sudo/Cron for privilege escalation.
title: Jay Deen. (2026, May). AI-Assisted Compromise of Mexican Water Utility with OT Implications. Retrieved September 2, 2026.

text:
Pay2Key can identify the IP and MAC addresses of the compromised host.
Pay2Key has designated machines in the compromised network to serve as reverse proxy pivot points to channel communications with C2.
Pay2Key can remove its log file from disk.
Pay2Key has sent its public key to the C2 server over TCP.
Pay2Key can stop the MS SQL service at the end of the encryption process to release files locked by the service.
Pay2Key has the ability to gather the hostname of the victim machine.
Pay2Key has used RSA encrypted communications with C2.
Pay2Key can encrypt data on victim's machines using RSA and AES algorithms in order to extort a ransom payment for decryption.
title: Check Point. (2020, November 6). Ransomware Alert: Pay2Key. Retrieved January 4, 2021.

text: ComRAT has used a task name associated with Windows SQM Consolidator. ComRAT can use email attachments for command and control. ComRAT can load a PE file from memory or the file system and execute it with CreateProcessW. ComRAT can check the victim's default browser to determine which process to inject its communications module into. ComRAT has used cmd.exe to execute commands. ComRAT can check the default browser by querying HKCR\http\shell\open\command. ComRAT has been programmed to sleep outside local business hours (9 to 5, Monday to Friday). ComRAT has used a portable FAT16 partition image placed in %TEMP% as a hidden file system.
title: Faou, M. (2020, May). From Agent.btz to ComRAT v4: A ten-year journey. Retrieved June 15, 2020.

text: Hikit is a Rootkit that has been used by Axiom. Hikit has used DLL to load oci.dll as a persistence mechanism.
title: Glyer, C., Kazanciyan, R. (2012, August 20). The “Hikit” Rootkit: Advanced and Persistent Attack Techniques (Part 1). Retrieved November 17, 2024.

text:
When executed, BPFDoor attempts to create and lock a runtime file, `/var/run/initd.lock`, and exits if it fails using the specified file, resulting in a makeshift mutex.
BPFDoor sets its process to ignore the following signals; `SIGHUP`, `SIGINT`, `SIGQUIT`, `SIGPIPE`, `SIGCHLD`, `SIGTTIN`, and `SIGTTOU`.
title: Shaul Vilkomir-Preisman and Eliran Nissan. (2023, May 10). BPFDoor Malware Evolves – Stealthy Sniffing Backdoor Ups Its Game. Retrieved September 19, 2024.

text: Octopus can collect system drive and disk size information. Octopus has used HTTP GET and POST requests for C2 communications. Octopus can capture screenshots of the victims’ machine. Octopus has used wmic.exe for local discovery information. Octopus can collect the computer name, OS version, and OS architecture information. Octopus can collect information on the Windows directory and searches for compressed RAR files on the host. Octopus can collect the username from the victim’s machine. Octopus has uploaded stolen files and data from a victim's machine over its C2 channel. Octopus can download additional files and tools onto the victim’s machine. Octopus has stored collected information in the Application Data directory on a compromised host. Octopus has been disguised as legitimate programs, such as Java and Telegram Messenger. Octopus can collect the host IP address from the victim’s machine. Octopus has encoded C2 communications in Base64. Octopus achieved persistence by placing a malicious executable in the startup directory and has added the HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run key to the Registry.
title: Kaspersky Lab's Global Research & Analysis Team. (2018, October 15). Octopus-infested seas of Central Asia. Retrieved November 14, 2018.

text:
StrelaStealer encrypts the payload of HTTP POST communications using the same XOR key used for the malware's DLL payload.
StrelaStealer uses XOR-encoded strings to obfuscate items.
StrelaStealer has sideloaded a DLL payload using a renamed, legitimate `msinfo32.exe` executable.
StrelaStealer automatically sends gathered email credentials following collection to command and control servers via HTTP POST.
StrelaStealer has used a renamed, legitimate `msinfo32.exe` executable to sideload the StrelaStealer payload during initial installation.
StrelaStealer has been distributed as a DLL/HTML polyglot file.
StrelaStealer has been distributed as a spearphishing attachment.
StrelaStealer relies on user execution of a malicious file for installation.
StrelaStealer has been distributed in ISO archives. StrelaStealer has been delivered in encrypted, password-protected ZIP archives.
title: DCSO CyTec Blog. (2022, November 8). #ShortAndMalicious: StrelaStealer aims for mail credentials. Retrieved December 31, 2024.

text: POWRUNER is written in PowerShell. POWRUNER may use WMI when collecting information about a victim. POWRUNER can capture a screenshot from a victim. POWRUNER may collect information about the system by running hostname and systeminfo on a victim. POWRUNER may collect information about the currently logged in user by running whoami on a victim. POWRUNER may collect information on the victim's anti-virus software. BONDUPDATER uses a DGA to communicate with command and control servers. POWRUNER may collect process information by running tasklist on a victim. POWRUNER may collect active network connections by running netstat -an on a victim. POWRUNER can use base64 encoded C2 communications. BONDUPDATER uses -windowstyle hidden to conceal a PowerShell window that downloads a payload. POWRUNER may collect local group information by running net localgroup administrators or a series of other commands on a victim. POWRUNER can execute commands from its C2 server. POWRUNER may enumerate user directories on a victim. POWRUNER may query the Registry by running reg query on a victim. POWRUNER can download or upload files from its C2 server. POWRUNER may collect user account information by running net user /domain or a series of other commands on a victim. POWRUNER may collect network configuration data by running ipconfig /all on a victim. POWRUNER may collect domain group information by running net group /domain or a series of other commands on a victim. POWRUNER persists through a scheduled task that executes it every minute.
title: Sardiwal, M, et al. (2017, December 7). New Targeted Attack in the Middle East by APT34, a Suspected Iranian Threat Group, Using CVE-2017-11882 Exploit. Retrieved December 20, 2017.

text:
AcidRain reboots the target system once the various wiping processes are complete.
AcidRain iterates over device file identifiers on the target, opens the device file, and either overwrites the file or calls various IOCTLS commands to erase it.
AcidRain performs an in-depth wipe of the target filesystem and various attached storage devices through either a data overwrite or calling various IOCTLS to erase it.
AcidRain identifies specific files and directories in the Linux operating system associated with storage devices.
title: Juan Andres Guerrero-Saade and Max van Amerongen, SentinelOne. (2022, March 31). AcidRain | A Modem Wiper Rains Down on Europe. Retrieved March 25, 2024.

text: DarkGate can masquerade as pirated media content for initial delivery to victims. DarkGate edits the Registry key HKCU\Software\Classes\mscfile\shell\open\command to execute a malicious AutoIt script. When eventvwr.exe is executed, this will call the Microsoft Management Console (mmc.exe), which in turn references the modified Registry key. DarkGate drops an encrypted PE file, pe.bin, and decrypts it during installation. DarkGate also uses custom base64 encoding schemas in later variations to obfuscate payloads. DarkGate starts a thread on execution that captures clipboard data and logs it to a predefined log file. DarkGate searches for stored credentials associated with cryptocurrency wallets and notifies the command and control server when identified. DarkGate uses AutoIt scripts dropped to a hidden directory during initial installation phases, such as `test.au3`. DarkGate will retrieved encrypted commands from its command and control server for follow-on actions such as cryptocurrency mining. DarkGate uses existing command and control channels to retrieve captured cryptocurrency wallet credentials. DarkGate retrieves cryptocurrency mining payloads and commands in encrypted traffic from its command and control server. DarkGate uses Windows Batch scripts executing the curl command to retrieve follow-on payloads. DarkGate has stolen `sitemanager.xml` and `recentservers.xml` from `%APPDATA%\FileZilla\` if present. DarkGate creates a log file for capturing keylogging, clipboard, and related data using the victim host's current date for the filename. DarkGate queries victim system epoch time during execution. DarkGate captures system time information as part of automated profiling on initial installation. DarkGate creates a local user account, SafeMode, via net user commands. DarkGate can delete system restore points through the command cmd.exe /c vssadmin delete shadows /for=c: /all /quiet”. DarkGate performs various checks for running processes, including security software by looking for hard-coded process name values. DarkGate uses two distinct User Account Control (UAC) bypass techniques to escalate privileges. DarkGate overrides the %windir% environment variable by setting a Registry key, HKEY_CURRENT_User\Environment\windir, to an alternate command to execute a malicious AutoIt script. This allows DarkGate to run every time the scheduled task DiskCleanup is executed as this uses the path value %windir%\system32\cleanmgr.exe for execution. DarkGate can cloak command and control traffic in DNS records from legitimate services to avoid reputation-based detection techniques. DarkGate will gather various system information such as domain, display adapter description, operating system type and version, processor type, and RAM amount. DarkGate can deploy payloads capable of capturing credentials related to cryptocurrency wallets. DarkGate can deploy follow-on cryptocurrency mining payloads. DarkGate queries system resources on an infected machine to identify if it is executing in a sandbox or virtualized environment. DarkGate leverages process hollowing techniques to evade detection, such as decrypting the content of an encrypted PE file and injecting it into the process vbc.exe. DarkGate initial infection payloads can masquerade as pirated media content requiring user interaction for code execution. DarkGate is distributed through phishing links to VBS or MSI objects requiring user interaction for execution. DarkGate can be distributed through emails with malicious attachments from a spoofed email address. DarkGate uses the native Windows API CallWindowProc() to decode and launch encoded shellcode payloads during execution. DarkGate can call kernel mode functions directly to hide the use of process hollowing methods during execution. DarkGate has also used the `CreateToolhelp32Snapshot`, `GetFileAttributesA` and `CreateProcessA` functions to obtain a list of running processes, to check for security products and to execute its malware. DarkGate looks for various security products by process name using hard-coded values in the malware. DarkGate will not execute its keylogging thread if a process name associated with Trend Micro anti-virus is identified, or if runtime checks identify the presence of Kaspersky anti-virus. DarkGate will initiate a new thread if certain security products are identified on the victim, and recreate any malicious files associated with it if it determines they were removed by security software in a new system location. DarkGate uses NirSoft tools to steal user credentials from the infected machine. NirSoft tools are executed via process hollowing in a newly-created instance of vbc.exe or regasm.exe. DarkGate installation includes AutoIt script execution creating a shortcut to itself as an LNK object, such as bill.lnk, in the victim startup folder. DarkGate installation finishes with the creation of a registry Run key. Some versions of DarkGate search for the hard-coded folder C:\Program Files\e Carte Bleue. DarkGate will spawn a thread on execution to capture all keyboard events and write them to a predefined log file. DarkGate installation includes binary code stored in a file located in a hidden directory, such as shell.txt, that is decrypted then executed. DarkGate uses hexadecimal-encoded shellcode payloads during installation that are called via Windows API CallWindowProc() to decode and then execute. DarkGate queries system locale information during execution. Later versions of DarkGate query GetSystemDefaultLCID for locale information to determine if the malware is executing in Russian-speaking countries. DarkGate initial infection mechanisms include masquerading as pirated media that launches malicious VBScript on the victim. DarkGate will search for cryptocurrency wallets by examining application window names for specific strings. DarkGate extracts information collected via NirSoft tools from the hosting process's memory by first identifying the window through the FindWindow API function. DarkGate can deploy follow-on ransomware payloads. DarkGate elevates accounts created through the malware to the local administration group during execution. DarkGate will terminate processes associated with several security software products if identified during execution. DarkGate uses the Delphi methods Sysutils::DiskSize and GlobalMemoryStatusEx to collect disk size and physical memory as part of the malware's anti-analysis checks for running in a virtualized environment.
title: Adi Zeligson & Rotem Kerner. (2018, November 13). Enter The DarkGate - New Cryptocurrency Mining and Ransomware Campaign. Retrieved February 9, 2024.

text:
BLINDINGCAN has encoded its C2 traffic with Base64.
BLINDINGCAN has attempted to hide its payload by using legitimate file names such as "iconcache.db".
BLINDINGCAN has loaded and executed DLLs in memory during runtime on a victim machine.
BLINDINGCAN has collected from a victim machine the system name, processor information, and OS version.
BLINDINGCAN has encrypted its C2 traffic with RC4.
BLINDINGCAN has deleted itself and associated artifacts from victim machines.
BLINDINGCAN has used AES and XOR to decrypt its DLLs.
BLINDINGCAN has collected the victim machine's local IP address information and MAC address.
BLINDINGCAN has downloaded files to a victim machine.
BLINDINGCAN has been delivered by phishing emails containing malicious Microsoft Office documents.
BLINDINGCAN has lured victims into executing malicious macros embedded within Microsoft Office documents.
BLINDINGCAN has used Rundll32 to load a malicious DLL.
BLINDINGCAN has been packed with the UPX packer.
BLINDINGCAN has been signed with code-signing certificates such as CodeRipper.
BLINDINGCAN has obfuscated code using Base64 encoding.
BLINDINGCAN has uploaded files from victim machines.
BLINDINGCAN has executed commands via cmd.exe.
BLINDINGCAN has collected disk information, including type and free space available.
BLINDINGCAN has used HTTPS over port 443 for command and control.
title: US-CERT. (2020, August 19). MAR-10295134-1.v1 – North Korean Remote Access Trojan: BLINDINGCAN. Retrieved August 19, 2020.

text:
HermeticWiper can determine the OS version and bitness on a targeted host.
HermeticWiper can disable the VSS service on a compromised host using the service control manager.
The HermeticWiper executable has been signed with a legitimate certificate issued to Hermetica Digital Ltd.
HermeticWiper can create system services to aid in executing the payload.
HermeticWiper has the ability to stop the Volume Shadow Copy service.
HermeticWiper can initiate a system shutdown.
HermeticWiper can enumerate physical drives on a targeted host.
HermeticWiper has the ability to set the `HKLM:\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Control\\CrashControl\CrashDumpEnabled` Registry key to `0` in order to disable crash dumps.
HermeticWiper has the ability to corrupt disk partitions, damage the Master Boot Record (MBR), and overwrite the Master File Table (MFT) of all available physical drives.
HermeticWiper has the ability to modify Registry keys to disable crash dumps, colors for compressed files, and pop-up information about folders and desktop items.
HermeticWiper can use `AdjustTokenPrivileges` to grant itself privileges for debugging with `SeDebugPrivilege`, creating backups with `SeBackupPrivilege`, loading drivers with `SeLoadDriverPrivilege`, and shutting down a local system with `SeShutdownPrivilege`.
HermeticWiper can enumerate common folders such as My Documents, Desktop, and AppData.
HermeticWiper can compress 32-bit and 64-bit driver files with the Lempel-Ziv algorithm.
HermeticWiper can call multiple Windows API functions used for privilege escalation, service execution, and to overwrite random bites of data.
title: Dani, M. (2022, March 1). Ukrainian Targets Hit by HermeticWiper, New Datawiper Malware. Retrieved March 25, 2022.

text: Hancitor has been delivered via phishing emails with malicious attachments. Hancitor has used PowerShell to execute commands. Hancitor has used malicious Microsoft Word documents, sent via email, which prompted the victim to enable macros. Hancitor has added Registry Run keys to establish persistence. Hancitor has delivered compressed payloads in ZIP files to victims. Hancitor has deleted files using the VBA kill function. Hancitor has used a macro to check that an ActiveDocument shape object in the lure message is present. If this object is not found, the macro will exit without downloading additional payloads. Hancitor has used CallWindowProc and EnumResourceTypesA to interpret and execute shellcode.
title: Anubhav, A., Jallepalli, D. (2016, September 23). Hancitor (AKA Chanitor) observed using multiple attack approaches. Retrieved August 13, 2020.

text: POWERSTATS has created a scheduled task named "MicrosoftEdge" to establish persistence. POWERSTATS can deobfuscate the main backdoor code. POWERSTATS can use JavaScript code for execution. POWERSTATS can use WMI queries to retrieve data from compromised hosts. POWERSTATS has established persistence through a scheduled task using the command ”C:\Windows\system32\schtasks.exe” /Create /F /SC DAILY /ST 12:00 /TN MicrosoftEdge /TR “c:\Windows\system32\wscript.exe C:\Windows\temp\Windows.vbe”.
title: ClearSky Cyber Security. (2018, November). MuddyWater Operations in Lebanon and Oman: Using an Israeli compromised domain for a two-stage campaign. Retrieved November 29, 2018.

text: SysUpdate can encrypt and encode its configuration file. SysUpdate can collect a system's drive information. SysUpdate has been packed with VMProtect. SysUpdate has the ability to set file attributes to hidden. Pandora can communicate over HTTP. SysUpdate can create a service to establish persistence. Pandora can load additional drivers and files onto a victim machine. SysUpdate has the ability to capture screenshots. SysUpdate can deobfuscate packed binaries in memory. Pandora can monitor processes on a compromised host. Pandora has the ability to encrypt communications with D3DES. Pandora has the ability to compress stings with QuickLZ. Pandora can write an encrypted token to the Registry to enable processing of remote commands. SysUpdate can manage services and processes. SysUpdate can store its encoded configuration file within Software\Classes\scConfig in either HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE or HKEY_CURRENT_USER. Pandora can identify if incoming HTTP traffic contains a token and if so it will intercept the traffic and process the received command. Pandora has the ability to gain system privileges through Windows services. SysUpdate can use a Registry Run key to establish persistence. Pandora can use DLL side-loading to execute malicious payloads. Pandora can use CVE-2017-15303 to disable Windows Driver Signature Enforcement (DSE) protection and load its driver. Pandora has the ability to install itself as a Windows service. Pandora can start and inject code into a new `svchost` process. SysUpdate has the ability to download files to a compromised host. SysUpdate can load DLLs through vulnerable legitimate executables. SysUpdate can collect a system's architecture, operating system version, and hostname. SysUpdate can search files on a compromised host. SysUpdate can delete its configuration file from the targeted system. SysUpdate can use WMI for execution on a compromised host. SysUpdate can write its configuration file to Software\Classes\scConfig in either HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE or HKEY_CURRENT_USER. Pandora can use CVE-2017-15303 to bypass Windows Driver Signature Enforcement (DSE) protection and load its driver. HyperBro has the ability to pack its payload.
title: Lunghi, D. and Lu, K. (2021, April 9). Iron Tiger APT Updates Toolkit With Evolved SysUpdate Malware. Retrieved November 12, 2021.

text: Agent Tesla has used SMTP for C2 communications.
title: James Arndt. (2023, February 21). The Rise of Agent Tesla: Understanding the Notorious Keylogger. Retrieved January 10, 2024.

text:
FIVEHANDS has the ability to decrypt its payload prior to execution.
FIVEHANDS can use an embedded NTRU public key to encrypt data for ransom.
FIVEHANDS has the ability to enumerate files on a compromised host in order to encrypt files with specific extensions.
The FIVEHANDS payload is encrypted with AES-128.
FIVEHANDS can receive a command line argument to limit file encryption to specified directories.
FIVEHANDS can enumerate network shares and mounted drives on a network.
title: Matthews, M. and Backhouse, W. (2021, June 15). Handy guide to a new Fivehands ransomware variant. Retrieved June 24, 2021.

text:
RotaJakiro uses a custom binary protocol using a type, length, value format over TCP.
RotaJakiro uses a custom binary protocol over TCP port 443.
RotaJakiro has used the filename `systemd-daemon` in an attempt to appear legitimate.
title: Alex Turing. (2021, May 6). RotaJakiro, the Linux version of the OceanLotus. Retrieved June 14, 2023.

text: Volgmer can gather system information, the computer name, OS version, drive and serial information from the victim's machine. Volgmer modifies the Registry to store an encoded configuration file in HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\WMI\Security. Volgmer installs a copy of itself in a randomly selected service, then overwrites the ServiceDLL entry in the service's Registry entry. Some Volgmer variants also install .dll files as services with names generated by a list of hard-coded strings. Volgmer can download remote files and additional payloads to the victim's machine. Volgmer can gather information about TCP connection state. Volgmer can gather a list of processes. Some Volgmer variants add new services with display names generated by a list of hard-coded strings such as Application, Background, Security, and Windows, presumably as a way to masquerade as a legitimate service. Volgmer stores an encoded configuration file in HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\WMI\Security. Volgmer can gather the IP address from the victim's machine.
title: Yagi, J. (2014, August 24). Trojan.Volgmer. Retrieved July 16, 2018.

text: HiddenWasp uses an RC4-like algorithm with an already computed PRGA generated key-stream for network communication. HiddenWasp encrypts its configuration and payload. HiddenWasp installs reboot persistence by adding itself to /etc/rc.local. HiddenWasp creates a user account as a means to provide initial persistence to the compromised machine. HiddenWasp adds itself as a shared object to the LD_PRELOAD environment variable. HiddenWasp downloads a tar compressed archive from a download server to the system. HiddenWasp communicates with a simple network protocol over TCP. HiddenWasp uses a script to automate tasks on the victim's machine and to assist in execution. HiddenWasp uses a cipher to implement a decoding function. HiddenWasp uses a rootkit to hook and implement functions on the system.
title: Sanmillan, I. (2019, May 29). HiddenWasp Malware Stings Targeted Linux Systems. Retrieved June 24, 2019.

text:
Small Sieve can obtain the id of a logged in user.
Small Sieve has the ability to use the Telegram Bot API from Telegram Messenger to send and receive messages.
Small Sieve has the ability to use a custom hex byte swapping encoding scheme combined with an obfuscated Base64 function to protect program strings and Telegram credentials.
Small Sieve can use `cmd.exe` to execute commands on a victim's system.
Small Sieve can obtain the IP address of a victim host.
Small Sieve has the ability to download files.
Small Sieve can use Python scripts to execute commands.
Small Sieve can only execute correctly if the word `Platypus` is passed to it on the command line.
Small Sieve can use variations of Microsoft and Outlook spellings, such as "Microsift", in its file names to avoid detection.
Small Sieve has the ability to add itself to `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\OutlookMicrosift` for persistence.
title: NCSC GCHQ. (2022, January 27). Small Sieve Malware Analysis Report. Retrieved August 22, 2022.

text:
RansomHub can use Elliptic Curve Encryption to encrypt files on targeted systems. RansomHub can also skip content at regular intervals (ex. encrypt 1 MB, skip 3 MB) to optomize performance and enable faster encryption for large files.
RansomHub has placed a ransom note on comrpomised systems to warn victims and provide directions for how to retrieve data.
RansomHub has used `vssadmin.exe` to delete volume shadow copies.
RansomHub can stop processes associated with files currently in use to maximize the impact of encryption.
title: CISA et al. (2024, August 29). #StopRansomware: RansomHub Ransomware. Retrieved March 17, 2025.

text: Bad Rabbit’s infpub.dat file creates a scheduled task to launch a malicious executable. Bad Rabbit used the EternalRomance SMB exploit to spread through victim networks. Bad Rabbit has attempted to bypass UAC and gain elevated administrative privileges. Bad Rabbit can enumerate all running processes to compare hashes. Bad Rabbit has masqueraded as a Flash Player installer through the executable file install_flash_player.exe. Bad Rabbit has used an executable that installs a modified bootloader to prevent normal boot-up. Bad Rabbit has used rundll32 to launch a malicious DLL as C:Windowsinfpub.dat. Bad Rabbit spread through watering holes on popular sites by injecting JavaScript into the HTML body or a .js file. Bad Rabbit has been executed through user installation of an executable disguised as a flash installer. Bad Rabbit’s infpub.dat file uses NTLM login credentials to brute force Windows machines. Bad Rabbit has encrypted files and disks using AES-128-CBC and RSA-2048.
title: Mamedov, O. Sinitsyn, F.  Ivanov, A.. (2017, October 24). Bad Rabbit ransomware. Retrieved January 28, 2021.

text: Kali365 has the ability to modify email rules to delete email based notifications prior to the victim seeing them.
title: Trevor Hilligoss. (2026, June 11). Kali365: Anatomy of a Microsoft 365 Phishing-as-a-Service Kit – From Telegram Hype to FBI Takedown Theater. Retrieved July 30, 2026.

text: PlugX checks if VMware tools is running in the background by searching for any process named "vmtoolsd".
title: Lancaster, T., Idrizovic, E. (2017, June 27). Paranoid PlugX. Retrieved April 19, 2019.

text: Bisonal has used the Windows API to communicate with the Service Control Manager to execute a thread. Bisonal can obtain a list of running processes on the victim’s machine. Bisonal's dropper creates VBS scripts on the victim’s machine. Bisonal has collected information from a compromised host. Bisonal has used raw sockets for network communication. Bisonal has been delivered as malicious email attachments. Bisonal has added the exfiltrated data to the URL over the C2 channel. Bisonal has encoded binary data with Base64 and ASCII. Bisonal has decoded strings in the malware using XOR and RC4. Bisonal's DLL file and non-malicious decoy file are encrypted with RC4 and some function name strings are obfuscated. Bisonal can execute ipconfig on the victim’s machine. Bisonal has been loaded through a `.wll` extension added to the ` %APPDATA%\microsoft\word\startup\` repository. Bisonal has renamed malicious code to `msacm32.dll` to hide within a legitimate library; earlier versions were disguised as `winhelp`. Bisonal has checked if the malware is running in a virtual environment with the anti-debug function GetTickCount() to compare the timing. Bisonal has used a dynamic DNS service for C2. Bisonal has added itself to the Registry key HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\CurrentVersion\Run\ for persistence. Bisonal has deleted Registry keys to clean up its prior activity. Bisonal can retrieve a file listing from the system. Bisonal has used the MPRESS packer and similar tools for obfuscation. Bisonal can check to determine if the compromised system is running on VMware. Bisonal has supported use of a proxy server. Bisonal has used the RegQueryValueExA function to retrieve proxy information in the Registry. Bisonal has launched cmd.exe and used the ShellExecuteW() API function to execute commands on the system. Bisonal has relied on users to execute malicious file attachments delivered via spearphishing emails. Bisonal will delete its dropper and VBS scripts from the victim’s machine. Bisonal has appended random binary data to the end of itself to generate a large binary. Bisonal has used commands and API calls to gather system information. Bisonal has been modified to be used as a Windows service. Bisonal dropped a decoy payload with a .jpg extension that contained a malicious Visual Basic script. Bisonal variants reported on in 2014 and 2015 used a simple XOR cipher for C2. Some Bisonal samples encrypt C2 communications with RC4. Bisonal has the capability to download files to execute on the victim’s machine.
title: Mercer, W., et al. (2020, March 5). Bisonal: 10 years of play. Retrieved January 26, 2022.

text:
MobileOrder has a command to upload to its C2 server victim browser bookmarks.
Psylo has commands to enumerate all storage devices and to find all files that start with a particular string.
The original variant of FakeM encrypts C2 traffic using a custom encryption cipher that uses an XOR key of “YHCRA” and bit rotation between each XOR operation. Some variants of FakeM use RC4 to encrypt C2 traffic.
CallMe has the capability to create a reverse shell on victims.
FakeM contains a keylogger module.
CallMe has the capability to download a file to the victim from the C2 server.
MobileOrder has a command to upload to its C2 server victim mobile device information, including IMEI, IMSI, SIM card serial number, phone number, Android version, and other information.
MobileOrder has a command to upload information about all running processes to its C2 server.
MobileOrder has a command to upload to its C2 server information about files on the victim mobile device, including SD card size, installed app list, SMS content, contacts, and calling history.
FakeM C2 traffic attempts to evade detection by resembling data generated by legitimate messenger applications, such as MSN and Yahoo! messengers. Additionally, some variants of FakeM use modified SSL code for communications back to C2 servers, making SSL decryption ineffective.
Psylo has a command to conduct timestomping by setting a specified file’s timestamps to match those of a system file in the System32 directory.
MobileOrder exfiltrates data to its C2 server over the same protocol as C2 communications.
Psylo uses HTTPS for C2.
Psylo exfiltrates data to its C2 server over the same protocol as C2 communications.
Some variants of FakeM use SSL to communicate with C2 servers.
MobileOrder has a command to download a file from the C2 server to the victim mobile device's SD card.
Psylo has a command to download a file to the system from its C2 server.
CallMe exfiltrates data to its C2 server over the same protocol as C2 communications.
MobileOrder exfiltrates data collected from the victim mobile device.
CallMe uses AES to encrypt C2 traffic.

text:
REvil has used obfuscated VBA macros for execution.
REvil has been executed via malicious MS Word e-mail attachments.
title: Han, Karsten. (2019, June 4). Strange Bits: Sodinokibi Spam, CinaRAT, and Fake G DATA. Retrieved August 4, 2020.

text: Ryuk has used Wake-on-Lan to power on turned off systems for lateral movement. Ryuk has used the C$ network share for lateral movement. Ryuk has called GetIpNetTable in attempt to identify all mounted drives and hosts that have Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) entries.
title: Abrams, L. (2021, January 14). Ryuk Ransomware Uses Wake-on-Lan To Encrypt Offline Devices. Retrieved February 11, 2021.

text: Kinsing has communicated with C2 over HTTP. Kinsing was run through a deployed Ubuntu container. Kinsing has created and run a Bitcoin cryptocurrency miner. Kinsing has used Unix shell scripts to execute commands in the victim environment. Kinsing was executed with an Ubuntu container entry point that runs shell scripts. Kinsing has attempted to brute force hosts over SSH. Kinsing has used chmod to modify permissions on key files for use. Kinsing has downloaded additional lateral movement scripts from C2. Kinsing has used crontab to download and run shell scripts every minute to ensure persistence. Kinsing has used ps to list processes. Kinsing has used a script to parse files like /etc/hosts and SSH known_hosts to discover remote systems. Kinsing has searched for private keys. Kinsing has used valid SSH credentials to access remote hosts. Kinsing has searched bash_history for credentials. Kinsing was executed in an Ubuntu container deployed via an open Docker daemon API. Kinsing has used the find command to search for specific files. Kinsing has used SSH for lateral movement.
title: Singer, G. (2020, April 3). Threat Alert: Kinsing Malware Attacks Targeting Container Environments. Retrieved April 1, 2021.

text:
TrickBot leverages a custom packer to obfuscate its functionality.
TrickBot collects a list of install programs and services on the system’s machine.
TrickBot collects local files and information from the victim’s local machine.
TrickBot uses an AES CBC (256 bits) encryption algorithm for its loader and configuration files.
TrickBot uses non-descriptive names to hide functionality.
title: Salinas, M., Holguin, J. (2017, June). Evolution of Trickbot. Retrieved July 31, 2018.

title: CISA. (2022, September 23). AA22-264A Iranian State Actors Conduct Cyber Operations Against the Government of Albania. Retrieved August 6, 2024.

text:
TSCookie has the ability to inject code into the svchost.exe, iexplorer.exe, explorer.exe, and default browser processes.
TSCookie has the ability to proxy communications with command and control (C2) servers.
TSCookie can use ICMP to receive information on the destination server.
title: Tomonaga, S.. (2019, September 18). Malware Used by BlackTech after Network Intrusion. Retrieved May 6, 2020.

text:
OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D can also use use HTTP POST and GET requests to send and receive C2 information.
OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D has disguised it's true file structure as an application bundle by adding special characters to the filename and using the icon for legitimate Word documents.
OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D has the ability to upload files from a compromised host.

text:
ROKRAT has used legitimate social networking sites and cloud platforms (including but not limited to Twitter, Yandex, Dropbox, and Mediafire) for C2 communications.
ROKRAT can use the `GetForegroundWindow` and `GetWindowText` APIs to discover where the user is typing.
ROKRAT can list the current running processes on the system.
ROKRAT can use `SetWindowsHookEx` and `GetKeyNameText` to capture keystrokes.
ROKRAT can send collected files back over same C2 channel.
title: Mercer, W., Rascagneres, P. (2017, April 03). Introducing ROKRAT. Retrieved May 21, 2018.

text:
Cobalt Strike can install a new service.
Cobalt Strike can use Window admin shares (C$ and ADMIN$) for lateral movement.
Cobalt Strike can query shared drives on the local system.
Cobalt Strike can perform pass the hash.

title: CyberESI. (2011). TROJAN.GTALK. Retrieved September 12, 2024.
