text:
Egregor contains functionality to query the local/system time.
Egregor has used regsvr32.exe to execute malicious DLLs.
Egregor can perform a long sleep (greater than or equal to 3 minutes) to evade detection.
title: Joe Security. (n.d.). Analysis Report fasm.dll. Retrieved November 17, 2024.

text: A module in Prikormka gathers logins and passwords stored in applications on the victims, including Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, and several other browsers. Prikormka creates a directory, %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\SKC\, which is used to store collected log files. After collecting documents from removable media, Prikormka compresses the collected files, and encrypts it with Blowfish. A module in Prikormka collects information from the victim about Windows OS version, computer name, battery info, and physical memory. After encrypting its own log files, the log encryption module in Prikormka deletes the original, unencrypted files from the host. A module in Prikormka collects information on available printers and disk drives. A module in Prikormka collects information from the victim about installed anti-virus software. Prikormka encrypts some C2 traffic with the Blowfish cipher. Prikormka contains a module that collects documents with certain extensions from removable media or fixed drives connected via USB. A module in Prikormka collects information about the paths, size, and creation time of files with specific file extensions, but not the actual content of the file. Prikormka adds itself to a Registry Run key with the name guidVGA or guidVSA. Some resources in Prikormka are encrypted with a simple XOR operation or encoded with Base64. Prikormka contains a module that captures screenshots of the victim's desktop. A module in Prikormka collects passwords stored in applications installed on the victim. Prikormka encodes C2 traffic with Base64. A module in Prikormka collects information from the victim about the current user name. Prikormka contains a keylogger module that collects keystrokes and the titles of foreground windows. Prikormka uses rundll32.exe to load its DLL. A module in Prikormka collects information from the victim about its IP addresses and MAC addresses. Prikormka uses DLL search order hijacking for persistence by saving itself as ntshrui.dll to the Windows directory so it will load before the legitimate ntshrui.dll saved in the System32 subdirectory.
title: Cherepanov, A.. (2016, May 17). Operation Groundbait: Analysis of a surveillance toolkit. Retrieved May 18, 2016.

text: LockBit 2.0 can automatically terminate processes that may interfere with the encryption or file extraction processes.
title: SentinelOne. (n.d.). LockBit 2.0: In-Depth Analysis, Detection, Mitigation, and Removal. Retrieved January 24, 2025.

text:
A JHUHUGIT variant takes screenshots by simulating the user pressing the "Take Screenshot" key (VK_SCREENSHOT), accessing the screenshot saved in the clipboard, and converting it to a JPG image.
JHUHUGIT uses a .bat file to execute a .dll.
JHUHUGIT is executed using rundll32.exe.
title: Mercer, W., et al. (2017, October 22). "Cyber Conflict" Decoy Document Used in Real Cyber Conflict. Retrieved November 2, 2018.

text:
Agent.btz obtains the victim username and saves it to a file.
Agent.btz saves system information into an XML file that is then XOR-encoded.
Agent.btz collects the network adapter’s IP and MAC address as well as IP addresses of the network adapter’s default gateway, primary/secondary WINS, DHCP, and DNS servers, and saves them into a log file.
Agent.btz attempts to download an encrypted binary from a specified domain.
Agent.btz drops itself onto removable media devices and creates an autorun.inf file with an instruction to run that file. When the device is inserted into another system, it opens autorun.inf and loads the malware.
title: Shevchenko, S.. (2008, November 30). Agent.btz - A Threat That Hit Pentagon. Retrieved April 8, 2016.

text: ShimRat can be issued a command shell function from the C2. ShimRat can uninstall itself from compromised hosts, as well create and modify directories, delete, move, copy, and rename files. ShimRat has used a secondary C2 location if the first was unavailable. ShimRat can list directories. ShimRat has used Windows API functions to install the service and shim. ShimRat communicated over HTTP and HTTPS with C2 servers. ShimRat can use pre-configured HTTP proxies. ShimRat has hijacked the cryptbase.dll within migwiz.exe to escalate privileges. This prevented the User Access Control window from appearing. ShimRat has the capability to upload collected files to a C2. ShimRat has decompressed its core DLL using shellcode once an impersonated antivirus component was running on a system. ShimRat can impersonate Windows services and antivirus products to avoid detection on compromised systems. ShimRat has installed a registry based start-up key HKCU\Software\microsoft\windows\CurrentVersion\Run to maintain persistence should other methods fail. ShimRat can hijack the cryptbase.dll within migwiz.exe to escalate privileges and bypass UAC controls. ShimRat has registered two registry keys for shim databases. ShimRat can enumerate connected drives for infected host machines. ShimRat has installed shim databases in the AppPatch folder. ShimRat's loader has been packed with the compressed ShimRat core DLL and the legitimate DLL for it to hijack. ShimRat has installed a Windows service to maintain persistence on victim machines. ShimRat has been delivered as a package that includes compressed DLL and shellcode payloads within a .dat file. ShimRat can sleep when instructed to do so by the C2. ShimRat can download additional files.
title: Yonathan Klijnsma. (2016, May 17). Mofang: A politically motivated information stealing adversary. Retrieved May 12, 2020.

text: BabyShark can execute additional VisualBasic content.
title: Mandiant. (2024, March 14). APT43: North Korean Group Uses Cybercrime to Fund Espionage Operations. Retrieved May 3, 2024.

text:
Mini Shai-Hulud has the ability to check system details for its language configuration and terminates actions when the system is configured for the Russian language.
Mini Shai-Hulud has utilized container administration commands to gather details of compromised hosts and gather credentials to include Kubernetes command-line utilities `kubectl get secrets`.
Mini Shai-Hulud has utilized Python scripts to execute payloads.
Mini Shai-Hulud has gathered and downloaded data stored on both compromised and publicly accessible code repositories.
Mini Shai-Hulud has accessed and propagated to AWS EC2 instances via SSM Send-Command.
title: Webb, M. (2026, May 20). TeamPCP Wave Four: GitHub Breach via Poisoned VS Code Extension, durabletask PyPI Worm, and ~4,000 Internal Repositories Exfiltrated. Retrieved July 16, 2026.

text:
After initial compromise, Chaos will download a second stage to establish a more permanent presence on the affected system.
Chaos provides a reverse shell connection on 8338/TCP, encrypted via AES.
Chaos provides a reverse shell is triggered upon receipt of a packet with a special string, sent to any port.
Chaos conducts brute force attacks against SSH services to gain initial access.
title: Sebastian Feldmann. (2018, February 14). Chaos: a Stolen Backdoor Rising Again. Retrieved March 5, 2018.

text:
Tsundere Botnet has been distributed via a PowerShell script.
Tsundere Botnet’s loader has decrypted obfuscated JavaScript files using the AES-256 CBC algorithm, a build-specific key, and initialization vector.
Tsundere Botnet has created a value in the `HKCU:\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run` Registry key, ensuring that it is run at login.
Tsundere Botnet’s loader contained AES-CBC/PKCS7 encrypted blobs, which were descrypted and written to disk.
Tsundere Botnet has obtained the WebSocket C2 address by making remote procedure call (RPC) APIs to Ethereum blockchain nodes.
Tsundere Botnet has obtained the C2 address from Ethereum blockchain nodes.
title: Ctrl-Alt-Intel. (2026, March 4). MuddyWater Exposed: Inside an Iranian APT operation . Retrieved April 6, 2026.

text: NanoCore gathers the IP address from the victim’s machine.
title: The DigiTrust Group. (2017, January 01). NanoCore Is Not Your Average RAT. Retrieved November 9, 2018.

text:
Embargo has been leveraged in double-extortion ransomware, exfiltrating files then encrypting them, to prompt victims to pay a ransom.
Embargo has utilized MS4Killer to detect running processes on the victim device. Embargo has also captured a snapshot of active running processes using the Windows API `CreateToolHelp32Snapshot()`.
Embargo has obtained active services running on the victim’s system through the functions `OpenSCManagerW()` and `EnumServicesStatusExW()`.
Embargo has searched for folders, subfolders and other networked or mounted drives for follow on encryption actions. Embargo has also iterated device volumes using `FindFirstVolumeW()` and `FindNextVolumeW()` functions and then calls the `GetVolumePathNamesForVolumeNameW()` function to retrieve a list of drive letters and mounted folder paths for each specified volume.
Embargo has utilized a hardcoded mutex name of “LoadUpOnGunsBringYourFriends” using the `CreateMutexW()` function. Embargo has also utilized a hardcoded mutex name of “IntoTheFloodAgainSameOldTrip."
Embargo has searched for folders, subfolders and other networked or mounted drives for follow-on encryption actions.
Embargo has cleared files from the recycle bin by invoking `SHEmptyRecycleBinW()` and disabled Windows recovery through `C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe /q /c bcdedit /set {default} recoveryenabled no`.
Embargo has terminated active processes and services based on a hardcoded list using the `CloseServiceHandle()` function. Embargo has also leveraged MS4Killer to terminate processes contained in an embedded list of security software process names that were XOR-encrypted.
Embargo has the ability to encrypt files with the ChaCha20 and Curve25519 cryptographic algorithms. Embargo also has the ability to encrypt system data and add a random six-letter extension consisting of hexadecimal characters such as ".b58eeb" or “.3d828a” to encrypted files.
Embargo has avoided encrypting specific files and directories by leveraging a regular expression within the ransomware binary.
Embargo has leveraged Windows Native API functions to execute its operations.
title: Cyble. (2024, May 24). The Rust Revolution: New Embargo Ransomware Steps In. Retrieved October 19, 2025.

text: GuLoader can delete its executable from the AppData\Local\Temp directory on the compromised host. NETWIRE has been executed through convincing victims into clicking malicious links. NETWIRE has been executed through luring victims into opening malicious documents. NETWIRE has been spread via e-mail campaigns utilizing malicious attachments. NETWIRE has been spread via e-mail campaigns utilizing malicious links. GuLoader can establish persistence via the Registry under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce. The GuLoader executable has been retrieved via embedded macros in malicious Word documents. GuLoader has been spread in phishing campaigns using malicious web links. GuLoader has relied upon users clicking on links to malicious documents.
title: Duncan, B. (2020, April 3). GuLoader: Malspam Campaign Installing NetWire RAT. Retrieved January 7, 2021.

text: MacSpy stores itself in ~/Library/.DS_Stores/ MacSpy deletes any temporary files it creates
title: PETER EWANE. (2017, June 9). MacSpy: OS X RAT as a Service. Retrieved September 21, 2018.

text:
MOPSLED can communicate to C2 nodes over HTTP.
RIFLESPINE can upload results from executed C2 commands to cloud storage.
MEDUSA can execute code through dynamic linker hijacking of the `LD_PRELOAD` library.
MEDUSA is a rootkit with command execution and credential logging capabilities.
RIFLESPINE can download and execute files.
REPTILE has used udev for persistence.
MOPSLED can use a custom binary protocol over TCP for C2 communication.
RIFLESPINE can use the AES algorithm to encrypt C2 data.
RIFLESPINE can execute commands with `/bin/sh`.
RIFLESPINE can use HTTP `GET` and `PUT` to upload and download files.
RIFLESPINE can collect system information after installation on infected systems.
The REPTILE reverse shell component can listen for a specialized packet in TCP, UDP, or ICMP for activation.
MEDUSA can be configured to capture SSH credentials via SSH hijacking.
REPTILE has the ability to control compromised endpoints via port knocking.
MOPSLED can decrypt obfuscated configuration files.
MEDUSA can XOR encrypt configuration strings.
MOPSLED has the ability to retrieve a C2 address from a dead drop URL.
The REPTILE launcher can daemonize a process.
MOPSLED can encrypt configuration files with a custom ChaCha20 algorithm.
REPTILE can deploy components automatically with shell scripts.
RIFLESPINE can deobfuscate encrypted files prior to execution on targeted hosts.
RIFLESPINE can create a systemd service file for execution.
RIFLESPINE can retrieve C2 commands from an encrypted file on Google Drive then upload the results of command execution back to Google Drive.
REPTILE can communicate using TLS over raw TCP.
The REPTILE rootkit is implemented as a loadable kernel module (LKM).
RIFLESPINE can stage the output from executed C2 commands to a temporary file.
MOPSLED can use third-party web services such as GitHub and Google Drive for C2.
REPTILE can use TLS over raw TCP for secure C2.
REPTILE has the ability to communicate with the kernel-mode component to hide files.
REPTILE has the ability to hook kernel functions and modify functions data to achieve rootkit functionality such as hiding processes and network connections.
The REPTILE launcher component can decrypt kernel module code from a file and load it into memory.
title: Punsaen Boonyakarn, Shawn Chew, Logeswaran Nadarajan, Mathew Potaczek, Jakub Jozwiak, and Alex Marvi. (2024, June 18). Cloaked and Covert: Uncovering UNC3886 Espionage Operations. Retrieved September 24, 2024.

text:
OopsIE uses the SmartAssembly obfuscator to pack an embedded .Net Framework assembly used for C2.
OopsIE uses the Confuser protector to obfuscate an embedded .Net Framework assembly used for C2. OopsIE also encodes collected data in hexadecimal format before writing to files on disk and obfuscates strings.
OopsIE compresses collected files with GZipStream before sending them to its C2 server.
OopsIE can upload files from the victim's machine to its C2 server.
OopsIE creates and uses a VBScript as part of its persistent execution.
OopsIE stages the output from command execution and collected files in specific folders before exfiltration.
OopsIE compresses collected files with a simple character replacement scheme before sending them to its C2 server.
OopsIE exfiltrates command output and collected files to its C2 server in 1500-byte blocks.
OopsIE can download files from its C2 server to the victim's machine.
OopsIE uses HTTP for C2 communications.
OopsIE encodes data in hexadecimal format over the C2 channel.
OopsIE creates a scheduled task to run itself every three minutes.
OopsIE uses the command prompt to execute commands on the victim's machine.
OopsIE concatenates then decompresses multiple resources to load an embedded .Net Framework assembly.
title: Lee, B., Falcone, R. (2018, February 23). OopsIE! OilRig Uses ThreeDollars to Deliver New Trojan. Retrieved July 16, 2018.

text: QakBot has stored stolen emails and other data into new folders prior to exfiltration.
title: Sette, N. et al. (2020, June 4). Qakbot Malware Now Exfiltrating Emails for Sophisticated Thread Hijacking Attacks. Retrieved September 27, 2021.

text:
REvil can download a copy of itself from an attacker controlled IP address to the victim machine.
REvil can use vssadmin to delete volume shadow copies and bcdedit to disable recovery features.
REvil has used PowerShell to delete volume shadow copies and download files.
REvil can use the Windows command line to delete volume shadow copies and disable recovery.
REvil can encrypt files on victim systems and demands a ransom to decrypt the files.
title: Cadieux, P, et al (2019, April 30). Sodinokibi ransomware exploits WebLogic Server vulnerability. Retrieved August 4, 2020.

text:
WhisperGate can deobfuscate downloaded files stored in reverse byte order and decrypt embedded resources using multiple XOR operations.
WhisperGate has used the `ExitWindowsEx` to flush file buffers to disk and stop running processes and other API calls.
WhisperGate can download and execute AdvancedRun.exe to disable the Windows Defender Theat Protection service and set an exclusion path for the C:\ drive.
WhisperGate can delete tools from a compromised host after execution.
WhisperGate can overwrite the Master Book Record (MBR) on victim systems with a malicious 16-bit bootloader.
WhisperGate can download additional stages of malware from a Discord CDN channel.
WhisperGate can use a Visual Basic script to exclude the `C:\` drive from Windows Defender.
WhisperGate can download additional payloads hosted on a Discord channel.
WhisperGate can use PowerShell to support multiple actions including execution and defense evasion.
WhisperGate can shutdown a compromised host through execution of `ExitWindowsEx` with the `EXW_SHUTDOWN` flag.
WhisperGate can overwrite sectors of a victim host's hard drive at periodic offsets.
WhisperGate can enumerate connected remote logical drives.
WhisperGate can corrupt files by overwriting the first 1 MB with `0xcc` and appending random extensions.
WhisperGate overwrites the MBR with a bootloader component that performs destructive wiping operations on hard drives and displays a fake ransom note when the host boots.
WhisperGate has the ability to enumerate fixed logical drives on a targeted system.
WhisperGate can Base64 encode strings, store downloaded files in reverse byte order, and use the Eazfuscator tool to obfuscate its third stage.
The WhisperGate third stage can use the AdvancedRun.exe tool to execute commands in the context of the Windows TrustedInstaller group via `%TEMP%\AdvancedRun.exe" /EXEFilename "C:\Windows\System32\sc.exe" /WindowState 0 /CommandLine "stop WinDefend" /StartDirectory "" /RunAs 8 /Run`.
WhisperGate has the ability to inject its fourth stage into a suspended process created by the legitimate Windows utility `InstallUtil.exe`.
WhisperGate can locate files based on hardcoded file extensions.
title: Biasini, N. et al.. (2022, January 21). Ukraine Campaign Delivers Defacement and Wipers, in Continued Escalation. Retrieved March 14, 2022.

text:
Lizar has a module to collect usernames and passwords stored in browsers.
Lizar can search for processes associated with an anti-virus product from list.
Lizar has used Python scripts (ps2x.py script and ps2p.py) to execute files on remote hosts using the Impacket library.
Lizar can collect the computer name from the machine.
Lizar has encrypted data before sending it to the server.
Lizar can collect the username from the system.
Lizar has a plugin to retrieve information about all active network sessions on the infected server.
Lizar has retrieved network information from a compromised host, such as the MAC address.
FIN7 has obtained and used tools such as Impacket, Mimikatz, and PsExec.
Lizar can execute PE files in the address space of the specified process.
Lizar can support encrypted communications between the client and server.
Lizar can retrieve browser history and database files.
Lizar has a command to open the command-line on the infected system.
Lizar has decrypted its configuration data, such as the C2 IP address, ports and other network communication.
Lizar has used various Windows API functions on a victim's machine.
Lizar has used PowerShell scripts.
Lizar has a plugin designed to obtain a list of processes.
Lizar has a plugin that can retrieve credentials from Internet Explorer and Microsoft Edge using `vaultcmd.exe` and another that can collect RDP access credentials using the `CredEnumerateW` function.
Lizar can run Mimikatz to harvest credentials.
Lizar can download additional plugins, files, and tools.
Lizar has used the PowerKatz plugin that can be loaded into the address space of a PowerShell process through reflective DLL loading.
Lizar can take JPEG screenshots of an infected system. Lizar has also used a plugin to take a screenshot of the infected system.
Lizar can collect email accounts from Microsoft Outlook and Mozilla Thunderbird.
Lizar can migrate the loader into another process.
title: BI.ZONE Cyber Threats Research Team. (2021, May 13). From pentest to APT attack: cybercriminal group FIN7 disguises its malware as an ethical hacker’s toolkit. Retrieved February 2, 2022.

text:
Cyclops Blink can use DNS over HTTPS (DoH) to resolve C2 nodes.
Cyclops Blink has the ability to create a pipe to enable inter-process communication.
title: Haquebord, F. et al. (2022, March 17). Cyclops Blink Sets Sights on Asus Routers. Retrieved March 17, 2022.

text:
Lokibot has the ability to initiate contact with command and control (C2) to exfiltrate stolen data.
Lokibot has the ability to discover the username on the infected host.
Lokibot has the ability to discover the computer name and Windows product name/version.
Lokibot has the ability to discover the domain name of the infected host.
Lokibot has the ability to capture input on the compromised host via keylogging.
title: Kazem, M. (2019, November 25). Trojan:W32/Lokibot. Retrieved May 15, 2020.

text:
MirrorStealer has the ability to steal credentials from email clients.
NOOPLDR can discover the device ID and hostname from the targeted machine to use for encryption keys.
NOOPLDR can decrypt its payload prior to execution.
HiddenFace can use RSA-2048 in addition to symmetric algorithms in C2.
LODEINFO has used Registry run keys to set persistence.
NOOPLDR can use native APIs `NtProtectVirtualMemory`, `NtWriteVirtualMemory`, and `NtCreateThreadEx` to aid process injection.
HiddenFace can act as an internal HTTP proxy within the targeted environment.
NOOPLDR can inject decrypted payloads into processes including wuauclt.exe., rdrleakdiag.exe, and tabcal.exe.
NOOPLDR can store its payload in the Registry using a random hex string in `HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\COM3`.
NOOPLDR can delete a file containing configuration instructions after use.
HiddenFace can use active and passive C2 modes that use different encryption algorithms and backdoor commands.
MirrorStealer can target Group Policy Preferences for credentials.
HiddenFace can check for the presence of specific analysis tools and will terminate itself if they are found.
The NOOPLDR payload is encrypted with AES256-CBC.
MirrorStealer can steal credentials stored in browsers.
title: Trend Micro. (2024, November 19). Spot the Difference: Earth Kasha's New LODEINFO Campaign And The Correlation Analysis With The APT10 Umbrella. Retrieved April 17, 2026.

text:
REvil attempts to create a mutex using a hard-coded value to ensure that no other instances of itself are running on the host.
REvil can query the Registry to get random file extensions to append to encrypted files.
REvil can launch an instance of itself with administrative rights using runas.
REvil can exfiltrate host and malware information to C2 servers.
title: Counter Threat Unit Research Team. (2019, September 24). REvil/Sodinokibi Ransomware. Retrieved August 4, 2020.

text:
Qilin has been deployed on VMware vCenter and ESXi servers via custom PowerShell script. Qilin has also used PowerShell for discovery in vCenter and Active Directory environments.
Qilin can reboot targeted systems in safe mode to avoid detection.
Qilin has pushed a scheduled task via a Group Policy Object for payload execution.
Qilin can use AES-256 or ChaCha20 for domain-wide encryption of victim servers and workstations and RSA-4096 or RSA-2048 to secure generated encryption keys.
Qilin has pushed scheduled tasks via Group Policy Objects (GPOs) for execution. Qilin has also created a scheduled task named TVInstallRestore, configured to run at logon using the `/SC ONLOGON` argument.
title: Thomas, W. (2024, June 12). Tracking Adversaries: The Qilin RaaS. Retrieved September 26, 2025.

text:
Sagerunex will gather system information such as MAC and IP addresses.
Sagerunex uses a custom decryption routine to unpack itself during installation.
Sagerunex encrypts collected system data then exfiltrates via existing command and control channels.
Sagerunex is designed to be dynamic link library (DLL) injected into an infected endpoint and executed directly in memory.
Sagerunex gathers information from the infected system such as hostname.
Sagerunex has used web services such as Twitter for command and control purposes.
Sagerunex has archived collected materials in RAR format.
Sagerunex uses a "servicemain" function to verify its environment to ensure it can only be executed as a service, as well as the existence of a configuration file in a specified directory.
Sagerunex gathers host information and stages it locally as a RAR file prior to exfiltration. Sagerunex stores logged data in an encrypted file located at `%TEMP%/TS_FB56.tmp` during execution.
Sagerunex uses several proxy configuration settings to ensure connectivity.
Sagerunex calls the `WaitForSingleObject` API function as part of time-check logic.
Sagerunex has used VMProtect to pack and obscure itself.
Sagerunex has used virtual private servers (VPS) for command and control traffic as well as third-party cloud services in more recent variants.

text: The Komplex trojan creates a persistent launch agent called with $HOME/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.updates.plist with launchctl load -w ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.updates.plist. The Komplex payload is stored in a hidden directory at /Users/Shared/.local/kextd. The OsInfo function in Komplex collects the current running username. The Komplex trojan supports file deletion. The OsInfo function in Komplex collects a running process list. The Komplex C2 channel uses HTTP POST requests. The Komplex C2 channel uses an 11-byte XOR algorithm to hide data.
title: Dani Creus, Tyler Halfpop, Robert Falcone. (2016, September 26). Sofacy's 'Komplex' OS X Trojan. Retrieved July 8, 2017.

text:
TONESHELL has an exception handler that executes when ESET antivirus applications `ekrn.exe` and `egui.exe` are not found and directly injects its code into waitfor.exe using Native Windows API including `WriteProcessMemory` and `CreateRemoteThreadEx`.
TONESHELL has injected its malicious payload into a running process through Windows utility Microsoft Application Virtualization Injector `MAVInject.exe`.
TONESHELL has used regsvr32.exe to execute the windows `DLLRegisterServer` function.
TONESHELL has checked for the presence of ESET antivirus applications `ekrn.exe` and `egui.exe`.
title: Nathaniel Morales, Nick Dai. (2025, February 18). Earth Preta Mixes Legitimate and Malicious Components to Sidestep Detection. Retrieved September 10, 2025.

text:
Smoke Loader searches for files named logins.json to parse for credentials.
Smoke Loader searches through Outlook files and directories (e.g., inbox, sent, templates, drafts, archives, etc.).
Smoke Loader scans processes to perform anti-VM checks.
Smoke Loader recursively searches through directories for files.
Smoke Loader searches for credentials stored from web browsers.
Smoke Loader launches a scheduled task.
Smoke Loader injects into the Internet Explorer process.
Smoke Loader deobfuscates its code.
title: Baker, B., Unterbrink H. (2018, July 03). Smoking Guns - Smoke Loader learned new tricks. Retrieved July 5, 2018.

text:
OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D has used a custom binary protocol over port 443 for C2 traffic.
For network communications, OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D loads a dynamic library (`.dylib` file) using `dlopen()` and obtains a function pointer to execute within that shared library using `dlsym()`.
OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D encrypts data sent back to the C2 using AES in CBC mode with a null initialization vector (IV) and a key sent from the server that is padded to 32 bytes.
OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D has used `zlib` to compress all data after 0x52 for the custom TCP C2 protocol.
OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D uses file naming conventions with associated executable locations to blend in with the macOS TimeMachine and OpenSSL services. Such as, naming a LaunchAgent plist file `com.apple.openssl.plist` which executes OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D from the user's `~/Library/OpenSSL/` folder upon user login.
OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D has used a custom binary protocol over TCP port 443 for C2.
OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D uses a decode routine combining bit shifting and XOR operations with a variable key that depends on the length of the string that was encoded. If the computation for the variable XOR key turns out to be 0, the default XOR key of 0x1B is used. This routine is also referenced as the `rotate` function in reporting.
OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D has used AES in CBC mode to encrypt collected data when saving that data to disk.
title: Erye Hernandez and Danny Tsechansky. (2017, June 22). The New and Improved macOS Backdoor from OceanLotus. Retrieved September 8, 2023.

text:
Emotet has obfuscated macros within malicious documents to hide the URLs hosting the malware, CMD.exe arguments, and PowerShell scripts.
Emotet has been delivered by phishing emails containing links.
Emotet has used HTTP over ports such as 20, 22, 443, 7080, and 50000, in addition to using ports commonly associated with HTTP/S.
Emotet has been delivered by phishing emails containing attachments.
Emotet has sent Microsoft Word documents with embedded macros that will invoke scripts to download additional payloads.
title: Brumaghin, E.. (2019, January 15). Emotet re-emerges after the holidays. Retrieved March 25, 2019.

text:
XTunnel relays traffic between a C2 server and a victim.
CHOPSTICK is capable of performing remote file transmission.
XTunnel has been used to execute remote commands.
title: Alperovitch, D.. (2016, June 15). Bears in the Midst: Intrusion into the Democratic National Committee. Retrieved August 3, 2016.

text:
Clop has used built-in API functions such as WNetOpenEnumW(), WNetEnumResourceW(), WNetCloseEnum(), GetProcAddress(), and VirtualAlloc().
Clop can use cmd.exe to help execute commands on the system.
Clop can use msiexec.exe to disable security tools on the system.
Clop has been packed to help avoid detection.
Clop can uninstall or disable security products.
Clop can make modifications to Registry keys.
Clop can search for processes with antivirus and antimalware product names.

text:
MgBot includes modules for collecting information on Active Directory domain accounts.
MgBot includes modules for dumping and capturing credentials from process memory.
MgBot includes modules for performing ARP scans of local connected systems.
MgBot includes modules for collecting information on local domain users and permissions.
MgBot includes keylogger payloads focused on the QQ chat application.
MgBot includes modules for performing HTTP and server service scans.
MgBot includes modules for identifying local administrator accounts on victim systems.
MgBot includes modules for stealing stored credentials from Outlook and Foxmail email client software.
MgBot can capture clipboard data.
MgBot includes modules for stealing credentials from various browsers and applications, including Chrome, Opera, Firefox, Foxmail, QQBrowser, FileZilla, and WinSCP.
MgBot can capture input and output audio streams from infected devices.
MgBot includes modules for identifying local users and administrators on victim machines.
MgBot includes a module for establishing a process watchdog for itself, identifying if the MgBot process is still running.
title: Threat Hunter Team. (2023, April 20). Daggerfly: APT Actor Targets Telecoms Company in Africa. Retrieved July 25, 2024.

text: BabyShark has executed the ver command. BabyShark has executed the reg query command for HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Terminal Server Client\Default. BabyShark has encoded data using certutil before exfiltration. BabyShark has used cmd.exe to execute commands. BabyShark has executed the tasklist command. BabyShark has used dir to search for "programfiles" and "appdata". BabyShark has executed the whoami command. BabyShark has added a Registry key to ensure all future macros are enabled for Microsoft Word and Excel as well as for additional persistence. BabyShark has executed the ipconfig /all command.
title: Unit 42. (2019, February 22). New BabyShark Malware Targets U.S. National Security Think Tanks. Retrieved October 7, 2019.

text:
Metamorfo has encrypted C2 commands with AES-256.
Metamorfo can send the data it collects to the C2 server.
Metamorfo has used YouTube to store and hide C&C server domains.
Metamorfo has collected the username from the victim's machine.
title: ESET Research. (2019, October 3). Casbaneiro: peculiarities of this banking Trojan that affects Brazil and Mexico. Retrieved September 23, 2021.

text:
KONNI has the capability to perform keylogging.
KONNI can delete files.
KONNI can collect the username from the victim’s machine.
KONNI had a feature to steal data from the clipboard.
KONNI has created a shortcut called "Anti virus service.lnk" in an apparent attempt to masquerade as a legitimate file.
KONNI can take screenshots of the victim’s machine.
KONNI can steal profiles (containing credential information) from Firefox, Chrome, and Opera.
A version of KONNI searches for filenames created with a previous version of the malware, suggesting different versions targeted the same victims and the versions may work together.
A version of KONNI has dropped a Windows shortcut into the Startup folder to establish persistence.
KONNI can collect the IP address from the victim’s machine.
A version of KONNI drops a Windows shortcut on the victim’s machine to establish persistence.
title: Rascagneres, P. (2017, May 03). KONNI: A Malware Under The Radar For Years. Retrieved November 5, 2018.

text: Zebrocy installs an application-defined Windows hook to get notified when a network drive has been attached, so it can then use the hook to call its RecordToFile file stealing method. Zebrocy identifies network drives when they are added to victim systems. Zebrocy has used a method similar to RC4 as well as AES for encryption and hexadecimal for encoding data before exfiltration. Zebrocy searches for files that are 60mb and less and contain the following extensions: .doc, .docx, .xls, .xlsx, .ppt, .pptx, .exe, .zip, and .rar. Zebrocy also runs the echo %APPDATA% command to list the contents of the directory. Zebrocy can obtain the current execution path as well as perform drive enumeration.
title: Kaspersky Lab's Global Research & Analysis Team. (2018, February 20). A Slice of 2017 Sofacy Activity. Retrieved November 27, 2018.

text:
ShrinkLocker will exit its "main" function if the victim domain name does not match provided criteria.
ShrinkLocker has used Diskpart to format newly-created partitions.
ShrinkLocker can initiate a destructive payload depending on the operating system check through resizing and reformatting portions of the victim machine's disk, leading to system instability and potential data corruption.
ShrinkLocker checks whether the Bitlocker Drive Encryption Tools service is running.
ShrinkLocker retrieves a system timestamp that is used in generating an encryption key.
title: Splunk Threat Research Team , Teoderick Contreras. (2024, September 5). ShrinkLocker Malware: Abusing BitLocker to Lock Your Data. Retrieved December 7, 2024.

text:
The primary delivered mechanism for Agent Tesla is through email phishing messages.
Agent Tesla can gather credentials from a number of browsers.
Agent Tesla has used wmi queries to gather information from the system.
Agent Tesla has the ability to use form-grabbing to extract data from web data forms.
Agent Tesla has been executed through malicious e-mail attachments
title: Arsene, L. (2020, April 21). Oil & Gas Spearphishing Campaigns Drop Agent Tesla Spyware in Advance of Historic OPEC+ Deal. Retrieved May 19, 2020.

text:
Babuk can stop anti-virus services on a compromised host.
Babuk has the ability to enumerate network shares.
title: Sogeti. (2021, March). Babuk Ransomware. Retrieved August 11, 2021.

text:
FunnyDream can identify the processes for Bkav antivirus.
FunnyDream can Base64 encode its C2 address stored in a template binary with the `xyz0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvw_-` or `xyz0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvw_=` character sets.
The FunnyDream FilepakMonitor component can detect removable drive insertion.
FunnyDream can parse the `ProxyServer` string in the Registry to discover http proxies.
Chinoxy can use a digitally signed binary ("Logitech Bluetooth Wizard Host Process") to load its dll into memory.
ccf32 can run on a daily basis using a scheduled task.
FunnyDream can identify files with .doc, .docx, .ppt, .pptx, .xls, .xlsx, and .pdf extensions and specific timestamps for collection.
FunnyDream can stage collected information including screen captures and logged keystrokes locally.
The FunnyDream Keyrecord component can capture keystrokes.
FunnyDream can check `Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Internet Settings` to extract the `ProxyServer` string.
FunnyDream has compressed collected files with zLib.
The FunnyDream FilePakMonitor component has the ability to collect files from removable devices.
FunnyDream has used a service named `WSearch` for execution.
ccf32 can be used to automatically collect files from a compromised host.
FunnyDream can use a Registry Run Key and the Startup folder to establish persistence.
FunnyDream can monitor files for changes and automatically collect them.
FunnyDream can download additional files onto a compromised host.
ccf32 can determine the local time on targeted machines.
FunnyDream can use com objects identified with `CLSID_ShellLink`(`IShellLink` and `IPersistFile`) and `WScript.Shell`(`RegWrite` method) to enable persistence mechanisms.
ccf32 has used `xcopy \\<target_host>\c$\users\public\path.7z c:\users\public\bin\<target_host>.7z /H /Y` to archive collected files.
FunnyDream can communicate with C2 over TCP and UDP.
Chinoxy has encrypted its configuration file.
FunnyDream can send compressed and obfuscated packets to C2.
FunnyDream can enumerate all logical drives on a targeted machine.
ccf32 can upload collected data and files to an FTP server.
ccf32 can delete files and folders from compromised machines.
Chinoxy has established persistence via the `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run` registry key and by loading a dropper to `(%COMMON_ STARTUP%\\eoffice.exe)`.
FunnyDream has compressed collected files with zLib and encrypted them using an XOR operation with the string key from the command line or `qwerasdf` if the command line argument doesn’t contain the key. File names are obfuscated using XOR with the same key as the compressed file content.
ccf32 can parse collected files to identify specific file extensions.
FunnyDream has the ability to discover application windows via execution of `EnumWindows`.
ccf32 has copied files to a remote machine infected with Chinoxy or another backdoor.
FunnyDream can delete files including its dropper component.
The Chinoxy dropping function can initiate decryption of its config file.
FunnyDream has the ability to gather user information from the targeted system using `whoami/upn&whoami/fqdn&whoami/logonid&whoami/all`.
FunnyDream can use `cmd.exe` for execution on remote hosts.
FunnyDream can use WMI to open a Windows command shell on a remote machine.
FunnyDream has the ability to discover processes, including `Bka.exe` and `BkavUtil.exe`.
FunnyDream can use `rundll32` for execution of its components.
FunnyDream can connect to HTTP proxies via TCP to create a tunnel to C2.
ccf32 can collect files from a compromised host.
FunnyDream can check system time to help determine when changes were made to specified files.
FunnyDream can identify and use configured proxies in a compromised network for C2 communication.
FunnyDream has established persistence by running `sc.exe` and by setting the `WSearch` service to run automatically.
The FunnyDream FilepakMonitor component can inject into the Bka.exe process using the `VirtualAllocEx`, `WriteProcessMemory` and `CreateRemoteThread` APIs to load the DLL component.
ccf32 has used `cmd.exe` for archiving data and deleting files.
ccf32 has created a hidden directory on targeted systems, naming it after the current local time (year, month, and day).
The FunnyDream ScreenCap component can take screenshots on a compromised host.
FunnyDream has the ability to clean traces of malware deployment.
FunnyDream can use Native API for defense evasion, discovery, and collection.
ccf32 can temporarily store files in a hidden directory on the local host.
Chinoxy has used the name `eoffice.exe` in attempt to appear as a legitimate file.
FunnyDream can execute commands, including gathering user information, and send the results to C2.

text:
Ursnif has used encoded data in HTTP URLs for C2.
Ursnif has used a DGA to generate domain names for C2.
Ursnif has used Registry modifications as part of its installation routine.
Ursnif has used crypto key information stored in the Registry to decrypt Tor clients dropped to disk.

RARSTONE downloads its backdoor component from a C2 server and loads it directly into memory.
RARSTONE uses SSL to encrypt its communication with its C2 server.
title: Aquino, M. (2013, June 13). RARSTONE Found In Targeted Attacks. Retrieved December 17, 2015.

text:
INC Ransomware has the ability to use wmic.exe to spread to multiple endpoints within a compromised environment.
INC Ransomware can push its encryption executable to multiple endpoints within compromised infrastructure.
title: Team Huntress. (2023, August 11). Investigating New INC Ransom Group Activity. Retrieved June 5, 2024.

text:
Torisma can use `WTSEnumerateSessionsW` to monitor remote desktop connections.
Torisma is only delivered to a compromised host if the victim's IP address is on an allow-list.
Torisma has used various Windows API calls.
Torisma can use `GetlogicalDrives` to get a bitmask of all drives available on a compromised system. It can also use `GetDriveType` to determine if a new drive is a CD-ROM drive.
Torisma can send victim data to an actor-controlled C2 server.
Torisma has encrypted its C2 communications using XOR and VEST-32.
Torisma can collect the local MAC address using `GetAdaptersInfo` as well as the system's IP address.
Torisma has used XOR and Base64 to decode C2 data.
Torisma can collect the current time on a victim machine.
Torisma has been packed with Iz4 compression.
Torisma has encoded C2 communications with Base64.
Torisma can use HTTP and HTTPS for C2 communications.
Torisma has been Base64 encoded and AES encrypted.
title: Beek, C. (2020, November 5). Operation North Star: Behind The Scenes. Retrieved December 20, 2021.

text: WastedLocker can perform a UAC bypass if it is not executed with administrator rights or if the infected host runs Windows Vista or later. WastedLocker checked if UCOMIEnumConnections and IActiveScriptParseProcedure32 Registry keys were detected as part of its anti-analysis technique. WastedLocker has a command to take ownership of a file and reset the ACL permissions using the takeown.exe /F filepath command. WastedLocker's custom crypter, CryptOne, leveraged the VirtualAlloc() API function to help execute the payload. WastedLocker's custom cryptor, CryptOne, used an XOR based algorithm to decrypt the payload. WastedLocker can delete shadow volumes. WastedLocker checks for specific registry keys related to the UCOMIEnumConnections and IActiveScriptParseProcedure32 interfaces. WastedLocker has performed DLL hijacking before execution. WastedLocker contains junk code to increase its entropy and hide the actual code. WastedLocker has copied a random file from the Windows System32 folder to the %APPDATA% location under a different hidden filename. WastedLocker can execute itself as a service. WastedLocker can enumerate files and directories just prior to encryption. The WastedLocker payload includes encrypted strings stored within the .bss section of the binary file. WastedLocker created and established a service that runs until the encryption process is complete. WastedLocker can encrypt data and leave a ransom note. WastedLocker can modify registry values within the Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Internet Settings\ZoneMap registry key. WastedLocker has used cmd to execute commands on the system.
title: Antenucci, S., Pantazopoulos, N., Sandee, M. (2020, June 23). WastedLocker: A New Ransomware Variant Developed By The Evil Corp Group. Retrieved September 14, 2021.

text:
Mini Shai-Hulud has used compromised accounts for Docker Hub and GitHub to publish malicious software packages.
Mini Shai-Hulud has utilized Python startup hooks to include the .pth import mechanism for execution.
Mini Shai-Hulud has discovered network configuration through the use of system commands to include `ip addr`, and `ip route`.
Mini Shai-Hulud has leveraged commands such as `whoami` to identify the system owner.
Mini Shai-Hulud has compressed collected credentials and data within tar archive files prior to exfiltration.
Mini Shai-Hulud has the ability to decrypt obfuscated payloads.
Mini Shai-Hulud has deleted all artifacts to include gathered credential archives to reduce disk persistence and detection.
title: Santos, J. and Navato, J.R. (2026, May 13). Analyzing TeamPCP’s Supply Chain Attacks: Checkmarx KICS and elementary-data in CI/CD Credential Theft. Retrieved July 16, 2026.

text: ThiefQuest uses the kill_unwanted function to get a list of running processes, compares each process with an encrypted list of “unwanted” security related programs, and kills the processes for security related programs. ThiefQuest invokes time call to check the system's time, executes a sleep command, invokes a second time call, and then compares the time difference between the two time calls and the amount of time the system slept to identify the sandbox. ThiefQuest uses the function kill_unwanted to obtain a list of running processes and kills each process matching a list of security related processes. When running with root privileges after a Launch Agent is installed, ThiefQuest installs a plist file to the /Library/LaunchDaemons/ folder with the RunAtLoad key set to true establishing persistence as a Launch Daemon. ThiefQuest installs a launch item using an embedded encrypted launch agent property list template. The plist file is installed in the ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ folder and configured with the path to the persistent binary located in the ~/Library/ folder. ThiefQuest obtains a list of running processes using the function kill_unwanted. ThiefQuest uses AppleScript's osascript -e command to launch ThiefQuest's persistence via Launch Agent and Launch Daemon. ThiefQuest hides a copy of itself in the user's ~/Library directory by using a . at the beginning of the file name followed by 9 random characters.
title: Patrick Wardle. (2020, June 29). OSX.EvilQuest Uncovered part i: infection, persistence, and more!. Retrieved March 18, 2021.

text:
WellMail can use hard coded client and certificate authority certificates to communicate with C2 over mutual TLS.
WellMail can identify the IP address of the victim system.
WellMail can identify the current username on the victim system.
WellMail has been observed using TCP port 25, without using SMTP, to leverage an open port for secure command and control communications.
WellMail can use TCP for C2 communications.
WellMail can exfiltrate files from the victim machine.
WellMail can archive files on the compromised host.
WellMail can decompress scripts received from C2.
WellMail can receive data and executable scripts from C2.
title: CISA. (2020, July 16). MAR-10296782-3.v1 – WELLMAIL. Retrieved September 29, 2020.

text: SombRAT has uploaded collected data and files from a compromised host to its C2 server. SombRAT can execute enum to enumerate files in storage on a compromised system. SombRAT can store harvested data in a custom database under the %TEMP% directory. SombRAT can SSL encrypt C2 traffic. PS1 can inject its payload DLL Into memory. SombRAT can communicate over DNS with the C2 server. SombRAT has collected data and files from a compromised host. CostaBricks can download additional payloads onto a compromised host. SombRAT can execute getinfo to enumerate the computer name and OS version of a compromised system. SombRAT can enumerate services on a victim machine. CostaBricks can implement a custom-built virtual machine mechanism to obfuscate its code. SombRAT can use the getprocesslist command to enumerate processes on a compromised host. CostaBricks has added the entire unobfuscated code of the legitimate open source application Blink to its code. SombRAT can use a custom DGA to generate a subdomain for C2. SombRAT can execute getinfo to identify the username on a compromised host. SombRAT has the ability to use TCP sockets to send data and ICMP to ping the C2 server. SombRAT has encrypted its C2 communications with AES. CostaBricks has used a number of API calls, including `VirtualAlloc`, `VirtualFree`, `LoadLibraryA`, `GetProcAddress`, and `ExitProcess`. PS1 can utilize a PowerShell loader. SombRAT can execute getinfo to discover the current time on a compromised host. SombRAT can execute loadfromfile, loadfromstorage, and loadfrommem to inject a DLL from disk, storage, or memory respectively. SombRAT can run upload to decrypt and upload files from storage. SombRAT has the ability to download and execute additional payloads. SombRAT has encrypted collected data with AES-256 using a hardcoded key. SombRAT can encrypt strings with XOR-based routines and use a custom AES storage format for plugins, configuration, C2 domains, and harvested data. SombRAT has the ability to run cancel or closeanddeletestorage to remove all files from storage and delete the storage temp file on a compromised host. CostaBricks can inject a payload into the memory of a compromised host. PS1 can use an XOR key to decrypt a PowerShell loader and payload binary. SombRAT has the ability to respawn itself using ShellExecuteW and CreateProcessW. CostaBricks has been used to load SombRAT onto a compromised host. CostaBricks has the ability to use bytecode to decrypt embedded payloads. PS1 is distributed as a set of encrypted files and scripts.
title: The BlackBerry Research and Intelligence Team. (2020, November 12). The CostaRicto Campaign: Cyber-Espionage Outsourced. Retrieved May 24, 2021.

text:
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can search GitHub for Actions runner processes.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can compress and encrypt data and exfiltrate it via POST to an attacker-controlled domain. If that method fails it can use the victim's own GitHub account to create a public repository and uploads the encrypted data as a release asset.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has searched victim hosts for TLS and SSH keys.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has searched for cryptocurrency wallets on targeted hosts.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can harvest credentials from cryptocurrency wallets and keystores such as Ethereum keystores, Cardano keys, Solana validator keypairs, Ledger device files, and Anchor deploy keys.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can create a repository in the victim's GitHub account using the victim's own GITHUB_TOKEN to upload stolen credentials.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can locate GitHub Actions runner processes.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can scrape memory from the Runner.Worker process by reading `/proc/<pid>/mem` to extract secrets including plaintext tokens.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has used multi-stage payloads with double Base64-encoded scripts to evade static analysis.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has encrypted collected data using a hybrid RSA-4096 and AES-256-encryption prior to exfiltration over 'curl`.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has encrypted collected data using a hybrid AES-256 and RSA-4096 encryption prior to exfiltration over 'curl`.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can search filesystems for cryptocurrency wallets such as Bitcoin, Litecoin, Dogecoin, Zcash, Dash, Ripple, and Monero.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can identify files containing environment variables, SSH keys, cloud credentials, access tokens, and cryptocurrency wallets.
title: Aqua Security . (2026, March 21). Trivy ecosystem supply chain temporarily compromised. Retrieved July 1, 2026.

text:
Emotet has relied upon users clicking on a malicious link delivered through spearphishing.
Emotet has been observed injecting in to Explorer.exe and other processes.
Emotet has relied upon users clicking on a malicious attachment delivered through spearphishing.
Emotet has been observed to hook network APIs to monitor network traffic.
title: Salvio, J.. (2014, June 27). New Banking Malware Uses Network Sniffing for Data Theft. Retrieved March 25, 2019.

text: Sibot has installed a second-stage script in the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\sibot registry key. Sibot has used a legitimate compromised website to download DLLs to the victim's machine. Sibot has downloaded a DLL to the C:\windows\system32\drivers\ folder and renamed it with a .sys extension. Sibot has modified the Registry to install a second-stage script in the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\sibot. GoldMax has used decoy traffic to surround its malicious network traffic to avoid detection. Sibot will delete an associated registry key if a certain server response is received. Sibot communicated with its C2 server via HTTP GET requests. Sibot can download and execute a payload onto a compromised system. Sibot has been executed via MSHTA application. Sibot has obfuscated scripts used in execution. GoldMax has used scheduled tasks to maintain persistence. GoldFinder has used HTTP for C2. GoldMax has impersonated systems management software to avoid detection. Sibot has queried the registry for proxy server information. GoldMax has set an execution trigger date and time, stored as an ASCII Unix/Epoch time value. Sibot checked if the compromised system is configured to use proxies. Sibot has retrieved a GUID associated with a present LAN connection on a compromised machine. Sibot has executed downloaded DLLs with rundll32.exe. GoldFinder logged and stored information related to the route or hops a packet took from a compromised machine to a hardcoded C2 server, including the target C2 URL, HTTP response/status code, HTTP response headers and values, and data received from the C2 node. GoldMax has RSA-encrypted its communication with the C2 server. Sibot executes commands using VBScript. GoldFinder performed HTTP GET requests to check internet connectivity and identify HTTP proxy servers and other redirectors that an HTTP request traveled through. Sibot can decrypt data received from a C2 and save to a file. Sibot has been executed via a scheduled task. GoldMax retrieved a list of the system's network interface after execution. Sibot will delete itself if a certain server response is received. Sibot has used WMI to discover network connections and configurations. Sibot has also used the Win32_Process class to execute a malicious DLL.
title: Nafisi, R., Lelli, A. (2021, March 4). GoldMax, GoldFinder, and Sibot: Analyzing NOBELIUM’s layered persistence. Retrieved March 8, 2021.

text: GrimAgent can use a hardcoded server public RSA key to encrypt the first request to C2. GrimAgent can enumerate the IP and domain of a target system. GrimAgent can identify the user id on a target machine. GrimAgent can identify the country code on a compromised host. GrimAgent can delete previously created tasks on a compromised host. GrimAgent can use Native API including GetProcAddress and ShellExecuteW. GrimAgent has the ability to set persistence using the Task Scheduler. GrimAgent has sent data related to a compromise host over its C2 channel. GrimAgent can pad C2 messages with random generated values. GrimAgent can use the Windows Command Shell to execute commands, including its own removal. GrimAgent has the ability to add bytes to change the file hash. GrimAgent can collect the OS, and build version on a compromised host. GrimAgent can use an AES key to encrypt C2 communications. GrimAgent has the ability to enumerate files and directories on a compromised host. GrimAgent can sleep for 195 - 205 seconds after payload execution and before deleting its task. GrimAgent can delete old binaries on a compromised host. GrimAgent has the ability to use HTTP for C2 communications. GrimAgent uses the last 64 bytes of the binary to compute a mutex name. If the generated name is invalid, it will default to the generic `mymutex`. GrimAgent can base64 encode C2 replies. GrimAgent can use a decryption algorithm for strings based on Rotate on Right (RoR) and Rotate on Left (RoL) functionality. GrimAgent has used Accept-Language to identify hosts in the United Kingdom, United States, France, and Spain. GrimAgent has used Rotate on Right (RoR) and Rotate on Left (RoL) functionality to encrypt strings. GrimAgent has the ability to download and execute additional payloads. GrimAgent can set persistence with a Registry run key. GrimAgent can collect data and files from a compromised host.
title: Priego, A. (2021, July). THE BROTHERS GRIM: THE REVERSING TALE OF GRIMAGENT MALWARE USED BY RYUK. Retrieved September 19, 2024.

text:
TrickBot can identify the groups the user on a compromised host belongs to.
TrickBot has come with a signed downloader component.
Anchor has obfuscated code with stack strings and string encryption.
TrickBot uses HTTPS to communicate with its C2 servers, to get malware updates, modules that perform most of the malware logic and various configuration files.
Anchor can self delete its dropper after the malware is successfully deployed.
Anchor can use secondary C2 servers for communication after establishing connectivity and relaying victim information to primary C2 servers.
TrickBot can enumerate computers and network devices.
TrickBot has been delivered via malicious links in phishing e-mails.
Anchor has used HTTP and HTTPS in C2 communications.
TrickBot can gather information about domain trusts by utilizing Nltest.
TrickBot decodes the configuration data and modules.
Anchor can establish persistence by creating a service.
Anchor has used ICMP in C2 communications.
Anchor has used NTFS to hide files.
Anchor can terminate itself if specific execution flags are not present.
Cobalt Strike can determine if the user on an infected machine is in the admin or domain admin group.
Anchor has come with a packed payload.
TrickBot can identify the user and groups the user belongs to on a compromised host.
TrickBot can steal passwords from the KeePass open source password manager.
Anchor can create a scheduled task for persistence.
TrickBot injects into the svchost.exe process.
The TrickBot downloader has used an icon to appear as a Microsoft Word document.
TrickBot can Base64-encode C2 commands.
TrickBot can use secondary C2 servers for communication after establishing connectivity and relaying victim information to primary C2 servers.
Anchor has used cmd.exe to run its self deletion routine.
Anchor has been signed with valid certificates to evade detection by security tools.
title: Dahan, A. et al. (2019, December 11). DROPPING ANCHOR: FROM A TRICKBOT INFECTION TO THE DISCOVERY OF THE ANCHOR MALWARE. Retrieved September 10, 2020.

text: Comnie executes the netstat -ano command. Comnie appends a total of 64MB of garbage data to a file to deter any security products in place that may be scanning files on disk. Comnie collects the hostname of the victim machine. Comnie attempts to detect several anti-virus products. Comnie uses HTTP for C2 communication. Comnie establishes persistence via a .lnk file in the victim’s startup path. Comnie uses RC4 and Base64 to obfuscate strings. Comnie encrypts command and control communications with RC4. Comnie runs the command: net start >> %TEMP%\info.dat on a victim. Comnie executes BAT scripts. Comnie executes a batch script to store discovery information in %TEMP%\info.dat and then uploads the temporarily file to the remote C2 server. Comnie uses the net user command. Comnie achieves persistence by adding a shortcut of itself to the startup path in the Registry. Comnie uses the tasklist to view running processes on the victim’s machine. Comnie executes VBS scripts. Comnie uses Rundll32 to load a malicious DLL. Comnie uses ipconfig /all and route PRINT to identify network adapter and interface information. Comnie uses blogs and third-party sites (GitHub, tumbler, and BlogSpot) to avoid DNS-based blocking of their communication to the command and control server.
title: Grunzweig, J. (2018, January 31). Comnie Continues to Target Organizations in East Asia. Retrieved June 7, 2018.

text: Hydraq uses basic obfuscation in the form of spaghetti code.
title: O'Gorman, G., and McDonald, G.. (2012, September 6). The Elderwood Project. Retrieved November 17, 2024.

text: INC Ransomware campaigns have used spearphishing emails for initial access.
title: SentinelOne. (n.d.). What Is Inc. Ransomware?. Retrieved June 5, 2024.

text:
StreamEx has the ability to modify the Registry.
StreamEx has the ability to enumerate drive types.
StreamEx obfuscates some commands by using statically programmed fragments of strings when starting a DLL. It also uses a one-byte xor against 0x91 to encode configuration data.
StreamEx has the ability to enumerate processes.
StreamEx establishes persistence by installing a new service pointing to its DLL and setting the service to auto-start.
StreamEx has the ability to remotely execute commands.
StreamEx uses rundll32 to call an exported function.
StreamEx has the ability to scan for security tools such as firewalls and antivirus tools.
StreamEx has the ability to enumerate system information.
title: Cylance SPEAR Team. (2017, February 9). Shell Crew Variants Continue to Fly Under Big AV’s Radar. Retrieved February 15, 2017.

text:
BONDUPDATER can download or upload files from its C2 server.
BONDUPDATER can read batch commands in a file sent from its C2 server and execute them with cmd.exe.
BONDUPDATER persists using a scheduled task that executes every minute.
BONDUPDATER is written in PowerShell.
BONDUPDATER can use DNS and TXT records within its DNS tunneling protocol for command and control.
title: Wilhoit, K. and Falcone, R. (2018, September 12). OilRig Uses Updated BONDUPDATER to Target Middle Eastern Government. Retrieved February 18, 2019.

text:
HexEval Loader has a function where the C2 endpoint can identify the geographical location of a victim host based on request headers, execution environment and runtime conditions.
HexEval Loader has collected the username from the victim host.
HexEval Loader has leveraged server-side client configurations to identify the public IP of the victim host.
HexEval Loader has identified the OS and MAC address of victim device through host fingerprinting scripting.
HexEval Loader has utilized a cross-platform keylogger that has the capability to capture keystrokes on Windows, macOS and Linux systems.
title: Kirill Boychenko. (2025, June 25). Another Wave: North Korean Contagious Interview Campaign Drops 35 New Malicious npm Packages. Retrieved October 19, 2025.

text: Skeleton Key is used to patch an enterprise domain controller authentication process with a backdoor password. It allows adversaries to bypass the standard authentication system to use a defined password for all accounts authenticating to that domain controller.
title: Dell SecureWorks. (2015, January 12). Skeleton Key Malware Analysis. Retrieved April 8, 2019.

text:
RTM has resolved Pony C2 server IP addresses by either converting Bitcoin blockchain transaction data to specific octets, or accessing IP addresses directly within the Namecoin blockchain.
RTM has used an RSS feed on Livejournal to update a list of encrypted C2 server names. RTM has also hidden Pony C2 server IP addresses within transactions on the Bitcoin and Namecoin blockchain.
title: Eisenkraft, K., Olshtein, A. (2019, October 17). Pony’s C&C servers hidden inside the Bitcoin blockchain. Retrieved June 15, 2020.

text: Cyclops Blink can use a custom binary scheme to encode messages with specific commands and parameters to be executed. Cyclops Blink can encrypt C2 messages with AES-256-CBC sent underneath TLS. OpenSSL library functions are also used to encrypt each message using a randomly generated key and IV, which are then encrypted using a hard-coded RSA public key. Cyclops Blink has the ability to upload exfiltrated files to a C2 server. Cyclops Blink can rename its running process to [kworker:0/1] to masquerade as a Linux kernel thread. Cyclops Blink has also named RC scripts used for persistence after WatchGuard artifacts. Cyclops Blink can modify the Linux iptables firewall to enable C2 communication on network devices via a stored list of port numbers. Cyclops Blink has the ability to query device information. Cyclops Blink can use the Linux API `if_nameindex` to gather network interface names. Cyclops Blink can use the Linux API `statvfs` to enumerate the current working directory. Cyclops Blink can use non-standard ports for C2 not typically associated with HTTP or HTTPS traffic. Cyclops Blink can upload files from a compromised host. Cyclops Blink has the ability to use the Linux API function `utime` to change the timestamps of modified firmware update images. Cyclops Blink can decrypt and parse instructions sent from C2. Cyclops Blink has maintained persistence by patching legitimate device firmware when it is downloaded, including that of WatchGuard devices. Cyclops Blink can download files via HTTP and HTTPS. Cyclops Blink can use various Linux API functions including those for execution and discovery. Cyclops Blink has the ability to download files to target systems. Cyclops Blink has the ability to execute on device startup, using a modified RC script named S51armled. Cyclops Blink can enumerate the process it is currently running under.
title: NCSC. (2022, February 23). Cyclops Blink Malware Analysis Report. Retrieved March 3, 2022.

text: HTTPBrowser deletes its original installer file once installation is complete. HTTPBrowser's installer contains a malicious file named navlu.dll to decrypt and run the RAT. navlu.dll is also the name of a legitimate Symantec DLL. HTTPBrowser has established persistence by setting the HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run key value for wdm to the path of the executable. It has also used the Registry entry HKEY_USERS\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run vpdn “%ALLUSERPROFILE%\%APPDATA%\vpdn\VPDN_LU.exe” to establish persistence. HTTPBrowser is capable of listing files, folders, and drives on a victim. HTTPBrowser abuses the Windows DLL load order by using a legitimate Symantec anti-virus binary, VPDN_LU.exe, to load a malicious DLL that mimics a legitimate Symantec DLL, navlu.dll. HTTPBrowser has also used DLL side-loading.
title: Desai, D.. (2015, August 14). Chinese cyber espionage APT group leveraging recently leaked Hacking Team exploits to target a Financial Services Firm. Retrieved January 26, 2016.

text: MarkiRAT can initiate communication over HTTP/HTTPS for its C2 server. MarkiRAT can masquerade as update.exe and svehost.exe; it has also mimicked legitimate Telegram and Chrome files. MarkiRAT can download additional files and tools from its C2 server, including through the use of BITSAdmin. MarkiRAT can upload data from the victim's machine to the C2 server. MarkiRAT can capture screenshots that are initially saved as ‘scr.jpg’. MarkiRAT can check for running processes on the victim’s machine to look for Kaspersky and Bitdefender antivirus products. MarkiRAT can store collected data locally in a created .nfo file. MarkiRAT can search for different processes on a system. MarkiRAT can utilize cmd.exe to execute commands in a victim's environment. MarkiRAT can capture all keystrokes on a compromised host. MarkiRAT can modify the shortcut that launches Telegram by replacing its path with the malicious payload to launch with the legitimate executable. MarkiRAT can exfiltrate locally stored data via its C2. MarkiRAT can gather information from the Keepass password manager. MarkiRAT can obtain the computer name from a compromised host. MarkiRAT can use the GetKeyboardLayout API to check if a compromised host's keyboard is set to Persian. MarkiRAT can drop its payload into the Startup directory to ensure it automatically runs when the compromised system is started. MarkiRAT can retrieve the victim’s username. MarkiRAT can look for files carrying specific extensions such as: .rtf, .doc, .docx, .xls, .xlsx, .ppt, .pptx, .pps, .ppsx, .txt, .gpg, .pkr, .kdbx, .key, and .jpb. MarkiRAT can capture clipboard content. MarkiRAT can use BITS Utility to connect with the C2 server. MarkiRAT can check for the Telegram installation directory by enumerating the files on disk. MarkiRAT can run the ShellExecuteW API via the Windows Command Shell.
title: GReAT. (2021, June 16). Ferocious Kitten: 6 Years of Covert Surveillance in Iran. Retrieved September 22, 2021.

text:
Kali365 has obtained OAuth access and refresh tokens by deceiving victims into completing actor-initiated device authorization requests, and intercepting authentication sessions with legitimate identity providers through adversary-in-the-middle reverse proxy infrastructure.
Kali365 has executed JavaScript within victims' browsers through a React frontend that detects browser sessions to evade automated analysis, auto-copies actor-generated device codes to the victim's clipboard, and polls the actor's C2 infrastructure every three seconds to confirm when OAuth token capture has completed..
Kali365 has generated tailored branded phishing lures to target victims utilizing a myriad of reputable services and brands that entice users to interact with the content. Kali365 has also been enabled with AI such as Claude Sonnet that evaluates emails and generates tailored responses to facilitate BEC activities.
Kali365 has used Cloudflare Workers to redirect traffic and to host malicious phishing pages. Kali365 has also leveraged Telegram chat to facilitate administrative tasks for the panel across affiliate users.
Kali365 has created obfuscated phishing landing pages that act as an adversary in the middle infrastructure that intercepts communications between the victim host and legitimate services to steal credentials and user sessions.
Kali365 has dynamically generated legitimate device codes that displays on the victims screen alongside instructions to copy and paste the device code to initiate and complete a successful authentication process.
title: Artic Wolf Labs. (2026, June 2). Retrieved July 30, 2026.

text:
LAMEHUG can encode queries sent to LLMs.
LAMEHUG can use SSH to transfer information to C2.
LAMEHUG can decode and drop a decoy file attached to spearphishing emails.
LAMEHUG has been distributed through spearphishing emails with various AI-themed malicious attachments.
LAMEHUG can use `cmd.exe` to display a decoy file to spearphishing victims.
LAMEHUG has been executed through victim interaction with malicious email attachments made to look like legitimate AI applications or documents.
LAMEHUG can use `whoami` to enumerate the system user.
LAMEHUG can xcopy for file collection on targeted systems.
LAMEHUG can use wmic to collect system information.
LAMEHUG can use HTTP POST requests to exfiltrate data from compromised hosts to C2.
title: Conteras, T., Splunk Research Team. (2025, September 25). From Prompt to Payload: LAMEHUG’s LLM-Driven Cyber Intrusion. Retrieved April 21, 2026.

text: Uroburos can use its kernel module to prevent its host components from being listed by the targeted system's OS and to mediate requests between user mode and concealed components. Epic heavily obfuscates its code to make analysis more difficult. Turla has used valid digital certificates from Sysprint AG to sign its Epic dropper. Epic uses the rem reg query command to obtain values from Registry keys. Epic uses the nbtstat -n and nbtstat -s commands on the victim’s machine. Epic uses the tasklist /svc command to list the services on the system. Epic uses the net time command to get the system time from the machine and collect the current date and time zone information. Epic searches for anti-malware services running on the victim’s machine and terminates itself if it finds them. Epic encrypts commands from the C2 server using a hardcoded key. Epic uses the net view command on the victim’s machine.
title: Kaspersky Lab's Global Research and Analysis Team. (2014, August 7). The Epic Turla Operation: Solving some of the mysteries of Snake/Uroburos. Retrieved December 11, 2014.

text: TajMahal has the ability to inject the LoadLibrary call template DLL into running processes. TajMahal has the ability to take screenshots on an infected host including capturing content from windows of instant messaging applications. TajMahal has used an encrypted Virtual File System to store plugins. TajMahal has the ability to capture webcam video. TajMahal has the ability to steal web session cookies from Internet Explorer, Netscape Navigator, FireFox and RealNetworks applications. TajMahal has the ability to identify which anti-virus products, firewalls, and anti-spyware products are in use. TajMahal can set the KeepPrintedJobs attribute for configured printers in SOFTWARE\\Microsoft\\Windows NT\\CurrentVersion\\Print\\Printers to enable document stealing. TajMahal has the ability to identify the MAC address on an infected host. TajMahal has the ability to capture keystrokes on an infected host. TajMahal has the ability to identify hardware information, the computer name, and OS information on an infected host. TajMahal has the ability to determine local time on a compromised host. TajMahal has the ability to identify the Internet Explorer (IE) version on an infected host. TajMahal has the ability to identify connected Apple devices. TajMahal has the ability to inject DLLs for malicious plugins into running processes. TajMahal has the ability to capture VoiceIP application audio on an infected host. TajMahal has the ability to send collected files over its C2. TajMahal has the ability to index and compress files into a send queue for exfiltration. TajMahal has the ability to identify running processes and associated plugins on an infected host. TajMahal has the ability to steal data from the clipboard of an infected host. TajMahal has the ability to steal written CD images and files of interest from previously connected removable drives when they become available again. TajMahal has the ability to index files from drives, user profiles, and removable drives. TajMahal has the ability to manage an automated queue of egress files and commands sent to its C2. TajMahal has the ability to use the open source libraries XZip/Xunzip and zlib to compress files. TajMahal has the ability to steal documents from the local system including the print spooler queue.
title: GReAT. (2019, April 10). Project TajMahal – a sophisticated new APT framework. Retrieved October 14, 2019.

text: Metamorfo has used raw TCP for C2. Metamorfo can collect screenshots of the victim’s machine. Metamorfo has automatically collected mouse clicks, continuous screenshots on the machine, and set timers to collect the contents of the clipboard and website browsing. Metamorfo has used mshta.exe to execute a HTA payload. Metamorfo has a command to delete a Registry key it uses, \Software\Microsoft\Internet Explorer\notes. Metamorfo has used VBS code on victims’ systems. Metamorfo has searched the compromised system for banking applications. Metamorfo has communicated with hosts over raw TCP on port 9999. Metamorfo can enumerate all windows on the victim’s machine. Metamorfo requires the user to double-click the executable to run the malicious HTA file or to download a malicious installer. Metamorfo has collected the hostname and operating system version from the compromised host. Metamorfo has displayed fake forms on top of banking sites to intercept credentials from victims. Metamorfo has been delivered to victims via emails with malicious HTML attachments.
title: Sierra, E., Iglesias, G.. (2018, April 24). Metamorfo Campaigns Targeting Brazilian Users. Retrieved July 30, 2020.

text:
InvisibleFerret has used FTP to exfiltrate files and directories using the command `ssh_upload` which contains with six subcommands of `.sdira`, `sdir`, `sfile`, `sfinda`, `sfindr` and `sfind` that had varying functions. InvisibleFerret has exfiltrated stolen files and data to the C2 servers over ports 1224, 2245 and 8637.
InvisibleFerret has been observed utilizing HTTP communications to the C2 server over ports 1224, 2245 and 8637.
InvisibleFerret has stolen login data, autofill data, cryptocurrency wallets, and payment information saved in web browsers such as Chrome, Brave, Opera, Yandex and Edge, to include versions affiliated with major operating systems on Windows, Linux, and macOS. InvisibleFerret has also leveraged the command `ssh_zcp` to copy browser data to include extensions and cryptocurrency wallet data.
title: eSentire Threat Response Unit (TRU). (2024, November 14). Bored BeaverTail & InvisibleFerret Yacht Club – A Lazarus Lure Pt.2. Retrieved October 17, 2025.

text: Power Loader overwrites Explorer’s Shell_TrayWnd extra window memory to redirect execution to a NTDLL function that is abused to assemble and execute a return-oriented programming (ROP) chain and create a malicious thread within Explorer.exe.
title: MalwareTech. (2013, August 13). PowerLoader Injection – Something truly amazing. Retrieved December 16, 2017.

text:
njRAT can identify remote hosts on connected networks.
njRAT can collect data from a local system.
njRAT enumerates the victim operating system and computer name during the initial infection.
njRAT uses Base64 encoding for C2 traffic.
njRAT gathers information about opened windows during the initial infection.
njRAT can launch a command shell interface for executing commands.
njRAT enumerates the current user during the initial infection.
njRAT can browse file systems using a file manager module.
title: Fidelis Cybersecurity. (2013, June 28). Fidelis Threat Advisory #1009: "njRAT" Uncovered. Retrieved June 4, 2019.

text: Raspberry Robin uses a RunOnce Registry key for persistence, where the key is removed after its use on reboot then re-added by the malware after it resumes execution. Raspberry Robin execution can rely on users directly interacting with malicious LNK files.
title: Microsoft Threat Intelligence. (2022, October 27). Raspberry Robin worm part of larger ecosystem facilitating pre-ransomware activity. Retrieved May 17, 2024.

text:
GoldenSpy's uninstaller can delete registry entries, files and folders, and finally itself once these tasks have been completed.
GoldenSpy's uninstaller has base64-encoded its variables.
title: Trustwave SpiderLabs. (2020, June 26). GoldenSpy: Chapter Two – The Uninstaller. Retrieved July 23, 2020.

text:
Black Basta has used WMI to execute files over the network.
QakBot can remotely create a temporary service on a target host.
Black Basta has used PowerShell scripts for discovery and to execute files over the network.
title: Inman, R. and Gurney, P. (2022, June 6). Shining the Light on Black Basta. Retrieved March 8, 2023.
