text: ThiefQuest uses a function named is_debugging to perform anti-debugging logic. The function invokes sysctl checking the returned value of P_TRACED. ThiefQuest also calls ptrace with the PTRACE_DENY_ATTACH flag to prevent debugging. ThiefQuest uses various API functions such as NSCreateObjectFileImageFromMemory to load and link in-memory payloads. ThiefQuest can download and execute payloads in-memory or from disk. ThiefQuest encrypts a set of file extensions on a host, deletes the original files, and provides a ransom note with no contact information. ThiefQuest uses various API to perform behaviors such as executing payloads and performing local enumeration.
title: Patrick Wardle. (2020, July 3). OSX.EvilQuest Uncovered part ii: insidious capabilities. Retrieved March 21, 2021.

text: Bonadan can create bind and reverse shells on the infected system. Kessel has exfiltrated data via hexadecimal-encoded subdomain fields of DNS queries. Kessel has decrypted the binary's configuration once the main function was launched. Kessel has exfiltrated information gathered from the infected system to the C2 server. Bonadan has maliciously altered the OpenSSH binary on targeted systems to create a backdoor. Kessel has trojanized the ssh_login and user-auth_pubkey functions to steal plaintext credentials. Kessel has collected the system architecture, OS version, and MAC address information. Bonadan can download an additional module which has a cryptocurrency mining extension. Kessel's configuration is hardcoded and RC4 encrypted within the binary. Bonadan can download additional modules from the C2 server. Bonadan has discovered the username of the user running the backdoor. Kessel has collected the DNS address of the infected host. Bonadan has discovered the OS version, CPU model, and RAM size of the system it has been installed on. Kessel can exfiltrate credentials and other information via HTTP POST request, TCP, and DNS. Kessel can RC4-encrypt credentials before sending to the C2. Kessel can split the data to be exilftrated into chunks that will fit in subdomains of DNS queries. Bonadan can find the external IP address of the infected host. Kessel has maliciously altered the OpenSSH binary on targeted systems to create a backdoor. Kessel can use a proxy during exfiltration if set in the configuration. Bonadan can XOR-encrypt C2 communications. Kessel can create a reverse shell between the infected host and a specified system. Kessel can download additional modules from the C2 server. Bonadan can use the ps command to discover other cryptocurrency miners active on the system.
title: Dumont, R., M.Léveillé, M., Porcher, H. (2018, December 1). THE DARK SIDE OF THE FORSSHE A landscape of OpenSSH backdoors. Retrieved July 16, 2020.

text:
Ebury can disable SELinux Role-Based Access Control and deactivate PAM modules.
Ebury has verified C2 domain ownership by decrypting the TXT record using an embedded RSA public key.
Ebury has used Python to implement its DGA.
Ebury has implemented a fallback mechanism to begin using a DGA when the attacker hasn't connected to the infected system for three days.
Ebury can deactivate PAM modules to tamper with the sshd configuration.
title: Vachon, F. (2017, October 30). Windigo Still not Windigone: An Ebury Update . Retrieved February 10, 2021.

text:
Hydraq creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can retrieve system information, such as CPU speed, from Registry keys.
Hydraq creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can download files and additional malware components.
Hydraq creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can clear all system event logs.
Hydraq creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can read data from files.
Hydraq creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can retrieve IP addresses of compromised machines.
Hydraq creates a Registry subkey to register its created service, and can also uninstall itself later by deleting this value. Hydraq's backdoor also enables remote attackers to modify and delete subkeys.
Hydraq creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can delete files.
Hydraq creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can load and call DLL functions.
Hydraq creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can monitor services.
Hydraq creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can check for the existence of files, including its own components, as well as retrieve a list of logical drives.
Hydraq creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can monitor processes.
title: Symantec Security Response. (2010, January 18). The Trojan.Hydraq Incident. Retrieved February 20, 2018.

text:
Bandook has modules that are capable of capturing audio.
Bandook can detect USB devices.
Bandook has modules that are capable of capturing video from a victim's webcam.
title: Galperin, E., Et al.. (2016, August). I Got a Letter From the Government the Other Day.... Retrieved April 25, 2018.

text: BoomBox can establish persistence by writing the Registry value MicroNativeCacheSvc to HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. BoomBox can download files from Dropbox using a hardcoded access token. BoomBox can enumerate the hostname, domain, and IP of a compromised host. BoomBox has the ability to mask malicious data strings as PDF files. VaporRage can use HTTP to download shellcode from compromised websites. BoomBox has the ability to download next stage malware components to a compromised system. BoomBox has used HTTP POST requests for C2. EnvyScout can call window.location.pathname to ensure that embedded files are being executed from the C: drive, and will terminate if they are not. EnvyScout has the ability to proxy execution of malicious files with Rundll32. BoomBox can enumerate the username on a compromised host. EnvyScout can Base64 encode payloads. EnvyScout can write files to disk with JavaScript using a modified version of the open-source tool FileSaver. EnvyScout can use hidden directories and files to hide malicious executables. EnvyScout can determine whether the ISO payload was received by a Windows or iOS device. EnvyScout has been distributed via spearphishing as an email attachment. BoomBox can execute an LDAP query to discover e-mail accounts for domain users. VaporRage has the ability to download malicious shellcode to compromised systems. NativeZone can display an RTF document to the user to enable execution of Cobalt Strike stage shellcode. EnvyScout has used folder icons for malicious files to lure victims into opening them. BoomBox can decrypt AES-encrypted files downloaded from C2. VaporRage can deobfuscate XOR-encoded shellcode prior to execution. EnvyScout has been executed through malicious files attached to e-mails. BoomBox has gained execution through user interaction with a malicious file. BoomBox can use RunDLL32 for execution. BoomBox can upload data to dedicated per-victim folders in Dropbox. EnvyScout can deobfuscate and write malicious ISO files to disk. BoomBox can check its current working directory and for the presence of a specific file and terminate if specific values are not found. BoomBox has the ability to execute an LDAP query to enumerate the distinguished name, SAM account name, and display name for all domain users. NativeZone has checked if Vmware or VirtualBox VM is running on a compromised host. BoomBox can encrypt data using AES prior to exfiltration. NativeZone can decrypt and decode embedded Cobalt Strike beacon stage shellcode. VaporRage has the ability to check for the presence of a specific DLL and terminate if it is not found. BoomBox can search for specific files and directories on a machine. EnvyScout contains JavaScript code that can extract an encoded blob from its HTML body and write it to disk. EnvyScout can collect sensitive NTLM material from a compromised host. EnvyScout can use cmd.exe to execute malicious files on compromised hosts. EnvyScout can use protocol handlers to coax the operating system to send NTLMv2 authentication responses to attacker-controlled infrastructure.
title: MSTIC. (2021, May 28). Breaking down NOBELIUM’s latest early-stage toolset. Retrieved August 4, 2021.

text: NavRAT leverages cmd.exe to perform discovery techniques. NavRAT loads malicious shellcode and executes it in memory. NavRAT uses tasklist /v to check running processes. NavRAT writes multiple outputs to a TMP file using the >> method. NavRAT uses systeminfo on a victim’s machine. NavRAT can download files remotely. NavRAT creates a Registry key to ensure a file gets executed upon reboot in order to establish persistence. NavRAT uses the email platform, Naver, for C2 communications, leveraging SMTP. NavRAT logs the keystrokes on the targeted system. NavRAT copies itself into a running Internet Explorer process to evade detection.
title: Mercer, W., Rascagneres, P. (2018, May 31). NavRAT Uses US-North Korea Summit As Decoy For Attacks In South Korea. Retrieved June 11, 2018.

text:
Some ZeroT DLL files have been packed with UPX.
Many ZeroT samples can perform UAC bypass by using eventvwr.exe to execute a malicious file.
ZeroT shellcode decrypts and decompresses its RC4-encrypted payload.
ZeroT gathers the victim's computer name, Windows version, and system language, and then sends it to its C2 server.
ZeroT can download additional payloads onto the victim.
ZeroT can add a new service to ensure PlugX persists on the system when delivered as another payload onto the system.
ZeroT has used RC4 to encrypt C2 traffic.
ZeroT gathers the victim's IP address and domain information, and then sends it to its C2 server.
ZeroT has encrypted its payload with RC4.
ZeroT has used HTTP for C2.
ZeroT has used DLL side-loading to load malicious payloads.
ZeroT has retrieved stage 2 payloads as Bitmap images that use Least Significant Bit (LSB) steganography.
ZeroT has obfuscated DLLs and functions using dummy API calls inserted between real instructions.
title: Huss, D., et al. (2017, February 2). Oops, they did it again: APT Targets Russia and Belarus with ZeroT and PlugX. Retrieved April 5, 2018.

text:
LockBit 2.0 can use wmic.exe to delete volume shadow copies.
LockBit 2.0 has the ability to delete volume shadow copies on targeted hosts.
title: Cybereason Global SOC Team. (n.d.). THREAT ANALYSIS REPORT: LockBit 2.0 - All Paths Lead to Ransom. Retrieved January 24, 2025.

text: Cheerscrypt can encrypt data on victim machines using a Sosemanuk stream cipher with an Elliptic-curve Diffie–Hellman (ECDH) generated key.
title: Biderman, O. et al. (2022, October 3). REVEALING EMPEROR DRAGONFLY: NIGHT SKY AND CHEERSCRYPT - A SINGLE RANSOMWARE GROUP. Retrieved December 6, 2023.

text: SamSam has been seen using AES or DES to encrypt payloads and payload components.
title: Ventura, V. (2018, January 22). SamSam - The Evolution Continues Netting Over $325,000 in 4 Weeks. Retrieved April 16, 2019.

text: Attor's Blowfish key is encrypted with a public RSA key. Attor's dispatcher disguises itself as a legitimate task (i.e., the task name and description appear legitimate). Attor can obtain application window titles and then determines which windows to perform Screen Capture on. Strings in Attor's components are encrypted with a XOR cipher, using a hardcoded key and the configuration data, log files and plugins are encrypted using a hybrid encryption scheme of Blowfish-OFB combined with RSA. Attor has used FTP protocol for C2 communication. Attor performs the injection by attaching its code into the APC queue using NtQueueApcThread API. Attor has a plugin that enumerates files with specific extensions on all hard disk drives and stores file information in encrypted log files. Attor has used Tor for C2 communication. Attor's dispatcher can execute additional plugins by loading the respective DLLs. Attor has a plugin that collects data stored in the Windows clipboard by using the OpenClipboard and GetClipboardData APIs. Attor's installer plugin can schedule rundll32.exe to load the dispatcher. One of Attor's plugins can collect user credentials via capturing keystrokes and can capture keystrokes pressed within the window of the injected process. Attor's has a plugin that is capable of recording audio using available input sound devices. Attor’s plugin deletes the collected files and log files after exfiltration. Attor has automatically collected data about the compromised system. Attor has a file uploader plugin that automatically exfiltrates the collected data and log files to the C2 server. Attor can download additional plugins, updates and other files. Attor's dispatcher can be executed as a service. Attor's installer plugin can schedule a new task that loads the dispatcher on boot/logon. Attor has a plugin that collects information about inserted storage devices, modems, and phone devices. Attor's dispatcher can establish persistence via adding a Registry key with a logon script HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Environment "UserInitMprLogonScript" . Attor has manipulated the time of last access to files and registry keys after they have been created or modified. Attor's dispatcher has used CreateProcessW API for execution. Attor encrypts collected data with a custom implementation of Blowfish and RSA ciphers. Attor has staged collected data in a central upload directory prior to exfiltration. Attor's dispatcher can modify the Run registry key. Attor has exfiltrated data over the C2 channel. Attor has encrypted data symmetrically using a randomly generated Blowfish (OFB) key which is encrypted with a public RSA key. Attor can detect whether it is executed in some virtualized or emulated environment by searching for specific artifacts, such as communication with I/O ports and using VM-specific instructions. Attor monitors the free disk space on the system. Attor's dispatcher can inject itself into running processes to gain higher privileges and to evade detection. Attor's has a plugin that captures screenshots of the target applications. Attor's dispatcher can establish persistence by registering a new service. Attor can set attributes of log files and directories to HIDDEN, SYSTEM, ARCHIVE, or a combination of those. Attor has opened the registry and performed query searches.
title: Hromcova, Z. (2019, October). AT COMMANDS, TOR-BASED COMMUNICATIONS: MEET ATTOR, A FANTASY CREATURE AND ALSO A SPY PLATFORM. Retrieved May 6, 2020.

text:
SombRAT has the ability to use an embedded SOCKS proxy in C2 communications.
FIVEHANDS has the ability to delete volume shadow copies on compromised hosts.
SombRAT can use a legitimate process name to hide itself.
FIVEHANDS can use WMI to delete files on a target machine.
title: CISA. (2021, May 6). Analysis Report (AR21-126A) FiveHands Ransomware. Retrieved June 7, 2021.

text: KOCTOPUS has executed a PowerShell command to download a file to the system. KOCTOPUS has checked the OS version using `wmic.exe` and the `find` command. KOCTOPUS has relied on victims clicking on a malicious link delivered via email. KOCTOPUS can set the AutoRun Registry key with a PowerShell command. KOCTOPUS will attempt to delete or disable all Registry keys and scheduled tasks related to Microsoft Security Defender and Security Essentials. KOCTOPUS has obfuscated scripts with the BatchEncryption tool. KOCTOPUS has added and deleted keys from the Registry. KOCTOPUS has used `cmd.exe` and batch files for execution. KOCTOPUS will perform UAC bypass either through fodhelper.exe or eventvwr.exe. KOCTOPUS has been distributed via spearphishing emails with malicious attachments. KOCTOPUS has used PowerShell commands to download additional files. KOCTOPUS has relied on victims clicking a malicious document for execution. KOCTOPUS can delete created registry keys used for persistence as part of its cleanup procedure. KOCTOPUS can use the `LoadResource` and `CreateProcessW` APIs for execution. KOCTOPUS has deployed a modified version of Invoke-Ngrok to expose open local ports to the Internet. KOCTOPUS has deobfuscated itself before executing its commands. KOCTOPUS has been distributed as a malicious link within an email. KOCTOPUS has used -WindowsStyle Hidden to hide the command window. KOCTOPUS has used VBScript to call wscript to execute a PowerShell command.
title: Jazi, H. (2021, February). LazyScripter: From Empire to double RAT. Retrieved November 17, 2024.

text:
JSS Loader has been executed through malicious attachments contained in spearphishing emails.
JSS Loader has been delivered by phishing emails containing malicious Microsoft Excel attachments.
title: eSentire. (2021, July 21). Notorious Cybercrime Gang, FIN7, Lands Malware in Law Firm Using Fake Legal Complaint Against Jack Daniels’ Owner, Brown-Forman Inc.. Retrieved September 20, 2021.

text:
InvisibleFerret has gathered installed programs and running processes.
InvisibleFerret has established persistence using LaunchAgents on macOS that run on Startup using a file named “com.avatar.update.wake.plist”.
InvisibleFerret has established persistence within GNOME-based Linux environments by placing entries within `.desktop` that run on Startup.
InvisibleFerret has established persistence within Windows devices by creating a .bat file “queue.bat” within the Startup folder to run a Python script.
InvisibleFerret has used HTTP communications to the “/Uploads” URI for file exfiltration.
title: Seongsu Park. (2024, November 4). From Pyongyang to Your Payroll: The Rise of North Korean Remote Workers in the West. Retrieved October 17, 2025.

text:
Qilin can bypass standard user access controls by using stolen tokens to launch processes at an elevated security context.
Qilin can initiate a reboot of the backup server to hinder recovery.
Qilin can employ an embedded Mimikatz module to dump LSASS memory.
Qilin can use an embedded Mimikatz module for token manipulation.
Qilin can require a specific password to be passed by command-line argument during execution which must match a pre-defined value in the configuration in order for it to continue execution.
title: Hacioglu, S. (2025, March 10). Qilin Ransomware: Exposing the TTPs Behind One of the Most Active Ransomware Campaigns of 2024. Retrieved September 26, 2025.

text:
BRICKSTORM has utilized a SOCKS proxy to tunnel access within the victim network and exfiltrate files from internal shares, code repositories, and other endpoints. BRICKSTORM has also leveraged Yamux for combining multiple concurrent logical streams over a single a socket.
BRICKSTORM has leveraged Base64 to encode C2 communications.
BRICKSTORM has embedded delayed-start logic that attempts to circumvent detection for long-term persistence. BRICKSTORM has been observed configured with a “delay” timer built-in that waited for a hard-coded date months in the future before beginning to beacon to the configured C2 domain.
BRICKSTORM has communicated to hardcoded C2 through WebSockets (WSS) to include domains associated with Cloudflare Workers. BRICKSTORM has also leveraged Gorilla mux library to serve its HTTP API calls.
BRICKSTORM has the ability to download files from the Adversaries C2 server to the compromised system.
BRICKSTORM has leveraged SOCKS Proxy to pivot into victim networks in attempts to resemble legitimate administrative traffic.
BRICKSTORM has uploaded files from the victim system to C2 servers.
BRICKSTORM has used DNS over HTTPS to resolve C2 infrastructure and obscure DNS traffic from inspection.
BRICKSTORM has the ability to delete files and directories. BRICKSTORM also has deleted installer files after execution to reduce detection.
BRICKSTORM has identified specific files and directories within targeted hosts and systems for modification, execution, collection and exfiltration.
title: NVISO Incident Response. (2025, April 1). BRICKSTORM  Backdoor Analysis: A Persistent Espionage Threat  to European Industries. Retrieved April 16, 2026.

text: RogueRobin uses a command prompt to run a PowerShell script from Excel. To assist in establishing persistence, RogueRobin creates %APPDATA%\OneDrive.bat and saves the following string to it:powershell.exe -WindowStyle Hidden -exec bypass -File “%APPDATA%\OneDrive.ps1”. RogueRobin uses WMI to check BIOS version for VBOX, bochs, qemu, virtualbox, and vm to check for evidence that the script might be executing within an analysis environment. RogueRobin uses Windows Script Components. RogueRobin uses various WMI queries to check if the sample is running in a sandbox. RogueRobin gathers BIOS versions and manufacturers, the number of CPU cores, the total physical memory, and the computer name. RogueRobin can save a new file to the system from the C2 server. RogueRobin created a shortcut in the Windows startup folder to launch a PowerShell script each time the user logs in to establish persistence. RogueRobin establishes persistence by creating a shortcut (.LNK file) in the Windows startup folder to run a script each time the user logs in. RogueRobin checks the running processes for evidence it may be running in a sandbox environment. It specifically enumerates processes for Wireshark and Sysinternals. RogueRobin has a command named $screenshot that may be responsible for taking screenshots of the victim machine. RogueRobin collects the victim’s username and whether that user is an admin. RogueRobin enumerates running processes to search for Wireshark and Windows Sysinternals suite. RogueRobin gathers the IP address and domain from the victim’s machine. RogueRobin base64 encodes strings that are sent to the C2 over its DNS tunnel.
title: Falcone, R., et al. (2018, July 27). New Threat Actor Group DarkHydrus Targets Middle East Government. Retrieved August 2, 2018.

text: TAINTEDSCRIBE can copy itself into the current user’s Startup folder as “Narrator.exe” for persistence. TAINTEDSCRIBE can download additional modules from its C2 server. TAINTEDSCRIBE can use DriveList to retrieve drive information. TAINTEDSCRIBE has used FakeTLS for session authentication. TAINTEDSCRIBE can randomly pick one of five hard-coded IP addresses for C2 communication; if one of the IP fails, it will wait 60 seconds and then try another IP address. TAINTEDSCRIBE can execute FileRecvWriteRand to append random bytes to the end of a file received from C2. TAINTEDSCRIBE uses a Linear Feedback Shift Register (LFSR) algorithm for network encryption. The TAINTEDSCRIBE main executable has disguised itself as Microsoft’s Narrator. TAINTEDSCRIBE can execute ProcessList for process discovery. TAINTEDSCRIBE can execute GetLocalTime for time discovery. TAINTEDSCRIBE can delete files from a compromised host. TAINTEDSCRIBE has used FileReadZipSend to compress a file and send to C2. TAINTEDSCRIBE can enable Windows CLI access and execute files. The TAINTEDSCRIBE command and execution module can perform target system enumeration. TAINTEDSCRIBE can change the timestamp of specified filenames. TAINTEDSCRIBE can use DirectoryList to enumerate files in a specified directory.
title: USG. (2020, May 12). MAR-10288834-2.v1 – North Korean Trojan: TAINTEDSCRIBE. Retrieved March 5, 2021.

text: IcedID has been executed through Word and Excel files with malicious embedded macros and through ISO and LNK files that execute the malicious DLL. IcedID has been delivered via phishing e-mails with malicious attachments. IcedID has used web injection attacks to redirect victims to spoofed sites designed to harvest banking and other credentials. IcedID can use a self signed TLS certificate in connection with the spoofed site and simultaneously maintains a live connection with the legitimate site to display the correct URL and certificates in the browser. IcedID has used WMI to execute binaries. IcedID has used obfuscated VBA string expressions. IcedID can inject itself into a suspended msiexec.exe process to send beacons to C2 while appearing as a normal msi application. IcedID has also used msiexec.exe to deploy the IcedID loader. IcedID has used HTTPS in communications with C2. IcedID has called ZwWriteVirtualMemory, ZwProtectVirtualMemory, ZwQueueApcThread, and NtResumeThread to inject itself into a remote process. IcedID has used SSL and TLS in communications with C2. IcedID has embedded binaries within RC4 encrypted .png files. IcedID has the ability to download additional modules and a configuration file from C2. IcedID has created a scheduled task to establish persistence. IcedID has utilzed encrypted binaries and base64 encoded strings. IcedID has packed and encrypted its loader module.
title: Kimayong, P. (2020, June 18). COVID-19 and FMLA Campaigns used to install new IcedID banking malware. Retrieved July 14, 2020.

text: Ramsay can hijack outdated Windows application dependencies with malicious versions of its own DLL payload. Ramsay can use ImprovedReflectiveDLLInjection to deploy components. Ramsay has been delivered using OLE objects in malicious documents. Ramsay has masqueraded as a JPG image file. Ramsay can insert itself into the address space of other applications using the AppInit DLL Registry key. Ramsay can use Windows API functions such as WriteFile, CloseHandle, and GetCurrentHwProfile during its collection and file storage operations. Ramsay can execute its embedded components via CreateProcessA and ShellExecute. Ramsay can collect data from removable media and stage it for exfiltration. Ramsay can use the Windows COM API to schedule tasks and maintain persistence. Ramsay can spread itself by infecting other portable executable files on networks shared drives. Ramsay can store collected documents in a custom container after encrypting and compressing them using RC4 and WinRAR. Ramsay has base64-encoded its portable executable and hidden itself under a JPG header. Ramsay can also embed information within document footers. Ramsay can conduct an initial scan for Microsoft Word documents on the local system, removable media, and connected network drives, before tagging and collecting them. It can continue tagging documents to collect with follow up scans. Ramsay can collect data from network drives and stage it for exfiltration. Ramsay has included a rootkit to evade defenses. Ramsay can spread itself by infecting other portable executable files on removable drives. Ramsay can extract its agent from the body of a malicious document. Ramsay can schedule tasks via the Windows COM API to maintain persistence.
title: Sanmillan, I.. (2020, May 13). Ramsay: A cyber‑espionage toolkit tailored for air‑gapped networks. Retrieved May 27, 2020.

text:
One version of Helminth consists of VBScript scripts.
Helminth can download additional files.
The executable version of Helminth has a module to log keystrokes.
Helminth can provide a remote shell. One version of Helminth uses batch scripting.
The Helminth config file is encrypted with RC4.
Helminth creates folders to store output from batch scripts prior to sending the information to its C2 server.
Helminth encrypts data sent to its C2 server over HTTP with RC4.
One version of Helminth uses a PowerShell script.
Helminth establishes persistence by creating a shortcut.
The executable version of Helminth has a module to log clipboard contents.
Helminth establishes persistence by creating a shortcut in the Start Menu folder.
Helminth splits data into chunks up to 23 bytes and sends the data in DNS queries to its C2 server.
Helminth can use DNS for C2.
A Helminth VBScript receives a batch script to execute a set of commands in a command prompt.
Helminth can use HTTP for C2.
For C2 over HTTP, Helminth encodes data with base64 and sends it via the "Cookie" field of HTTP requests. For C2 over DNS, Helminth converts ASCII characters into their hexadecimal values and sends the data in cleartext.
title: Falcone, R. and Lee, B.. (2016, May 26). The OilRig Campaign: Attacks on Saudi Arabian Organizations Deliver Helminth Backdoor. Retrieved May 3, 2017.

text:
Final1stspy creates a Registry Run key to establish persistence.
Final1stspy obtains victim Microsoft Windows version information and CPU architecture.
Final1stspy uses HTTP for C2.
Final1stspy obfuscates strings with base64 encoding.
DOGCALL can capture microphone data from the victim's machine.
DOGCALL is encrypted using single-byte XOR.
DOGCALL can download and execute additional payloads.
DOGCALL is capable of leveraging cloud storage APIs such as Cloud, Box, Dropbox, and Yandex for C2.
DOGCALL is capable of logging keystrokes.
DOGCALL is capable of capturing screenshots of the victim's machine.
Final1stspy obtains a list of running processes.
Final1stspy uses Python code to deobfuscate base64-encoded strings.
title: Grunzweig, J. (2018, October 01). NOKKI Almost Ties the Knot with DOGCALL: Reaper Group Uses New Malware to Deploy RAT. Retrieved November 5, 2018.

text:
POWERTON has used HTTP/HTTPS for C2 traffic.
POWERTON has used AES for encrypting C2 traffic.
POWERTON can install a Registry Run key for persistence.
POWERTON has the ability to dump password hashes.
POWERTON can use WMI for persistence.
POWERTON is written in PowerShell.
title: Ackerman, G., et al. (2018, December 21). OVERRULED: Containing a Potentially Destructive Adversary. Retrieved January 17, 2019.

text: Calisto uses a hidden directory named .calisto to store data from the victim’s machine before exfiltration. Calisto collects information on bookmarks from Google Chrome. Calisto adds a .plist file to the /Library/LaunchAgents folder to maintain persistence. Calisto's installation file is an unsigned DMG image under the guise of Intego’s security solution for mac. Calisto has the capability to use rm -rf to remove folders and files from the victim's machine. Calisto collects Keychain storage data and copies those passwords/tokens to a file. Calisto can collect data from user directories. Calisto runs the ifconfig command to obtain the IP address from the victim’s machine. Calisto uses the zip -r command to compress the data collected on the local system. Calisto uses launchctl to enable screen sharing on the victim’s machine.
title: Kuzin, M., Zelensky S. (2018, July 20). Calisto Trojan for macOS. Retrieved September 7, 2018.

text:
IcedID can identify AV products on an infected host using the following command: ` WMIC.exe WMIC /Node:localhost /Namespace:\\root\SecurityCenter2 Path AntiVirusProduct Get * /Format:List`.
IcedID has exfiltrated collected data via HTTPS.
IcedID used Nltest during initial discovery.
title: DFIR. (2021, March 29). Sodinokibi (aka REvil) Ransomware. Retrieved July 22, 2024.

text:
SysUpdate has named their unit configuration file similarly to other unit files residing in the same directory, `/usr/lib/systemd/system/`, to appear benign.
SysUpdate can collect a list of services on a victim machine.
SysUpdate can collect information about running processes.
SysUpdate has used Base64 to encode its C2 traffic.
SysUpdate can copy a script to the user owned `/usr/lib/systemd/system/` directory with a symlink mapped to a `root` owned directory, `/etc/ystem/system`, in the unit configuration file's `ExecStart` directive to establish persistence and elevate privileges.
SysUpdate can call the `GetNetworkParams` API as part of its C2 establishment process.
SysUpdate can collected the IP address and domain name of a compromised host.
SysUpdate can collect information and files from a compromised host.
SysUpdate has used DES to encrypt all C2 communications.
SysUpdate can collect the username from a compromised host.
SysUpdate has used DNS TXT requests as for its C2 communication.
SysUpdate can contact the DNS server operated by Google as part of its C2 establishment process.
SysUpdate has been signed with stolen digital certificates.
SysUpdate has exfiltrated data over its C2 channel.
title: Daniel Lunghi. (2023, March 1). Iron Tiger’s SysUpdate Reappears, Adds Linux Targeting. Retrieved March 20, 2023.

text:
BRICKSTORM has leveraged DNS web services to resolve C2 IP addresses including sslip.io and nip.io. BRICKSTORM has also utilized Cloudflare Workers for C2 communications.
BRICKSTORM has utilized DNS services sslip.io and nip.io to resolve C2 IP addresses.
BRICKSTORM has appeared to resemble legitimate processes to include the vCenter process `vami-http`. BRICKSTORM has also leveraged legitimate names of VMware vSphere platform such as `vmsrc` or `vmware-sphere`.
BRICKSTORM has decoded its encrypted C2 traffic prior to execution. BRICKSTORM also has the ability to decode its obfuscated payload before execution.
BRICKSTORM has utilized Go libraries to include Garble to obfuscate code.
title: Sarah Yoder, John Wolfram, Ashley Pearson, Doug Bienstock, Josh Madeley, Josh Murchie, Brad Slaybaugh, Matt Lin, Geoff Carstairs, Austin Larsen. (2025, September 24). Another BRICKSTORM: Stealthy Backdoor Enabling Espionage into Tech and Legal Sectors. Retrieved April 16, 2026.

text:
KARAE was distributed through torrent file-sharing websites to South Korean victims, using a YouTube video downloader application as a lure.
SLOWDRIFT downloads additional payloads.
POORAIM can enumerate processes.
CORALDECK searches for specified files.
KARAE can use public cloud-based storage providers for command and control.
WINERACK can gather information about the host.
KARAE can collect system information.
can collect the victim user name.
POORAIM can identify system information, including battery status.
POORAIM can perform screen capturing.
can collect system information, including computer name, system manufacturer, IsDebuggerPresent state, and execution path.
CORALDECK has created password-protected RAR, WinImage, and zip archives to be exfiltrated.
WINERACK can gather information on the victim username.
SHUTTERSPEED can collect system information.
WINERACK can enumerate processes.
SLOWDRIFT uses cloud based services for C2.
WINERACK can enumerate services.
CORALDECK has exfiltrated data in HTTP POST headers.
POORAIM has used AOL Instant Messenger for C2.
WINERACK can enumerate active windows.
POORAIM has been delivered through compromised sites acting as watering holes.
WINERACK can enumerate files and directories.
SHUTTERSPEED can capture screenshots.
SHUTTERSPEED can download and execute an arbitary executable.
SLOWDRIFT collects and sends system information to its C2.
WINERACK can create a reverse shell that utilizes statically-linked Wine cmd.exe code to emulate Windows command prompt commands.
POORAIM can conduct file browsing.
KARAE can upload and download files, including second-stage malware.
can download and execute a second-stage payload.
title: FireEye. (2018, February 20). APT37 (Reaper): The Overlooked North Korean Actor. Retrieved November 17, 2024.

text:
QakBot has been delivered in ZIP files via HTML smuggling.
QakBot has the ability to use DLL side-loading for execution.
Black Basta will check for the presence of a hard-coded mutex `dsajdhas.0` before executing.
Black Basta can use `cmd.exe` to enable shadow copy deletion.
title: Vilkomir-Preisman, S. (2022, August 18). Beating Black Basta Ransomware. Retrieved March 8, 2023.

text:
BabyShark has used mshta.exe to download and execute applications from a remote server.
BabyShark has the ability to decode downloaded files prior to execution.
title: CISA, FBI, CNMF. (2020, October 27). https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-301a. Retrieved November 4, 2020.

text:
XORIndex Loader has leveraged webservices to identify the public IP of the victim host.
HexEval Loader has been used to download a malicious payload to include BeaverTail.
XORIndex Loader has been used to download a malicious payload to include BeaverTail.
XORIndex Loader has exfiltrated victim data using HTTPS POST requests to its C2 servers.
XORIndex Loader has obfuscated strings using ASCII buffers and TextDecoder.
XORIndex Loader has leveraged legitimate package names to mimic frequently utilized tools to entice victims to download and execute malicious payloads.
BeaverTail has exfiltrated data collected from victim devices to C2 servers.
XORIndex Loader has the ability to collect the hostname, OS Username, Geolocation, and OS version of an infected host.
XORIndex Loader has collected the username from the victim host.
BeaverTail has collected keys associated with macOS within `/Library/Keychains/login.keychain`.
BeaverTail has searched the victim device for browser extensions including those commonly associated with cryptocurrency wallets.
BeaverTail has staged collected data to the system’s temporary directory.
HexEval Loader has used HTTP and HTTPS POST requests to communicate with C2.
XORIndex Loader has used HTTPS POST to communicate with C2.
HexEval Loader has decoded its payload prior to execution.
BeaverTail has searched for .ldb and .log files stored in browser extension directories for collection and exfiltration.
BeaverTail has exfiltrated data collected from local systems.
BeaverTail has collected and archived sensitive data in a zip file.
BeaverTail has deleted files from a compromised host after they were exfiltrated.
XORIndex Loader has encoded module names and C2 URLs as hexadecimal strings in attempts to evade analysis.
BeaverTail has used HTTP GET request to download malicious payloads to include InvisibleFerret and HTTP POST to exfiltrate data to C2 infrastructure.
XORIndex Loader can decode its payload prior to execution.
BeaverTail has been used to download a malicious payload to include Python based malware InvisibleFerret.
XORIndex Loader has executed malicious JavaScript code.
XORIndex Loader can identify the geographical location of a victim host.
BeaverTail has stolen passwords saved in web browsers. BeaverTail has also been known to collect login data from Firefox within key3.db, key4.db and logins.json from `/.mozilla/firefox/` for exfiltration.
title: Kirill Boychenko. (2025, July 14). Contagious Interview Campaign Escalates With 67 Malicious npm Packages and New Malware Loader. Retrieved October 19, 2025.

text: Turian can download additional files and tools from its C2. Turian can establish persistence by adding Registry Run keys. Turian has the ability to use Python to spawn a Unix shell. Turian can store copied files in a specific directory prior to exfiltration. Turian can create a remote shell and execute commands using cmd. Turian can use WinRAR to create a password-protected archive for files of interest. Turian can retrieve usernames. Turian can insert pseudo-random characters into its network encryption setup. Turian has the ability to use HTTP for its C2. Turian can retrieve system information including OS version, memory usage, local hostname, and system adapter information. Turian has the ability to take screenshots. Turian can search for specific files and list directories. Turian can retrieve the internal IP address of a compromised host. Turian can scan for removable media to collect data. Turian can disguise as a legitimate service to blend into normal operations. Turian can use VMProtect for obfuscation. Turian has the ability to use /bin/sh to execute commands. Turian has the ability to use a XOR decryption key to extract C2 server domains and IP addresses.
title: Adam Burgher. (2021, June 10). BackdoorDiplomacy: Upgrading from Quarian to Turian. Retrieved September 1, 2021

text:
LockBit 2.0 will not execute on hosts where the system language is set to a language spoken in the Commonwealth of Independent States region.
LockBit 2.0 can delete log files through the use of wevtutil.
LockBit 2.0 can enumerate local drive configuration.
LockBit 2.0 can enumerate system information including hostname and domain information.
LockBit 2.0 can be executed via scheduled task.
LockBit 2.0 can check if a targeted machine is using a set of Eastern European languages and exit without infection if so.
LockBit 2.0 can decode scripts and strings in loaded modules.
LockBit 2.0 can execute command line arguments in a hidden window.
LockBit 2.0 can bypass UAC through creating the Registry key `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\ICM\Calibration`.
LockBit 2.0 has been observed creating accounts for persistence using simple names like "a".
LockBit 2.0 can delete itself from disk after execution.
LockBit 2.0 can disable firewall rules and anti-malware and monitoring software including Windows Defender.
LockBit 2.0 can use the PowerShell module `InvokeGPUpdate` to modify Group Policy.
LockBit 2.0 has the ability to move laterally via SMB.
LockBit 2.0 can modify Group Policy to disable Windows Defender and to automatically infect devices in Windows domains.
LockBit 2.0 can use the Windows command shell for multiple post-compromise actions on objective.
LockBit 2.0 can use standard AES and elliptic-curve cryptography algorithms to encrypt victim data.
title: Elsad, A. et al. (2022, June 9). LockBit 2.0: How This RaaS Operates and How to Protect Against It. Retrieved January 24, 2025.

text: LoJax is a UEFI BIOS rootkit deployed to persist remote access software on some targeted systems. LoJax has modified the Registry key ‘HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\BootExecute’ from ‘autocheck autochk *’ to ‘autocheck autoche *’ in order to execute its payload during Windows startup. LoJax has modified the Registry key ‘HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\BootExecute’ from ‘autocheck autochk *’ to ‘autocheck autoche *’. LoJax has loaded an embedded NTFS DXE driver to be able to access and write to NTFS partitions.
title: ESET. (2018, September). LOJAX First UEFI rootkit found in the wild, courtesy of the Sednit group. Retrieved July 2, 2019.

text:
WastedLocker can identify network adjacent and accessible drives.
WastedLocker can enumerate removable drives prior to the encryption process.
WastedLocker has the ability to save and execute files as an alternate data stream (ADS).
title: Walter, J.. (2020, July 23). WastedLocker Ransomware: Abusing ADS and NTFS File Attributes. Retrieved September 14, 2021.

text: As part of the data reconnaissance phase, Proxysvc grabs the system time to send back to the control server. Proxysvc uses HTTP over SSL to communicate commands with the control server. Proxysvc can overwrite files indicated by the attacker before deleting them. Proxysvc automatically collects data about the victim and sends it to the control server. Proxysvc performs data exfiltration over the control server channel using a custom protocol. Proxysvc executes a binary on the system and logs the results into a temp file by using: cmd.exe /c " > %temp%\PM* .tmp 2>&1". Proxysvc gathers product names from the Registry key: HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion ProductName and the processor description from the Registry key HKLM\HARDWARE\DESCRIPTION\System\CentralProcessor\0 ProcessorNameString. Proxysvc lists files in directories. Proxysvc collects the OS version, country name, MAC address, computer name, and physical memory statistics. Proxysvc registers itself as a service on the victim’s machine to run as a standalone process. Proxysvc collects volume information for all drives on the system. Proxysvc can delete files indicated by the attacker and remove itself from disk using a batch file. Proxysvc lists processes running on the system. Proxysvc searches the local system and gathers data. Proxysvc collects the network adapter information and domain/username information based on current remote sessions.
title: Sherstobitoff, R., Malhotra, A. (2018, April 24). Analyzing Operation GhostSecret: Attack Seeks to Steal Data Worldwide. Retrieved May 16, 2018.

text:
TONESHELL has retrieved the disk serial number of the device using WMI query `SELECT volumeserialnumber FROM win32_logicaldisk where Name =’C:` to identify the victim machine.
TONESHELL has used WMI queries to gather information from the system.
title: Ken Towne, Francis Guibernau. (2023, March 23). Emulating the Politically Motivated Chinese APT Mustang Panda. Retrieved September 10, 2025.

text: Data captured by RawPOS is placed in a temporary file under a directory named "memdump".
title: Nesbit, B. and Ackerman, D. (2017, January). Malware Analysis Report - RawPOS Malware: Deconstructing an Intruder’s Toolkit. Retrieved October 4, 2017.

text:
Egregor has used multiple anti-analysis and anti-sandbox techniques to prevent automated analysis by sandboxes.
Egregor has used DLL side-loading to execute its payload.
Egregor has checked for the LogMein event log in an attempt to encrypt files in remote machines.
Egregor has used the Windows API to make detection more difficult.
Egregor's payloads are custom-packed, archived and encrypted to prevent analysis.
Egregor can inject its payload into iexplore.exe process.
title: Cybleinc. (2020, October 31). Egregor Ransomware – A Deep Dive Into Its Activities and Techniques. Retrieved December 29, 2020.

text:
BLUELIGHT can use HTTP/S for C2 using the Microsoft Graph API.
BLUELIGHT can collect the username on a compromised host.
BLUELIGHT can zip files before exfiltration.
BLUELIGHT can download additional files onto the host.
BLUELIGHT can enumerate files and collect associated metadata.
BLUELIGHT can uninstall itself.
BLUELIGHT can collect passwords stored in web browers, including Internet Explorer, Edge, Chrome, and Naver Whale.
BLUELIGHT has captured a screenshot of the display every 30 seconds for the first 5 minutes after initiating a C2 loop, and then once every five minutes thereafter.
BLUELIGHT can harvest cookies from Internet Explorer, Edge, Chrome, and Naver Whale browsers.
BLUELIGHT can collect IP information from the victim’s machine.
BLUELIGHT can collect the local time on a compromised host.
BLUELIGHT can check to see if the infected machine has VM tools running.
BLUELIGHT has exfiltrated data over its C2 channel.
BLUELIGHT can collect a list of anti-virus products installed on a machine.
BLUELIGHT has collected the computer name and OS version from victim machines.
BLUELIGHT can collect process filenames and SID authority level.
BLUELIGHT has a XOR-encoded payload.
BLUELIGHT can use different cloud providers for its C2.
BLUELIGHT has encoded data into a binary blob using XOR.
title: Cash, D., Grunzweig, J., Meltzer, M., Adair, S., Lancaster, T. (2021, August 17). North Korean APT InkySquid Infects Victims Using Browser Exploits. Retrieved September 30, 2021.

text: MultiLayer Wiper uses a batch script to clear file system cache memory via the ProcessIdleTasks export in advapi32.dll as an anti-analysis and anti-forensics technique. MultiLayer Wiper reboots the infected system following wiping and related tasks to prevent system recovery. MultiLayer Wiper wipes the boot sector of infected systems to inhibit system recovery. MultiLayer Wiper changes timestamps of overwritten files to either 1601.1.1 for NTFS filesystems, or 1980.1.1 for all other filesystems. MultiLayer Wiper changes the original path information of deleted files to make recovery efforts more difficult. MultiLayer Wiper uses a batch script launched via a scheduled task to delete Windows Event Logs. MultiLayer Wiper opens a handle to \\\\\\\\.\\\\PhysicalDrive0 and wipes the first 512 bytes of data from this location, removing the boot sector. MultiLayer Wiper deletes files on network drives, but corrupts and overwrites with random data files stored locally. BFG Agonizer wipes the boot sector of infected machines to inhibit system recovery. BFG Agonizer uses DLL unhooking to remove user mode inline hooks that security solutions often implement. BFG Agonizer also uses IAT unhooking to remove user-mode IAT hooks that security solutions also use. MultiLayer Wiper contains two binaries in its resources section, MultiList and MultiWip. MultiLayer Wiper drops and executes each of these items when run, then deletes them after execution. MultiLayer Wiper generates a list of all files and paths on the fixed drives of an infected system, enumerating all files on the system except specific folders defined in a hardcoded list. MultiLayer Wiper removes Windows event logs during execution. MultiLayer Wiper removes the Volume Shadow Copy (VSS) service from infected devices along with all present shadow copies. MultiLayer Wiper creates a malicious scheduled task that launches a batch file to remove Windows Event Logs. BFG Agonizer retrieves a device handle to \\\\.\\PhysicalDrive0 to wipe the boot sector of a given disk. BFG Agonizer uses elevated privileges to call NtRaiseHardError to induce a "blue screen of death" on infected systems, causing a system crash. Once shut down, the system is no longer bootable. MultiLayer Wiper uses a batch file, remover.bat to delete malware artifacts and the batch file itself during execution.
title: Or Chechik, Tom Fakterman, Daniel Frank & Assaf Dahan. (2023, November 6). Agonizing Serpens (Aka Agrius) Targeting the Israeli Higher Education and Tech Sectors. Retrieved May 22, 2024.

text: Zeroaccess is a kernel-mode rootkit.
title: Wyke, J. (2012, April). ZeroAccess. Retrieved July 18, 2016.

text:
Black Basta can make a random number of calls to the `kernel32.beep` function to hinder log analysis.
The Black Basta dropper has been digitally signed with a certificate issued by Akeo Consulting for legitimate executables used for creating bootable USB drives.
The Black Basta dropper has mimicked an application for creating USB bootable drivers.
Black Basta can use LDAP queries to connect to AD and iterate over connected workstations.
Black Basta can check system flags and libraries, process timing, and API's to detect code emulation or sandboxing.
The Black Basta dropper can check system flags, CPU registers, CPU instructions, process timing, system libraries, and APIs to determine if a debugger is present.
Black Basta can enumerate specific files for encryption.
Black Basta had added data prior to the Portable Executable (PE) header to prevent automatic scanners from identifying the payload.
title: Check Point. (2022, October 20). BLACK BASTA AND THE UNNOTICED DELIVERY. Retrieved March 8, 2023.

text:
HAWKBALL has used an OLE object that uses Equation Editor to drop the embedded shellcode.
HAWKBALL has leveraged several Windows API calls to create processes, gather disk information, and detect debugger activity.
HAWKBALL has encrypted data with XOR before sending it over the C2 channel.
HAWKBALL has created a cmd.exe reverse shell, executed commands, and uploaded output via the command line.
HAWKBALL has exploited Microsoft Office vulnerabilities CVE-2017-11882 and CVE-2018-0802 to deliver the payload.
HAWKBALL can collect the user name of the system.
HAWKBALL has the ability to delete files.
HAWKBALL has used HTTP to communicate with a single hard-coded C2 server.
HAWKBALL can collect the OS version, architecture information, and computer name.
HAWKBALL has encrypted the payload with an XOR-based algorithm.
HAWKBALL has sent system information and files over the C2 channel.
title: Patil, S. and Williams, M.. (2019, June 5). Government Sector in Central Asia Targeted With New HAWKBALL Backdoor Delivered via Microsoft Office Vulnerabilities. Retrieved June 20, 2019.

text: Clop can delete the shadow volumes with vssadmin Delete Shadows /all /quiet and can use bcdedit to disable recovery options. Clop has searched folders and subfolders for files to encrypt. Clop has used a simple XOR operation to decrypt strings. Clop can enumerate all processes on the victim's machine. Clop can enumerate network shares. Clop has checked the keyboard language using the GetKeyboardLayout() function to avoid installation on Russian-language or other Commonwealth of Independent States-language machines; it will also check the GetTextCharset function.
title: Mundo, A. (2019, August 1). Clop Ransomware. Retrieved May 10, 2021.

text: Flagpro can execute malicious VBA macros embedded in .xlsm files. Flagpro has been distributed via spearphishing as an email attachment. Flagpro has been used to execute net view on a targeted system. Flagpro has the ability to wait for a specified time interval between communicating with and executing commands from C2. Flagpro can use Native API to enable obfuscation including `GetLastError` and `GetTickCount`. Flagpro has exfiltrated data to the C2 server. Flagpro has encoded bidirectional data communications between a target system and C2 server using Base64. Flagpro has dropped an executable file to the startup directory. Flagpro has relied on users clicking a malicious attachment delivered through spearphishing. Flagpro can close specific Windows Security and Internet Explorer dialog boxes to mask external connections. Flagpro can download additional malware from the C2 server. Flagpro has been used to execute the net localgroup administrators command on a targeted system. Flagpro has been used to execute the ipconfig /all command on a victim system. Flagpro can check the name of the window displayed on the system. Flagpro has been used to run the whoami command on the system. Flagpro has been used to execute `net view` to discover mapped network shares. Flagpro has been delivered within ZIP or RAR password-protected archived files. Flagpro can collect data from a compromised host, including Windows authentication information. Flagpro can communicate with its C2 using HTTP. Flagpro can check whether the target system is using Japanese, Taiwanese, or English through detection of specific Windows Security and Internet Explorer dialog. Flagpro has been used to execute netstat -ano on a compromised host. Flagpro can download malicious files with a .tmp extension and append them with .exe prior to execution. Flagpro can use `cmd.exe` to execute commands received from C2. Flagpro has been used to run the tasklist command on a compromised system.
title: Hada, H. (2021, December 28).  Flagpro The new malware used by BlackTech. Retrieved March 25, 2022.

text:
MuddyViper has decrypted the embedded HackBrowserData tool prior to execution.
Fooder has used a custom delay function (`delayExecution(integer)`) and Sleep API calls (`Sleep(integer)`) to slow code execution.
MuddyViper has launched a reverse shell using a provided command line.
Fooder has frequently masqueraded as the Snake game, using strings such as “Welcome to snake Game” and mutexes such as “SNAKE_G.”
LP-Notes has used a custom addition-based function and a string stacking function for string encryption.
Fooder has used the `DuplicateTokenEx` API to duplicate the token of a specified process, and `CreateProcessAsUserA` to execute its payload.
MuddyViper has the ability to establish persistence by configuring its installation directory as a Windows Startup folder by setting the following Registry values to `%APPDATALOCAL%\Microsoft\Windows\PPBCompatCache\ManagerCache`: `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\User Shell Folders\Startup` and `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\Shell Folders\Startup`.
Fooder has stored its embedded payload in encrypted form within the binary, using a hardcoded key modified at runtime to produce the AES decryption key.
LP-Notes has stored collected credentials in ` C:\Users\Public\Downloads\lp-notes.txt`.
MuddyViper has displayed a fake Windows Security dialog to gather credentials.
MuddyViper has the ability to sleep for a certain amount of time, with the default being one minute.
MuddyViper has used cmd.exe to launch a reverse shell.
LP-Notes has used the `ImpersonateLoggedOnUser` API to impersonate the security context of the taskhostw.exe process. Additionally, LP-Notes has also used the `CredUIPromptForWindowsCredentialsW` API to obtain Windows credentials.
MuddyViper has the ability to download files from the C2 server. Additionally, MuddyViper has the ability to download a file in chunks with sleep time between each chunk.
LP-Notes has used stolen Windows credentials to log in as the users.
Fooder has decrypted payloads using the WinCrypt API and the AES key.
MuddyViper has archived collected web browser data into a file named CacheDump.zip.
MuddyViper has the ability to collect running processes.
LP-Notes has decrypted strings with lengths ranging from 15 to 19 characters using the same decryption key for each string.
LP-Notes has encrypted collected credentials using AES-CBC from the CNG API and the key ED15C8344B45DAED1E0578F8BC1A32411812C61F4CB45D89B107287DE0E09FFC and the initialization vector 91A4E6F6D51DAEE773A8F00279792578.
MuddyViper has reflectively loaded the decrypted HackBrowserData tool in a new thread.
MuddyViper has uploaded files to the C2 server. Additionally, MuddyViper has the ability to upload the specified file in chunks with sleep time between each chunk.
LP-Notes has searched for the process taskhostw.exe.
LP-Notes has dynamically resolved API functions during the C runtime startup.
MuddyViper has the ability to clear the Registry values in the Windows Startup folder that were previously set for persistence.
LP-Notes has displayed a fake Windows Security dialog box to prompt for Windows credentials.
LP-Notes has impersonated the security context of the taskhostw.exe process via the `ImpersonateLoggedOnUser` API.
MuddyViper has used HTTP GET requests over port 443 and with the WINHTTP_FLAG_SECURE set to SSL/TLS via the WinHTTP API.
Fooder has used the WinCrypt API for payload decryption, `DuplicateTokenEx` to duplicate the token of a specified process, and `CreateProcessAsUserA` for payload execution.
MuddyViper has the ability to relaunch itself using the `CreateProcessW` API.
LP-Notes has been downloaded and executed by PowerShell’s`Invoke-WebRequest` and `Invoke-Expression` cmdlets.
MuddyViper has used PowerShell.exe to launch a reverse shell.
Fooder has reflectively loaded a payload into memory.
MuddyViper has the ability to establish persistence by creating a scheduled task named ManageOnDriveUpdater to launch itself during system startup.
MuddyViper has the ability to check for a specified list of security tools in the compromised environment.
MuddyViper has the ability to encrypt C2 communication using AES-CBC using the CNG API, the key `0608101047106453101617106423101013101012101083109710108585106969`, and the initialization vector `0`.
title: ESET Research. (2025, December 2). MuddyWater: Snakes by the riverbank. Retrieved February 17, 2026.

text:
QakBot can move laterally using worm-like functionality through exploitation of SMB.
QakBot can use MSIExec to spawn multiple cmd.exe processes.
title: CS. (2020, October 7). Duck Hunting with Falcon Complete: A Fowl Banking Trojan Evolves, Part 2. Retrieved September 27, 2021.

text: HyperStack can enumerate all account names on a remote share. Kazuar has used internal nodes on the compromised network for C2 communications. HyperStack can connect to the IPC$ share on remote machines. Carbon decrypts task and configuration files for execution. HyperStack can add the name of its communication pipe to HKLM\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Services\\lanmanserver\\parameters\NullSessionPipes. HyperStack has used RSA encryption for C2 communications. Carbon encrypts configuration files and tasks for the malware to complete using CAST-128 algorithm. HyperStack can use default credentials to connect to IPC$ shares on remote machines. Carbon can use Pastebin to receive C2 commands. HyperStack can use Windows API's ConnectNamedPipe and WNetAddConnection2 to detect incoming connections and connect to remote shares. Carbon has used RSA encryption for C2 communications. Carbon can use HTTP in C2 communications.
title: Accenture. (2020, October). Turla uses HyperStack, Carbon, and Kazuar to compromise government entity. Retrieved December 2, 2020.

text:
AuTo Stealer can collect data such as PowerPoint files, Word documents, Excel files, PDF files, text files, database files, and image files from an infected machine.
Action RAT has the ability to collect the MAC address of an infected host.
AuTo Stealer can use HTTP to communicate with its C2 servers.
AuTo Stealer can use TCP to communicate with command and control servers.
Action RAT has the ability to download additional payloads onto an infected machine.
Action RAT has the ability to collect drive and file information on an infected machine.
Action RAT has the ability to collect the username from an infected host.
Action RAT can use Base64 to decode actor-controlled C2 server communications.
AuTo Stealer has the ability to collect the username from an infected host.
AuTo Stealer can store collected data from an infected host to a file named `Hostname_UserName.txt` prior to exfiltration.
AuTo Stealer can exfiltrate data over actor-controlled C2 servers via HTTP or TCP.
Action RAT's commands, strings, and domains can be Base64 encoded within the payload.
Action RAT can identify AV products on an infected host using the following command: `cmd.exe WMIC /Node:localhost /Namespace:\\root\SecurityCenter2 Path AntiVirusProduct Get displayName /Format:List`.
AuTo Stealer can place malicious executables in a victim's AutoRun registry key or StartUp directory, depending on the AV product installed, to maintain persistence.
Action RAT can use HTTP to communicate with C2 servers.
Action RAT has the ability to collect the hostname, OS version, and OS architecture of an infected host.
Action RAT can use WMI to gather AV products installed on an infected host.
Action RAT can use `cmd.exe` to execute commands on an infected host.
AuTo Stealer has the ability to collect the hostname and OS information from an infected host.
AuTo Stealer can use `cmd.exe` to execute a created batch file.
Action RAT can collect local data from an infected machine.
AuTo Stealer has the ability to collect information about installed AV products from an infected host.
title: Threat Intelligence Team. (2021, December 2). SideCopy APT: Connecting lures victims, payloads to infrastructure. Retrieved June 13, 2022.

text:
Remsec can ping or traceroute a remote host.
Remsec has a plugin that can perform ARP scanning as well as port scanning.
Remsec can add or remove applications or ports on the Windows firewall or disable it entirely.
Remsec schedules the execution one of its modules by creating a new scheduler task.
Remsec can perform DLL injection.
Remsec can obtain information about the current user.
Remsec can obtain the OS version information, computer name, processor architecture, machine role, and OS edition.
Remsec has a package that collects documents from any inserted USB sticks.
Remsec can obtain a list of active connections and open ports.
Remsec can obtain a list of users.
Remsec has a plugin to drop and execute vulnerable Outpost Sandbox or avast! Virtualization drivers in order to gain kernel mode privileges.
Remsec has a plugin detect security products via active drivers.
Remsec can dump the SAM database.
Remsec can obtain a process list from the victim.
Remsec can obtain information about network configuration, including the routing table, ARP cache, and DNS cache.
Remsec has a plugin to detect active drivers of some security products.
title: Kaspersky Lab's Global Research & Analysis Team. (2016, August 9). The ProjectSauron APT. Technical Analysis. Retrieved August 17, 2016.

text:
gh0st RAT can capture the victim’s screen remotely.
gh0st RAT is able to open a remote shell to execute commands.
gh0st RAT uses RC4 and XOR to encrypt C2 traffic.
title: Pantazopoulos, N. (2018, April 17). Decoding network data from a Gh0st RAT variant. Retrieved November 2, 2018.

text: FinFisher uses DLL side-loading to load malicious programs. A FinFisher variant also uses DLL search order hijacking. FinFisher creates a new Windows service with the malicious executable for persistence. FinFisher contains junk code in its functions in an effort to confuse disassembly programs. FinFisher obtains the hardware device list and checks if the MD5 of the vendor ID is equal to a predefined list in order to check for sandbox/virtualized environments. FinFisher renames one of its .dll files to uxtheme.dll in an apparent attempt to masquerade as a legitimate file. FinFisher injects itself into various processes depending on whether it is low integrity or high integrity. FinFisher establishes persistence by creating the Registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\Run. FinFisher queries Registry values as part of its anti-sandbox checks. FinFisher performs UAC bypass. FinFisher clears the system event logs using OpenEventLog/ClearEventLog APIs . FinFisher extracts and decrypts stage 3 malware, which is stored in encrypted resources. FinFisher takes a screenshot of the screen and displays it on top of all other windows for few seconds in an apparent attempt to hide some messages showed by the system during the setup process. FinFisher checks if the victim OS is 32 or 64-bit. FinFisher is heavily obfuscated in many ways, including through the use of spaghetti code in its functions in an effort to confuse disassembly programs. It also uses a custom XOR algorithm to obfuscate code. FinFisher uses token manipulation with NtFilterToken as part of UAC bypass. FinFisher enumerates directories and scans for certain files. Some FinFisher variants incorporate an MBR rootkit. FinFisher checks its parent process for indications that it is running in a sandbox setup.
title: Allievi, A.,Flori, E. (2018, March 01). FinFisher exposed: A researcher’s tale of defeating traps, tricks, and complex virtual machines. Retrieved July 9, 2018.

text:
LODEINFO can halt execution if the “en_US” locale is identified on a victim's machine.
LODEINFO can encrypt C2 communication with a hardcoded (NV4HDOeOVyL) Vigenere cipher key.
LODEINFO can use a hashing algorithm to dynamically resolve API function addresses.
LODEINFO can looks for the “en_US” locale on the victim’s machine.
LODEINFO can append C2 communication with randomly generated junk data.
LODEINFO can use Windows APIs such as `VirtualAllocEx()`, `WriteProcessMemory()`, `CreateRemoteThread()`, `NtAllocateVirtualMemory()`, `NtWriteVirtualMemory()`, and `RtlCreateUserThread()` to enable memory injection of shellcode.
LODEINFO can capture system time to send to the C2.
title: Ishimaru, S. (2022, October 31). APT10: Tracking down LODEINFO 2022, part II. Retrieved April 17, 2026.

text:
EKANS looks for processes from a hard-coded list.
EKANS can determine the domain of a compromised host.
title: Singleton, C. and Kiefer, C. (2020, September 28). Ransomware 2020: Attack Trends Affecting Organizations Worldwide. Retrieved September 20, 2021.

text:
Gootloader can insert malicious scripts to compromise vulnerable content management systems (CMS).
Gootloader can use an embedded script to check the IP address of potential victims visiting compromised websites.
Gootloader has used compromised legitimate domains to as a delivery network for malicious payloads.
Gootloader can use IP geolocation to determine if the person browsing to a compromised site is within a targeted territory such as the US, Canada, Germany, and South Korea.
Gootloader can determine if a targeted system is part of an Active Directory domain by expanding the %USERDNSDOMAIN% environment variable.
Gootloader can retrieve a Base64 encoded stager from C2.
title: Pirozzi, A. (2021, June 16). Gootloader: ‘Initial Access as a Service’ Platform Expands Its Search for High Value Targets. Retrieved May 28, 2024.

text: ZxShell can leverage native API including RegisterServiceCtrlHandler to register a service.RegisterServiceCtrlHandler
title: MITRE ATT&CK software S0412

text: EvilBunny's dropper has checked the number of processes and the length and strings of its own file name to identify if the malware is in a sandbox environment. EvilBunny has used various API calls as part of its checks to see if the malware is running in a sandbox. EvilBunny has used the API calls NtQuerySystemTime, GetSystemTimeAsFileTime, and GetTickCount to gather time metrics as part of its checks to see if the malware is running in a sandbox. EvilBunny has created Registry keys for persistence in [HKLM|HKCU]\…\CurrentVersion\Run. EvilBunny has executed C2 commands directly via HTTP. EvilBunny has used time measurements from 3 different APIs before and after performing sleep operations to check and abort if the malware is running in a sandbox. EvilBunny has exploited CVE-2011-4369, a vulnerability in the PRC component in Adobe Reader. EvilBunny has been observed querying installed antivirus software. EvilBunny has an integrated scripting engine to download and execute Lua scripts. EvilBunny has downloaded additional Lua scripts from the C2. EvilBunny has used WMI to gather information about the system. EvilBunny has used EnumProcesses() to identify how many process are running in the environment. EvilBunny has executed commands via scheduled tasks. EvilBunny has deleted the initial dropper after running through the environment checks.
title: Marschalek, M.. (2014, December 16). EvilBunny: Malware Instrumented By Lua. Retrieved June 28, 2019.

text:
Caterpillar WebShell has a module to perform brute force attacks on a system.
Caterpillar WebShell has a module to collect information from the local database.
Explosive has encrypted communications with the RC4 method.
Caterpillar WebShell can run commands on the compromised asset with CMD functions.
Caterpillar WebShell has a module to use a port scanner on a system.
Caterpillar WebShell can obtain a list of the services from a system.
Caterpillar WebShell has a module to download and upload files to the system.
Caterpillar WebShell can upload files over the C2 channel.
Caterpillar WebShell can search for files in directories.
Caterpillar WebShell can gather the IP address from the victim's machine using the IP config command.
Caterpillar WebShell has a command to modify a Registry key.
Caterpillar WebShell has a module to use a rootkit on a system.
Caterpillar WebShell can obtain a list of local groups of users from a system.
Caterpillar WebShell has a module to gather information from the compromised asset, including the computer version, computer name, IIS version, and more.
Caterpillar WebShell can gather a list of processes running on the machine.
Caterpillar WebShell can obtain a list of user accounts from a victim's machine.
title: ClearSky Cyber Security. (2021, January). “Lebanese Cedar” APT Global Lebanese Espionage Campaign Leveraging Web Servers. Retrieved February 10, 2021.

text: HTTPBrowser has used HTTP and HTTPS for command and control. OwaAuth is a Web shell that appears to be exclusively used by Threat Group-3390. It is installed as an ISAPI filter on Exchange servers and shares characteristics with the China Chopper Web shell. OwaAuth uses the filename owaauth.dll, which is a legitimate file that normally resides in %ProgramFiles%\Microsoft\Exchange Server\ClientAccess\Owa\Auth\; the malicious file by the same name is saved in %ProgramFiles%\Microsoft\Exchange Server\ClientAccess\Owa\bin\. HTTPBrowser is capable of capturing keystrokes on victims. PlugX can be configured to use DNS for command and control. HTTPBrowser has used DNS for command and control. OwaAuth DES-encrypts captured credentials using the key 12345678 before writing the credentials to a log file. HTTPBrowser is capable of writing a file to the compromised system from the C2 server. OwaAuth has a command to timestop a file or directory. OwaAuth uses incoming HTTP requests with a username keyword and commands and handles them as instructions to perform actions. PlugX can be configured to use raw TCP or UDP for command and control. ASPXSpy is a Web shell. The ASPXTool version used by Threat Group-3390 has been deployed to accessible servers running Internet Information Services (IIS). HTTPBrowser is capable of spawning a reverse shell on a victim. OwaAuth has been loaded onto Exchange servers and disguised as an ISAPI filter (owaauth.dll). The IIS w3wp.exe process then loads the malicious DLL. HTTPBrowser's code may be obfuscated through structured exception handling and return-oriented programming. OwaAuth captures and DES-encrypts credentials before writing the username and password to a log file, C:\log.txt. OwaAuth has a command to list its directory and logical drives.
title: Dell SecureWorks Counter Threat Unit Threat Intelligence. (2015, August 5). Threat Group-3390 Targets Organizations for Cyberespionage. Retrieved August 18, 2018.

text:
Mispadu collects the OS version, computer name, and language ID.
Mispadu has the ability to capture and replace Bitcoin wallet data in the clipboard on a compromised host.
Mispadu uses RunDLL32 for execution via its injector DLL.
Mispadu searches for various filesystem paths to determine what banking applications are installed on the victim’s machine.
Mispadu can enumerate the running processes on a compromised host.
Mispadu utilizes malicious Google Chrome browser extensions to steal financial data.
title: ESET Security. (2019, November 19). Mispadu: Advertisement for a discounted Unhappy Meal. Retrieved March 13, 2024.

text: XAgentOSX contains the deletFileFromPath function to delete a specified file using the NSFileManager:removeFileAtPath method. XAgentOSX contains the getProcessList function to run ps aux to get running processes. XAgentOSX contains the readFiles function to return a detailed listing (sometimes recursive) of a specified directory. XAgentOSX contains the showBackupIosFolder function to check for IOS device backups by running ls -la ~/Library/Application\ Support/MobileSync/Backup/. XAgentOSX contains the getFirefoxPassword function to attempt to locate Firefox passwords. XAgentOSX contains the takeScreenShot (along with startTakeScreenShot and stopTakeScreenShot) functions to take screenshots using the CGGetActiveDisplayList, CGDisplayCreateImage, and NSImage:initWithCGImage methods. XAgentOSX contains the getInfoOSX function to return the OS X version as well as the current user. XAgentOSX contains the getInstalledAPP function to run ls -la /Applications to gather what applications are installed. XAgentOSX contains keylogging functionality that will monitor for active application windows and write them to the log, it can handle special characters, and it will buffer by default 50 characters before sending them out over the C2 infrastructure. XAgentOSX contains the ftpUpload function to use the FTPManager:uploadFile method to upload files from the target system. XAgentOSX contains the execFile function to execute a specified file on the system using the NSTask:launch method.
title: Robert Falcone. (2017, February 14). XAgentOSX: Sofacy's Xagent macOS Tool. Retrieved July 12, 2017.

text: Sakula calls cmd.exe to run various DLL files via rundll32. Sakula contains UAC bypass code for both 32- and 64-bit systems. Sakula uses single-byte XOR obfuscation to obfuscate many of its files. Some Sakula samples use cmd.exe to delete temporary files. Most Sakula samples maintain persistence by setting the Registry Run key SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\ in the HKLM or HKCU hive, with the Registry value and file name varying by sample. Sakula uses HTTP for C2. Sakula has the capability to download files. Sakula calls cmd.exe to run various DLL files via rundll32 and also to perform file cleanup. Sakula also has the capability to invoke a reverse shell. Sakula uses DLL side-loading, typically using a digitally signed sample of Kaspersky Anti-Virus (AV) 6.0 for Windows Workstations or McAfee's Outlook Scan About Box to load malicious DLL files. Sakula encodes C2 traffic with single-byte XOR keys. Some Sakula samples install themselves as services for persistence by calling WinExec with the net start argument.
title: Dell SecureWorks Counter Threat Unit Threat Intelligence. (2015, July 30). Sakula Malware Family. Retrieved January 26, 2016.

text: CharmPower can use PowerShell for payload execution and C2 communication. CharmPower has the ability to list running processes through the use of `tasklist`. CharmPower can remove persistence-related artifacts from the Registry. CharmPower can use `netsh wlan show profiles` to list specific Wi-Fi profile details. CharmPower can use HTTP to communicate with C2. CharmPower has the ability to capture screenshots. CharmPower can send additional modules over C2 encoded with base64. CharmPower can exfiltrate gathered data to a hardcoded C2 URL via HTTP POST. CharmPower has the ability to download additional modules to a compromised host. CharmPower can delete created files from a compromised system. CharmPower can enumerate the OS version and computer name on a targeted system. CharmPower can enumerate drives and list the contents of the C: drive on a victim's computer. The C# implementation of the CharmPower command execution module can use cmd. CharmPower can collect data and files from a compromised host. CharmPower can use `wmic` to gather information from a system. CharmPower has the ability to use ipconfig to enumerate system network settings. CharmPower can send victim data via FTP with credentials hardcoded in the script. CharmPower has the ability to enumerate `Uninstall` registry values. CharmPower can send additional modules over C2 encrypted with a simple substitution cipher. CharmPower can change its C2 channel once every 360 loops by retrieving a new domain from the actors’ S3 bucket. CharmPower can download additional modules from actor-controlled Amazon S3 buckets. CharmPower can decrypt downloaded modules prior to execution. CharmPower can list the installed applications on a compromised host. CharmPower can retrieve C2 domain information from actor-controlled S3 buckets.
title: Check Point. (2022, January 11). APT35 exploits Log4j vulnerability to distribute new modular PowerShell toolkit. Retrieved January 24, 2022.

text: PlugX allows actors to spawn a reverse shell on a victim. PlugX has a module to enumerate drives and find files recursively. PlugX has also checked the path from which it is running for specific parameters prior to execution. PlugX has a module to create, delete, or modify Registry keys. PlugX can enumerate and query for information contained within the Windows Registry. PlugX adds Run key entries in the Registry to establish persistence. PlugX has established persistence via the registry keys `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run` and `HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run`. PlugX has a module to download and execute files on the compromised machine. PlugX decompresses and decrypts itself using the Microsoft API call RtlDecompressBuffer. PlugX has also decrypted its payloads in memory. PlugX has a module for enumerating TCP and UDP network connections and associated processes using the netstat command. PlugX can be added as a service to establish persistence. PlugX also has a module to change service configurations as well as start, control, and delete services. PlugX has a module for capturing keystrokes per process including window titles. PlugX has a module to enumerate network shares. PlugX has a module to list the processes running on a machine. PlugX allows the operator to capture screenshots.
title: Computer Incident Response Center Luxembourg. (2013, March 29). Analysis of a PlugX variant. Retrieved November 5, 2018.

text:
Shai-Hulud has used JavaScript to create JSON file output and run scripts using node.js.
Shai-Hulud has destroyed the victim’s home directory by overwriting and deleting every writable file within the user's home folder. Shai-Hulud has also utilized the `shred` command on Linux devices.
Shai-Hulud has stolen access tokens and API tokens from with CI/CD pipeline solutions and repositories.
Shai-Hulud has stopped `systemd-resolved` in order to manipulate DNS and firewalls.
Shai-Hulud has masqueraded as a legitimate Bun installer.
