Shai-Hulud has created a repository named `Shai-Hulud` under the compromised account that commits a JSON dump that contains system information, environment variables and collected secrets. Shai-Hulud has also posted stolen credentials to public GitHub repositories.
Shai-Hulud has augmented its installation process by having its original install process exit cleanly to provide the user with the illusion that the service is installed normally.
Shai-Hulud has published itself on compromised code repository maintainers within infected packages in attempts to propagate to other victims. Shai-Hulud has also modified versions of code packages.
Shai-Hulud has gathered secrets from AWS Secrets and GCP Secret Manager. Shai-Hulud has also gathered data from Azure Key Vault.
Shai-Hulud has utilized double-base64 encoding to store stolen secrets within the Github Action Logs within the victim account. Shai-Hulud has also leveraged three layers of base64 encoding of exfiltrated data for anti-forensic purposes.
Shai-Hulud has downloaded packages from code repositories. Shai-Hulud has also downloaded and executed the secrets-discovery tool TruffleHog to gather sensitive data.
Shai-Hulud has also leveraged GitHub actions from stolen accounts in order to create a malicious Github workflow within `.github/workflows/discussion.yaml`.
Shai-Hulud has leveraged captured valid NPM tokens to enumerate and update packages on compromised accounts. Shai-Hulud has also utilized stolen GitHub access tokens to access compromised accounts.
Shai-Hulud has utilized Linux shell commands to modify configuration files.
Shai-Hulud has replaced DNS configuration from `/tmp/resolved.conf` in order to gain control of network-level control within CI environments and has flushed iptables rules using `sudo iptables -F OUTPUT` and `sudo iptables -F DOCKER-USER`.
Shai-Hulud has gathered victim system information.
Shai-Hulud has inserted a new lifecycle hook to include `postinstall`. Shai-Hulud has also leveraged the NPM lifecycle hook `preinstall`.
Shai-Hulud has attempted to gain root access by leveraging `sudo` and `/etc/sudoers.d`.
Shai-Hulud has suppressed NPM warnings by silently exiting through the use of the NPM success code that has a setting that all errors exit with `code 0`.
Shai-Hulud has suppressed victim NPM warnings using `process[“exit’](0x0);` which results in having all errors exit with code 0.
Shai-Hulud has gathered sensitive data stored in the Node.JS file `process.env` to include credentials and API keys. Shai-Hulud has harvested credentials stored in config files and credential files in victim environments to include `~/.aws/credentials`, `application_default_credentials.json`, and `azureProfile.json`. Shai-Hulud has also targeted credentials and tokens stored in NPM files `.npmrc` and GitHub config files.
title: Socket Research Team. (2025, November 24). Shai Hulud Strikes Again (v2). Retrieved April 9, 2026.

text:
Kasidet has the ability to change firewall settings to allow a plug-in to be downloaded.
Kasidet has the ability to search for a given process name in processes currently running in the system.
Kasidet has the ability to download and execute additional files.
Kasidet has the ability to obtain a victim's system name and operating system version.
Kasidet has the ability to identify any anti-virus installed on the infected system.
Kasidet can execute commands using cmd.exe.
Kasidet has the ability to initiate keylogging.
Kasidet has the ability to search for a given filename on a victim.
Kasidet creates a Registry Run key to establish persistence.
Kasidet has the ability to initiate keylogging and screen captures.
title: Yadav, A., et al. (2016, January 29). Malicious Office files dropping Kasidet and Dridex. Retrieved March 24, 2016.

text:
ShadowPad has sent data back to C2 every 8 hours.
ShadowPad has encoded data as readable Latin characters.
ShadowPad has downloaded code from a C2 server.
ShadowPad has encrypted its payload, a virtual file system, and various files.
title: GReAT. (2017, August 15). ShadowPad in corporate networks. Retrieved March 22, 2021.

text:
Bumblebee can inject code into multiple processes on infected endpoints.
Bumblebee can compress data stolen from the Registry and volume shadow copies prior to exfiltration.
Bumblebee has the ability to bypass UAC to deploy post exploitation tools with elevated privileges.
Bumblebee has been spread through e-mail campaigns with malicious links.
Bumblebee has relied upon a user downloading a file from a OneDrive link for execution.
Bumblebee can capture and compress stolen credentials from the Registry and volume shadow copies.
Bumblebee can use `odbcconf.exe` to run DLLs on targeted hosts.
title: Cybereason. (2022, August 17). Bumblebee Loader – The High Road to Enterprise Domain Control. Retrieved August 29, 2022.

text:
Valak has the ability to enumerate domain admin accounts.
Valak can execute JavaScript containing configuration data for establishing persistence.
Valak has the ability to identify the domain and the MAC and IP addresses of an infected machine.
Valak can collect sensitive mailing information from Exchange servers, including credentials and the domain certificate of an enterprise.
Valak has the ability to take screenshots on a compromised host.
Valak has the ability to enumerate local admin accounts.
Valak has the ability to enumerate running processes on a compromised host.
Valak can determine if a compromised host has security products installed.
Valak can gather information regarding the user.
Valak has used PowerShell to download additional modules.
title: Salem, E. et al. (2020, May 28). VALAK: MORE THAN MEETS THE EYE . Retrieved June 19, 2020.

text: HyperBro has the ability to download additional files. HyperBro can run shellcode it injects into a newly created process. HyperBro has the ability to take screenshots. HyperBro has used HTTPS for C2 communications. HyperBro can list all services and their configurations. HyperBro has the ability to start and stop a specified service. HyperBro has the ability to run an application (CreateProcessW) or script/file (ShellExecuteW) via API. HyperBro has the ability to delete a specified file. HyperBro has used a legitimate application to sideload a DLL to decrypt, decompress, and run a payload.
title: Falcone, R. and Lancaster, T. (2019, May 28). Emissary Panda Attacks Middle East Government Sharepoint Servers. Retrieved July 9, 2019.

text: NETWIRE can create a scheduled task to establish persistence. NETWIRE can use Native API including CreateProcess GetProcessById, and WriteProcessMemory. NETWIRE has used a custom encryption algorithm to encrypt collected data. NETWIRE can capture session logon details from a compromised host. NETWIRE has used a custom obfuscation algorithm to hide strings including Registry keys, APIs, and DLL names. NETWIRE has been executed through use of VBScripts. The NETWIRE binary has been executed via PowerShell script. NETWIRE can discover processes on compromised hosts. NETWIRE has the ability to write collected data to a file created in the ./LOGS directory. NETWIRE has used web services including Paste.ee to host payloads. NETWIRE can downloaded payloads from C2 to the compromised host.
title: Maniath, S. and Kadam P. (2019, March 19). Dissecting a NETWIRE Phishing Campaign's Usage of Process Hollowing. Retrieved January 7, 2021.

text:
Carberp has maintained persistence by placing itself inside the current user's startup folder.
Carberp has collected the operating system version from the infected system.
Carberp has exploited multiple Windows vulnerabilities (CVE-2010-2743, CVE-2010-3338, CVE-2010-4398, CVE-2008-1084) and a .NET Runtime Optimization vulnerability for privilege escalation.
Carberp has attempted to disable security software by creating a suspended process for the security software and injecting code to delete antivirus core files when the process is resumed.
Carberp has used user mode rootkit techniques to remain hidden on the system.
Carberp has queried the infected system's registry searching for specific registry keys associated with antivirus products.
Carberp can capture display screenshots with the screens_dll.dll plugin.
Carberp's passw.plug plugin can gather passwords saved in Opera, Internet Explorer, Safari, Firefox, and Chrome.
Carberp has queued an APC routine to explorer.exe by calling ZwQueueApcThread.
Carberp has searched the Image File Execution Options registry key for "Debugger" within every subkey.
Carberp's passw.plug plugin can gather account information from multiple instant messaging, email, and social media services, as well as FTP, VNC, and VPN clients.
Carberp has used XOR-based encryption to mask C2 server locations within the trojan.
Carberp has hooked several Windows API functions to steal credentials.
Carberp can start a remote VNC session by downloading a new plugin.
title: Giuliani, M., Allievi, A. (2011, February 28). Carberp - a modular information stealing trojan. Retrieved September 12, 2024.

text:
WhisperGate can use `cmd.exe` to execute commands.
WhisperGate can recognize the presence of monitoring tools on a target system.
WhisperGate has used `InstallUtil.exe` as part of its process to disable Windows Defender.
WhisperGate can stop its execution when it recognizes the presence of certain monitoring tools.
title: Falcone, R. et al.. (2022, January 20). Threat Brief: Ongoing Russia and Ukraine Cyber Conflict. Retrieved March 10, 2022.

text:
IOCONTROL has used the Ultimate Packer for eXecutables (UPX) to pack the malware.
IOCONTROL has used the AES-256-CBC algorithm to decrypt configuration files associated with the malware.
IOCONTROL has used the Advanced Encryption Standard 256-bit Cypher Block Chaining (AES-256-CBC) algorithm to encrypt its configuration files which are used to store information like file paths and IP addresses to connect to.
title: Dragos. (2026, February 17). Dragos 2026 OT/ICS Cybersecurity Report and Year in Review. Retrieved September 2, 2026.

text:
Daserf uses RC4 encryption to obfuscate HTTP traffic.
Daserf uses custom base64 encoding to obfuscate HTTP traffic.
Daserf uses HTTP for C2.
title: Counter Threat Unit Research Team. (2017, October 12). BRONZE BUTLER Targets Japanese Enterprises. Retrieved January 4, 2018.

text:
Dacls can collect data on running and parent processes.
Dacls has had its payload named with a dot prefix to make it hidden from view in the Finder application.
Dacls can encrypt its configuration file with AES CBC.
Dacls can scan directories on a compromised host.
Dacls can establish persistence via a Launch Daemon.
Dacls can establish persistence via a LaunchAgent.
Dacls can use HTTPS in C2 communications.
Dacls can download its payload from a C2 server.
title: Mabutas, G. (2020, May 11). New MacOS Dacls RAT Backdoor Shows Lazarus’ Multi-Platform Attack Capability. Retrieved August 10, 2020.

text: DynoWiper has enumerated and overwritten files on all removeable and fixed drives.
title: ESET. (2026, January 30). Russian Sandworm group attacks energy company in Poland with DynoWiper, ESET Research discovers. Retrieved April 22, 2026.

text:
FlawedAmmyy can collect clipboard data.
Amadey has decoded antivirus name strings.
Amadey has modified the `:Zone.Identifier` in the ADS area to zero.
FlawedAmmyy has been installed via `msiexec.exe`.
SDBbot has sent collected data from a compromised host to its C2 servers.
FlawedAmmyy has used `rundll32` for execution.
Amadey has used fast flux DNS for its C2.
FlawedAmmyy can collect keyboard events.
FlawedAmmyy enumerates the current user during the initial infection.
Amadey has searched for folders associated with antivirus software.
SDBbot has used rundll32.exe to execute DLLs.
FlawedAmmyy has collected information and files from a compromised machine.
SDBbot has the ability to identify the OS version, OS bit information and computer name.
FlawedAmmyy has established persistence via the `HKCU\SOFTWARE\microsoft\windows\currentversion\run` registry key.
SDBbot can collected the country code of a compromised machine.
FlawedAmmyy can collect mouse events.
FlawedAmmyy can capture screenshots.
FlawedAmmyy has used PowerShell to execute commands.
FlawedAmmyy has sent data collected from a compromised host to its C2 servers.
SDBbot can enumerate a list of running processes on a compromised machine.
FlawedAmmyy has used `cmd` to execute commands on a compromised host.
FlawedAmmyy enumerates the privilege level of the victim during the initial infection.
FlawedAmmyy can execute batch scripts to delete files.
FlawedAmmyy can transfer files from C2.
title: Financial Security Institute. (2020, February 28). Profiling of TA505 Threat Group That Continues to Attack the Financial Sector. Retrieved July 14, 2022.

text:
Black Basta can encrypt files with the ChaCha20 cypher and using a multithreaded process to increase speed. Black Basta has also encrypted files while the victim system is in safe mode, appending `.basta` upon completion.
Black Basta has set the desktop wallpaper on victims' machines to display a ransom note.
title: Ballmer, D. (2022, May 6). Black Basta: Rebrand of Conti or Something New?. Retrieved March 7, 2023.

text:
Cobalt Strike can inject a variety of payloads into processes dynamically chosen by the adversary.
Conti can utilize command line options to allow an attacker control over how it scans and encrypts files.
Cobalt Strike can use WMI to deliver a payload to a remote host.
Cobalt Strike can use `rundll32.exe` to load DLL from the command line.
title: DFIR Report. (2021, November 29). CONTInuing the Bazar Ransomware Story. Retrieved September 29, 2022.

text: Bazar can attempt to overload sandbox analysis by sending 1550 calls to printf. The Bazar loader has used dual-extension executable files such as PreviewReport.DOC.exe. Bazar can enumerate remote systems using Net View. Bazar can identify the installed antivirus engine. Bazar can launch cmd.exe to perform reconnaissance commands. Bazar can implement DGA using the current date as a seed variable. Bazar can inject code through calling VirtualAllocExNuma. Bazar can identity the current process on a compromised host. Bazar can retrieve information from the infected machine. Bazar has been signed with fake certificates including those appearing to be from VB CORPORATE PTY. LTD. Bazar has a variant with a packed payload. Bazar can query the Registry for installed applications. Bazar can use various APIs to allocate memory and facilitate code execution/injection. Bazar can create a task named to appear benign. Bazar downloads have been hosted on Google Docs. The Bazar loader is used to download and execute the Bazar backdoor. Bazar can collect the IP address and NetBIOS name of an infected machine.
title: Cybereason Nocturnus. (2020, July 16). A BAZAR OF TRICKS: FOLLOWING TEAM9’S DEVELOPMENT CYCLES. Retrieved November 18, 2020.

text:
WarzoneRAT has the ability of performing remote desktop access via a hVNC window for decreased visibility.
TrickBot has been known to use PowerShell to download new payloads, open documents, and upload data to command and control servers.
TrickBot downloads several additional files and saves them to the victim's machine.
Some TrickBot samples have used HTTP over ports 447 and 8082 for C2. Newer versions of TrickBot have been known to use a custom communication protocol which sends the data unencrypted over port 443.
TrickBot can send information about the compromised host and upload data to a hardcoded C2 server.
TrickBot has used a VNC module to monitor the victim and collect information to pivot to valuable systems on the network
title: Radu Tudorica. (2021, July 12). A Fresh Look at Trickbot’s Ever-Improving VNC Module. Retrieved September 28, 2021.

text:
Cobian RAT obfuscates communications with the C2 server using Base64 encoding.
Cobian RAT has a feature to perform screen capture.
Cobian RAT has a feature to perform voice recording on the victim’s machine.
Cobian RAT creates an autostart Registry key to ensure persistence.
Cobian RAT has a feature to perform keylogging on the victim’s machine.
Cobian RAT has a feature to access the webcam on the victim’s machine.
Cobian RAT can launch a remote command shell interface for executing commands.
Cobian RAT uses DNS for C2.
title: Yadav, A., et al. (2017, August 31). Cobian RAT – A backdoored RAT. Retrieved November 13, 2018.

text:
POSHSPY uses a DGA to derive command and control URLs from a word list.
POSHSPY downloads and executes additional PowerShell code and Windows binaries.
POSHSPY modifies timestamps of all downloaded executables to match a randomly selected file created prior to 2013.
POSHSPY uses a WMI event subscription to establish persistence.
POSHSPY uses PowerShell to execute various commands, one to execute its payload.
POSHSPY encrypts C2 traffic with AES and RSA.
POSHSPY uploads data in 2048-byte chunks.
POSHSPY appends a file signature header (randomly selected from six file types) to encrypted data prior to upload or download.
title: Dunwoody, M.. (2017, April 3). Dissecting One of APT29’s Fileless WMI and PowerShell Backdoors (POSHSPY). Retrieved April 5, 2017.

text: Bundlore creates a new key pair with ssh-keygen and drops the newly created user key in authorized_keys to enable remote login. Bundlore can use AppleScript to inject malicious JavaScript into a browser. Bundlore has been spread through malicious advertisements on websites. Bundlore can persist via a LaunchDaemon. Bundlore can persist via a LaunchAgent. Bundlore uses HTTP requests for C2. Bundlore can execute JavaScript by injecting it into the victim's browser. Bundlore has used the ps command to list processes. Bundlore has used Python scripts to execute payloads. Bundlore has obfuscated data with base64, AES, RC4, and bz2. Bundlore can download and execute new versions of itself. Bundlore can install malicious browser extensions that are used to hijack user searches. Bundlore prompts the user for their credentials. Bundlore has disguised a malicious .app file as a Flash Player update. Bundlore has the ability to enumerate what browser is being used as well as version information for Safari. Bundlore has used openssl to decrypt AES encrypted payload data. Bundlore has also used base64 and RC4 with a hardcoded key to deobfuscate data. Bundlore has attempted to get users to execute a malicious .app file that looks like a Flash Player update. Bundlore has leveraged /bin/sh and /bin/bash to execute commands on the victim machine.
title: Sushko, O. (2019, April 17). macOS Bundlore: Mac Virus Bypassing macOS Security Features. Retrieved June 30, 2020.

text:
A Volgmer variant is encoded using a simple XOR cipher.
Volgmer uses a simple XOR cipher to encrypt traffic and files.
Volgmer deobfuscates its strings and APIs once its executed.
Volgmer can delete files and itself after infection to avoid analysis.
Volgmer checks the system for certain Registry keys.
Volgmer executes payloads using the Windows API call CreateProcessW().
title: US-CERT. (2017, November 01). Malware Analysis Report (MAR) - 10135536-D. Retrieved July 16, 2018.

text:
Raccoon Stealer queries the Windows Registry to fingerprint the infected host via the `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Cryptography\MachineGuid` key.
Raccoon Stealer gathers information on the infected system owner and user.
Raccoon Stealer is capable of identifying running software on victim machines.
Raccoon Stealer can remove files related to use and installation.
Raccoon Stealer collects files and directories from victim systems based on configuration data downloaded from command and control servers.
Raccoon Stealer uses RC4 encryption for strings and command and control addresses to evade static detection.
Raccoon Stealer uses RC4-encrypted, base64-encoded strings to obfuscate functionality and command and control servers.
Raccoon Stealer dynamically links key WinApi functions during execution.
Raccoon Stealer will automatically collect and exfiltrate data identified in received configuration files from command and control nodes.
Raccoon Stealer uses HTTP, and particularly HTTP POST requests, for command and control actions.
Raccoon Stealer uses existing HTTP-based command and control channels for exfiltration.
title: Quentin Bourgue, Pierre le Bourhis, & Sekoia TDR. (2022, June 28). Raccoon Stealer v2 - Part 1: The return of the dead. Retrieved August 1, 2024.

text:
A gh0st RAT variant has used rundll32 for execution.
A gh0st RAT variant has used DLL side-loading.
title: Sabo, S. (2018, February 15). Musical Chairs Playing Tetris. Retrieved February 19, 2018.

text:
HTTPTroy has the ability to generate a reverse shell using the command `conn <IP_ADDRESS> <PORT>`.
HTTPTroy has obfuscated HTTP POST request communications utilizing XOR with a designated key of 0x56, followed by Base64 encoding.
HTTPTroy has the ability to download files from C2 using the `down <FILENAME>` command.
HTTPTroy has decoded strings encoded with Base64 and XOR prior to execution.
HTTPTroy has used HTTP POST requests to communicate with C2.
HTTPTroy has obtained screen captures leveraging the `screen` command which captures, encrypts and uploads the stolen image to the adversary controlled C2 server.
HTTPTroy has exfiltrated encrypted data over the C2 channel using the `up <FILENAME>` command.
HTTPTroy has obfuscated strings using Single Instruction Multiple Data (SIMD) instructions to hinder analysis and detection.
HTTPTroy has utilized dynamic API resolution by reconstructing API calls during runtime using combinations of arithmetic and logical operations to complicate static analysis.
HTTPTroy has leveraged the ability to execute commands with system privileges using the `srun <EXECUTABLE> <ARGS>` command.
HTTPTroy has leveraged Windows Native API calls, including `GetProcAddress` to execute functions in memory.
HTTPTroy has obfuscated request communications utilizing XOR encryption.
HTTPTroy can terminate its running process and then remove traces of itself through the `die <COMMAND>` command.
title: Alexndru-Cristian Bardas. (2025, October 30). DPRK’s Playbook: Kimsuky’s HttpTroy and Lazarus’s New BLINDINGCAN Variant. Retrieved April 8, 2026.

text: FrameworkPOS can identifiy payment card track data on the victim and copy it to a local file in a subdirectory of C:\Windows\.
title: FireEye Threat Intelligence. (2016, April). Follow the Money: Dissecting the Operations of the Cyber Crime Group FIN6. Retrieved November 17, 2024.

text:
Vasport copies itself to disk and creates an associated run key Registry entry to establish.
Vasport is capable of tunneling though a proxy.
Vasport creates a backdoor by making a connection using a HTTP POST.
Vasport can download files.
title: Zhou, R. (2012, May 15). Backdoor.Vasport. Retrieved February 22, 2018.

text:
HUI Loader has the ability to disable Windows Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) and Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) functions.
HUI Loader can be deployed to targeted systems via legitimate programs that are vulnerable to DLL search order hijacking.
HUI Loader can decrypt and load files containing malicious payloads.
title: Counter Threat Unit Research Team . (2022, June 23). BRONZE STARLIGHT RANSOMWARE OPERATIONS USE HUI LOADER. Retrieved December 7, 2023.

text:
PoisonIvy creates a mutex using either a custom or default value.
PoisonIvy uses the Camellia cipher to encrypt communications.
PoisonIvy contains a keylogger.
PoisonIvy can inject a malicious DLL into a process.
title: FireEye. (2014). POISON IVY: Assessing Damage and Extracting Intelligence. Retrieved September 19, 2024.

text: Fysbis can perform keylogging. Fysbis has the ability to create and execute commands in a remote shell for CLI. Fysbis has used the command ls /etc | egrep -e"fedora\*|debian\*|gentoo\*|mandriva\*|mandrake\*|meego\*|redhat\*|lsb-\*|sun-\*|SUSE\*|release" to determine which Linux OS version is running.
title: Bryan Lee and Rob Downs. (2016, February 12). A Look Into Fysbis: Sofacy’s Linux Backdoor. Retrieved September 10, 2017.

text:
SVCReady can use `WMI` queries to detect the presence of a virtual machine environment.
SVCReady can collect time zone information.
SVCReady has relied on users clicking a malicious attachment delivered through spearphishing.
SVCReady can collect a list of running processes from an infected host.
SVCReady can encrypt victim data with an RC4 cipher.
SVCReady has the ability to collect information such as computer name, computer manufacturer, BIOS, operating system, and firmware, including through the use of `systeminfo.exe`.
SVCReady can create a scheduled task named `RecoveryExTask` to gain persistence.
SVCReady can communicate with its C2 servers via HTTP.
SVCReady has been distributed via spearphishing campaigns containing malicious Mircrosoft Word documents.
SVCReady can check for the number of devices plugged into an infected host.
SVCReady can collect a list of installed software from an infected host.
SVCReady can use Windows API calls to gather information from an infected host.
SVCReady has named a task `RecoveryExTask` as part of its persistence activity.
SVCReady can enter a sleep stage for 30 minutes to evade detection.
SVCReady has used `rundll32.exe` for execution.
SVCReady can search for the `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\HARDWARE\DESCRIPTION\System` Registry key to gather system information.
SVCReady has created the `HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Classes\CLSID\{E6D34FFC-AD32-4d6a-934C-D387FA873A19}` Registry key for persistence.
SVCReady has used VBA macros to execute shellcode.
SVCReady has the ability to determine if its runtime environment is virtualized.
SVCReady has the ability to download additional tools such as the RedLine Stealer to an infected host.
SVCReady can take a screenshot from an infected host.
SVCReady can collect data from an infected host.
SVCReady can send collected data in JSON format to its C2 server.
SVCReady can collect the username from an infected host.
title: Schlapfer, Patrick. (2022, June 6). A New Loader Gets Ready. Retrieved December 13, 2022.

text: Green Lambert can delete the original executable after initial installation in addition to unused functions. Green Lambert can use shell scripts for execution, such as /bin/sh -c. Green Lambert has created a new executable named `Software Update Check` to appear legitimate. Green Lambert can create a Launch Agent with the `RunAtLoad` key-value pair set to true, ensuring the `com.apple.GrowlHelper.plist` file runs every time a user logs in. Green Lambert can add init.d and rc.d files in the /etc folder to establish persistence. Green Lambert can obtain proxy information from a victim's machine using system environment variables. Green Lambert can use Keychain Services API functions to find and collect passwords, such as `SecKeychainFindInternetPassword` and `SecKeychainItemCopyAttributesAndData`. Green Lambert can collect data from a compromised host. Green Lambert can use DNS for C2 communications. Green Lambert can use proxies for C2 traffic. Green Lambert can add Login Items to establish persistence. Green Lambert has encrypted strings. Green Lambert can use multiple custom routines to decrypt strings prior to execution. Green Lambert can collect the date and time from a compromised host. Green Lambert can establish persistence on a compromised host through modifying the `profile`, `login`, and run command (rc) files associated with the `bash`, `csh`, and `tcsh` shells. Green Lambert has been disguised as a Growl help file. Green Lambert can add a plist file in the `Library/LaunchDaemons` to establish persistence. Green Lambert can use `uname` to identify the operating system name, version, and processor type.
title: Sandvik, Runa. (2021, October 1). Made In America: Green Lambert for OS X. Retrieved March 21, 2022.

text:
Raccoon Stealer collects passwords, cookies, and autocomplete information from various popular web browsers.
Raccoon Stealer attempts to steal cookies and related information in browser history.
Raccoon Stealer gathers victim machine timezone information.
Raccoon Stealer identifies target files and directories for collection based on a configuration file.
Raccoon Stealer gathers information on infected systems such as operating system, processor information, RAM, and display information.
Raccoon Stealer collects data from victim machines based on configuration information received from command and control nodes.
Raccoon Stealer gathers information from repositories associated with cryptocurrency wallets and the Telegram messaging service.
Raccoon Stealer can capture screenshots from victim systems.
Raccoon Stealer downloads various library files enabling interaction with various data stores and structures to facilitate follow-on information theft.
Raccoon Stealer checks the privileges of running processes to determine if the running user is equivalent to `NT Authority\System`.
Raccoon Stealer archives collected system information in a text f ile, `System info.txt`, prior to exfiltration.
title: Pierre Le Bourhis, Quentin Bourgue, & Sekoia TDR. (2022, June 29). Raccoon Stealer v2 - Part 2: In-depth analysis. Retrieved August 1, 2024.

text:
ServHelper will attempt to enumerate the username of the victim.
ServHelper contains modules that will use schtasks to carry out malicious operations.
ServHelper may set up a reverse SSH tunnel to give the attacker access to services running on the victim, such as RDP.
ServHelper has created a new user named `supportaccount`.
ServHelper will attempt to enumerate Windows version and system architecture.
ServHelper uses HTTP for C2.
ServHelper has created a new user named "supportaccount".
ServHelper has added a user named "supportaccount" to the Remote Desktop Users and Administrators groups.
ServHelper has commands for adding a remote desktop user and sending RDP traffic to the attacker through a reverse SSH tunnel.
FlawedGrace encrypts its C2 configuration files with AES in CBC mode.
title: Schwarz, D. and Proofpoint Staff. (2019, January 9). ServHelper and FlawedGrace - New malware introduced by TA505. Retrieved May 28, 2019.

text: Ursnif has registered itself as a system service in the Registry for automatic execution at system startup.
title: Trend Micro. (2014, December 11). PE_URSNIF.A2. Retrieved June 5, 2019.

text: AppleJeus has XOR-encrypted collected system information prior to sending to a C2. AppleJeus has also used the open source ADVObfuscation library for its components. AppleJeus has exfiltrated collected host information to a C2 server. AppleJeus has deleted the MSI file after installation. AppleJeus has presented the user with a UAC prompt to elevate privileges while installing. FALLCHILL has been installed as a Windows service. AppleJeus has waited a specified time before downloading a second stage payload. AppleJeus has required user execution of a malicious MSI installer. AppleJeus has been distributed via spearphishing link. AppleJeus has decoded files received from a C2. AppleJeus has been installed via MSI installer. AppleJeus has used a valid digital signature from Sectigo to appear legitimate. FALLCHILL encrypts C2 data with RC4 encryption. AppleJeus's spearphishing links required user interaction to navigate to the malicious website. AppleJeus has created a scheduled SYSTEM task that runs when a user logs in. AppleJeus has added a leading . to plist filenames, unlisting them from the Finder app and default Terminal directory listings. AppleJeus can install itself as a service. AppleJeus has collected the victim host information after infection. AppleJeus has loaded a plist file using the launchctl command.
title: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. (2021, February 21). AppleJeus: Analysis of North Korea’s Cryptocurrency Malware. Retrieved March 1, 2021.

text:
SystemBC has collected username , build number and serial number, then sent the information to the C2 server. SystemBC has also gathered device name, operating system, and processor type.
SystemBC has the ability to decrypt RC4 encrypted packets and to decode obfuscated data before C2 communication. Additionally, SystemBC has decrypted its config file that was encoded with XOR and a hardcoded 40-byte key.
SystemBC has used raw TCP on non-standard ports, such as 4044, for C2 communications and for HTTP communications, which include downloading binaries.
title: AhnLab. (2022, April 4). SystemBC Being Used by Various Attackers . Retrieved June 18, 2025.

text: Olympic Destroyer will attempt to enumerate mapped network shares to later attempt to wipe all files on those shares. Olympic Destroyer uses the native Windows utilities vssadmin, wbadmin, and bcdedit to delete and disable operating system recovery features such as the Windows backup catalog and Windows Automatic Repair. Olympic Destroyer attempts to copy itself to remote machines on the network. Olympic Destroyer uses API calls to enumerate the infected system's ARP table. Olympic Destroyer contains a module that tries to obtain credentials from LSASS, similar to Mimikatz. These credentials are used with PsExec and Windows Management Instrumentation to help the malware propagate itself across a network. Olympic Destroyer will shut down the compromised system after it is done modifying system configuration settings. Olympic Destroyer will attempt to clear the System and Security event logs using wevtutil. Olympic Destroyer contains a module that tries to obtain stored credentials from web browsers. Olympic Destroyer uses WMI to help propagate itself across a network. Olympic Destroyer uses the API call ChangeServiceConfigW to disable all services on the affected system. Olympic Destroyer utilizes PsExec to help propagate itself across a network. Olympic Destroyer uses Windows Management Instrumentation to enumerate all systems in the network. Olympic Destroyer overwrites files locally and on remote shares.
title: Mercer, W. and Rascagneres, P. (2018, February 12). Olympic Destroyer Takes Aim At Winter Olympics. Retrieved March 14, 2019.

text: VBShower has the ability to download VBS files to the target computer. VBShower used HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\\[a-f0-9A-F]{8} to maintain persistence. VBShower has attempted to complicate forensic analysis by deleting all the files contained in %APPDATA%\..\Local\Temporary Internet Files\Content.Word and %APPDATA%\..\Local Settings\Temporary Internet Files\Content.Word\. PowerShower has the ability to encode C2 communications with base64 encoding. PowerShower has the ability to identify the current user on the infected host. VBShower has attempted to obtain a VBS script from command and control (C2) nodes over HTTP. PowerShower has used a PowerShell document stealer module to pack and exfiltrate .txt, .pdf, .xls or .doc files smaller than 5MB that were modified during the past two days. PowerShower has used 7Zip to compress .txt, .pdf, .xls or .doc files prior to exfiltration. VBShower has the ability to execute VBScript files. PowerShower has the ability to deploy a reconnaissance module to retrieve a list of the active processes. PowerShower has the ability to identify the current Windows domain of the infected host.
title: GReAT. (2019, August 12). Recent Cloud Atlas activity. Retrieved May 8, 2020.

text:
TrickBot module shareDll/mshareDll discovers network shares via the WNetOpenEnumA API.
TrickBot uses brute-force attack against RDP with rdpscanDll module.
TrickBot uses vncDll module to remote control the victim machine.
TrickBot uses module networkDll for process list discovery.
title: Tudorica, R., Maximciuc, A., Vatamanu, C. (2020, March 18). New TrickBot Module Bruteforces RDP Connections, Targets Select Telecommunication Services in US and Hong Kong. Retrieved March 15, 2021.

text: Spark has run the whoami command and has a built-in command to identify the user logged in. Spark has used a splash screen to check whether an user actively clicks on the screen before running malicious code. Spark has used HTTP POST requests to communicate with its C2 server to receive commands. Spark has used a custom XOR algorithm to decrypt the payload. Spark has checked the results of the GetKeyboardLayoutList and the language name returned by GetLocaleInfoA to make sure they contain the word “Arabic” before executing. Spark can collect the hostname, keyboard layout, and language from the system. Spark has exfiltrated data over the C2 channel. Spark has been packed with Enigma Protector to obfuscate its contents. Spark can use cmd.exe to run commands. Spark has encoded communications with the C2 server with base64.
title: Falcone, R., et al. (2020, March 3). Molerats Delivers Spark Backdoor to Government and Telecommunications Organizations. Retrieved December 14, 2020.

text:
Machete has a feature to copy files from every drive onto a removable drive in a hidden folder.
Machete used the startup folder for persistence.
Machete hijacks the clipboard data by creating an overlapped window that listens to keyboard events.
The different components of Machete are executed by Windows Task Scheduler.
Machete renamed payloads to masquerade as legitimate Google Chrome, Java, Dropbox, Adobe Reader and Python executables.
Machete has used base64 encoding.
title: Kaspersky Global Research and Analysis Team. (2014, August 20). El Machete. Retrieved September 13, 2019.

text:
Ursnif has dropped payload and configuration files to disk. Ursnif has also been used to download and execute additional payloads.
Ursnif has injected HTML codes into banking sites to steal sensitive online banking information (ex: usernames and passwords).
Ursnif has collected files from victim machines, including certificates and cookies.
Ursnif has used Registry Run keys to establish automatic execution at system startup.
title: Sioting, S. (2013, June 15). BKDR_URSNIF.SM. Retrieved June 5, 2019.

text:
Vidar has been distributed via malicious advertisements when users searched for “Notepad++.”
Vidar has compiled collected data into a randomly generated directory in the ProgramData folder.
Vidar has downloaded additional binaries from the C2 server such as sqlx[1].dll, a sqlite3 binary for data harvesting and exfiltration. Vidar has also ownloaded get.zip, an archive containing several DLL libraries that extracted data from applications and browsers.
Vidar has used process hollowing to inject itself into an AppLaunch.exe process.
Vidar has used a hidden directory in the ProgramData directory to store collected data.
Vidar has set the Registry value associated with User Access Control (UAC) (i.e. `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\EnableLUA`) to `0`, which disabled UAC.
Vidar has used Telegram and Steam dead drop resolvers to recover its C2 domain.
Vidar has used the function `TerminateProcess` to terminate processes. Vidar has forcefully terminated a process named Devil.exe using the command `C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe” /c taskkill /im Devil.exe /f`.
Vidar has used HTTP/HTTPS to retrieve and send data and beacons.
Vidar has self-deleted its initial executable to operate in memory. Vidar has deleted collected data after exfiltration. Vidar has also deleted the file Malware.exe and all .dll files in the ProgramData folder using the command `del /f /q “C:\Users\MalWorkstation\Desktop\Malware.exe” & del C:\ProgramData\*.dll`.
Vidar has bypassed UAC by setting the Registry value `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\EnableLUA` to `0`, which disabled UAC.
Vidar has used PowerShell commands to modify Windows Defender’s list of excluded file extensions.
Vidar has waited for six seconds using the command `timeout /t 6`.
Vidar has collected browser history from the victim machine.
title: Khadgi, N. (n.d.). A Comprehensive Overview on Stealer Malware Families. Retrieved August 25, 2026.

text:
Saint Bot had used `InstallUtil.exe` to download and deploy executables.
Saint Bot has used Base64 to encode its C2 communications.
Saint Bot can collect files and information from a compromised host.
Saint Bot has used `regsvr32` to execute scripts.
Saint Bot has used different API calls, including `GetProcAddress`, `VirtualAllocEx`, `WriteProcessMemory`, `CreateProcessA`, and `SetThreadContext`.
Saint Bot has been distributed as malicious attachments within spearphishing emails.
Saint Bot can collect the username from a compromised host.
Saint Bot has renamed malicious binaries as `wallpaper.mp4` and `slideshow.mp4` to avoid detection.
Saint Bot has written its payload into a newly-created `EhStorAuthn.exe` process using `ZwWriteVirtualMemory` and executed it using `NtQueueApcThread` and `ZwAlertResumeThread`.
Saint Bot has used HTTP for C2 communications.
Saint Bot has used `is_debugger_present` as part of its environmental checks.
Saint Bot has used `check_registry_keys` as part of its environmental checks.
Saint Bot has conducted system locale checks to see if the compromised host is in Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, Armenia, Kazakhstan, or Moldova.
Saint Bot has established persistence by being copied to the Startup directory or through the `\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run` registry key.
Saint Bot has relied on users to execute a malicious attachment delivered via spearphishing.
Saint Bot has injected its DLL component into `EhStorAurhn.exe`.
Saint Bot has been disguised as a legitimate executable, including as Windows SDK.
Saint Bot has created a scheduled task named "Maintenance" to establish persistence.
Saint Bot can deobfuscate strings and files for execution.
Saint Bot has been packed using a dark market crypter.
Saint Bot can identify the OS version, CPU, and other details from a victim's machine.
Saint Bot can collect the IP address of a victim machine.
title: Hasherezade. (2021, April 6). A deep dive into Saint Bot, a new downloader. Retrieved June 9, 2022.

text:
Kerrdown has been distributed through malicious e-mail attachments.
Kerrdown has gained execution through victims opening malicious links.
Kerrdown has been distributed via e-mails containing a malicious link.
title: Amnesty International. (2021, February 24). Vietnamese activists targeted by notorious hacking group. Retrieved March 1, 2021.

text:
PlugX has made calls to Windows API `CheckRemoteDebuggerPresent` and exits if it detects a debugger.
PlugX has leveraged a mutex in its infection process.
title: Secureworks Counter Threat Unit Research Team. (2022, September 8). BRONZE PRESIDENT Targets Government Officials. Retrieved September 9, 2025.

text: Ursnif has used CreateProcessW to create child processes. Ursnif has used process hollowing to inject into child processes.
title: Vaish, A. & Nemes, S. (2017, November 28). Newly Observed Ursnif Variant Employs Malicious TLS Callback Technique to Achieve Process Injection. Retrieved June 5, 2019.

text:
Xbash has maliciously encrypted victim's database systems and demanded a cryptocurrency ransom be paid.
Xbash can collect IP addresses and local intranet information from a victim’s machine.
Xbash can obtain a webpage hosted on Pastebin to update its C2 domain list.
Xbash can create a Startup item for persistence if it determines it is on a Windows system.
Xbash has destroyed Linux-based databases as part of its ransomware capabilities.
Xbash can use mshta for executing scripts.
Xbash can download additional malicious files from its C2 server.
Xbash can attempt to exploit known vulnerabilities in Hadoop, Redis, or ActiveMQ when it finds those services running in order to conduct further execution.
Xbash can create a cronjob for persistence if it determines it is on a Linux system.
Xbash uses HTTP for C2 communications.
Xbash can execute malicious JavaScript payloads on the victim’s machine.
Xbash can execute malicious VBScript payloads on the victim’s machine.
Xbash can use regsvr32 for executing scripts.
Xbash can obtain a list of weak passwords from the C2 server to use for brute forcing as well as attempt to brute force services with open ports.
Xbash can perform port scanning of TCP and UDP ports.
Xbash can use scripts to invoke PowerShell to download a malicious PE executable or PE DLL for execution.
title: Xiao, C. (2018, September 17). Xbash Combines Botnet, Ransomware, Coinmining in Worm that Targets Linux and Windows. Retrieved November 14, 2018.

text:
SDBbot has the ability to use application shimming for persistence if it detects it is running as admin on Windows XP or 7, by creating a shim database to patch services.exe.
SDBbot has the ability to delete files from a compromised host.
SDBbot has the ability to get directory listings or drive information on a compromised host.
SDBbot has the ability to determine the domain name and whether a proxy is configured on a compromised host.
Get2 has the ability to run executables with command-line arguments.
SDBbot has the ability to inject a downloaded DLL into a newly created rundll32.exe process.
SDBbot has the ability to clean up and remove data structures from a compromised host.
SDBbot has the ability to XOR the strings for its installer component with a hardcoded 128 byte key.
SDBbot has the ability to use the command shell to execute commands on a compromised host.
Get2 has the ability to identify the current username of an infected host.
Get2 has the ability to identify the computer name and Windows version of an infected host.
Get2 has the ability to identify running processes on an infected host.
SDBbot has the ability to access the file system on a compromised host.
SDBbot has the ability to download a DLL from C2 to a compromised host.
SDBbot has the ability to communicate with C2 with TCP over port 443.
SDBbot has the ability to use port forwarding to establish a proxy between a target host and C2.
SDBbot has the ability to use RDP to connect to victim's machines.
SDBbot has the ability to use image file execution options for persistence if it detects it is running with admin privileges on a Windows version newer than Windows 7.
Get2 has the ability to use HTTP to send information collected from an infected host to C2.
SDBbot has the ability to identify the user on a compromised host.
Get2 has the ability to inject DLLs into processes.
title: Schwarz, D. et al. (2019, October 16). TA505 Distributes New SDBbot Remote Access Trojan with Get2 Downloader. Retrieved May 29, 2020.

text:
XLoader can collect data stored in the victim's clipboard.
XLoader can use an AutoIT script to decrypt a payload file, load it into victim memory, then execute it on the victim machine.
XLoader can capture keystrokes from the victim machine.
XLoader can conduct form grabbing, steal cookies, and extract data from HTTP sessions.
XLoader uses HTTP and HTTPS for command and control communication.
XLoader uses XOR and RC4 algorithms to decrypt payloads and functions. XLoader can be distributed as a self-extracting RAR archive that launches an AutoIT loader.
XLoader establishes persistence by copying its executable in a subdirectory of `%APPDATA%` or `%PROGRAMFILES%`, and then modifies Windows Registry Run keys or policies keys to execute the executable on system start.
XLoader can capture screenshots on compromised hosts.
XLoader uses anti-debugging mechanisms such as calling `NtQueryInformationProcess` with `InfoClass=7`, referencing `ProcessDebugPort`, to determine if it is being analyzed.
XLoader performs timing checks using the Read-Time Stamp Counter (RDTSC) instruction on the victim CPU.
XLoader can collect credentials stored in email clients.
XLoader can initiate a system reboot or shutdown.
XLoader can capture web session cookies and session information from victim browsers.
XLoader has been delivered as a phishing attachment, including PDFs with embedded links, Word and Excel files, and various archive files (ZIP, RAR, ACE, and ISOs) containing EXE payloads.
XLoader can gather credentials from several web browsers.
title: Nart Villeneuve, Randi Eitzman, Sandor Nemes & Tyler Dean, Google Cloud. (2017, October 5). Significant FormBook Distribution Campaigns Impacting the U.S. and South Korea. Retrieved March 11, 2025.

text:
STARWHALE has the ability to hex-encode collected data from an infected host.
STARWHALE can gather the username from an infected host.
STARWHALE has been obfuscated with hex-encoded strings.
PowGoop can receive encrypted commands from C2.
Small Sieve can use SSL/TLS for its HTTPS Telegram Bot API-based C2 channel.
STARWHALE can exfiltrate collected data to its C2 servers.
STARWHALE has the ability to collect the IP address of an infected host.
PowGoop has used a DLL named Goopdate.dll to impersonate a legitimate Google update file.
Small Sieve can use a custom hex byte swapping encoding scheme to obfuscate tasking traffic.
PowGoop has the ability to use PowerShell scripts to execute commands.
STARWHALE can collect data from an infected local host.
STARWHALE can establish persistence by installing itself in the startup folder, whereas the GO variant has created a `HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\OutlookM` registry key.
STARWHALE has the ability to contact actor-controlled C2 servers via HTTP.
Mori has obfuscated the FML.dll with 200MB of junk data.
Mori can read data from the Registry including from `HKLM\Software\NFC\IPA` and `HKLM\Software\NFC\`.
PowGoop has disguised a PowerShell script as a .dat file (goopdate.dat).
STARWHALE has relied on victims opening a malicious Excel file for execution.
Mori can use Base64 encoded JSON libraries used in C2.
Mori can resolve networking APIs from strings that are ADD-encrypted.
PowGoop can decrypt PowerShell scripts for execution.
PowGoop can side-load `Goopdate.dll` into `GoogleUpdate.exe`.
Mori can write data to `HKLM\Software\NFC\IPA` and `HKLM\Software\NFC\` and delete Registry values.
Mori can communicate using HTTP over IPv4 or IPv6 depending on a flag set.
STARWHALE can gather the computer name of an infected host.
Mori can use DNS tunneling to communicate with C2.
Small Sieve can contact actor-controlled C2 servers by using the Telegram API over HTTPS.
Mori can delete its DLL file and related files by Registry value.
Mori can use `regsvr32.exe` for DLL execution.
title: FBI, CISA, CNMF, NCSC-UK. (2022, February 24). Iranian Government-Sponsored Actors Conduct Cyber Operations Against Global Government and Commercial Networks. Retrieved September 27, 2022.

text: POWERSTATS encoded C2 traffic with base64.
title: Lancaster, T.. (2017, November 14). Muddying the Water: Targeted Attacks in the Middle East. Retrieved March 15, 2018.

text:
RedLine Stealer has stolen browser cookies and settings.
RedLine Stealer has obtained credentials from VPN services, FTP clients and Instant Messenger (IM)/Chat clients.
RedLine Stealer was designed to steal sensitive information from web browsers, including credit card details, saved credentials, and autocomplete data. RedLine Stealer can also gather credentials from several browsers.
RedLine Stealer malware has masqueraded as legitimate software such as "PDF Converter Software" which has been distributed through poisoned search engine results often resembling legitimate software lures with the combination of typo squatted domains.
RedLine Stealer has gathered detailed information about victims’ systems, such as IP addresses, and geolocation. RedLine Stealer has also checked the IP from where it was being executed and leveraged an opensource geolocation IP-lookup service.
RedLine Stealer can enumeate information about victims’ systems including IP addresses.
title: George Glass. (2024, August 14). REDLINESTEALER Malware Driving the Initial Access Broker Market. Retrieved September 17, 2025.

text: Crocodilus has stolen cryptocurrency wallet details from victim devices.
title: ThreatFabric. (2025, June 3). Crocodilus Mobile Malware: Evolving Fast, Going Global. Retrieved November 24, 2025.

text:
macOS.OSAMiner has used `launchctl` to restart the Launch Agent.
macOS.OSAMiner has placed a Stripped Payloads with a `plist` extension in the Launch Agent's folder.
macOS.OSAMiner has used `osascript` to call itself via the `do shell script` command in the Launch Agent `.plist` file.
macOS.OSAMiner has embedded Stripped Payloads within another run-only Stripped Payloads.
macOS.OSAMiner can parse the output of the native `system_profiler` tool to determine if the machine is running with 4 cores.
macOS.OSAMiner can gather the device serial number.
macOS.OSAMiner has used `ps ax | grep <name> | grep -v grep | ...` and `ps ax | grep -E...` to conduct process discovery.
macOS.OSAMiner has checked to ensure there is enough disk space using the Unix utility `df`.
macOS.OSAMiner has used run-only Applescripts, a compiled and stripped version of AppleScript, to remove human readable indicators to evade detection.
macOS.OSAMiner has searched for the Activity Monitor process in the System Events process list and kills the process if running. macOS.OSAMiner also searches the operating system's `install.log` for apps matching its hardcoded list, killing all matching process names.
title: Phil Stokes. (2021, January 11). FADE DEAD | Adventures in Reversing Malicious Run-Only AppleScripts. Retrieved September 29, 2022.

text:
HALFBAKED can obtain information about running processes on the victim.
HALFBAKED can obtain screenshots from the victim.
HALFBAKED can obtain information about the OS, processor, and BIOS.
HALFBAKED can use WMI queries to gather system information.
HALFBAKED can delete a specified file.
HALFBAKED can execute PowerShell scripts.
title: Carr, N., et al. (2017, April 24). FIN7 Evolution and the Phishing LNK. Retrieved April 24, 2017.

text:
SocGholish can identify the victim's browser in order to serve the correct fake update page.
SocGholish can list processes on targeted hosts.
SocGholish can use IP-based geolocation to limit infections to victims in North America, Europe, and a small number of Asian-Pacific nations.
title: Secureworks. (n.d.). GOLD PRELUDE . Retrieved March 22, 2024.

text: Zebrocy runs the ipconfig /all command. Zebrocy has the capability to upload dumper tools that extract credentials from web browsers and store them in database files. Zebrocy uses netstat -aon to gather network connection information. Zebrocy executes the reg query command to obtain information in the Registry.
title: ESET Research. (2019, May 22). A journey to Zebrocy land. Retrieved June 20, 2019.

text: Trojan.Mebromi performs BIOS modification and can download and execute a file as well as protect itself from removal.
title: Ge, L. (2011, September 9). BIOS Threat is Showing up Again!. Retrieved November 14, 2014.

text:
BlackMould can send commands to C2 in the body of HTTP POST requests.
BlackMould can run cmd.exe with parameters.
BlackMould can copy files on a compromised host.
BlackMould has the ability to download files to the victim's machine.
BlackMould can enumerate local drives on a compromised host.
BlackMould has the ability to find files on the targeted system.
title: MSTIC. (2019, December 12). GALLIUM: Targeting global telecom. Retrieved January 13, 2021.

text:
PlugX has obtained the location of the victim device by leveraging `GetSystemDefaultLCID`.
PlugX has leveraged XOR encryption with the key of 123456789.
PlugX has created a scheduled task to execute additional malicious software, as well as maintain persistence.
PlugX has leveraged obfuscated Windows API function calls that were concealed as unique names, or hashes of the Windows API.
PlugX has the ability to execute a command on a hidden desktop.
PlugX has utilized junk code and opaque predicates in payloads to hinder analysis.
PlugX has collected system information including OS version, processor information, RAM size, location, host name, IP, and screen size of the infected host.
PlugX has the ability to gather the username from the victim’s machine.
PlugX has identified system time through its GetSystemInfo command.
PlugX has deleted registry keys that store data and maintained persistence.
PlugX has collected a list of all mapped drives on the infected host.
title: Alexandre Cote Cyr. (2022, March 23). Mustang Panda’s Hodur: Old tricks, new Korplug variant. Retrieved September 9, 2025.

text: SQLRat has used a character insertion obfuscation technique, making the script appear to contain Chinese characters. SQLRat has used been observed deleting scripts once used. SQLRat has scripts that are responsible for deobfuscating additional scripts. SQLRat has used PowerShell to create a Meterpreter session. SQLRat has created scheduled tasks in %appdata%\Roaming\Microsoft\Templates\. SQLRat can make a direct SQL connection to a Microsoft database controlled by the attackers, retrieve an item from the bindata table, then write and execute the file on disk. SQLRat has used SQL to execute JavaScript and VB scripts on the host system. SQLRat relies on users clicking on an embedded image to execute the scripts.
title: Platt, J. and Reeves, J.. (2019, March). FIN7 Revisited: Inside Astra Panel and SQLRat Malware. Retrieved June 18, 2019.

text: Dtrack has used cmd.exe to add a persistent service. Dtrack contains a function that calls LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress. Dtrack can collect a variety of information from victim machines. One of Dtrack can hide in replicas of legitimate programs like OllyDbg, 7-Zip, and FileZilla. Dtrack can collect the RegisteredOwner, RegisteredOrganization, and InstallDate registry values. Dtrack can add a service called WBService to establish persistence. One of Dtrack can replace the normal flow of a program execution with malicious code. Dtrack used hard-coded credentials to gain access to a network share.
title: Hod Gavriel. (2019, November 21). Dtrack: In-depth analysis of APT on a nuclear power plant. Retrieved January 20, 2021.

text: KillDisk overwrites the first sector of the Master Boot Record with “0x00”. KillDisk uses VMProtect to make reverse engineering the malware more difficult. KillDisk has called the Windows API to retrieve the hard disk handle and shut down the machine. KillDisk retrieves the hard disk name by calling the CreateFileA to \\.\PHYSICALDRIVE0 API. KillDisk loads and executes functions from a DLL.
title: Fernando Merces, Byron Gelera, Martin Co. (2018, June 7). KillDisk Variant Hits Latin American Finance Industry. Retrieved January 12, 2021.

text: QUADAGENT stores a session identifier unique to the compromised system as well as a pre-shared key used for encrypting and decrypting C2 communications within a Registry key (such as `HKCU\Office365DCOMCheck`) in the `HKCU` hive. QUADAGENT uses DNS for C2 communications. QUADAGENT checks if a value exists within a Registry key in the HKCU hive whose name is the same as the scheduled task it has created. QUADAGENT uses cmd.exe to execute scripts and commands on the victim’s machine. QUADAGENT used the PowerShell filenames Office365DCOMCheck.ps1 and SystemDiskClean.ps1. QUADAGENT uses VBScripts. QUADAGENT encodes C2 communications with base64. QUADAGENT has a command to delete its Registry key and scheduled task. QUADAGENT uses HTTPS and HTTP for C2 communications. QUADAGENT gathers the victim username. QUADAGENT gathers the current domain the victim system belongs to. QUADAGENT creates a scheduled task to maintain persistence on the victim’s machine. QUADAGENT uses PowerShell scripts for execution. QUADAGENT modifies an HKCU Registry key to store a session identifier unique to the compromised system as well as a pre-shared key used for encrypting and decrypting C2 communications. QUADAGENT uses AES and a preshared key to decrypt the custom Base64 routine used to encode strings and scripts. QUADAGENT uses multiple protocols (HTTPS, HTTP, DNS) for its C2 server as fallback channels if communication with one is unsuccessful.
title: Lee, B., Falcone, R. (2018, July 25). OilRig Targets Technology Service Provider and Government Agency with QUADAGENT. Retrieved August 9, 2018.

text:
SamSam uses custom batch scripts to execute some of its components.
SamSam has used garbage code to pad some of its malware components.
SamSam has been seen deleting its own files and payloads to make analysis of the attack more difficult.
SamSam encrypts victim files using RSA-2048 encryption and demands a ransom be paid in Bitcoin to decrypt those files.
title: Palotay, D. and Mackenzie, P. (2018, April). SamSam Ransomware Chooses Its Targets Carefully. Retrieved April 15, 2019.

text:
LazyWiper can disable Microsoft Windows Defender Real-Time Monitoring with the `Set-MpPreference` cmdlet.
DynoWiper has utilized a five-second delay using `Sleep(5000)` between two of the three phases of the attack that involves file overwriting, file deletion, and system reboot.
DynoWiper has been named after well-known files schtask.exe, schtask2.exe, and <redacted>_update.exe.
DynoWiper has used the Microsoft Windows native `FindFirstFile()` and `FindNextFile()` to recursively enumerate directories and files on the system.
LazyWiper has used PowerShell to enable data destruction on targeted systems.
DynoWiper has recursively enumerated directories with the exception of the following: System32, Windows, Program Files, Program Files(x86), Temp, Recycle.Bin, $Recycle.Bin, Boot, PerfLogs, AppData, Documents and Settings.
DynoWiper has used the Microsoft Windows native `ExitWindowsEx()` function to log off the interactive user and shutdown the system.
LazyWiper is believed to have been generated by a large language model (LLM) due to the non-sensical comments in the code.
DynoWiper has overwritten files with 16-byte sequences of random data generated by the Mersenne Twister algorithm using the Microsoft Windows native `CreateFileW()` function to open the file and the `SetFilePointerEx()` and `WriteFile()` functions to overwrite the file. Additionally, versions of DynoWiper can also delete files using the `DeleteFileW` API.
DynoWiper has used the Microsoft Windows native `GetLogicalDrives()` and `GetDriveType()` functions to enumerate all the drives visible to the system.
LazyWiper can halt execution if `[System.Net.Dns]::GetHostName()` or `$env:COMPUTERNAME` contains `“pe-dc”`.
LazyWiper has used `[System.Net.Dns]::GetHostName()` and `$env:COMPUTERNAME` to enumerate the hostname of a system and determine if it is a domain controller.
LazyWiper can enumerate the hostname of the system to determine if it is a domain controller and exclude it from being wiped if so.
LazyWiper has overwritten files with pseudorandom 32‑byte sequences written at 16‑byte intervals making the file unrecoverable.
LazyWiper can specifically target multiple files by extension including: .rar, .tar.gz, .zip, .7z, .json, .bcp, .bak, .gho, .erf, .edb, .onepkg, .pst, and .ldiff.
DynoWiper has used multiple native Windows functions, such as `GetLogicalDrives` and `FindNextFile` for discovery and file deletion.
title: CERT Polska. (2026, January 30). Energy Sector Incident  Report – 29 December. Retrieved April 22, 2026.

text:
YAHOYAH checks for the system’s Windows OS version and hostname.
YAHOYAH uses HTTP GET requests to download other files that are executed in memory.
YAHOYAH decrypts downloaded files before execution.
YAHOYAH encrypts its configuration file using a simple algorithm.
YAHOYAH uses HTTP for C2.
YAHOYAH checks for antimalware solution processes on the system.
title: Alintanahin, K. (2015). Operation Tropic Trooper: Relying on Tried-and-Tested Flaws to Infiltrate Secret Keepers. Retrieved June 14, 2019.

text:
LockBit 3.0 can use PsExec to execute commands and payloads.
LockBit 3.0 can identify and terminate specific services.
title: CISA et al. (2023, June 14). UNDERSTANDING RANSOMWARE THREAT ACTORS: LOCKBIT. Retrieved February 5, 2025.

text:
The Exaramel for Windows dropper creates and starts a Windows service named wsmprovav with the description “Windows Check AV.”
The Exaramel for Windows dropper creates and starts a Windows service named wsmprovav with the description “Windows Check AV” in an apparent attempt to masquerade as a legitimate service.
Exaramel for Windows stores the backdoor's configuration in the Registry in XML format.
Exaramel for Windows adds the configuration to the Registry in XML format.
Exaramel for Windows specifies a path to store files scheduled for exfiltration.
Exaramel for Windows has a command to execute VBS scripts on the victim’s machine.
Exaramel for Windows automatically encrypts files before sending them to the C2 server.
Exaramel for Windows has a command to launch a remote shell and executes commands on the victim’s machine.
title: Cherepanov, A., Lipovsky, R. (2018, October 11). New TeleBots backdoor: First evidence linking Industroyer to NotPetya. Retrieved November 27, 2018.

text:
Uroburos can store configuration information in the Registry including the initialization vector and AES key needed to find and decrypt other Uroburos components.
Uroburos has used a combination of a Diffie-Hellman key exchange mixed with a pre-shared key (PSK) to encrypt its top layer of C2 communications.
Uroburos uses a custom packer.
Uroburos can use concealed storage mechanisms including an NTFS or FAT-16 filesystem encrypted with CAST-128 in CBC mode.
Uroburos can search for specific files on a compromised system.
Uroburos has encoded outbound C2 communications in DNS requests consisting of character strings made to resemble standard domain names. The actual information transmitted by Uroburos is contained in the part of the character string prior to the first ‘.’ character.
Uroburos has the ability to move data between its kernel and user mode components, generally using named pipes.
Uroburos can use AES and CAST-128 encryption to obfuscate resources.
Uroburos has the ability to gather basic system information and run the POSIX API `gethostbyname`.
Uroburos can run a `Clear Agents Track` command on an infected machine to delete Uroburos-related logs.
Uroburos can use custom communications protocols that ride over SMTP.
Uroburos can use its `Process List` command to enumerate processes on compromised hosts.
Uroburos can use a `Put` command to write files to an infected machine.
Uroburos can store configuration information for the kernel driver and kernel driver loader components in an encrypted blob typically found at `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Classes\.wav\OpenWithProgIds.`
Uroburos can use custom communication methodologies that ride over common protocols including TCP, UDP, HTTP, SMTP, and DNS in order to blend with normal network traffic.
Uroburos can query the Registry, typically `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Classes\.wav\OpenWithProgIds`, to find the key and path to decrypt and load its kernel driver and kernel driver loader.
Uroburos can use implants on multiple compromised machines to proxy communications through its worldwide P2P network.
Uroburos has the ability to communicate over custom communications methodologies that ride over common network protocols including raw TCP and UDP sockets, HTTP, SMTP, and DNS.
Uroburos can encrypt the data beneath its http2 or tcp encryption at the session layer with CAST-128, using a different key for incoming and outgoing data.
Uroburos can use a custom base62 and a de-facto base32 encoding that uses digits 0-9 and lowercase letters a-z in C2 communications.
Uroburos can use a custom HTTP-based protocol for large data communications that can blend with normal network traffic by riding on top of standard HTTP.
Uroburos can intercept the first client to server packet in the 3-way TCP handshake to determine if the packet contains the correct unique value for a specific Uroburos implant. If the value does not match, the packet and the rest of the TCP session are passed to the legitimate listening application.
Individual Uroburos implants can use multiple communication channels based on one of four available modes of operation.
Uroburos has the ability to load new modules directly into memory using its `Load Modules Mem` command.
Uroburos has the ability to use the command line for execution on the targeted system.
Uroburos can use up to 10 channels to communicate between implants.
Uroburos can use native Windows APIs including `GetHostByName`.
Uroburos can use DLL injection to load embedded files and modules.
Uroburos can decrypt command parameters sent through C2 and use unpacking code to extract its packed executable.
Uroburos can add extra characters in encoded strings to help mimic DNS legitimate requests.
Uroburos has registered a service named `WerFaultSvc`, likely to spoof the legitimate Windows error reporting service.
The Uroburos Queue file contains embedded executable files along with key material, communication channels, and modes of operation.
Uroburos can communicate through custom methodologies for UDP, ICMP, and TCP that use distinct sessions to ride over the legitimate protocols.
Uroburos can use its `Get` command to exfiltrate specified files from the compromised system.
Uroburos has registered a service, typically named `WerFaultSvc`, to decrypt and find a kernel driver and kernel driver loader to maintain persistence.
title: FBI et al. (2023, May 9). Hunting Russian Intelligence “Snake” Malware. Retrieved June 8, 2023.

text:
ProLock can encrypt files on a compromised host with RC6, and encrypts the key with RSA-1024.
ProLock can use vssadmin.exe to remove volume shadow copies.
QakBot has the ability to modify the Registry to add its binaries to the Windows Defender exclusion list.
QakBot can enumerate a list of installed programs.
ProLock can use WMIC to execute scripts on targeted hosts.
ProLock can remove files containing its payload after they are executed.
QakBot can use large file sizes to evade detection.
ProLock can use CVE-2019-0859 to escalate privileges on a compromised host.
The QakBot payload has been disguised as a PNG file and hidden within LNK files using a Microsoft File Explorer icon.
ProLock can use .jpg and .bmp files to store its payload.
QakBot can use PowerShell to download and execute payloads.
ProLock can use BITS jobs to download its malicious payload.
title: Group IB. (2020, September). LOCK LIKE  A PRO. Retrieved November 17, 2024.

text: HARDRAIN uses FakeTLS to communicate with its C2 server.
title: US-CERT. (2018, February 5). Malware Analysis Report (MAR) - 10135536-F. Retrieved August 15, 2024.

text:
Lizar has used a complex XOR operation to obfuscate C2 communications.
Lizar has obfuscated the fingerprint of the victim system, the local IP address, and the Fowler-Noll-V 1 (FNV-1) hash of the local IP address using an XOR operation. The data is then sent to the C2 server.
Lizar has used the Reflective DLL injection module from Github to inject itself into a process’s memory.
Lizar has used a raw TCP connection to communicate with the C2 server.
title: Bourhis, P., Sekoia TDR. (2024, February 1). Unveiling the intricacies of DiceLoader. Retrieved May 14, 2025.

text:
Crimson contains a command to retrieve files from its C2 server.
Crimson can exfiltrate stolen information over its C2.
Crimson contains a command to perform screen captures.
Crimson can use a module to perform keylogging on compromised hosts.
Crimson contains commands to list files and directories, as well as search for files matching certain extensions from a defined list.
Crimson can collect information from a compromised host.
Crimson contains a command to collect disk drive information.
Crimson contains a command to collect the victim PC name and operating system.
Crimson can identify the user on a targeted system.
Crimson contains a command to list processes.
Crimson has the ability to delete files from a compromised host.
title: N. Baisini. (2022, July 13). Transparent Tribe begins targeting education sector in latest campaign. Retrieved September 22, 2022.

text:
TinyZBot contains keylogger functionality.
TinyZBot can install as a Windows service for persistence.
TinyZBot supports execution from the command-line.
Net Crawler uses PsExec to perform remote service manipulation to execute a copy of itself as part of lateral movement.
Net Crawler uses a list of known credentials gathered through credential dumping to guess passwords to accounts as it spreads throughout a network.
TinyZBot contains functionality to collect information from the clipboard.
TinyZBot can disable Avira anti-virus.
Net Crawler uses Windows admin shares to establish authenticated sessions to remote systems over SMB as part of lateral movement.
TinyZBot can create a shortcut in the Windows startup folder for persistence.
Net Crawler uses credential dumpers such as Mimikatz and Windows Credential Editor to extract cached credentials from Windows systems.
TinyZBot contains screen capture functionality.
title: Cylance. (2014, December). Operation Cleaver. Retrieved September 14, 2017.

text: QakBot can capture keystrokes on a compromised host. QakBot has the ability to use HTTP and HTTPS in communication with C2 servers. QakBot can Base64 encode system information sent to C2. QakBot can run nltest /domain_trusts /all_trusts for domain trust discovery. QakBot can conduct brute force attacks to capture credentials. QakBot can execute WMI queries to gather information. QakBot can RC4 encrypt strings in C2 communication. QakBot can identify the system time on a targeted host. The QakBot proxy module can encapsulate SOCKS5 protocol within its own proxy protocol. QakBot can inject itself into processes including explore.exe, Iexplore.exe, Mobsync.exe., and wermgr.exe. QakBot can use net localgroup to enable discovery of local groups. QakBot has the ability use TCP to send or receive C2 packets. The QakBot web inject module can inject Java Script into web banking pages visited by the victim. QakBot can identify the user name on a compromised system. QakBot can measure the download speed on a targeted host. QakBot can use net config workstation, arp -a, `nslookup`, and ipconfig /all to gather network configuration information. QakBot can use netstat to enumerate current network connections. QakBot can identify remote systems through the net view command. QakBot has a module that can proxy C2 communications. QakBot can use net share to identify network shares for use in lateral movement. QakBot can target and steal locally stored emails to support thread hijacking phishing campaigns. QakBot can send stolen information to C2 nodes including passwords, accounts, and emails. QakBot has collected usernames and passwords from Firefox and Chrome. QakBot has the ability to capture web session cookies.
title: Kuzmenko, A. et al. (2021, September 2). QakBot technical analysis. Retrieved September 27, 2021.

text:
Some Volgmer variants use SSL to encrypt C2 communications.
Volgmer can execute commands on the victim's machine.
Volgmer can list directories on a victim.
Volgmer queries the system to identify existing services.
title: US-CERT. (2017, November 22). Alert (TA17-318B): HIDDEN COBRA – North Korean Trojan: Volgmer. Retrieved December 7, 2017.

text: Cobalt Strike can conduct peer-to-peer communication over Windows named pipes encapsulated in the SMB protocol. All protocols use their standard assigned ports. Cobalt Strike has the ability to use an Excel Workbook to execute additional code by enabling Office to trust macros and execute code without user permission. Cobalt Strike can use self signed Java applets to execute signed applet attacks. Cobalt Strike's Beacon payload can collect information on process details. Cobalt Strike uses the native Windows Network Enumeration APIs to interrogate and discover targets in a Windows Active Directory network. Cobalt Strike has the ability to use AES-256 symmetric encryption in CBC mode with HMAC-SHA-256 to encrypt task commands and XOR to encrypt shell code and configuration data. Cobalt Strike can query HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Office\\Excel\Security\AccessVBOM\ to determine if the security setting for restricting default programmatic access is enabled. Cobalt Strike can perform port scans from an infected host. Cobalt Strike has the ability to load DLLs via reflective injection. Cobalt Strike can exploit Oracle Java vulnerabilities for execution, including CVE-2011-3544, CVE-2013-2465, CVE-2012-4681, and CVE-2013-2460. Cobalt Strike can produce a sessions report from compromised hosts. Cobalt Strike can hash functions to obfuscate calls to the Windows API and use a public/private key pair to encrypt Beacon session metadata. Cobalt Strike uses a command-line interface to interact with systems. The Cobalt Strike System Profiler can use JavaScript to perform reconnaissance actions. Cobalt Strike can deliver additional payloads to victim machines. Cobalt Strike can use RSA asymmetric encryption with PKCS1 padding to encrypt data sent to the C2 server. Cobalt Strike can be configured to use TCP, ICMP, and UDP for C2 communications. Cobalt Strike can use a custom command and control protocol that can be encapsulated in DNS. All protocols use their standard assigned ports. Cobalt Strike can modify Registry values within HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Office\\Excel\Security\AccessVBOM\ to enable the execution of additional code. Cobalt Strike can download a hosted "beacon" payload using BITSAdmin. Cobalt Strike has the ability to use Smart Applet attacks to disable the Java SecurityManager sandbox.
title: Mavis, N. (2020, September 21). The Art and Science of Detecting Cobalt Strike. Retrieved September 12, 2024.

text:
XTunnel is capable of probing the network for open ports.
XTunnel is capable of accessing locally stored passwords on victims.
title: Belcher, P.. (2016, July 28). Tunnel of Gov: DNC Hack and the Russian XTunnel. Retrieved August 3, 2016.

text:
FrameworkPOS can enumerate and exclude selected processes on a compromised host to speed execution of memory scraping.
FrameworkPOS can XOR credit card information before exfiltration.
FrameworkPOS can collect elements related to credit card data from process memory.
FrameworkPOS can use DNS tunneling for exfiltration of credit card data.
title: Kremez, V. (2019, September 19). FIN6 “FrameworkPOS”: Point-of-Sale Malware Analysis & Internals. Retrieved September 8, 2020.

text: HotCroissant has used the open source UPX executable packer. HotCroissant has the ability to clean up installed files, delete files, and delete itself from the victim’s machine. Rifdoor has created a new registry entry at HKEY_CURRENT_USERS\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\Graphics with a value of C:\ProgramData\Initech\Initech.exe /run. HotCroissant has the ability to list running processes on the infected host. Rifdoor has added four additional bytes of data upon launching, then saved the changed version as C:\ProgramData\Initech\Initech.exe. Rifdoor has the ability to identify the username on the compromised host. Rifdoor has the ability to identify the Windows version on the compromised host. HotCroissant has attempted to install a scheduled task named “Java Maintenance64” on startup to establish persistence. HotCroissant has the ability to download files from the infected host to the command and control (C2) server. Rifdoor has encrypted command and control (C2) communications with a stream cipher. HotCroissant has the ability to do real time screen viewing on an infected host. HotCroissant can remotely open applications on the infected host with the ShellExecuteA command. Rifdoor has the ability to identify the IP address of the compromised host. HotCroissant has the ability to hide the window for operations performed on a given file. Rifdoor has been distributed in e-mails with malicious Excel or Word documents. HotCroissant has the ability to list the names of all open windows on the infected host.
