HotCroissant can retrieve a list of applications from the SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\App Paths registry key. HotCroissant has the ability to retrieve a list of services on the infected host. Rifdoor has encrypted strings with a single byte XOR algorithm. Rifdoor has been executed from malicious Excel or Word documents containing macros. HotCroissant has the ability to collect the username on the infected host. HotCroissant has the ability to stop services on the infected host. HotCroissant has the ability to upload a file from the command and control (C2) server to the victim machine. HotCroissant has the ability to retrieve a list of files in a given directory as well as drives and drive types. HotCroissant has encrypted strings with single-byte XOR and base64 encoded RC4. HotCroissant has compressed network communications and encrypted them with a custom stream cipher.
title: Knight, S.. (2020, April 16). VMware Carbon Black TAU Threat Analysis: The Evolution of Lazarus. Retrieved May 1, 2020.

text: Denis exploits a security vulnerability to load a fake DLL and execute its code.
title: Dahan, A. (2017, May 24). OPERATION COBALT KITTY: A LARGE-SCALE APT IN ASIA CARRIED OUT BY THE OCEANLOTUS GROUP. Retrieved November 5, 2018.

text:
PlugX has used random, high-number, non-standard ports to listen for subsequent actions and C2 activities.
PlugX has modified local firewall rules on victim machines to enable a random, high-number listening port for subsequent access and C2 activity.
title: Sygnia Team. (2024, June 3). China-Nexus Threat Group ‘Velvet Ant’ Abuses F5 Load Balancers for Persistence. Retrieved March 14, 2025.

text:
Mispadu creates a link in the startup folder for persistence. Mispadu adds persistence via the registry key `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run`.
Mispadu can list installed security products in the victim’s environment.
title: Garcia, F., Regalado, D. (2023, March 7). Inside Mispadu massive infection campaign in LATAM. Retrieved March 15, 2024.

text: njRAT can access the victim's webcam.
title: Scott-Railton, J., et al. (2016, August 2). Group5: Syria and the Iranian Connection. Retrieved September 26, 2016.

text:
AcidPour includes a self-delete function where the malware deletes itself from disk after execution and program load into memory.
AcidPour can identify specific files and directories within the Linux operating system corresponding with storage devices for follow-on wiping activity, similar to AcidRain.
AcidPour can perform an in-depth wipe of victim filesystems and attached storage devices through either data overwrite or calling various IOCTLS to erase them, similar to AcidRain.
AcidPour can identify various system locations and mapped devices on Linux systems as a precursor to wiping activity.
AcidPour includes functionality to identify MMC and SD cards connected to the victim device.
AcidPour includes functionality to overwrite victim devices with the content of a buffer to wipe disk content.
AcidPour includes functionality to reboot the victim system following wiping actions, similar to AcidRain.
title: Juan Andrés Guerrero-Saade & Tom Hegel. (2024, March 21). AcidPour | New Embedded Wiper Variant of AcidRain Appears in Ukraine. Retrieved November 25, 2024.

text:
Royal can identify specific files and directories to exclude from the encryption process.
Royal can use `RmShutDown` to kill applications and services using the resources that are targeted for encryption.
Royal can use `GetLogicalDrives` to enumerate logical drives.
Royal establishes a TCP socket for C2 communication using the API `WSASocketW`.
Royal can use multiple APIs for discovery, communication, and execution.
Royal can use SMB to connect to move laterally.
Royal can enumerate the shared resources of a given IP addresses using the API call `NetShareEnum`.
Royal can enumerate IP addresses using `GetIpAddrTable`.
Royal uses a multi-threaded encryption process that can partially encrypt targeted files with the OpenSSL library and the AES256 algorithm.
Royal can use `GetCurrentProcess` to enumerate processes.
Royal can use `GetNativeSystemInfo` to enumerate system processors.
Royal can scan the network interfaces of targeted systems.
title: Cybereason Global SOC and Cybereason Security Research Teams. (2022, December 14). Royal Rumble: Analysis of Royal Ransomware. Retrieved March 30, 2023.

text:
ROADSWEEP has dropped ransom notes in targeted folders prior to encrypting the files.
ROADSWEEP has been placed in the start up folder to trigger execution upon user login.
title: MSTIC. (2022, September 8). Microsoft investigates Iranian attacks against the Albanian government. Retrieved August 6, 2024.

text:
StoneDrill has a disk wiper module that targets files other than those in the Windows directory.
StoneDrill can check for antivirus and antimalware programs.
StoneDrill has obfuscated its module with an alphabet-based table or XOR encryption.
StoneDrill can take screenshots.
StoneDrill has downloaded and dropped temporary files containing scripts; it additionally has a function to upload files from the victims machine.
StoneDrill has several VBS scripts used throughout the malware's lifecycle.
StoneDrill has used several anti-emulation techniques to prevent automated analysis by emulators or sandboxes.
StoneDrill has relied on injecting its payload directly into the process memory of the victim's preferred browser.
StoneDrill has used the WMI command-line (WMIC) utility to run tasks.
StoneDrill has been observed deleting the temporary files once they fulfill their task.
StoneDrill has the capability to discover the system OS, Windows version, architecture and environment.
StoneDrill has looked in the registry to find the default browser path.
StoneDrill can obtain the current date and time of the victim machine.
title: Kaspersky Lab. (2017, March 7). From Shamoon to StoneDrill: Wipers attacking Saudi organizations and beyond. Retrieved March 14, 2019.

text: gh0st RAT has a keylogger.
title: Alintanahin, K. (2014, March 13). Kunming Attack Leads to Gh0st RAT Variant. Retrieved November 12, 2014.

text:
Unknown Logger is capable of stealing usernames and passwords from browsers on the victim machine.
TINYTYPHON searches through the drive containing the OS, then all drive letters C through to Z, for documents matching certain extensions.
AutoIt backdoor downloads a PowerShell script that decodes to a typical shellcode loader.
Unknown Logger has functionality to disable security tools, including Kaspersky, BitDefender, and MalwareBytes.
Unknown Logger can obtain information about the victim's IP address.
Unknown Logger can obtain information about the victim computer name, physical memory, country, and date.
TINYTYPHON installs itself under Registry Run key to establish persistence.
Unknown Logger is capable of recording keystrokes.
TINYTYPHON has used XOR with 0x90 to obfuscate its configuration file.
Unknown Logger can obtain information about the victim usernames.
AutoIt backdoor has sent a C2 response that was base64-encoded.
BADNEWS installs a registry Run key to establish persistence.
When it first starts, BADNEWS crawls the victim's mapped drives and collects documents with the following extensions: .doc, .docx, .pdf, .ppt, .pptx, and .txt.
After encrypting C2 data, BADNEWS converts it into a hexadecimal representation and then encodes it into base64.
AutoIt backdoor is capable of identifying documents on the victim with the following extensions: .doc; .pdf, .csv, .ppt, .docx, .pst, .xls, .xlsx, .pptx, and .jpeg.
AutoIt backdoor attempts to escalate privileges by bypassing User Access Control.
Unknown Logger is capable of spreading to USB devices.
When a document is found matching one of the extensions in the configuration, TINYTYPHON uploads it to the C2 server.
Unknown Logger is capable of downloading remote files.
title: Settle, A., et al. (2016, August 8). MONSOON - Analysis Of An APT Campaign. Retrieved September 22, 2016.

text:
ROAMINGHOUSE can embed a ZIP file containing UPPERCUT components into three base64 encoded parts.
ANELLDR code implements anti-analysis techniques including control flow flattening and Mixed Boolean Arithmetic (MBA).
ROAMINGHOUSE has been loaded as a Word Template file when victims opened a decoy document placed in `%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Templates` alongside a ROAMINGHOUSE macro.
UPPERCUT can upload files to the C2 from infected machines.
ANELLDR can use DLL sideloading from a legitimate application to initiate execution.
ROAMINGHOUSE can use a legitimate EXE to sideload a malicious DLL named JSFC.dll. ROAMINGHOUSE has also used ScnCfg32.exe to sideload vsodscpl.dll to enable UPPERCUT execution.
During Operation AkaiRyū, MirrorFace used malicious files to drop ROAMINGHOUSE.
ANELLDR can enumerate files in the current directory to search for encrypted payload files.
ANELLDR can use the `ZwSetInformationThread` to enable debugger evasion.
UPPERCUT can base64 encode C2 communications.
ANELLDR can call `ZwSetInformationThread` with the second argument set to `ThreadHideFromDebugger (0x11)` to evade being debugged.
UPPERCUT can use a sleep function to delay execution.
ANELLDR can decrypt encrypted payload data using AES-256-CBC and subsequently execute the payload in memory.
ROAMINGHOUSE can use WMI to launch a legitimate executable later used to enable DLL sideloading.
UPPERCUT contains functionality to bypass UAC.

Mafalda can use a variety of API calls. metaMain can inject the loader file, Speech02.db, into a process. Mafalda can delete Windows Event logs by invoking the `OpenEventLogW` and `ClearEventLogW` functions. metaMain has the ability to log keyboard events. Mafalda can enumerate running processes on a machine. Mafalda can decrypt files and data. metaMain has stored the collected system files in a working directory. Mafalda can collect a Chrome encryption key used to protect browser cookies. metaMain can encrypt the data that it sends and receives from the C2 server using an RC4 encryption algorithm. Mafalda can collect files and information from a compromised host. Mafalda can send network system data and files to its C2 server. metaMain can establish an indirect and raw TCP socket-based connection to the C2 server. Mafalda can use the `GetAdaptersInfo` function to retrieve information about network adapters and the `GetIpNetTable` function to retrieve the IPv4 to physical network address mapping table. Mafalda can collect the contents of the `%USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\Google\Chrome\User Data\LocalState` file. metaMain can execute an operator-provided Windows command by leveraging functions such as `WinExec`, `WriteFile`, and `ReadFile`. Mafalda can use HTTP for C2. Mafalda can search for files and directories. metaMain can download files onto compromised systems. Mafalda can place retrieved files into a destination directory. metaMain can take and save screenshots. metaMain can collect files and system information from a compromised host. Mafalda can collect the computer name of a compromised host. Mafalda can enumerate all drives on a compromised host. Mafalda has been obfuscated and contains encrypted functions.

text: Shamoon creates a new service named “ntssrv” to execute the payload. Newer versions create the "MaintenaceSrv" and "hdv_725x" services. Shamoon attempts to copy itself to remote machines on the network. Shamoon attempts to overwrite operating system files and disk structures with image files. In a later variant, randomly generated data was used for data overwrites. Shamoon obtains the system time and will only activate if it is greater than a preset date. Shamoon obtains the victim's operating system version and keyboard layout and sends the information to the C2 server. Shamoon contains base64-encoded strings. Shamoon copies an executable payload to the target system by using SMB/Windows Admin Shares and then scheduling an unnamed task to execute the malware. Shamoon has been seen overwriting features of disk structure such as the MBR. Shamoon creates a new service named “ntssrv” that attempts to appear legitimate; the service's display name is “Microsoft Network Realtime Inspection Service” and its description is “Helps guard against time change attempts targeting known and newly discovered vulnerabilities in network time protocols.” Newer versions create the "MaintenaceSrv" service, which misspells the word "maintenance." Shamoon queries several Registry keys to identify hard disk partitions to overwrite. Shamoon creates a new service named “ntssrv” to execute the payload. Shamoon can also spread via PsExec. Once Shamoon has access to a network share, it enables the RemoteRegistry service on the target system. It will then connect to the system with RegConnectRegistryW and modify the Registry to disable UAC remote restrictions by setting SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy to 1. Shamoon attempts to disable UAC remote restrictions by modifying the Registry. Shamoon has an operational mode for encrypting data instead of overwriting it. Shamoon has used HTTP for C2. Shamoon obtains the target's IP address and local network segment. Shamoon can download an executable to run on the victim.

text: APIs and strings in some TYPEFRAME variants are RC4 encrypted. Another variant is encoded with XOR. TYPEFRAME can search directories for files on the victim’s machine. TYPEFRAME has used ports 443, 8080, and 8443 with a FakeTLS method. TYPEFRAME can gather the disk volume information. A Word document delivering TYPEFRAME prompts the user to enable macro execution. TYPEFRAME has used a malicious Word document for delivery with VBA macros for execution. TYPEFRAME can open the Windows Firewall on the victim’s machine to allow incoming connections. TYPEFRAME can upload and download files to the victim’s machine. TYPEFRAME can delete files off the system. TYPEFRAME variants can add malicious DLL modules as new services.TYPEFRAME can also delete services from the victim’s machine. TYPEFRAME can install and store encrypted configuration data under the Registry key HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\ShellCompatibility\Applications\laxhost.dll and HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\PrintConfigs. One TYPEFRAME variant decrypts an archive using an RC4 key, then decompresses and installs the decrypted malicious DLL module. Another variant decodes the embedded file by XORing it with the value "0x35". TYPEFRAME can install encrypted configuration data under the Registry key HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\ShellCompatibility\Applications\laxhost.dll and HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\PrintConfigs. A TYPEFRAME variant can force the compromised system to function as a proxy server. TYPEFRAME can uninstall malware components using a batch script. TYPEFRAME can execute commands using a shell.
title: US-CERT. (2018, June 14). MAR-10135536-12 – North Korean Trojan: TYPEFRAME. Retrieved July 13, 2018.

text: ROKRAT can access the HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\mssmbios\Data\SMBiosData Registry key to obtain the System manufacturer value to identify the machine type. ROKRAT can steal credentials by leveraging the Windows Vault mechanism. ROKRAT can steal credentials stored in Web browsers by querying the sqlite database.
title: Mercer, W., Rascagneres, P. (2018, January 16). Korea In The Crosshairs. Retrieved May 21, 2018.

text:
Gomir uses reverse proxy functionality that employs SSL to encrypt communications.
Gomir can start a reverse proxy to initiate connections to arbitrary endpoints in victim networks.
Gomir probes arbitrary network endpoints for TCP connectivity.
Gomir uses a custom encryption algorithm for content sent to command and control infrastructure.
Gomir will configure a crontab for process execution to start the backdoor on reboot if it is not initially running under group 0 privileges.
Gomir collects information about directory and file structures, including total number of subdirectories, total number of files, and total size of files on infected systems.
Gomir creates a systemd service named `syslogd` for persistence.
GoBear is installed through droppers masquerading as legitimate, signed software installers.
Gomir checks the effective group ID of its process when initially executed to determine if it is in group 0, denoting superuser privileges in Linux environments.
Gomir reads command line arguments and parses them for functionality when executed from a Linux shell, and can execute arbitrary strings passed to it as shell commands.
Gomir deletes its original executable and terminates its original process after creating a systemd service.
Gomir collects information on infected systems such as hostname, username, CPU, and RAM information.
Gomir periodically communicates to its command and control infrastructure through HTTP POST requests.
Gomir uses Base64-encoded content in HTTP communications to command and control infrastructure.
Gomir collects network information on infected systems such as listing interface names, MAC and IP addresses, and IPv6 addresses.
title: Symantec Threat Hunter Team. (2024, May 16). Springtail: New Linux Backdoor Added to Toolkit. Retrieved January 17, 2025.

text:
Gazer versions are signed with various valid certificates; one was likely faked and issued by Comodo for "Solid Loop Ltd," and another was issued for "Ultimate Computer Support Ltd."
Gazer logs its actions into files that are encrypted with 3DES. It also uses RSA to encrypt resources.
Gazer uses custom encryption for C2 that uses 3DES.
Gazer performs thread execution hijacking to inject its orchestrator into a running thread from a remote process.
Gazer uses custom encryption for C2 that uses RSA.
Gazer has commands to delete files and persistence mechanisms from the victim.
Gazer can execute a task to download a file.
Gazer obtains the current user's security identifier.
Gazer can establish persistence by creating a .lnk file in the Start menu.
Gazer can establish persistence by creating a scheduled task.
Gazer injects its communication module into an Internet accessible process through which it performs C2.
Gazer can establish persistence by creating a .lnk file in the Start menu or by modifying existing .lnk files to execute the malware through cmd.exe.
title: Kaspersky Lab's Global Research & Analysis Team. (2017, August 30). Introducing WhiteBear. Retrieved September 21, 2017.

text: Mivast has the capability to open a remote shell and run basic commands. Mivast has the capability to download and execute .exe files. Mivast creates the following Registry entry: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\Micromedia. Mivast has the capability to gather NTLM password information.
title: Stama, D.. (2015, February 6). Backdoor.Mivast. Retrieved February 15, 2016.

text: PLEAD has the ability to steal saved passwords from Microsoft Outlook.
title: Cherepanov, A.. (2018, July 9). Certificates stolen from Taiwanese tech‑companies misused in Plead malware campaign. Retrieved May 6, 2020.

text:
Hannotog uses non-standard listening ports, such as UDP 5900, for command and control purposes.
Hannotog creates a new service for persistence.
Hannotog can stop Windows services.
Hannotog can download additional files to the victim machine.
Sagerunex finds the `explorer.exe` process after execution and uses it to change the token of its executing thread.
Sagerunex can be passed a reference to an XOR-encrypted configuration file at runtime.
Hannotog can execute various `cmd.exe /c %s` commands.
Sagerunex identifies the `explorer.exe` process on the executing system.
Sagerunex communicates via HTTPS, at times using a hard-coded User Agent of `Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; MSIE 7.0; Win32)`.
Hannotog can modify local firewall settings via `netsh` commands to open a listening UDP port.
Hannotog can upload encyrpted data for exfiltration.
Sagerunex uses HTTPS for command and control communication.
title: Symntec Threat Hunter Team. (2022, November 12). Billbug: State-sponsored Actor Targets Cert Authority, Government Agencies in Multiple Asian Countries. Retrieved March 15, 2025.

text:
TrickBot can implant malicious code into a compromised device's firmware.
TrickBot module "Trickboot" can write or erase the UEFI/BIOS firmware of a compromised device.
TrickBot gathers the OS version, machine name, CPU type, amount of RAM available, and UEFI/BIOS firmware information from the victim’s machine.
title: Eclypsium, Advanced Intelligence. (2020, December 1). TRICKBOT NOW OFFERS ‘TRICKBOOT’: PERSIST, BRICK, PROFIT. Retrieved March 15, 2021.

text:
Ursnif droppers have used COM objects to execute the malware's full executable payload.
Ursnif droppers have used WMI classes to execute PowerShell commands.
Ursnif droppers have used COM properties to execute malware in hidden windows.
Ursnif droppers have used PowerShell in download cradles to download and execute the malware's full executable payload.
Ursnif droppers execute base64 encoded PowerShell commands.
Ursnif droppers have used VBA macros to download and execute the malware's full executable payload.
Ursnif has used an XOR-based algorithm to encrypt Tor clients dropped to disk. Ursnif droppers have also been delivered as password-protected zip files that execute base64 encoded PowerShell commands.
title: Holland, A. (2019, March 7). Tricks and COMfoolery: How Ursnif Evades Detection. Retrieved June 10, 2019.

text:
J-magic can compare the host and remote IPs to check if a received packet is from the infected machine.
J-magic can monitor incoming C2 communications sent over TCP to the compromised host.
J-magic can communicate back to send a challenge to C2 infrastructure over SSL.
The J-magic agent is executed through a command line argument which specifies an interface and listening port.
cd00r can monitor for a single TCP-SYN packet to be sent in series to a configurable set of ports (200, 80, 22, 53 and 3 in the original code) before opening a port for communication.
J-magic can rename itself as “[nfsiod 0]” to masquerade as the local Network File System (NFS) asynchronous I/O server.
cd00r can monitor incoming C2 communications sent over TCP to the compromised host.
J-magic has a pcap listener function that can create an Extended Berkley Packet Filter (eBPF) on designated interfaces and ports.
J-magic can overwrite previously executed command line arguments.
J-magic can monitor TCP traffic for packets containing one of five different predefined parameters and will spawn a reverse shell if one of the parameters and the proper response string to a subsequent challenge is received.
title: Black Lotus Labs. (2025, January 23). The J-Magic Show: Magic Packets and Where to find them. Retrieved February 17, 2025.

text: Chaes has a module to perform any API hooking it desires. Chaes changed the template target of the settings.xml file embedded in the Word document and populated that field with the downloaded URL of the next payload. Chaes has used a script that extracts the web session cookie and sends it to the C2 server. Chaes has used an unsigned, crafted DLL module named hha.dll that was designed to look like a legitimate 32-bit Windows DLL. Chaes has collected system information, including the machine name and OS version. Chaes can download additional files onto an infected machine. Chaes has used HTTP for C2 communications. Chaes used the CreateFileW() API function with read permissions to access downloaded payloads. Some versions of Chaes stored its instructions (otherwise in a `instructions.ini` file) in the Registry. Chaes requires the user to click on the malicious Word document to execute the next part of the attack. Chaes has used the Puppeteer module to hook and monitor the Chrome web browser to collect user information from infected hosts. Chaes can capture screenshots of the infected machine. Chaes has been delivered by sending victims a phishing email containing a malicious .docx file. Chaes has used .MSI files as an initial way to start the infection chain. Chaes has used Python scripts for execution and the installation of additional files. Chaes has used search order hijacking to load a malicious DLL. Chaes has used JavaScript and Node.Js information stealer script that exfiltrates data using the node process. Chaes has used encryption for its C2 channel. Chaes has used VBscript to execute malicious code. Chaes has used Installutill to download content. Chaes has decrypted an AES encrypted binary file to trigger the download of other files. Chaes has collected the username and UID from the infected machine. Chaes has used Base64 to encode C2 communications. Chaes has used cmd to execute tasks on the system. Chaes has added persistence via the Registry key software\microsoft\windows\currentversion\run\microsoft windows html help. Chaes has exfiltrated its collected data from the infected machine to the C2, sometimes using the MIME protocol. Chaes can steal login credentials and stored financial information from the browser. Chaes can modify Registry values to stored information and establish persistence.
title: Salem, E. (2020, November 17). CHAES: Novel Malware Targeting Latin American E-Commerce. Retrieved June 30, 2021.

text:
BRICKSTORM has utilized XOR cipher encryption to hide key strings within their code, to include IPv4 addresses of public DNS-over-HTTPS (DOH) servers.
BRICKSTORM has impaired command logging through the use of `dev/null` which prevents generating output from the command and does not wait for input.
BRICKSTORM has terminated an existing process to ensure that its own new process can execute.
BRICKSTORM has communicated with C2 infrastructure via TLS.
BRICKSTORM has commands that allow the actor download files from the compromised host to the C2 server, and to also download specific sections of a file.
BRICKSTORM has checked hard-coded paths of `/etc/sysconfig/` or `/etc/sysconfig/network` prior to execution and loading file contents from that path.
BRICKSTORM has the ability to check if it is running as an active child process through the detection of a specific environment variable.
BRICKSTORM has created a new background session and has spawned a child process of a parent process when it determines it is not running in its intended state.
BRICKSTORM has copied itself to the `usr/sbin/` folder.
title: DHS/CISA. (2026, February 11). AR25-338A: BRICKSTORM Backdoor. Retrieved April 16, 2026.

text:
Tomiris can download files and execute them on a victim's system.
Tomiris can upload files matching a hardcoded set of extensions, such as .doc, .docx, .pdf, and .rar, to its C2 server.
Tomiris has connected to a signalization server that provides a URL and port, and then Tomiris sends a GET request to that URL to establish C2.
Tomiris has the ability to collect recent files matching a hardcoded list of extensions prior to exfiltration.
Tomiris can use HTTP to establish C2 communications.
Tomiris has the ability to sleep for at least nine minutes to evade sandbox-based analysis systems.
Tomiris has been packed with UPX.
Tomiris has used `SCHTASKS /CREATE /SC DAILY /TN StartDVL /TR "[path to self]" /ST 10:00` to establish persistence.
title: Kwiatkoswki, I. and Delcher, P. (2021, September 29). DarkHalo After SolarWinds: the Tomiris connection. Retrieved December 27, 2021.

text:
BADFLICK has delayed communication to the actor-controlled IP address by 5 minutes.
BADFLICK has searched for files on the infected host.
BADFLICK has compressed data using the aPLib compression library.
BADFLICK has relied upon users clicking on a malicious attachment delivered through spearphishing.
BADFLICK has download files from its C2 server.
BADFLICK has been distributed via spearphishing campaigns containing malicious Microsoft Word documents.
BADFLICK has captured victim IP address details.
BADFLICK has captured victim computer name, memory space, and CPU details.
BADFLICK has uploaded files from victims' machines.
BADFLICK can decode shellcode using a custom rotating XOR cipher.
title: Accenture iDefense Unit. (2019, March 5). Mudcarp's Focus on Submarine Technologies. Retrieved August 24, 2021.

text: LockerGoga has been observed deleting its original launcher after execution.
title: CarbonBlack Threat Analysis Unit. (2019, March 22). TAU Threat Intelligence Notification – LockerGoga Ransomware. Retrieved April 16, 2019.

text:
CorKLOG has leveraged legitimate binaries to conduct DLL side-loading.
PAKLOG has collected a timestamp to log the precise time a key was pressed, formatted as %Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.
SplatDropper has created a service to execute a payload.
SplatCloak has used a revoked certificate to exploit Windows driver execution policy where certificates issued before a specific date could still load.
SplatDropper has deleted its malicious payload and removed its own created service to avoid leaving traces of its presence on victim devices.
CorKLOG has stored the captured data in an encrypted file using a 48-character RC4 key.
SplatDropper has leveraged hashed Windows API calls using a seed value of "131313".
SplatDropper has also utilized XOR encrypted payload.
SplatDropper has decoded XOR encrypted payload.
PAKLOG has detected and logged the full path of processes active in the foreground using Windows API calls.
CorKLOG has captured keystrokes.
SplatCloak has identified drivers of AV solutions by searching for related filenames, keywords and signed certificates.
SplatDropper has utilized hashed Native Windows API calls.
SplatDropper has used legitimate signed binaries such as BugSplatHD64.exe for follow-on execution of malicious DLLs through DLL side-loading.
SplatCloak has identified and disabled API callback features of Windows Defender and Kaspersky.
SplatCloak has collected the Windows build number using the windows kernel API `RtlGetVersion` to determine if the response is 19000 or higher (Windows 10 version 2004 or later).
PAKLOG has stored the captured data in a file located `C:\\Users\\Public\\Libraries\\record.txt`.
CorKLOG has used legitimate signed binaries such as lcommute.exe for follow-on execution of malicious DLLs through DLL side-loading.
PAKLOG has utilized a simple encoding mechanism to encode characters in the buffer.
PAKLOG has used Windows API `SetWindowsHookExW` with `idHook` set to `WH_KEYBOARD_LL` and a custom hook procedure to support its keylogging functions.
CorKLOG has encrypted collected contents using RC4. CorKLOG has also utilized XOR encrypted strings.
CorKLOG has created a service to establish persistence.
PAKLOG has monitored and extracted clipboard contents.
PAKLOG has used legitimate signed binaries such as PACLOUD.exe for follow-on execution of malicious DLLs through DLL Side-Loading.
CorKLOG has achieved persistence through the creation of a scheduled task named TableInputServices by using the command `schtasks /create /tn TabletlnputServices /tr /sc minute /mo 10 /f`.
PAKLOG has captured keystrokes using Windows API.
SplatDropper has leveraged legitimate binaries to conduct DLL side-loading.
CorKLOG has decoded XOR encrypted strings.
PAKLOG has used `GetForegroundWindow` to access the foreground window. PAKLOG has also captured text from the foreground windows.
PAKLOG has leveraged legitimate binaries to conduct DLL side-loading.
SplatCloak has utilized Native Windows API calls dynamically through `ZwQuerySystemInformation`.
SplatCloak has used Windows API to identify files associated with Windows Defender and Kaspersky.
title: Sudeep Singh. (2025, April 16). Latest Mustang Panda Arsenal: PAKLOG, CorKLOG, and SplatCloak | P2. Retrieved September 12, 2025.

text:
Nidiran can download and execute files.
Nidiran can create a new service named msamger (Microsoft Security Accounts Manager).
title: Sponchioni, R.. (2016, March 11). Backdoor.Nidiran. Retrieved August 3, 2016.

text:
hcdLoader provides command-line access to the compromised system.
hcdLoader installs itself as a service for persistence.
title: Carvey, H.. (2014, September 2). Where you AT?: Indicators of lateral movement using at.exe on Windows 7 systems. Retrieved January 25, 2016.

text:
AvosLocker’s Linux variant has terminated ESXi virtual machines.
AvosLocker has been executed via the `RunOnce` Registry key to run itself on safe mode.
AvosLocker has been disguised as a .jpg file.
title: Trend Micro Research. (2022, April 4). Ransomware Spotlight AvosLocker. Retrieved January 11, 2023.

text: OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D has changed permissions of a second-stage payload to an executable via chmod. OSX_OCEANLOTUS.D uses a shell script as the main executable inside an app bundle and drops an embedded base64-encoded payload to the /tmp folder.
title: Phil Stokes. (2020, December 2). APT32 Multi-stage macOS Trojan Innovates on Crimeware Scripting Technique. Retrieved September 13, 2021.

text:
Winnti for Linux has used a custom TCP protocol with four-byte XOR for command and control (C2).
Winnti for Linux has the ability to deploy modules directly from command and control (C2) servers, possibly for remote command execution, file exfiltration, and socks5 proxying on the infected host.
Winnti for Linux has used a modified copy of the open-source userland rootkit Azazel, named libxselinux.so, to hide the malware's operations and network activity.
Winnti for Linux can encode its configuration file with single-byte XOR encoding.
Winnti for Linux has used HTTP in outbound communications.
Winnti for Linux has used a passive listener, capable of identifying a specific magic value before executing tasking, as a secondary command and control (C2) mechanism.
Winnti for Linux has used ICMP, custom TCP, and UDP in outbound communications.
Winnti for Linux has decoded XOR encoded strings holding its configuration upon execution.
title: Chronicle Blog. (2019, May 15). Winnti: More than just Windows and Gates. Retrieved April 29, 2020.

text: Derusbi injects itself into the secure shell (SSH) process.
title: Perigaud, F. (2015, December 15). Newcomers in the Derusbi family. Retrieved September 12, 2024.

text:
Kevin has renamed an image of `cmd.exe` with a random name followed by a `.tmpl` extension.
Variants of Kevin can communicate with C2 over HTTP.
Kevin can create directories to store logs and other collected data.
Kevin can download files to the compromised host.
Kevin can assign hard-coded fallback domains for C2.
Kevin can Base32 encode chunks of output files during exfiltration.
Kevin can use a renamed image of `cmd.exe` for execution.
Milan can use the API `DnsQuery_A` for DNS resolution.
Kevin has Base64-encoded its configuration file.
Kevin can use a custom protocol tunneled through DNS or HTTP.
Milan can use HTTPS for communication with C2.
Kevin can exfiltrate data to the C2 server in 27-character chunks.
Variants of Kevin can communicate over DNS through queries to the server for constructed domain names with embedded information.
Kevin can delete files created on the victim's machine.
Kevin can compile randomly-generated MOF files into the WMI repository to persistently run malware.
Kevin can use the `ShowWindow` API to avoid detection.
Milan can use a custom protocol tunneled through DNS or HTTP.
Kevin can generate a sequence of dummy HTTP C2 requests to obscure traffic.
Kevin can sleep for a time interval between C2 communication attempts.
Milan can encode files containing information about the targeted system.
Kevin can send data from the victim host through a DNS C2 channel.
Milan has the ability to use DNS for C2 communications.
Kevin can upload logs and other data from a compromised host.
Kevin can hide the current window from the targeted user via the `ShowWindow` API function.
Kevin can enumerate the OS version and hostname of a targeted machine.
Kevin can collect the MAC address and other information from a victim machine using `ipconfig/all`.
title: Kayal, A. et al. (2021, October). LYCEUM REBORN: COUNTERINTELLIGENCE IN THE MIDDLE EAST. Retrieved June 14, 2022.

text:
Micropsia can perform microphone recording.
Micropsia can perform a recursive directory listing for all volume drives available on the victim's machine and can also fetch specific files by their paths.
Micropsia has keylogging capabilities.
Micropsia creates a RAR archive based on collected files on the victim's machine.
Micropsia executes an RAR tool to recursively archive files based on a predefined list of file extensions (*.xls, *.xlsx, *.csv, *.odt, *.doc, *.docx, *.ppt, *.pptx, *.pdf, *.mdb, *.accdb, *.accde, *.txt).
Micropsia creates a new hidden directory to store all components' outputs in a dedicated sub-folder for each.
Micropsia takes screenshots every 90 seconds by calling the Gdi32.BitBlt API.
Micropsia creates a command-line shell using cmd.exe.
title: Tsarfaty, Y. (2018, July 25). Micropsia Malware. Retrieved November 13, 2018.

text: NGLite will use an AES encrypted channel for command and control purposes, in one case using the key WHATswrongwithUu. NGLite will run the whoami command to gather system information and return this to the command and control server. NGLite will initially beacon out to the NKN network via an HTTP POST over TCP 30003. NGLite has abused NKN infrastructure for its C2 communication. NGLite identifies the victim system MAC and IPv4 addresses and uses these to establish a victim identifier.
title: Robert Falcone, Jeff White, and Peter Renals. (2021, November 7). Targeted Attack Campaign Against ManageEngine ADSelfService Plus Delivers Godzilla Webshells, NGLite Trojan and KdcSponge Stealer. Retrieved February 8, 2024.

text:
Diavol can collect the computer name and OS version from the system.
Diavol can delete specified files from a targeted system.
Diavol has Base64 encoded the RSA public key used for encrypting files.
Diavol has used several API calls like `GetLogicalDriveStrings`, `SleepEx`, `SystemParametersInfoAPI`, `CryptEncrypt`, and others to execute parts of its attack.
Diavol has used `CreateToolhelp32Snapshot`, `Process32First`, and `Process32Next` API calls to enumerate the running processes in the system.
Diavol can receive configuration updates and additional payloads including wscpy.exe from C2.
Diavol can delete shadow copies using the `IVssBackupComponents` COM object to call the `DeleteSnapshots` method.
Diavol has used HTTP GET and POST requests for C2.
Diavol can enumerate victims' local and external IPs when registering with C2.
Diavol has obfuscated its main code routines within bitmap images as part of its anti-analysis techniques.
Diavol has a command to traverse the files and directories in a given path.
Diavol can attempt to stop security software.
Diavol has encrypted files using an RSA key though the `CryptEncrypt` API and has appended filenames with ".lock64".
Diavol will terminate services using the Service Control Manager (SCM) API.
Diavol has a `ENMDSKS` command to enumerates available network shares.
After encryption, Diavol will capture the desktop background window, set the background color to black, and change the desktop wallpaper to a newly created bitmap image with the text “All your files are encrypted! For more information see “README-FOR-DECRYPT.txt".
Diavol can collect the username from a compromised host.
Diavol can spread throughout a network via SMB prior to encryption.
Diavol can use the ARP table to find remote hosts to scan.
title: Neeamni, D., Rubinfeld, A.. (2021, July 1). Diavol - A New Ransomware Used By Wizard Spider?. Retrieved November 12, 2021.

text:
Catchamas collects keystrokes from the victim’s machine.
Catchamas adds a new service named NetAdapter to establish persistence.
Catchamas captures screenshots based on specific keywords in the window’s title.
Catchamas creates three Registry keys to establish persistence by adding a Windows Service.
Catchamas steals data stored in the clipboard.
Catchamas adds a new service named NetAdapter in an apparent attempt to masquerade as a legitimate service.
Catchamas gathers the Mac address, IP address, and the network adapter information from the victim’s machine.
Catchamas stores the gathered data from the machine in .db files and .bmp files under four separate locations.
Catchamas obtains application windows titles and then determines which windows to perform Screen Capture on.
title: Balanza, M. (2018, April 02). Infostealer.Catchamas. Retrieved November 17, 2024.

text: NOKKI has established persistence by writing the payload to the Registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. NOKKI can delete files to cover tracks. NOKKI has downloaded a remote module for execution. NOKKI is written to %LOCALAPPDATA%\MicroSoft Updatea\svServiceUpdate.exe prior being executed in a new process in an apparent attempt to masquerade as a legitimate folder and file. NOKKI has used FTP for C2 communications. NOKKI has used HTTP for C2 communications. NOKKI can collect data from the victim and stage it in LOCALAPPDATA%\MicroSoft Updatea\uplog.tmp. NOKKI can gather information on drives on the victim’s machine. NOKKI uses Base64 encoding for strings. NOKKI uses the Windows call SetWindowsHookEx and begins injecting it into every GUI process running on the victim's machine. NOKKI has used rundll32 for execution. NOKKI can collect the username from the victim’s machine. NOKKI can gather information on the operating system on the victim’s machine. NOKKI can gather information on the victim IP address. NOKKI uses a unique, custom de-obfuscation technique. NOKKI can collect the current timestamp of the victim's machine.
title: Grunzweig, J., Lee, B. (2018, September 27). New KONNI Malware attacking Eurasia and Southeast Asia. Retrieved November 5, 2018.

text: Azorult can collect the time zone information from the system. Azorult can capture screenshots of the victim’s machines. Azorult uses an XOR key to decrypt content and uses Base64 to decode the C2 address. Azorult can steal credentials in files belonging to common software such as Skype, Telegram, and Steam. Azorult can call WTSQueryUserToken and CreateProcessAsUser to start a new process with local system privileges. Azorult can decrypt the payload into memory, create a new suspended process of itself, then inject a decrypted payload to the new process and resume new process execution. Azorult can collect the username from the victim’s machine. Azorult can download and execute additional files. Azorult has also downloaded a ransomware payload called Hermes. Azorult can steal credentials from the victim's browser. Azorult can collect a list of running processes by calling CreateToolhelp32Snapshot. Azorult can recursively search for files in folders and collects files from the desktop with certain extensions. Azorult can collect host IP information from the victim’s machine. Azorult can check for installed software on the system under the Registry key Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall. Azorult can delete files from victim machines. Azorult can encrypt C2 traffic using XOR. Azorult can collect the machine information, system architecture, the OS version, computer name, Windows product name, the number of CPU cores, video card information, and the system language.
title: Yan, T., et al. (2018, November 21). New Wine in Old Bottle: New Azorult Variant Found in FindMyName Campaign using Fallout Exploit Kit. Retrieved November 29, 2018.

text: DustySky searches for removable media and duplicates itself onto it. The DustySky dropper uses a function to obfuscate the name of functions and other parts of the malware. DustySky searches for network drives and removable media and duplicates itself onto them. DustySky checks for the existence of anti-virus. The DustySky dropper uses Windows Management Instrumentation to extract information about the operating system and whether an anti-virus is active. DustySky has used both HTTP and HTTPS for C2. DustySky has two hard-coded domains for C2 servers; if the first does not respond, it will try the second. DustySky extracts basic information about the operating system. DustySky contains a keylogger. DustySky achieves persistence by creating a Registry entry in HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run.
title: ClearSky. (2016, January 7). Operation DustySky. Retrieved January 8, 2016.

text: NETWIRE can use XDG Autostart Entries to establish persistence on Linux systems. NETWIRE can retrieve passwords from messaging and mail client applications. NETWIRE can perform keylogging. NETWIRE has masqueraded as legitimate software including TeamViewer and macOS Finder. If executing without root privileges, Fysbis adds a `.desktop` configuration file to the user's `~/.config/autostart` directory. The NETWIRE payload has been injected into benign Microsoft executables via process hollowing. NETWIRE can capture the victim's screen. NETWIRE can persist via startup options for Login items. NETWIRE has the ability to steal credentials from web browsers including Internet Explorer, Opera, Yandex, and Chrome. NETWIRE has the ability to communicate over HTTP. NETWIRE can copy itself to and launch itself from hidden folders. NETWIRE can use crontabs to establish persistence. NETWIRE has the ability to compress archived screenshots. NETWIRE can use AES encryption for C2 data transferred. CrossRAT can use an XDG Autostart to establish persistence. NETWIRE can collect the IP address of a compromised host. NETWIRE can store its configuration information in the Registry under `HKCU:\Software\Netwire`. NETWIRE can encrypt C2 communications. NETWIRE can automatically archive collected data. NETWIRE can inject code into system processes including notepad.exe, svchost.exe, and vbc.exe. NETWIRE has the ability to use /bin/bash and /bin/sh to execute commands. NETWIRE can use TCP in C2 communications. NETWIRE can modify the Registry to store its configuration information. NETWIRE can issue commands using cmd.exe. NETWIRE can use launch agents for persistence. NETWIRE can discover and close windows on controlled systems. NETWIRE has used .NET packer tools to evade detection. NETWIRE can implement use of proxies to pivot traffic. NETWIRE creates a Registry start-up entry to establish persistence.
title: Lambert, T. (2020, January 29). Intro to Netwire. Retrieved January 7, 2021.

text: ServHelper has the ability to execute a PowerShell script to get information from the infected host.

text:
PHASEJAM has launched a webshell using the `MIME::Base64` module that encoded and decoded Base64 commands.
PHASEJAM has disabled the `cgi-server` process on Ivanti Connect Secure appliances.
PHASEJAM has modified legitimate components to enable persistence and execution, including inserting a web shell into `getComponent.cgi` and `restAuth.cgi`, modifying `DSUpgrade.pm` to block system upgrades, and overwriting `remotedebug` to execute arbitrary commands when specific parameters are provided.
DRYHOOK has the ability to interact with Ivanti Connect Secure environments and to modify system components.
PHASEJAM has modified Ivanti Connect Secure appliances and blocks the system upgrades by altering the DSUpgrade.pm file.
DRYHOOK has stored stolen credentials for future use in the temp folder of a victimized Ivanti Connect Secure VPN device, specifically in the file location `/tmp/cmmmap.kumMW`.
PHASEJAM has prevented legitimate Ivanti Connect Secure system upgrades by intercepting the upgrade command and rendering fake HTML upgrade progress bar through a function called `processUpgradeDisplay()` which allowed the compromised device to remain under the control of the adversary.
PHASEJAM has leveraged native commands associated with the compromised network appliance to execute code.
PHASEJAM has blocked legitimate upgrades of Ivanti Connect Secure systems and falsely indicates a successful upgrade while operating on an older version.
DRYHOOK has modified the Ivanti Connect Secure VPN authentication Perl module `DSAuth.pm` by reading its contents in the buffer, then finding and replacing select lines of code.
SPAWNCHIMERA can persist across system upgrades by hijacking the execution flow of dspkginstall, a binary used during the system upgrade process.
DRYHOOK has killed all instances of the `cgi-server` process in order for the modified Perl module to be activated.
PHASEJAM has inserted Perl-based web shells into legitimate files that provided threat actors with remote access and code execution capabilities on the compromised network appliance.
PHASEJAM has the ability to upload files onto the compromised appliance.
PHASEJAM has the ability to exfiltrate data from the victim appliance.
DRYHOOK has encrypted stolen credentials strings within a file using both Base64 and RC4 with a hard-coded key.
PHASEJAM has renamed the file `/home/bin/remotedebug` to `remotedebug.bak`, allowing the threats actors to write a malicious `/home/bin/remotedebug` shell script.
SPAWNCHIMERA has generated RSA keys against modified files to sign the manifest file, so they appear legitimate.
PHASEJAM has encoded commands with Base64.
DRYHOOK is a Python-based script that executes within the victim environment.
PHASEJAM has used the `sleep` command within its code to generate a fake HTML upgrade progress bar that mimics a running process.
DRYHOOK has captured user credentials and passwords in plaintext and has encrypted them in a stored file on the network device.
SPAWNCHIMERA has monitored and filtered network traffic on compromised edge devices, allowing legitimate traffic to pass while redirecting attacker-controlled traffic to infrastructure under adversary control.
DRYHOOK has intercepted and logged user credentials by modifying the Perl module in Ivanti Connect Secure VPN edge-devices located within `/home/perl/DSAuth.pm`.
SPAWNCHIMERA has created SSH tunnels to facilitate C2 communications.
DRYHOOK has patched victim appliances authentication routines to capture credentials in plaintext as users log in.
PHASEJAM has the ability to decode Base64 commands and data.
DRYHOOK has terminated all instances of the `cgi-server` process before activating the modified DSAuth.pm file.
DRYHOOK has the ability to remount the filesystem as “read-write” to make changes and then restores it to “read-only” prior to killing processes to apply the modifications.
PHASEJAM has used a bash script to modify components on Ivanti Connect Secure appliances and execute files via `/bin/bash`.[1] It has also used the Linux stream editor (`sed`) to execute commands.
title: John Wolfram, Josh Murchie, Matt Lin, Daniel Ainsworth, Robert Wallace, Dimiter Andonov, Dhanesh Kizhakkinan, Jacob Thompson. (2025, January 8). Ivanti Connect Secure VPN Targeted in New Zero-Day Exploitation. Retrieved April 14, 2026.

Hi-Zor encrypts C2 traffic with TLS.

text: The Akira _v2 encryptor targets the `/vmfs/volumes/` path by default and can use the rust-crypto 0.2.36 library crate for the encryption processes. Akira can encrypt victim filesystems for financial extortion purposes including through the use of the ChaCha20 and ChaCha8 stream ciphers. Akira _v2 can enumerate the trace, debug, error, info, and warning logs on targeted systems. Akira _v2 can stop running virtual machines. Akira _v2 can target specific files and folders for encryption. Akira _v2 will fail to execute if the targeted `/vmfs/volumes/` path does not exist or is not defined. Megazord can encrypt files on targeted Windows hosts leaving them with a ".powerranges" file extension. Akira examines files prior to encryption to determine if they meet requirements for encryption and can be encrypted by the ransomware. These checks are performed through native Windows functions such as GetFileAttributesW.
title: Nutland, J. and Szeliga, M. (2024, October 21). Akira ransomware continues to evolve. Retrieved December 10, 2024.

text: Havoc can facilitate the execution of PowerShell commands.

text:
Tsundere Botnet has the ability to run JavaScript code from the C2 server. Additionally, Tsundere Botnet has used Node.js to execute JavaScript code for the loader component.
Tsundere Botnet has collected the machine’s MAC address, total memory, GPU information and other system information.
Tsundere Botnet has checked the victim machine’s location by obtaining the culture name of the machine.
Tsundere Botnet’s loader component has downloaded the zip file node-v18.17.0-win-x64.zip from the official Node.js website, as well as pm2, a Node.js process management tool.
Tsundere Botnet’s MSI installer has used `-WindowStyle Hidden` to hide Tsundere Botnet’s execution from the user.
Tsundere Botnet has disguised its MSI installer as a fake installer for popular games and software.
Tsundere Botnet has checked the victim machine’s location to avoid infecting in the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) region.
Tsundere Botnet has been distributed via an MSI installer.
Tsundere Botnet’s MSI installer has Base64-encoded command execution.
Tsundere Botnet has used the Node Package Manager (npm) to download malicious packages and to deliver the payload.
title: Ubiedo, L. (2025, November 20). Blockchain and Node.js abused by Tsundere: an emerging botnet. Retrieved April 6, 2026.

text:
RustyWater has encrypted encoded data with XOR before sending it to the C2 server.
RustyWater has used the WriteHexToFile function to transform an embedded hex string to the payload CertificationKit.ini.
RustyWater has gathered the victim machine’s computer name.
RustyWater has generated random sleep intervals between C2 communication.
RustyWater has used reddit.exe as its file name and a Cloudflare logo.
RustyWater has sent spearphishing emails with the attachment Cybersecurity.doc, which served as the primary payload for the next stage.
RustyWater has encrypted all strings in the code using position independent XOR encryption.
RustyWater has used `CreateObject` to instantiate a WScript.Shell Component Object Model (COM) object. Additionally, RustyWater has used `VirtualAllocEx` and `WriteProcessMemory` to inject shellcode into explorer.exe.
RustyWater has encoded collected data with Base64.
RustyWater has gathered the victim machine’s username.
RustyWater has established persistence by adding `C:\ProgramData\CertificationKit.ini` to a Windows startup Registry key or to a Run or RunOnce Registry key.
RustyWater has an obfuscated function (i.e. love_me__()) that dynamically reconstructs the string WScript.Shell using hard-coded ASCII values and the Chr() function.
RustyWater has attempted to detect more than 25 antivirus and EDR tools.
RustyWater has registered a Vectored Exception Handler (VEH) to catch debugging efforts.
RustyWater has used a Word document with a malicious Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) macro; when enabled, the CertificationKit.ini payload is constructed and executed.
RustyWater has used the Rust request library for HTTP C2 communication.
RustyWater has used a WScript.Shell COM object to execute the CertificationKit.ini file.
RustyWater has injected its shellcode into explorer.exe by allocating memory via `VirtualAllocEx`, then by writing the payload via `WriteProcessMemory`.
RustyWater has gathered the domain membership of the victim machine’s user.
RustyWater has impersonated TMCell (Altyn Asyr CJSC), the primary mobile operator in Turkmenistan, sending phishing emails with the email domain `info@tmcell`.
title: Awasthi, P. (2026, January 8). Reborn in Rust: Muddy Water Evolves Tooling with RustyWater Implant. Retrieved March 19, 2026.

text:
Seth-Locker can encrypt files on a targeted system, appending them with the suffix .seth.
Seth-Locker can execute commands via the command line shell.
Seth-Locker has the ability to download and execute files on a compromised host.

text:
TRAILBLAZE has injected a hook into an existing process to load BRUSHFIRE in the spaces allocated memory to include the Ivanti Connect Secure (ICS) web process named `web`.
BRUSHFIRE has executed its commands within memory and is not saved on disk.
BRUSHFIRE has decrypted XOR strings prior to execution.
SPAWNCHIMERA has extracted the device’s Linux kernel image (vmlinux).
TRAILBLAZE has leveraged raw syscalls to execute commands.
SPAWNCHIMERA has disabled logging and log forwarding on Ivanti devices targeting the `dslogserver` process.
TRAILBLAZE has conducted process discovery by searching for specific named processes such as `/home/bin/web`.
TRAILBLAZE has the ability to delete temporary files and contents in specified directories to cover its tracks.

text: POWERSOURCE is a PowerShell backdoor. POWERSOURCE achieves persistence by setting a Registry Run key, with the path depending on whether the victim account has user or administrator access. POWERSOURCE queries Registry keys in preparation for setting Run keys to achieve persistence. If the victim is using PowerShell 3.0 or later, POWERSOURCE writes its decoded payload to an alternate data stream (ADS) named kernel32.dll that is saved in %PROGRAMDATA%\Windows\. POWERSOURCE uses DNS TXT records for C2. TEXTMATE executes cmd.exe to provide a reverse shell to adversaries.
title: Brumaghin, E. and Grady, C.. (2017, March 2). Covert Channels and Poor Decisions: The Tale of DNSMessenger. Retrieved March 8, 2017.

PureCrypter can decrypt downloaded resources and parse internal files to determine its settings.
HeartCrypt can pack malicious Windows x86 and .NET payloads in order to evade detection.
PureCrypter can download additional payloads for execution on the compromised host.
PureCrypter can maintain persistence with scheduled tasks.
PureCrypter can execute PowerShell commands to exclude files from EDR and to self-delete.
PureCrypter can enumerate a targeted system's SerialNumber and Version.
PureCrypter has used SmartAssembly and NET-Reactor for string encryption and control flow obfuscation.
PureCrypter can set `ProcessWindowStyle.Hidden` to hide windows on victim machines.
HeartCrypt can decrypt payloads prior to execution.
PureCrypter can retrieve the username from targeted machines.
PureCrypter can identify installed antivirus solutions.
PureCrypter can use AES to encrypt system information sent to the C2.
PureCrypter can enumerate processes on compromised hosts.

text:

RDFSNIFFER hooks several Win32 API functions to hijack elements of the remote system management user-interface.
BOOSTWRITE has used a a 32-byte long multi-XOR key to decode data inside its payload.
RDFSNIFFER has used several Win32 API functions to interact with the victim machine.
BOOSTWRITE has used the DWriteCreateFactory() function to load additional modules.
BOOSTWRITE has been signed by a valid CA.
RDFSNIFFER has the capability of deleting local files.
BOOSTWRITE has encoded its payloads using a ChaCha stream cipher with a 256-bit key and 64-bit Initialization vector (IV) to evade detection.

PlugX has the remove itself and other artifacts.

Felismus collects the victim LAN IP address and sends it to the C2 server.

Felismus collects the current username and sends it to the C2 server.

HELLOKITTY has the ability to enumerate network resources.

HELLOKITTY can delete volume shadow copies on compromised hosts.

HELLOKITTY can enumerate logical drives on a target system.

text: Stuxnet attempts to impersonate an anonymous token to enumerate bindings in the service control manager. Stuxnet uses encrypted configuration blocks and writes encrypted files to disk. Stuxnet transforms encrypted binary data into an ASCII string in order to use it as a URL parameter value. Stuxnet encodes the payload of system information sent to the command and control servers using a one byte 0xFF XOR key. Stuxnet also uses a 31-byte long static byte string to XOR data sent to command and control servers. The servers use a different static key to encrypt replies to the implant. Stuxnet enumerates user accounts of the local host. Stuxnet collects the IP address of a compromised system. Stuxnet uses a driver registered as a boot start service as the main load-point. Stuxnet calls LoadLibrary then executes exports from a DLL. Stuxnet infects remote servers via network shares and by infecting WinCC database views with malicious code. Stuxnet uses the SetSecurityDescriptorDacl API to reduce object integrity levels. Stuxnet enumerates the directories of a network resource. Stuxnet used MS10-073 and an undisclosed Task Scheduler vulnerability to escalate privileges on local Windows machines. Stuxnet can propagate via peer-to-peer communication and updates using RPC. Stuxnet used xp_cmdshell to store and execute SQL code. Stuxnet reduces the integrity level of objects to allow write actions. Stuxnet extracts and writes driver files that match the times of other legitimate files. Stuxnet decrypts resources that are loaded into memory and executed. Stuxnet can create registry keys to load driver files. Stuxnet propagates using the MS10-061 Print Spooler and MS08-067 Windows Server Service vulnerabilities. Stuxnet used WMI with an explorer.exe token to execute on a remote share. Stuxnet attempts to access network resources with a domain account’s credentials. Stuxnet can propagate via removable media using an autorun.inf file or the CVE-2010-2568 LNK vulnerability. Stuxnet infected WinCC machines via a hardcoded database server password. Stuxnet enumerates removable drives for infection. Stuxnet used a digitally signed driver with a compromised Realtek certificate. Stuxnet checks for specific operating systems on 32-bit machines, Registry keys, and dates for vulnerabilities, and will exit execution if the values are not met. Stuxnet collects system information including computer and domain names, OS version, and S7P paths. Stuxnet enumerates the currently running processes related to a variety of security products. Stuxnet uses a driver to scan for specific filesystem driver objects. Stuxnet schedules a network job to execute two minutes after host infection. Stuxnet uses HTTP to communicate with a command and control server. Stuxnet installs an RPC server for P2P communications. Stuxnet propagates to available network shares. Stuxnet enumerates user accounts of the domain. Stuxnet encrypts exfiltrated data via C2 with static 31-byte long XOR keys. Stuxnet sends compromised victim information via HTTP. Stuxnet injects an entire DLL into an existing, newly created, or preselected trusted process. Stuxnet uses an RPC server that contains a file dropping routine and support for payload version updates for P2P communications within a victim network. Stuxnet collects the time and date of a system when it is infected. Stuxnet uses an RPC server that contains a routine for file deletion and also removes itself from the system through a DLL export by deleting specific files. Stuxnet searches the Registry for indicators of security programs. Stuxnet uses a Windows rootkit to mask its binaries and other relevant files. Stuxnet has the ability to generate new C2 domains. Stuxnet can delete OLE Automation and SQL stored procedures used to store malicious payloads.
title: Nicolas Falliere, Liam O Murchu, Eric Chien 2011, February W32.Stuxnet Dossier (Version 1.4) Retrieved November 17, 2024.

text:
Pasam creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can retrieve lists of running processes.
Pasam creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can retrieve information like hostname.
Pasam creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can retrieve information like free disk space.
Pasam creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can upload files.
Pasam creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can retrieve files.
Pasam establishes by infecting the Security Accounts Manager (SAM) DLL to load a malicious DLL dropped to disk.
Pasam creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can delete files.
Pasam creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can retrieve lists of files.

NETWIRE can discover and collect victim system information.
The NETWIRE client has been signed by fake and invalid digital certificates.

text: yty gets an output of running processes using the tasklist command. yty collects screenshots of the victim machine. yty collects the victim’s username. yty gathers information on victim’s drives and has a plugin for document listing. yty runs ipconfig /all and collects the domain name. yty uses the net view command for discovery. yty packs a plugin with UPX. yty communicates to the C2 server by retrieving a Google Doc. yty contains junk code in its binary, likely to confuse malware analysts. yty establishes persistence by creating a scheduled task with the command SchTasks /Create /SC DAILY /TN BigData /TR “ + path_file + “/ST 09:30“. yty has some basic anti-sandbox detection that tries to detect Virtual PC, Sandboxie, and VMware. yty gathers the the serial number of the main disk volume. yty collects files with the following extensions: .ppt, .pptx, .pdf, .doc, .docx, .xls, .xlsx, .docm, .rtf, .inp, .xlsm, .csv, .odt, .pps, .vcf and sends them back to the C2 server. yty gathers the computer name, CPU information, Microsoft Windows version, and runs the command systeminfo. yty uses a keylogger plugin to gather keystrokes.
title: Schwarz, D., Sopko J. (2018, March 08). Donot Team Leverages New Modular Malware Framework in South Asia. Retrieved June 11, 2018.

text:
StrelaStealer variants have used PowerShell scripts to download or drop payloads, including obfuscated variants to connect to a WebDAV server to download and executed an encrypted DLL for installation.
StrelaStealer variants use COM objects to enumerate installed applications from the "AppsFolder" on victim machines.
StrelaStealer payloads have tailored filenames to include names identical to the name of the targeted organization or company.
StrelaStealer variants have used valid code signing certificates.
StrelaStealer variants collect victim system information for exfiltration.
StrelaStealer installers have used obfuscated PowerShell scripts to retrieve follow-on payloads from WebDAV servers.
StrelaStealer PE executable payloads have used uncommon but legitimate extensions such as `.com` instead of `.exe`.
StrelaStealer utilizes a hard-coded XOR key to encrypt the content of HTTP POST requests to command and control infrastructure.
StrelaStealer DLL payloads have been executed via `rundll32.exe`.

text:
TRANSLATEXT has the ability to capture screenshots of new browser tabs, based on the presence of the `Capture` flag.
TRANSLATEXT has been named `GoogleTranslate.crx` to masquerade as a legitimate Chrome extension.
TRANSLATEXT has used a dead drop resolver to retrieve configurations and commands from a public blog site.
TRANSLATEXT has the ability to capture credentials, cookies, browser screenshots, etc. and to exfiltrate data.
TRANSLATEXT has exfiltrated collected credentials to the C2 server.
TRANSLATEXT has modified the following registry key to install itself as the value, granting permission to install specified extensions: ` HKCU\Software\Policies\Google\Chrome\ExtensionInstallForcelist`.
TRANSLATEXT has stolen credentials stored in Chrome.
TRANSLATEXT has queried the following registry key to check for installed Chrome extensions: ` HKCU\Software\Policies\Google\Chrome\ExtensionInstallForcelist `.
TRANSLATEXT has exfiltrated collected email addresses to the C2 server.
TRANSLATEXT has the ability to use form-grabbing and event-listening to extract data from web data forms.
TRANSLATEXT has used HTTP to communicate with the C2 server.
TRANSLATEXT has used a Github repository for C2.
TRANSLATEXT has used PowerShell to collect system information and to upload the collected data to a Github repository.
TRANSLATEXT has exfiltrated updated cookies from Google, Naver, Kakao or Daum to the C2 server.
TRANSLATEXT has redirected clients to legitimate Gmail, Naver or Kakao pages if the clients connect with no parameters.
title: Park, S. (2024, June 27). Kimsuky deploys TRANSLATEXT to target South Korean academia. Retrieved October 14, 2024.

text: WindTail has the ability to use HTTP for C2 communications. WindTail has the ability to use the macOS built-in zip utility to archive files. WindTail can invoke Apple APIs contentsOfDirectoryAtPath, pathExtension, and (string) compare. WindTail can identify and add files that possess specific file extensions to an array for archiving. WindTail has the ability to receive and execute a self-delete command. WindTail has the ability to automatically exfiltrate files using the macOS built-in utility /usr/bin/curl. WindTail can be delivered as a compressed, encrypted, and encoded payload.
title: Wardle, Patrick. (2019, January 15). Middle East Cyber-Espionage analyzing WindShift's implant: OSX.WindTail (part 2). Retrieved October 3, 2019.

text:
GreyEnergy encrypts communications using AES256.
GreyEnergy can securely delete a file by hooking into the DeleteFileA and DeleteFileW functions in the Windows API.
GreyEnergy modifies conditions in the Registry and adds keys.
FELIXROOT collects information about the network including the IP address and DHCP server.
GreyEnergy encrypts communications using RSA-2048.
FELIXROOT checks for installed security software like antivirus and firewall.
GreyEnergy uses cmd.exe to execute itself in-memory.
GreyEnergy has a module to harvest pressed keystrokes.
FELIXROOT uses WMI to query the Windows Registry.
FELIXROOT gathers the time zone information from the victim’s machine.
GreyEnergy is packed for obfuscation.
GreyEnergy has used Tor relays for Command and Control servers.
GreyEnergy digitally signs the malware with a code-signing certificate.
FELIXROOT adds a shortcut file to the startup folder for persistence.
GreyEnergy enumerates all Windows services.
FELIXROOT collects a list of running processes.
FELIXROOT creates a .LNK file for persistence.
GreyEnergy has a module to inject a PE binary into a remote process.
GreyEnergy has a module for Mimikatz to collect Windows credentials from the victim’s machine.
GreyEnergy can download additional modules and payloads.
GreyEnergy chooses a service, drops a DLL file, and writes it to that serviceDLL Registry key.
GreyEnergy encrypts its configuration files with AES-256 and also encrypts its strings.
GreyEnergy uses HTTP and HTTPS for C2 communications.
GreyEnergy uses PsExec locally in order to execute rundll32.exe at the highest privileges (NTAUTHORITY\SYSTEM).
title: Cherepanov, A. (2018, October). GREYENERGY A successor to BlackEnergy. Retrieved November 15, 2018.

text: Skidmap has the ability to install several loadable kernel modules (LKMs) on infected machines. Skidmap has encrypted it's main payload using 3DES. Skidmap has checked for the existence of specific files including /usr/sbin/setenforce and /etc/selinux/config. It also has the ability to monitor the cryptocurrency miner file and process. Skidmap has the ability to replace the pam_unix.so file on an infected machine with its own malicious version that accepts a specific backdoor password for all users. Skidmap has the ability to set SELinux to permissive mode. Skidmap has the ability to check whether the infected system’s OS is Debian or RHEL/CentOS to determine which cryptocurrency miner it should use. Skidmap has monitored critical processes to ensure resiliency. Skidmap is a kernel-mode rootkit used for cryptocurrency mining. Skidmap has the ability to check if /usr/sbin/setenforce exists. This file controls what mode SELinux is in. Skidmap has used pm.sh to download and install its main payload. Skidmap has the ability to add the public key of its handlers to the authorized_keys file to maintain persistence on an infected host. Skidmap has the ability to download files on an infected host. Skidmap has the ability to download, unpack, and decrypt tar.gz files . Skidmap has installed itself via crontab. Skidmap is a kernel-mode rootkit that has the ability to hook system calls to hide specific files and fake network and CPU-related statistics to make the CPU load of the infected machine always appear low. Skidmap has created a fake rm binary to replace the legitimate Linux binary.
title: Remillano, A., Urbanec, J. (2019, September 19). Skidmap Linux Malware Uses Rootkit Capabilities to Hide Cryptocurrency-Mining Payload. Retrieved June 4, 2020.

text:
WEBC2 can download and execute a file.
BISCUIT malware contains a secondary fallback command and control server that is contacted after the primary command and control server.
BISCUIT has a command to collect the processor type, operation system, computer name, and whether the system is a laptop or PC.
WEBC2 can open an interactive command shell.
BISCUIT has a command to collect the system `UPTIME`.
The CALENDAR malware communicates through the use of events in Google Calendar.
title: Mandiant. (n.d.). APT1 Exposing One of China’s Cyber Espionage Units. Retrieved July 18, 2016.

text:

text: SUNSPOT monitored running processes for instances of MsBuild.exe by hashing the name of each running process and comparing it to the corresponding value 0x53D525. It also extracted command-line arguments and individual arguments from the running MsBuild.exe process to identify the directory path of the Orion software Visual Studio solution. SUNSPOT enumerated the Orion software Visual Studio solution directory path. SUNBURST source code used generic variable names and pre-obfuscated strings, and was likely sanitized of developer comments before being added to SUNSPOT. SUNSPOT malware was designed and used to insert SUNBURST into software builds of the SolarWinds Orion IT management product. Following the successful injection of SUNBURST, SUNSPOT deleted a temporary file it created named InventoryManager.bk after restoring the original SolarWinds Orion source code to the software library. SUNSPOT modified its security token to grants itself debugging privileges by adding SeDebugPrivilege. SUNSPOT only replaces SolarWinds Orion source code if the MD5 checksums of both the original source code file and backdoored replacement source code match hardcoded values. SUNSPOT created a copy of the SolarWinds Orion software source file with a .bk extension to backup the original content, wrote SUNBURST using the same filename but with a .tmp extension, and then moved SUNBURST using MoveFileEx to the original filename with a .cs extension so it could be compiled within Orion software. SUNSPOT was identified on disk with a filename of taskhostsvc.exe and it created an encrypted log file at C:\Windows\Temp\vmware-vmdmp.log. SUNSPOT decrypts SUNBURST, which was stored in AES128-CBC encrypted blobs. SUNSPOT encrypted log entries it collected with the stream cipher RC4 using a hard-coded key. It also uses AES128-CBC encrypted blobs for SUNBURST source code and data extracted from the SolarWinds Orion process. SUNSPOT creates a mutex using the hard-coded value ` {12d61a41-4b74-7610-a4d8-3028d2f56395}` to ensure that only one instance of itself is running. SUNSPOT used Windows API functions such as MoveFileEx and NtQueryInformationProcess as part of the SUNBURST injection process.

BlackEnergy is capable of taking screenshots.
BlackEnergy has run a keylogger plug-in on a victim.

text: Conficker uses the current UTC victim system date for domain generation and connects to time servers to determine the current date. Conficker adds keys to the Registry at HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services and various other Registry locations. Conficker has used a DGA that seeds with the current UTC victim system date to generate domains. Conficker downloads an HTTP server to the infected machine. Conficker resets system restore points and deletes backup files. Conficker variants used the Windows AUTORUN feature to spread through USB propagation. Conficker exploited the MS08-067 Windows vulnerability for remote code execution through a crafted RPC request. Conficker scans for other machines to infect. Conficker variants spread through NetBIOS share propagation. Conficker terminates various services related to system security and Windows. Conficker copies itself into the %systemroot%\system32 directory and registers as a service.

text: Dtrack has used process hollowing shellcode to target a predefined list of processes from %SYSTEM32%. Dtrack has used a dropper that embeds an encrypted payload as extra data. Dtrack can collect network and active connection information. Dtrack can retrieve browser history. Dtrack can collect the host's IP addresses using the ipconfig command. Dtrack’s dropper contains a keylogging executable. Dtrack’s RAT makes a persistent target file with auto execution on the host start. Dtrack can remove its persistence and delete itself. Dtrack can list files on available disk volumes. Dtrack’s dropper can list all running processes. Dtrack can save collected data to disk, different file formats, and network shares. Dtrack has used a decryption routine that is part of an executable physical patch. Dtrack can collect the victim's computer name, hostname and adapter information to create a unique identifier. Dtrack packs collected data into a password protected archive. Dtrack’s can download and upload a file to the victim’s computer.

text:
Dyre has the ability to identify the computer name, OS version, and hardware configuration on a compromised host.
Dyre has the ability to identify the users on a compromised host.
Dyre has the ability to identify network settings on a compromised host.
Dyre has the ability to send information staged on a compromised host externally to C2.
