text: Chrommme has the ability to obtain the computer name of a compromised host. Chrommme can encrypt and store on disk collected data before exfiltration. Gelsemium can retrieve data from specific Windows directories, as well as open random files as part of Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion. Chrommme can exfiltrate collected data via C2. Chrommme can retrieve the username from a targeted system. Gelsemium can determine the operating system and whether a targeted machine has a 32 or 64 bit architecture. Gelsemium can use a batch script to delete itself. Gelsemium can use dynamic DNS domain names in C2. Chrommme can store captured system information locally prior to exfiltration. Chrommme can download its code from C2. Gelsemium can modify the Registry to store its components. Gelsemium can drop itself in C:\Windows\System32\spool\prtprocs\x64\winprint.dll to be loaded automatically by the spoolsv Windows service. Chrommme can encrypt sections of its code to evade detection. Gelsemium can use multiple domains and protocols in C2. Gelsemium has the ability to perform timestomping of files on targeted systems. Gelsemium has the ability to use DNS in communication with C2. Chrommme has the ability to capture screenshots. Chrommme can use Windows API including `WinExec` for execution. Gelsemium can use HTTP/S in C2 communications. Gelsemium has named malicious binaries `serv.exe`, `winprint.dll`, and `chrome_elf.dll` and has set its persistence in the Registry with the key value Chrome Update to appear legitimate. Gelsemium can use custom shellcode to map embedded DLLs into memory. Gelsemium can open random files and Registry keys to obscure malware behavior from sandbox analysis. Gelsemium can delete its dropper component from the targeted system. Gelsemium can use token manipulation to bypass UAC on Windows7 systems. Gelsemium has the ability to inject DLLs into specific processes. Gelsemium has used unverified signatures on malicious DLLs. Chrommme can set itself to sleep before requesting a new command from C2. Gelsemium can set persistence with a Registry run key. Gelsemium has the ability to distinguish between a standard user and an administrator on a compromised host. Gelsemium can drop itself in `C:\Windows\System32\spool\prtprocs\x64\winprint.dll` as an alternative Print Processor to be loaded automatically when the spoolsv Windows service starts. Gelsemium can check for the presence of specific security products. Gelsemium has the ability to compress its components. Gelsemium can store its components in the Registry. Gelsemium has the ability to use various Windows API functions to perform tasks. Gelsemium can download additional plug-ins to a compromised host. Gelsemium can bypass UAC to elevate process privileges on a compromised host. Chrommme can collect data from a local system. Gelsemium can use junk code to generate random activity to obscure malware behavior. Chrommme can decrypt its encrypted internal code. Gelsemium can use the `IARPUinstallerStringLauncher` COM interface are part of its UAC bypass process. Gelsemium can collect data from a compromised host. Gelsemium can enumerate running processes. Chrommme has the ability to list drives. Gelsemium can decompress and decrypt DLLs and shellcode. Chrommme can enumerate the IP address of a compromised host. Gelsemium can use junk code to hide functions and evade detection. Gelsemium has the ability to use TCP and UDP in C2 communications.

text: Kwampirs collects a list of files and directories in C:\ with the command dir /s /a c:\ >> "C:\windows\TEMP\[RANDOM].tmp". Kwampirs collects OS version information such as registered owner details, manufacturer details, processor type, available storage, installed patches, hostname, version info, system date, and other system information by using the commands systeminfo, net config workstation, hostname, ver, set, and date /t. Kwampirs collects a list of active and listening connections by using the command netstat -nao as well as a list of available network mappings with net use. Kwampirs creates a new service named WmiApSrvEx to establish persistence. Kwampirs decrypts and extracts a copy of its main DLL payload when executing. Kwampirs collects a list of available servers with the command net view. Kwampirs collects a list of accounts with the command net users. Kwampirs collects registered owner details by using the commands systeminfo and net config workstation. Kwampirs collects a list of users belonging to the local users and administrators groups with the commands net localgroup administrators and net localgroup users. Kwampirs uses a large list of C2 servers that it cycles through until a successful connection is established. Kwampirs uses rundll32.exe in a Registry value added to establish persistence. Kwampirs establishes persistence by adding a new service with the display name "WMI Performance Adapter Extension" in an attempt to masquerade as a legitimate WMI service. Kwampirs collects password policy information with the command net accounts. Before writing to disk, Kwampirs inserts a randomly generated string into the middle of the decrypted payload in an attempt to evade hash-based detections. Kwampirs collects network adapter and interface information by using the commands ipconfig /all, arp -a and route print. It also collects the system's MAC address with getmac and domain configuration with net config workstation. Kwampirs collects a list of running services with the command tasklist /svc. Kwampirs collects a list of network shares with the command net share. Kwampirs collects a list of running services with the command tasklist /v. Kwampirs collects a list of domain groups with the command net localgroup /domain. Kwampirs copies itself over network shares to move laterally on a victim network.

text: Raspberry Robin contains multiple payloads that are packed for defense evasion purposes and unpacked on runtime. Raspberry Robin will execute its payload prior to initializing command and control traffic by impersonating one of several legitimate program names such as dllhost.exe, regsvr32.exe, or rundll32.exe. Raspberry Robin will execute a legitimate process, then suspend it to inject code for a Tor client into the process, followed by resumption of the process to enable Tor client execution. Raspberry Robin can execute via LNK containing a command to run a legitimate executable, such as wmic.exe, to download a malicious Windows Installer (MSI) package. Raspberry Robin leverages anti-debugging mechanisms through the use of ThreadHideFromDebugger. Raspberry Robin determines whether it is successfully running on a victim system by querying the running account information to determine if it is running in Session 0, indicating running with elevated privileges. Raspberry Robin creates an elevated COM object for CMLuaUtil and uses this to set a registry value that points to the malicious LNK file during execution. Raspberry Robin will use a Registry key to achieve persistence through reboot, setting a RunOnce key such as: HKEY_CURRENT_USER\\Software\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\RunOnce {random value name} = “rundll32 shell32 ShellExec_RunDLLA REGSVR /u /s “{dropped copy path and file name}”” . Raspberry Robin contains real and fake second-stage payloads following initial execution, with the real payload only delivered if the malware determines it is not running in a virtualized environment. Raspberry Robin implements a variation of the ucmDccwCOMMethod technique abusing the Windows AutoElevate backdoor to bypass UAC while elevating privileges. Raspberry Robin contains an embedded custom Tor network client that communicates with the primary payload via shared process memory. Raspberry Robin contains several layers of obfuscation to hide malicious code from detection and analysis. Raspberry Robin will drop a copy of itself to a subfolder in %Program Data% or %Program Data%\\Microsoft\\ to attempt privilege elevation and defense evasion if not running in Session 0.
title: Christopher So. (2022, December 20). Raspberry Robin Malware Targets Telecom, Governments. Retrieved May 17, 2024.

text:

TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can deobfuscate an encoded Python script prior to execution.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has exfiltrated collected data to typosquat C2 domains including scan.aquasecurtiy[.]org.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has checked if it is running on a developer machine (rather than GitHub Actions) before executing a Python script for persistence. The script has also polled C2 every 50 minutes for additional payloads and aborted if the returned value contained YouTube.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has bundled collected data into a file named tpcp.tar.gz for exfiltration.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can identify Docker and Kubernetes environments for credentials.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has the ability to remove all staged files after exfiltration.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can target sensitive file paths in Git repos to extract credentials.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can use `kubectl get secrets` to extract credentials from Kubernetes.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has detected if it is on a developer machine by checking if the environmental variable GITHUB_ACTIONS != “true”. TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has also identified readable memory regions on CI/CD runners and enumerated system information using `hostname` and `uname-a`.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can use `sudo` for code execution.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has the ability to enumerate network interfaces.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can identify and collect credentials across over 50 file paths in Cloud, CI/CD, developer tooling, and container enviornments.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can create a systemd unit to execute a python script for persistence.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can use `whoami` on self-hosted runners to identify the current user.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can extract credentials from multiple database configuration files including ~/.pgpass, ~/.my.cnf, ~/.mongorc.js, and /etc/mysql/my.cnf.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has leveraged a persistence script that will sleep for five minutes before additional execution.

text: Epic gathers information on local group names. Epic compresses the collected data with bzip2 before sending it to the C2 server. Epic uses the tasklist /v command to obtain a list of processes. Epic collects the user name from the victim’s machine. Epic encrypts collected data using a public key framework before sending it over the C2 channel. Some variants encrypt the collected data with AES and encode it with base64 before transmitting it to the C2 server. Epic collects the OS version, hardware information, computer name, available system memory status, and system and user language settings. Epic uses HTTP and HTTPS for C2 communications. Epic has a command to delete a file from the machine. Epic collects disk space information. Epic gathers a list of all user accounts, privilege classes, and time of last logon. Epic recursively searches for all .doc files on the system and collects a directory listing of the Desktop, %TEMP%, and %WINDOWS%\Temp directories. Epic uses the net use, net session, and netstat commands to gather information on network connections.

text:
Nightdoor uses scheduled tasks for persistence to load the final malware payload into memory.
Nightdoor creates a cmd.exe shell to send and receive commands from the command and control server via open pipes.
Nightdoor embeds code from the public `al-khaser` project, a repository that works to detect virtual machines, sandboxes, and malware analysis environments.
Nightdoor uses TCP and UDP communication for command and control traffic.
Nightdoor stores network configuration data in a file XOR encoded with the key value of `0x7A`.
Nightdoor can utilize Microsoft OneDrive or Google Drive for command and control purposes.
Nightdoor uses a legitimate executable to load a malicious DLL file for installation.

text:
InvisibleFerret has collected OS type, hostname and system version through the "pay" module. InvisibleFerret has also queried the victim device using Python scripts to obtain the User and Hostname.
InvisibleFerret is written in Python and has used Python scripts for execution.
InvisibleFerret has the capability to scan for file names, file extensions, and avoids pre-designated path names and file types.
InvisibleFerret has the capability to query installed programs and running processes. InvisibleFerret has also identified running processes using the Python project “psutil”.
InvisibleFerret has terminated Chrome and Brave browsers using the `taskkill` command on Windows and the `killall` command on other systems such as Linux and macOS. InvisibleFerret has also utilized it’s `ssh_kill` command to terminate Chrome and Brave browser processes.
InvisibleFerret has utilized the XOR and Base64 encoding for each of its modules. InvisibleFerret has also obfuscated files with a combination of zlib, Base64 and reverse string order. InvisibleFerret has also utilized the XOR and Base64 encoding some of its Python scripts.
InvisibleFerret has collected the local IP address, and external IP.
InvisibleFerret has downloaded “AnyDesk.exe” into the user’s home directory from the C2 server when checks for the service fail to identify its presence in the victim environment. InvisibleFerret has also been configured to download additional payloads using a command which calls to the /bow URI.
InvisibleFerret has established a connection with the C2 server over TCP traffic. InvisibleFerret has also created a TCP reverse shell communicating via a socket connection over ports 1245, 80, 2245, 3001, and 5000.
InvisibleFerret has collected mouse and keyboard events using “pyWinhook”.
InvisibleFerret has utilized remote access software including AnyDesk client through the “adc” module. InvisibleFerret has also downloaded the AnyDesk client should it not already exist on the compromised host by searching for `C:/Program Files(x86)/AnyDesk/AnyDesk.exe`.
InvisibleFerret has queried the victim device using Python scripts to obtain the User and Hostname.
InvisibleFerret has collected the internal IP address, IP geolocation information of the infected host and sends the data to a C2 server. InvisibleFerret has also leveraged the “pay” module to obtain region name, country, city, zip code, ISP, latitude and longitude using “http://ip-api.com/json”.
BeaverTail has been known to collect basic system information. BeaverTail has also collected data to include hostname and current timestamp prior to uploading data to the API endpoint `/uploads` on the C2 server.
InvisibleFerret has used HTTP for C2 communications.
InvisibleFerret has conducted keylogging using the Python project “pyWinHook” and "Pyhook". InvisibleFerret has also captured keylogging thread checks for changes in an active window and key presses.
InvisibleFerret has searched the victim device credentials and files commonly associated with cryptocurrency wallets.
InvisibleFerret has stolen data from the clipboard using the Python project “pyperclip”. InvisibleFerret has also captured clipboard contents during copy and paste operations.
InvisibleFerret has identified the user’s UUID and username through the "pay" module.

text: RTM can scan victim drives to look for specific banking software on the machine to determine next actions. RTM has the ability to remove Registry entries that it created for persistence. RTM samples have been signed with a code-signing certificates. RTM uses the command line and rundll32.exe to execute. RTM can obtain the victim username and permissions. RTM has the capability to download a VNC module from command and control (C2). RTM can obtain the victim time zone. RTM used Port 44443 for its VNC module. RTM can attempt to run the program as admin, then show a fake error message and a legitimate UAC bypass prompt to the user in an attempt to socially engineer the user into escalating privileges. RTM tries to add a Registry Run key under the name "Windows Update" to establish persistence. RTM can use the FindNextUrlCacheEntryA and FindFirstUrlCacheEntryA functions to search for specific strings within browser history. RTM can delete all Registry entries created during its execution. RTM can obtain the computer name, OS version, and default language identifier. RTM encrypts C2 traffic with a custom RC4 variant. RTM can obtain information about security software on the victim. RTM can search for specific strings within browser tabs using a Dynamic Data Exchange mechanism. RTM can obtain information about process integrity levels.
title: Faou, M. and Boutin, J. (2017, February). Read The Manual: A Guide to the RTM Banking Trojan. Retrieved March 9, 2017.

CrossRAT is capable of taking screen captures.
CrossRAT can list all files on a system.

CrossRAT creates a Launch Agent on macOS.

MiniBus has the ability to detect security applications.
MiniBike has leveraged HTTP calls to the C2.
MiniBike has been deployed using a launcher, which has been executed via search-order-hijacking (SoH).

text: PowerDuke has a command to write random data across a file and delete it. PowerDuke has commands to get information about the victim's name, build, version, serial number, and memory usage. PowerDuke has commands to get the current directory name as well as the size of a file. It also has commands to obtain information about logical drives, drive type, and free space. PowerDuke uses steganography to hide backdoors in PNG files, which are also encrypted using the Tiny Encryption Algorithm (TEA). PowerDuke has a command to get text of the current foreground window. PowerDuke has commands to get the time the machine was built, the time, and the time zone. PowerDuke has a command to download a file. PowerDuke hides many of its backdoor payloads in an alternate data stream (ADS). PowerDuke runs cmd.exe /c and sends the output to its C2. PowerDuke has a command to list the victim's processes. PowerDuke has a command to get the victim's domain and NetBIOS name. PowerDuke has commands to get the current user's name and SID. PowerDuke uses rundll32.exe to load. PowerDuke achieves persistence by using various Registry Run keys.

text: KillDisk has used the FindNextFile command as part of its file deletion process. KillDisk attempts to reboot the machine by terminating specific processes. KillDisk has called GetCurrentProcess. KillDisk has attempted to get the access token of a process by calling OpenProcessToken. If KillDisk gets the access token, then it attempt to modify the token privileges with AdjustTokenPrivileges. KillDisk terminates various processes to get the user to reboot the victim machine.

text: Netwalker has been written in PowerShell and executed directly in memory, avoiding detection. Netwalker can determine the system architecture it is running on to choose which version of the DLL to use. Netwalker's DLL has been embedded within the PowerShell script in hex format. Netwalker can use Windows API functions to inject the ransomware DLL. Netwalker can encrypt files on infected machines to extort victims. Netwalker can delete the infected system's Shadow Volumes to prevent recovery. Netwalker can add the following registry entry: HKEY_CURRENT_USER\SOFTWARE\{8 random characters}. Netwalker can terminate system processes and services, some of which relate to backup software. The Netwalker DLL has been injected reflectively into the memory of a legitimate running process. Netwalker can use WMI to delete Shadow Volumes. Netwalker's PowerShell script has been obfuscated with multiple layers including base64 and hexadecimal encoding and XOR-encryption, as well as obfuscated PowerShell functions and variables. Netwalker can detect and terminate active security software-related processes on infected systems.
title: Victor, K.. (2020, May 18). Netwalker Fileless Ransomware Injected via Reflective Loading . Retrieved May 26, 2020.

text: T9000 gathers and beacons the MAC and IP addresses during installation. T9000 gathers and beacons the operating system build number and CPU Architecture (32-bit/64-bit) during installation. If a victim meets certain criteria, T9000 uses the AppInit_DLL functionality to achieve persistence by ensuring that every user mode process that is spawned will load its malicious DLL, ResN32.dll. It does this by creating the following Registry keys: HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows\AppInit_DLLs – %APPDATA%\Intel\ResN32.dll and HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows\LoadAppInit_DLLs – 0x1. T9000 searches removable storage devices for files with a pre-defined list of file extensions (e.g. * .doc, *.ppt, *.xls, *.docx, *.pptx, *.xlsx). Any matching files are encrypted and written to a local user directory. During the T9000 installation process, it drops a copy of the legitimate Microsoft binary igfxtray.exe. The executable contains a side-loading weakness which is used to load a portion of the malware. T9000 performs checks for various antivirus and security products during installation. T9000 gathers and beacons the username of the logged in account during installation. It will also gather the username of running processes to determine if it is running as SYSTEM. T9000 uses the Skype API to record audio and video calls. It writes encrypted data to %APPDATA%\Intel\Skype. T9000 gathers and beacons the system time during installation. T9000 can take screenshots of the desktop and target application windows, saving them to user directories as one byte XOR encrypted .dat files. T9000 searches through connected drives for removable storage devices. T9000 encrypts collected data using a single byte XOR key.
title: Grunzweig, J. and Miller-Osborn, J.. (2016, February 4). T9000: Advanced Modular Backdoor Uses Complex Anti-Analysis Techniques. Retrieved April 15, 2016.

text:
QUIETCANARY has the ability to stage data prior to exfiltration.
KOPILUWAK had used Javascript to perform its core functions.
KOPILUWAK can use netstat and Net to discover network shares.
QUIETCANARY can use a custom parsing routine to decode the command codes and additional parameters from the C2 before executing them.
KOPILUWAK has been delivered to victims as a malicious email attachment.
QUIETCANARY has the ability to retrieve information from the Registry.
QUIETCANARY can identify the default proxy setting on a compromised host.
KOPILUWAK can gather information from compromised hosts.
KOPILUWAK can use netstat, Arp, and Net to discover current TCP connections.

KOPILUWAK has exfiltrated collected data to its C2 via POST requests.
KOPILUWAK can use Arp to discover a target's network configuration setttings.

KOPILUWAK can conduct basic network reconnaissance on the victim machine with `whoami`, to get user details.
KOPILUWAK has used HTTP POST requests to send data to C2.

ANDROMEDA has been delivered through a LNK file disguised as a folder.
QUIETCANARY can execute processes in a hidden window.
ANDROMEDA can download additional payloads from C2.
QUIETCANARY can RC4 encrypt C2 communications.
QUIETCANARY can base64 encode C2 communications.
KOPILUWAK can enumerate current running processes on the targeted machine.
ANDROMEDA has been spread via infected USB keys.
KOPILUWAK has piped the results from executed C2 commands to `%TEMP%\result2.dat` on the local machine.
KOPILUWAK has gained execution through malicious attachments.
KOPILUWAK can discover logical drive information on compromised hosts.
ANDROMEDA has the ability to make GET requests to download files from C2.

EVILNUM can harvest cookies and upload them to the C2 server.
EVILNUM can obtain the username from the victim's machine.
EVILNUM has changed the creation date of files.

text: Astaroth has obfuscated and randomized parts of the JScript code it is initiating. Astaroth uses the LoadLibraryExW() function to load additional modules. Astaroth executes embedded JScript or VBScript in an XSL stylesheet located on a remote domain. Astaroth spawns a CMD process to execute commands. Astaroth loads its module with the XSL script parameter vShow set to zero, which opens the application with a hidden window. Astaroth can be loaded through regsvr32.exe. Astaroth searches for different processes on the system. Astaroth has used a DGA in C2 communications. Astaroth uses a software packer called Pe123\RPolyCryptor. Astaroth uses an external software known as NetPass to recover passwords. Astaroth exfiltrates collected information from its r1.log file to the external C2 server. Astaroth collects information from the clipboard by using the OpenClipboard() and GetClipboardData() libraries.

NotPetya searches for files ending with dozens of different file extensions prior to encryption.
NotPetya determines if specific antivirus programs are running on an infected host machine.

TrickBot has been known to reach a command and control server via one of nine proxy IP addresses.
TrickBot uses a custom crypter leveraging Microsoft’s CryptoAPI to encrypt C2 traffic.Newer versions of TrickBot have been known to use `bcrypt` to encrypt and digitally sign responses to their C2 server.

text: NotPetya can use PsExec to help propagate itself across a network. NotPetya can use wmic to help propagate itself across a network. NotPetya will reboot the system one hour after infection. NotPetya uses wevtutil to clear the Windows event logs. NotPetya drops PsExec with the filename dllhost.dat. NotPetya can use two exploits in SMBv1, EternalBlue and EternalRomance, to spread itself to other remote systems on the network. NotPetya uses rundll32.exe to install itself on remote systems when accessed via PsExec or wmic. NotPetya contains a modified version of Mimikatz to help gather credentials that are later used for lateral movement. NotPetya can use valid credentials with PsExec or wmic to spread itself to remote systems. NotPetya creates a task to reboot the system one hour after infection. NotPetya encrypts user files and disk structures like the MBR with 2048-bit RSA.
title: Chiu, A. (2016, June 27). New Ransomware Variant "Nyetya" Compromises Systems Worldwide. Retrieved March 26, 2019.

AppleJeus has placed a plist file within the LaunchDaemons folder and launched it manually. During AppleJeus's installation process, it uses `postinstall` scripts to extract a hidden plist from the application's `/Resources` folder and execute the `plist` file as a Launch Daemon with elevated permissions.

Hydraq includes a component based on the code of VNC that can stream a live feed of the desktop of an infected host.
Hydraq connects to a predefined domain on port 443 to exfil gathered information.
Hydraq creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can adjust token privileges.
Hydraq C2 traffic is encrypted using bitwise NOT and XOR operations.

Sys10 collects the computer name, OS versioning information, and OS install date and sends the information to the C2.

HDoor kills anti-virus found on the victim.

SslMM identifies and kills anti-malware processes.
WinMM collects the system name, OS version including service pack, and system install date and sends the information to the C2 server.

SslMM sends the logged-on username to its hard-coded C2.
Sys10 uses HTTP for C2.
SslMM contains a feature to manipulate process privileges and tokens.
SslMM creates a new thread implementing a keylogging facility using Windows Keyboard Accelerators.
SslMM sends information to its hard-coded C2, including OS version, service pack information, processor speed, system name, and OS install date.

text:
Pcexter has the ability to search for files in specified directories.
The Ninja loader can call Windows APIs for discovery, process injection, and payload decryption.
Ninja can enumerate processes on a targeted host.
Pcexter can upload stolen files to OneDrive storage accounts via HTTP `POST`.
Ninja can obtain the computer name and information on the OS from targeted hosts.
Ninja has compressed its data with the LZSS algorithm.
LoFiSe can collect all the files from the working directory every three hours and place them into a password-protected archive for further exfiltration.
Ninja can forward TCP packets between the C2 and a remote host.
LoFiSe can save files to be evaluated for further exfiltration in the `C:\Programdata\Microsoft\` and `C:\windows\temp\` folders.
Pcexter can upload files from targeted systems.
The Ninja loader component can decrypt and decompress the payload.
Ninja can proxy C2 communications including to and from internal agents without internet connectivity.
Ninja has used legitimate looking filenames for its loader including update.dll and x64.dll.
The Ninja payload is XOR encrypted and compressed. Ninja has also XORed its configuration data with a constant value of `0xAA`.
Ninja loader components can be executed through rundll32.exe.
LoFiSe can collect files of interest from targeted systems.
Ninja loaders can be side-loaded with legitimate and signed executables including the VLC.exe media player.
LoFiSe can monitor the file system to identify files less than 6.4 MB in size with file extensions including .doc, .docx, .xls, .xlsx, .ppt, .pptx, .pdf, .rtf, .tif, .odt, .ods, .odp, .eml, and .msg.
LoFiSe can collect files into password-protected ZIP-archives for exfiltration.
Ninja has the ability to enumerate directory content.

Ninja can obtain information on physical drives from targeted hosts.
LoFiSe has been executed as a file named DsNcDiag.dll through side-loading.
Ninja has the ability to inject an agent module into a new process and arbitrary shellcode into running processes.
title: Dedola, G. et al. (2023, October 12). ToddyCat: Keep calm and check logs. Retrieved January 3, 2024.

text: GravityRAT has been delivered via Word documents using DDE for execution. GravityRAT collects the volumes mapped on the system, and also steals files with the following extensions: .docx, .doc, .pptx, .ppt, .xlsx, .xls, .rtf, and .pdf. GravityRAT collects the victim username along with other account information (account type, description, full name, SID and status). GravityRAT has used HTTP over a non-standard port, such as TCP port 46769. GravityRAT steals files with the following extensions: .docx, .doc, .pptx, .ppt, .xlsx, .xls, .rtf, and .pdf. GravityRAT steals files based on an extension list if a USB drive is connected to the system. GravityRAT uses WMI to check the BIOS and manufacturer information for strings like "VMWare", "Virtual", and "XEN" and another WMI request to get the current temperature of the hardware to determine if it's a virtual machine environment. GravityRAT supports file encryption (AES with the key "lolomycin2017"). GravityRAT can obtain the date and time of a system. GravityRAT uses the netstat command to find open ports on the victim’s machine. GravityRAT collects the MAC address, computer name, and CPU information. GravityRAT executes commands remotely on the infected host. GravityRAT creates a scheduled task to ensure it is re-executed everyday. GravityRAT lists the running processes on the system. GravityRAT collects the victim IP address, MAC address, as well as the victim account domain name. GravityRAT uses HTTP for C2. GravityRAT has a feature to list the available services on the system. The author of GravityRAT submitted samples to VirusTotal for testing, showing that the author modified the code to try to hide the DDE object in a different part of the document. GravityRAT collects various information via WMI requests, including CPU information in the Win32_Processor entry (Processor ID, Name, Manufacturer and the clock speed).
title: Mercer, W., Rascagneres, P. (2018, April 26). GravityRAT - The Two-Year Evolution Of An APT Targeting India. Retrieved May 16, 2018.

text: Goopy has the ability to communicate with its C2 over HTTP. Denis uses ipconfig to gather the IP address from the system. Denis deploys additional backdoors and hacking tools to the system. Denis queries the Registry for keys and values. Denis will decrypt important strings used for C&C communication. Denis used the IsDebuggerPresent, OutputDebugString, and SetLastError APIs to avoid debugging. Denis used GetProcAddress and LoadLibrary to dynamically resolve APIs. Denis also used the Wow64SetThreadContext API as part of a process hollowing process. Denis enumerates and collects the username from the victim’s machine. Goopy has the ability to maintain persistence by creating scheduled tasks set to run every hour. Goopy has checked for the Google Updater process to ensure Goopy was loaded properly. Denis has used DNS tunneling for C2 communications. Denis performed process hollowing through the API calls CreateRemoteThread, ResumeThread, and Wow64SetThreadContext. Goopy has the ability to communicate with its C2 over DNS. Goopy has impersonated the legitimate goopdate.dll, which was dropped on the target system with a legitimate GoogleUpdate.exe. Goopy has the ability to disable Microsoft Outlook's security policies to disable macro warnings. Goopy has the ability to side-load malicious DLLs with legitimate applications from Kaspersky, Microsoft, and Google. Goopy has the ability to enumerate the infected system's user name. Denis collects OS information and the computer name from the victim’s machine. Denis has several commands to search directories for files. Goopy's decrypter have been inflated with junk code in between legitimate API functions, and also included infinite loops to avoid analysis. Goopy has used a polymorphic decryptor to decrypt itself at runtime. Goopy has the ability to exfiltrate data over the Microsoft Outlook C2 channel. Denis has a version written in PowerShell. Goopy has had null characters padded in its malicious DLL payload. Denis has encoded its PowerShell commands in Base64. Denis has a command to delete files from the victim’s machine. Denis obfuscates its code and encrypts the API names. Goopy has the ability to delete emails used for C2 once the content has been copied. Goopy has the ability to use a Microsoft Outlook backdoor macro to communicate with its C2. Denis ran multiple system checks, looking for processor and register characteristics, to evade emulation and analysis. Denis replaces the nonexistent Windows DLL "msfte.dll" with its own malicious version, which is loaded by the SearchIndexer.exe and SearchProtocolHost.exe. Goopy has the ability to exfiltrate documents from infected systems. Denis can launch a remote shell to execute arbitrary commands on the victim’s machine. Denis encodes the data sent to the server in Base64. Goopy has the ability to use cmd.exe to execute commands passed from an Outlook C2 channel. Goopy has the ability to enumerate the infected system's user name via GetUserNameW.
title: Dahan, A. (2017). Operation Cobalt Kitty. Retrieved December 27, 2018.

text: Conti can enumerate remote open SMB network shares using NetShareEnum(). Conti can enumerate through all open processes to search for any that have the string “sql” in their process name. Conti has used API calls during execution. Conti has decrypted its payload using a hardcoded AES-256 key. Conti can discover files on a local system. Conti can use compiler-based obfuscation for its code, encrypt DLLs, and hide Windows API calls. Conti can delete Windows Volume Shadow Copies using vssadmin. Conti can spread itself by infecting other remote machines via network shared drives. Conti can retrieve the ARP cache from the local system by using the GetIpNetTable() API call and check to ensure IP addresses it connects to are for local, non-Internet, systems. Conti can stop up to 146 Windows services related to security, backup, database, and email solutions through the use of net stop. Conti can enumerate routine network connections from a compromised host. Conti has loaded an encrypted DLL into memory and then executes it. Conti can spread via SMB and encrypts files on different hosts, potentially compromising an entire network.
title: Baskin, B. (2020, July 8). TAU Threat Discovery: Conti Ransomware. Retrieved February 17, 2021.

text: Sykipot may use net view /domain to display hostnames of available systems on a network. Sykipot may use netstat -ano to display active network connections. Sykipot may use ipconfig /all to gather system network configuration details. Sykipot may gather a list of running processes by running tasklist /v. Sykipot may use net start to display running services. Sykipot injects itself into running instances of outlook.exe, iexplore.exe, or firefox.exe. Sykipot may use net group "domain admins" /domain to display accounts in the "domain admins" permissions group and net localgroup "administrators" to list local system administrator group membership.
title: Blasco, J. (2011, December 12). Another Sykipot sample likely targeting US federal agencies. Retrieved March 28, 2016.

text:

The Gentlemen Ransomware has enumerated files and directories using WMI and PowerShell commands.

text: BackConfig can download and execute additional payloads on a compromised host. BackConfig has the ability to use scheduled tasks to repeatedly execute malicious payloads on a compromised host. BackConfig has the ability to use HTTPS for C2 communiations. BackConfig has the ability to use hidden columns in Excel spreadsheets to store executable files or commands for VBA macros. BackConfig has been signed with self signed digital certificates mimicking a legitimate software company. BackConfig can download and run batch files to execute commands on a compromised host. BackConfig has the ability to identify folders and files related to previous infections. BackConfig has used compressed and decimal encoded VBS scripts. BackConfig has the ability to remove files and folders related to previous infections. BackConfig has the ability to set folders or files to be hidden from the Windows Explorer default view. BackConfig has hidden malicious payloads in %USERPROFILE%\Adobe\Driver\dwg\ and mimicked the legitimate DHCP service binary. BackConfig can leverage API functions such as ShellExecuteA and HttpOpenRequestA in the process of downloading and executing files. BackConfig has used a custom routine to decrypt strings. BackConfig has compromised victims via links to URLs hosting malicious content. BackConfig has the ability to gather the victim's computer name. BackConfig has used VBS to install its downloader component and malicious documents with VBA macro code.
title: Hinchliffe, A. and Falcone, R. (2020, May 11). Updated BackConfig Malware Targeting Government and Military Organizations in South Asia. Retrieved June 17, 2020.

text:
The Gentlemen Ransomware has disabled Microsoft Defender utilizing PowerShell commands to include the cmdlet `Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true -Force`. The Gentlemen Ransomware has also utilized the `TaskKill` command to target specific processes associated with backup software, endpoint detection, and office applications.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has deleted Volume Shadow Copies through the use of `vssadmin delete shadows /all /quiet` and `wmic shadowcopy delete`. The Gentlemen Ransomware has also inhibited system recovery by stopping backup services, disabling endpoint protection agents and remote access tools.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has utilized `esxcli` to execute commands on compromised ESXi systems and VMs.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has leveraged ephemeral Curve25519 keys with XChaCha20 stream ciphers to encrypt files.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has created hidden SMB share folder named “share$” that allowed anonymous access.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has utilized wmic to execute commands on victim devices. The Gentlemen Ransomware has also leveraged WMI to enumerate volumes and drives.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has deleted forensic artifacts to include prefetch files, defender diagnostic and support logs using both `del /f /q C:\Windows\Prefetch\*.*` and `del /f /q C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Support\*.*`. The Gentlemen Ransomware has also used a batch script named after itself (`<filename>.exe.bat`) to delete The Gentlemen Ransomware and the batch script.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has written registry keys within HKLM and HKCU to gain persistence device wide and to have redundancy. The Gentlemen Ransomware has added registry keys to maintain persistence through `reg add HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run /v GupdateS /t REG_SZ /d “<malware_path>” /f` and `reg add HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run /v GupdateU /t REG_SZ /d “<malware_path>” /f`.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has prevented command logging through the use of `/dev/null 2 &1` that silences output and discards any written data.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has utilized SMB to enable lateral movement and file transfers. The Gentlemen Ransomware has leveraged network shares to distribute the ransomware payload to other victim devices throughout the domain.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has removed RDP Logs by leveraging the command `del /f /q %SystemRoot%\System32\LogFiles\RDP*\*\*.*`.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has modified anti-virus settings to add its own executable to the exclusion list of the endpoint detection solution using the PowerShell command `Add-MpPreference -ExclusionProcess <malware path> -force`.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has utilized PowerShell to execute commands. The Gentlemen Ransomware has also leveraged PowerShell cmdlets to disable real-time monitoring and set exclusions.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has copied malware executables, such as PsExec.exe, to the local `C:\Temp` directory. The Gentlemen Ransomware had also enabled a hidden SMB share pointed at the `C:\Temp` folder to allow anonymous access. The Gentlemen Ransomware has also consolidated data in `C:\ProgramData\data\`.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has discovered and enumerated network shares using `net use` with corresponding sequential drive letters from A through Z. The Gentlemen Ransomware has also enumerated network shares using Windows APIs to include `WnetOpenEnumW`, `WNetEnumResourceW`, and `WNetCloseEnum`.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has the ability to change the system’s desktop wallpaper using a bitmap image file stored as `%TEMP%\gentlemen.bmp`.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has modified registry keys to allow more permissive access controls to include LSA anonymous access controls.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has used Wevtutil to clear event logs within system, application and security using the commands `wevtutil cl System`, `wevtutil cl Application`, and `wevtutil cl Security`.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has the ability to modify Group Policy on victim Domain Controllers through a PowerShell script that enables simultaneous ransomware detonation on every computer in domain.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has utilized a wipe feature that writes 64 MB chunks of data to a targeted drive to exhaust all free space and overwrites previously deleted file content, reducing recovery capabilities.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has leveraged `crontab` to launch the ransomware after a 60-second delay upon reboot using `echo '@reboot sleep 60 && /bin/.vmware-authd <original_argv>' | crontab - 2>/dev/null`.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has modified the ownership and access control settings to ensure it has unrestricted write access to target file paths prior to encryption. The Gentlemen Ransomware has leveraged the `takeown`, `icacls` and `attrib` commands to modify permissions on files and folders.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has the functionality to delay for a specified number of minutes before file encryption.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has utilized Windows APIs to facility network share discovery actions.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has conducted clean shutdowns of running VMs in ESXI environments using `vim-cmd vmsvc/power.off <vmid> > /dev/null 2>&1`. The Gentlemen Ransomware has also forcibly terminated running VM processes using `esxcli vm process kill --type=force --world-id=<world_id> > /dev/null 2>&1`.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has discovered and enumerated valid drives through a PowerShell script. The Gentlemen Ransomware has also scanned for letter drives from A: to Z: using `os.Stat` to determine valid drives.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has excluded the `C:\` volume from scanning to reduce its likelihood of being detected during the encryption process using the PowerShell cmdlet `Add-MpPreference – ExclusionPath C:\ -Force`. The Gentlemen Ransomware has also excluded encryption of specified file names, and file extensions, to include those associated with critical system functionality.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has utilized ESXi administration commands to include `vmkfstools` to modify the compromised system.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has leveraged scheduled tasks to execute itself as system. The Gentlemen Ransomware has also established persistence through the creation of scheduled tasks to include `schtasks /Create /SC ONSTART /TN UpdateSystem /TR “<malware_path>” /RU SYSTEM` and `schtasks /Create /SC ONSTART /TN UpdateUser /TR “<malware_path>”`. The Gentlemen Ransomware has deleted pre-existing scheduled tasks using `schtasks /Delete /TN UpdateSystem /F` and `schtasks /Delete /TN UpdateUser /F`.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has executed service commands using `sc.exe` to modify configurations and set the service to “start-auto” to run automatically when the system restarted to include `fdrespub`, `fdPHost`, `SSDPSRV` and `upnphost`.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has utilized Windows Command Shell to execute commands to facilitate lateral movement and other actions.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has used the following command to re-enable SMB1: `Enable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol -NoRestart`.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has utilized RC scripts to establish persistence in ESXi service.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has deleted preexisting scheduled tasks and created malicious versions of the same named task to execute automatically at system start to include tasks named `UpdateSystem` and `UpdateUser`. The Gentlemen Ransomware has also leveraged naming conventions that mimic legitimate VMware services.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has terminated active processes on the victim device. The Gentlemen Ransomware has stopped Windows services using `sc config <service name> start=disabled`, `net stop <service name>` and `sc stop <service name>`. The Gentlemen Ransomware has also disabled running processes using the `taskkill` command for specified processes.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has modified windows firewall rules to allow for discovery actions using `netsh advfirewall firewall set rule group=”Network Discovery” new enable=Yes` and using the PowerShell command `-Command Get-NetFirewall Rule -DisplayGroup “Network Discovery” | Enable-NetFirewallRule`. The Gentlemen Ransomware has also modified firewall rules to allow remote desktop access using the command `netsh firewall set service type remotedesktop mode enable` or `netsh advfirewall firewall set rule group="remote desktop" new enable=Yes`. The Gentlemen Ransomware has also deactivated Windows firewall rules using the command ` netsh advfirewall set allprofiles state off`. The Gentlemen Ransomware has disabled the Windows Firewall settings using the PowerShell cmdlet `powershell -Command Set-NetFirewallProfile -Profile Domain,Public,Private -Enabled False`.
title: Check Point Research. (2026, April 20). DFIR Report – The Gentlemen & SystemBC: A Sneak Peek Behind the Proxy. Retrieved September 18, 2026.

text: Revenge RAT has a plugin for credential harvesting. Revenge RAT collects the IP address and MAC address from the system. Revenge RAT creates a Registry key at HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\Shell to survive a system reboot. Revenge RAT gathers the username from the system. Revenge RAT collects the CPU information, OS information, and system language. Revenge RAT uses Base64 to encode information sent to the C2 server. Revenge RAT has the ability to upload and download files. Revenge RAT has a plugin to perform RDP access. Revenge RAT has a plugin for screen capture.

text: WannaCry utilizes wmic to delete shadow copies. WannaCry uses vssadmin, wbadmin, bcdedit, and wmic to delete and disable operating system recovery features. WannaCry creates the service "mssecsvc2.0" with the display name "Microsoft Security Center (2.0) Service." WannaCry uses attrib +h and icacls . /grant Everyone:F /T /C /Q to make some of its files hidden and grant all users full access controls. WannaCry uses an exploit in SMBv1 to spread itself to other remote systems on a network. WannaCry enumerates current remote desktop sessions and tries to execute the malware on each session. WannaCry searches for variety of user files by file extension before encrypting them using RSA and AES, including Office, PDF, image, audio, video, source code, archive/compression format, and key and certificate files. WannaCry encrypts user files and demands that a ransom be paid in Bitcoin to decrypt those files. WannaCry attempts to copy itself to remote computers after gaining access via an SMB exploit.
title: Noerenberg, E., Costis, A., and Quist, N. (2017, May 16). A Technical Analysis of WannaCry Ransomware. Retrieved December 8, 2024.

text: Aria-body has used ZIP to compress data gathered on a compromised host. Aria-body has the ability to inject itself into another process such as rundll32.exe and dllhost.exe. Aria-body has the ability to decrypt the loader configuration and payload DLL. Aria-body has the ability to identify the location, public IP address, and domain name on a compromised host. Aria-body has the ability to delete files and directories on compromised hosts. Aria-body has the ability to download additional payloads from C2. Aria-body has the ability to gather metadata from a file and to search for file and directory names. Aria-body has used HTTP in C2 communications. Aria-body has used an encrypted configuration file for its loader. Aria-body has the ability to capture screenshots on compromised hosts. Aria-body has the ability to gather TCP and UDP table status listings. Aria-body has the ability to identify the titles of running windows on a compromised host. Aria-body has the ability to duplicate a token from ntprint.exe. Aria-body has the ability to identify the hostname, computer name, Windows version, processor speed, and machine GUID on a compromised host. Aria-body has used TCP in C2 communications. Aria-body has the ability to enumerate loaded modules for a process.. Aria-body has the ability to use a reverse SOCKS proxy module. Aria-body has the ability to collect data from USB devices. Aria-body has the ability to identify disk information on a compromised host. Aria-body has the ability to identify the username on a compromised host. Aria-body has the ability to use a DGA for C2 communications. Aria-body has established persistence via the Startup folder or Run Registry key. Aria-body has the ability to launch files using ShellExecute. Aria-body has the ability to execute a process using runas.

StrongPity can use multiple layers of proxy servers to hide terminal nodes in its infrastructure.
StrongPity has used HTTPS over port 1402 in C2 communication.
StrongPity can download files to specified targets.

StrongPity has been signed with self-signed certificates.

text:
Rising Sun used dynamic API resolutions to various Windows APIs by leveraging `LoadLibrary()` and `GetProcAddress()`.
Rising Sun can enumerate information about files from the infected system, including file size, attributes, creation time, last access time, and write time. Rising Sun can enumerate the compilation timestamp of Windows executable files.
Rising Sun has identified the OS product name from a compromised host by searching the registry for `SOFTWARE\MICROSOFT\Windows NT\ CurrentVersion | ProductName`.
Configuration data used by Rising Sun has been encrypted using an RC4 stream algorithm.
Rising Sun has collected data and files from a compromised host.
Rising Sun can test a connection to a specified network IP address over a specified port number.
Rising Sun can detect the username of the infected host.
Rising Sun can clear a memory blog in the process by overwriting it with junk bytes.
Rising Sun can send data gathered from the infected machine via HTTP POST request to the C2.
Rising Sun can delete files and artifacts it creates.
Rising Sun can detect network adapter and IP address information.
Rising Sun can modify file attributes to hide files.
Rising Sun can detect drive information, including drive type, total number of bytes on disk, total number of free bytes on disk, and name of a specified volume.
Rising Sun can enumerate all running processes and process information on an infected machine.
Rising Sun has decrypted itself using a single-byte XOR scheme. Additionally, Rising Sun can decrypt its configuration data at runtime.
Rising Sun has executed commands using `cmd.exe /c “<command> > <%temp%>\AM<random>. tmp” 2>&1`.
Rising Sun can detect the computer name and operating system.
Rising Sun has used HTTP and HTTPS for command and control.
Rising Sun can archive data using RC4 encryption and Base64 encoding prior to exfiltration.
title: Sherstobitoff, R., Malhotra, A., et. al.. (2018, December 18). Operation Sharpshooter Campaign Targets Global Defense, Critical Infrastructure. Retrieved May 14, 2020.

text:
CASTLETAP can execute a C2 command to transfer files from victim machines.
CASTLETAP has the ability to spawn BusyBox command shell in victim environments.
THINCRUST can use Python scripts for command execution.
THINCRUST can use HTTP POST requests in C2 communications.
CASTLETAP can transfer files to compromised network devices.
CASTLETAP can filter and deobfuscate an XOR encrypted activation string in the payload of an ICMP echo request.
THINCRUST can use the Django python module "django.views.decorators.csrf” along with the decorator “csrf_exempt” within victim firewalls to disable cross-site request forgery protections.
THINCRUST can deobfuscate RSA encrypted C2 commands received through the DEVICEID cookie.
CASTLETAP can listen for a specialized ICMP packet for activation on compromised network devices.
THINCRUST can process RSA encryted C2 commands.
CASTLETAP can initiate a C2 connection over an SSL socket.
CASTLETAP has the ability to create a raw promiscuous socket to sniff network traffic.
CASTLETAP can receive a 9-byte XOR encrypted activation string in the payload of an ICMP echo request packet.

Mafalda can encode data using Base64 prior to exfiltration.
Mafalda can manipulate the system registry on a compromised host.
metaMain can log mouse events.
metaMain can collect the computer name from a compromised host.
Mafalda can execute shell commands using `cmd.exe`.
Mafalda can download additional files onto the compromised host.
Mafalda can conduct mouse event logging.
Mafalda can dump password hashes from `LSASS.exe`.
metaMain can collect the username from a compromised host.

Mafalda can search for debugging tools on a compromised host.
Mafalda can use `AdjustTokenPrivileges()` to elevate privileges.
Mafalda can collect the username from a compromised host.
Mafalda can execute PowerShell commands on a compromised machine.
metaMain can create a named pipe to listen for and send data to a named pipe-based C2 server.
metaMain's module file has been encrypted via XOR.
metaMain can change the `CreationTime`, `LastAccessTime`, and `LastWriteTime` file time attributes when executed with `SYSTEM` privileges.
metaMain can support an HKCMD sideloading start method.
Mafalda can create a token for a different user.
Mafalda can create a remote service, let it run once, and then delete it.
Mafalda can enumerate Registry keys with all subkeys and values.
Mafalda can establish an SSH connection from a compromised host to a server.
metaMain can upload collected files and data to its C2 server.

text: DarkGate tries to elevate privileges to SYSTEM using PsExec to locally execute as a service, such as cmd /c c:\temp\PsExec.exe -accepteula -j -d -s [Target Binary]. DarkGate use Nirsoft Network Password Recovery or NetPass tools to steal stored RDP credentials in some malware versions. DarkGate relies on parent PID spoofing as part of its "rootkit-like" functionality to evade detection via Task Manager or Process Explorer. DarkGate includes one infection vector that leverages a malicious "KeyScramblerE.DLL" library that will load during the execution of the legitimate KeyScrambler application. DarkGate masquerades malicious LNK files as PDF objects using the double extension .pdf.lnk. DarkGate is distributed in phishing emails containing links to distribute malicious VBS or MSI files. DarkGate uses applications such as Microsoft Teams for distributing links to payloads. DarkGate command and control includes hard-coded domains in the malware masquerading as legitimate services such as Akamai CDN or Amazon Web Services. DarkGate checks the BeingDebugged flag in the PEB structure during execution to identify if the malware is being debugged. DarkGate command and control includes hard-coded domains in the malware chosen to masquerade as legitimate services such as Akamai CDN or Amazon Web Services. DarkGate executes a Windows Batch script during installation that creases a randomly-named directory in the C:\\ root directory that copies and renames the legitimate Windows curl command to this new location. DarkGate uses per-victim links for hosting malicious archives, such as ZIP files, in services such as SharePoint to prevent other entities from retrieving them. DarkGate uses a hard-coded string as a seed, along with the victim machine hardware identifier and input text, to generate a unique string used as an internal mutex value to evade static detection based on mutexes.
title: Ernesto Fernández Provecho, Pham Duy Phuc, Ciana Driscoll & Vinoo Thomas. (2023, November 21). The Continued Evolution of the DarkGate Malware-as-a-Service. Retrieved February 9, 2024.

text:
DarkComet has dropped itself onto victim machines with file names such as WinDefender.Exe and winupdate.exe in an apparent attempt to masquerade as a legitimate file.
DarkComet gathers the username from the victim’s machine.
DarkComet has a keylogging capability.

text:
NetTraveler reports window names along with keylogger information to provide application context.
NetTraveler contains a keylogger.

text:
Kobalos is triggered by an incoming TCP connection to a legitimate service from a specific source port.
Kobalos encrypts all strings using RC4 and bundles all functionality into a single function call.
Kobalos has used a compromised SSH client to capture the hostname, port, username and password used to establish an SSH connection from the compromised host.
Kobalos can spawn a new pseudo-terminal and execute arbitrary commands at the command prompt.
Kobalos's post-authentication communication channel uses a 32-byte-long password with RC4 for inbound and outbound traffic.
Kobalos can chain together multiple compromised machines as proxies to reach their final targets.
Kobalos's authentication and key exchange is performed using RSA-512.
Kobalos can remove all command history on compromised hosts.

text:
Exbyte decodes and decrypts data stored in the configuration file with a key provided on the command line during execution.
BlackByte 2.0 Ransomware modifies the victim Registry to allow for elevated execution.
BlackByte 2.0 Ransomware can timestomp files for defense evasion and anti-forensics purposes.
Exbyte checks for the presence of a configuration file before completing execution.
BlackByte 2.0 Ransomware injects into a newly-created `svchost.exe` process prior to device encryption.
Exbyte will self-delete if a hard-coded configuration file is not found.
BlackByte 2.0 Ransomware executes as a service when deployed.
BlackByte 2.0 Ransomware modifies volume shadow copies during execution in a way that destroys them on the victim machine.
BlackByte 2.0 Ransomware exploits a vulnerability in the RTCore64.sys driver (CVE-2019-16098) to enable privilege escalation and defense evasion when run as a service.
BlackByte 2.0 Ransomware can terminate running services.
BlackByte 2.0 Ransomware modifies the Windows firewall during execution.

text: The "Uploader" variant of HAMMERTOSS visits a hard-coded server over HTTP/S to download the images HAMMERTOSS uses to receive commands. The "tDiscoverer" variant of HAMMERTOSS establishes a C2 channel by downloading resources from Web services like Twitter and GitHub. HAMMERTOSS binaries contain an algorithm that generates a different Twitter handle for the malware to check for instructions every day. HAMMERTOSS is known to use PowerShell. HAMMERTOSS exfiltrates data by uploading it to accounts created by the actors on Web cloud storage providers for the adversaries to retrieve later. Before being appended to image files, HAMMERTOSS commands are encrypted with a key composed of both a hard-coded value and a string contained on that day's tweet. To decrypt the commands, an investigator would need access to the intended malware sample, the day's tweet, and the image file containing the command.

Another JHUHUGIT variant gathers the victim storage volume serial number and the storage device name. JHUHUGIT obtains a list of running processes on the victim. JHUHUGIT variants have communicated with C2 servers over HTTP and HTTPS. JHUHUGIT has used a Registry Run key to establish persistence by executing JavaScript code within the rundll32.exe process. JHUHUGIT can retrieve an additional payload from its C2 server. JHUHUGIT has a command to download files to the victim’s machine. The JHUHUGIT dropper can delete itself from the victim. Another JHUHUGIT variant has the capability to delete specified files.

text: Pikabot uses base64 encoding in conjunction with symmetric encryption mechanisms to obfuscate command and control communications. Pikabot performs a variety of system checks to determine if it is running in an analysis environment or sandbox, such as checking the number of processors (must be greater than two), and the amount of RAM (must be greater than 2GB). Earlier Pikabot variants use a custom encryption procedure leveraging multiple mechanisms including AES with multiple rounds of Base64 encoding for its command and control communication. Later Pikabot variants eliminate the use of AES and instead use RC4 encryption for transmitted information. Pikabot will gather information concerning the Windows Domain the victim machine is a member of during execution. Pikabot will retrieve the name of the user associated with the thread under which the malware is executing. Pikabot reflectively loads stored, previously encrypted components of the PE file into memory of the currently executing process to avoid writing content to disk on the executing machine. Pikabot uses non-standard ports, such as 2967, 2223, and others, for HTTPS command and control communication. Some versions of Pikabot build the final PE payload in memory to avoid writing contents to disk on the executing machine. Pikabot stops execution if the infected system language matches one of several languages, with various versions referencing: Georgian, Kazakh, Uzbek, Tajik, Russian, Ukrainian, Belarussian, and Slovenian. Pikabot decrypts command and control URIs using ADVobfuscator, and decrypts IP addresses and port numbers with a custom algorithm. Other versions of Pikabot decode chunks of stored stage 2 payload content in the initial payload .text section before consolidating them for further execution. Overall LunarMail is associated with multiple encoding and encryption mechanisms to obfuscate the malware's presence and avoid analysis or detection. Pikabot can create a suspended instance of a legitimate process (e.g., ctfmon.exe), allocate memory within the suspended process corresponding to Pikabot's core module, then redirect execution flow via `SetContextThread` API so that when the thread resumes the Pikabot core module is executed. During the initial Pikabot command and control check-in, Pikabot will transmit collected system information encrypted using RC4. Pikabot performs a variety of system checks and gathers system information, including commands such as whoami. Pikabot features several methods to evade debugging by analysts, including checks for active debuggers, the use of breakpoints during execution, and checking various system information items such as system memory and the number of processors. Pikabot further decrypts information embedded via steganography using AES-CBC with the same 32 bit key as initial XOR operations combined with the first 16 bytes of the encrypted data as an initialization vector. Other Pikabot variants include encrypted, chunked sections of the stage 2 payload in the initial loader .text section before decrypting and assembling these during execution. Pikabot uses native Windows APIs to determine if the process is being debugged and analyzed, such as `CheckRemoteDebuggerPresent`, `NtQueryInformationProcess`, `ProcessDebugPort`, and `ProcessDebugFlags`. Other Pikabot variants populate a global list of Windows API addresses from the `NTDLL` and `KERNEL32` libraries, and references these items instead of calling the API items to obfuscate execution.

text: Bazar has been downloaded via Windows BITS functionality. Bazar has the ability to use an alternative C2 server if the primary server fails. Bazar can execute a PowerShell script received from C2. Bazar can identify the username of the infected user. Bazar can download and deploy additional payloads, including ransomware and post-exploitation frameworks such as Cobalt Strike. Bazar can perform a check to ensure that the operating system's keyboard and language settings are not set to Russian. The Bazar loader has named malicious shortcuts "adobe" and mimicked communications software. Bazar can fingerprint architecture, computer name, and OS version on the compromised host. Bazar can also check if the Russian language is installed on the infected machine and terminate if it is found. Bazar can use HTTP and HTTPS over ports 80 and 443 in C2 communications. Bazar can collect the time on the compromised host. Bazar can send C2 communications with XOR encryption. Bazar can establish persistence by writing shortcuts to the Windows Startup folder. Bazar can enumerate shared drives on the domain. Bazar can inject into a target process including Svchost, Explorer, and cmd using process hollowing. Bazar's loader can delete scheduled tasks created by a previous instance of the malware. Bazar has used XOR, RSA2, and RC4 encrypted files. Bazar can use a timer to delay execution of core functionality. Bazar can create a scheduled task for persistence. Bazar can use Nltest tools to obtain information about the domain. Bazar can query Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall for installed applications. Bazar can identify administrator accounts on an infected host. Bazar can create or add files to Registry Run Keys to establish persistence. Bazar has the ability to identify domain administrator accounts. Bazar can inject into a target process using process doppelgänging. Bazar can enumerate the victim's desktop. Bazar has manually loaded ntdll from disk in order to identity and remove API hooks set by security products. Bazar can hash then resolve API calls at runtime. Bazar can delete its loader using a batch file in the Windows temporary folder. Bazar can decrypt downloaded payloads. Bazar also resolves strings and other artifacts at runtime.

BlackByte Ransomware is distributed as a JavaScript launcher file.
