text:
VIRTUALPITA can execute commands on guest virtual machines from compromised ESXi hypervisors.
VIRTUALPIE has file transfer capabilities.
VIRTUALPITA samples have been found in `/usr/libexec/setconf/ksmd` and `/usr/bin/ksmd`, named to spoof the legitimate Kernel Same-Page Merging Daemon binary.
VIRTUALPIE has created listeners on hard coded TCP port 546.
VIRTUALPITA can target specific guest virtual machines for script execution.
VIRTUALPITA can persist as an init.d startup service on Linux vCenter systems.
VIRTUALPITA has created listeners on hard coded TCP ports such as 2233, 7475, and 18098.
VIRTUALPITA has the ability to spawn a bash shell for script execution.
VIRTUALPITA can call a Python script to run commands on a targeted guest virtual machine.
VIRTUALPIE is capable of command line execution on compromised ESXi servers.
VIRTUALPIE has been installed on VMware ESXi servers through malicious vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs).
VIRTUALPITA can start and stop the `vmsyslogd` service.
VIRTUALPITA is capable of file transfer and arbitrary command execution.
VIRTUALPIE can use a custom RC4 encrypted protocol for C2 communications.
VIRTUALPITA has utilized VMware service names and ports to masquerade as legitimate services.
VIRTUALPITA has the ability to upload and download files.
VIRTUALPIE is a Python-based backdoor malware.
VIRTUALPITA can impair logging by setting the `HISTFILE` environmental variable to `0` and stopping the `vmsyslogd` service.
title: Alexander Marvi, Jeremy Koppen, Tufail Ahmed, and Jonathan Lepore. (2022, September 29). Bad VIB(E)s Part One: Investigating Novel Malware Persistence Within ESXi Hypervisors. Retrieved March 26, 2025.

text: EvilBunny has used Lua scripts to execute payloads.
title: Marschalek, Marion. (2014, December 16). EvilBunny: Malware Instrumented By Lua. Retrieved August 5, 2024.

text: JCry has used VBS scripts. JCry has used cmd.exe to launch PowerShell. JCry has used PowerShell to execute payloads. JCry has created payloads in the Startup directory to maintain persistence. JCry has achieved execution by luring users to click on a file that appeared to be an Adobe Flash Player update installer. JCry has been observed deleting shadow copies to ensure that data cannot be restored easily. JCry has encrypted files and demanded Bitcoin to decrypt those files.
title: Lee, S.. (2019, May 14). JCry Ransomware. Retrieved June 18, 2019.

text: Ixeshe is capable of executing commands via cmd. Ixeshe can download and execute additional files. Ixeshe can list running processes. Ixeshe sets its own executable file's attributes to hidden. Ixeshe can list file and directory information. Ixeshe can collect data from a local system. Ixeshe collects the username from the victim’s machine. Ixeshe enumerates the IP address, network proxy settings, and domain name from a victim's system. Ixeshe can list running services. Ixeshe can achieve persistence by adding itself to the HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run Registry key. Ixeshe has used registry values and file names associated with Adobe software, such as AcroRd32.exe. Ixeshe has a command to delete a file from the machine. Ixeshe collects the computer name of the victim's system during the initial infection.
title: Sancho, D., et al. (2012, May 22). IXESHE An APT Campaign. Retrieved June 7, 2019.

text: TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can compress and encrypt data and exfiltrate it via POST to scan.aquasecurtiy[.]org. If that method fails it attempts to use a stolen GITHUB_TOKEN to create a repo and exfiltrate the data there.
title: McCarthy, R. (2026, March 20). Trivy Compromised: Everything You Need to Know about the Latest Supply Chain Attack. Retrieved July 1, 2026.

text: KONNI has used HTTP POST for C2. KONNI has been delivered via spearphishing campaigns through a malicious Word document. KONNI has pretended to be the xmlProv Network Provisioning service. KONNI has registered itself as a service using its export function. KONNI used PowerShell to download and execute a specific 64-bit version of the malware. KONNI has used Rundll32 to execute its loader for privilege escalation purposes. KONNI has stored collected information and discovered processes in a tmp file. KONNI has bypassed UAC by performing token impersonation as well as an RPC-based method, this included bypassing UAC set to “AlwaysNotify". KONNI has relied on a victim to enable malicious macros within an attachment delivered via email. KONNI has sent data and files to its C2 server. KONNI can gather the OS version, architecture information, hostname, and RAM size information from the victim’s machine and has used cmd /c systeminfo command to get a snapshot of the current system state of the target machine. KONNI can download files and execute them on the victim’s machine. KONNI has used cmd.exe to execute arbitrary commands on the infected host across different stages of the infection chain. KONNI has duplicated the token of a high integrity process to spawn an instance of cmd.exe under an impersonated user. KONNI has used net session on the victim's machine. KONNI has used parent PID spoofing to spawn a new `cmd` process using `CreateProcessW` and a handle to `Taskmgr.exe`. KONNI has encrypted data and files prior to exfiltration. KONNI has hardcoded API calls within its functions to use on the victim's machine. KONNI has modified registry keys of ComSysApp, Svchost, and xmlProv on the machine to gain persistence. KONNI has executed malicious JavaScript code. KONNI has used the command cmd /c tasklist to get a snapshot of the current processes on the target machine. KONNI is heavily obfuscated and includes encrypted configuration files. KONNI has used certutil to download and decode base64 encoded strings and has also devoted a custom section to performing all the components of the deobfuscation process. KONNI can gather information on connected drives and disk space from the victim’s machine.
title: Threat Intelligence Team. (2021, August 23). New variant of Konni malware used in campaign targetting Russia. Retrieved January 5, 2022.

text:
Qilin can exclude specific directories and files from encryption.
Qilin can check `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Control SystemStartOptions` to determine if a machine is running in safe mode.
Qilin can configure a Winlogon registry entry.
Qilin can list all local users found on a targeted system.
Qilin can inject pwndll.dll, a patched DLL from the legitimate DLL WICloader.dll, into svchost.exe for continuous execution.
Qilin can accept a command line argument identifying specific IPs.
title: Magdy, S. et al. (2022, August 25). New Golang Ransomware Agenda Customizes Attacks. Retrieved September 26, 2025.

text:
Okrum's loader can detect presence of an emulator by using two calls to GetTickCount API, and checking whether the time has been accelerated.
Okrum's payload is encrypted and embedded within its loader, or within a legitimate PNG file.
Okrum has used a custom implementation of AES encryption to encrypt collected data.
Okrum can establish persistence by creating a .lnk shortcut to itself in the Startup folder.
Okrum was seen using a keylogger tool to capture keystrokes.
To establish persistence, Okrum can install itself as a new service named NtmSsvc.
Okrum has used DriveLetterView to enumerate drive information.
Okrum can impersonate a logged-on user's security context using a call to the ImpersonateLoggedOnUser API.
Okrum can obtain the date and time of the compromised system.
Okrum has built-in commands for uploading, downloading, and executing files to the system.
Before exfiltration, Okrum's backdoor has used hidden files to store logs and outputs from backdoor commands.
Okrum leverages the HTTP protocol for C2 communication, while hiding the actual messages in the Cookie and Set-Cookie headers of the HTTP requests.
Okrum's loader can decrypt the backdoor code, embedded within the loader or within a legitimate PNG file. A custom XOR cipher or RC4 is used for decryption.
Okrum can collect the victim username.
Okrum can collect computer name, locale information, and information about the OS and architecture.
Okrum's loader can create a new service named NtmsSvc to execute the payload.
Okrum uses AES to encrypt network traffic. The key can be hardcoded or negotiated with the C2 server in the registration phase.
Okrum has used base64 to encode C2 communication.
Okrum can establish persistence by adding a new service NtmsSvc with the display name Removable Storage to masquerade as a legitimate Removable Storage Manager.
Okrum was seen using modified Quarks PwDump to perform credential dumping.
Okrum can identify proxy servers configured and used by the victim, and use it to make HTTP requests to C2 its server.
Okrum was seen using NetSess to discover NetBIOS sessions.
Okrum's installer can attempt to achieve persistence by creating a scheduled task.
Okrum was seen using a RAR archiver tool to compress/decompress data.
Okrum uses HTTP for communication with its C2.
Okrum's backdoor deletes files after they have been successfully uploaded to C2 servers.
Okrum loader only executes the payload after the left mouse button has been pressed at least three times, in order to avoid being executed within virtualized or emulated environments.
Okrum's backdoor has used cmd.exe to execute arbitrary commands as well as batch scripts to update itself to a newer version.
Okrum was seen using MimikatzLite to perform credential dumping.
Okrum establishes persistence by creating a .lnk shortcut to itself in the Startup folder.
Okrum can collect network information, including the host IP address, DNS, and proxy information.
Okrum's loader can check the amount of physical memory and terminates itself if the host has less than 1.5 Gigabytes of physical memory in total.
Data exfiltration is done by Okrum using the already opened channel with the C2 server.
title: Hromcova, Z. (2019, July). OKRUM AND KETRICAN: AN OVERVIEW OF RECENT KE3CHANG GROUP ACTIVITY. Retrieved May 6, 2020.

text: SUPERNOVA contained Base64-encoded strings.
title: CISA. (2021, January 27). Malware Analysis Report (AR21-027A). Retrieved February 22, 2021.

text: OSX/Shlayer has used the `nohup` command to instruct executed payloads to ignore hangup signals.
title: Jaron Bradley. (2021, April 26). Shlayer malware abusing Gatekeeper bypass on macOS. Retrieved September 22, 2021.

text:
Lumma Stealer has used PowerShell for initial user execution and other fuctions.
Lumma Stealer has detected antivirus processes using commands such as “tasklist” and “findstr.”
Lumma Stealer has used mshta.exe to execute additional content.
Lumma Stealer has used HTTP and HTTP for command and control communication.
Lumma Stealer has exfiltrated collected data over existing HTTP and HTTPS C2 channels.
Lumma Stealer has utilized AutoIt malware scripts and AutoIt executables.
Lumma Stealer has used AES-encrypted payloads contained within PowerShell scripts.
Lumma Stealer has been distributed through a fake CAPTCHA that presents instructions to the victim to open Windows Run window (“Windows Button + R”) and paste clipboard contents (“CTRL + V”) and press “Enter” to execute a Base64-encoded PowerShell.
Lumma Stealer has used process hollowing leveraging a legitimate program such as “BitLockerToGo.exe” to inject a malicious payload.
title: Vishwajeet Kumar, Qualys. (2024, October 20). Unmasking Lumma Stealer: Analyzing Deceptive Tactics with Fake CAPTCHA. Retrieved March 22, 2025.

text: Rover searches for files on attached removable drives based on a predefined list of file extensions every five seconds. Rover automatically searches for files on local drives based on a predefined list of file extensions. Rover takes screenshots of the compromised system's desktop and saves them to C:\system\screenshot.bmp for exfiltration every 60 minutes. Rover automatically collects files from the local system and removable drives based on a predefined list of file extensions on a regular timeframe. Rover persists by creating a Registry entry in HKEY_CURRENT_USER\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\. Rover searches for files on local drives based on a predefined list of file extensions. Rover automatically searches for files on local drives based on a predefined list of file extensions and sends them to the command and control server every 60 minutes. Rover also automatically sends keylogger files and screenshots to the C2 server on a regular timeframe. Rover has functionality to remove Registry Run key persistence as a cleanup procedure. Rover has keylogging functionality. Rover copies files from removable drives to C:\system.
title: Ray, V., Hayashi, K. (2016, February 29). New Malware ‘Rover’ Targets Indian Ambassador to Afghanistan. Retrieved February 29, 2016.

text: SystemBC has used DNS servers to resolve .bit domains to C2 infrastructure.
title: Harmon, K., et al. (2019, August 1). SystemBC is like Christmas in July for SOCKS5 Malware and Exploit Kits . Retrieved June 13, 2025.

text:
DarkTortilla has used `%HiddenReg%` and `%HiddenKey%` as part of its persistence via the Windows registry.
DarkTortilla has modified registry keys for persistence.
DarkTortilla can decrypt its payload and associated configuration elements using the Rijndael cipher.
DarkTortilla can retrieve information about a compromised system's running services.
DarkTortilla can download a clipboard information stealer module.
DarkTortilla can check for the Kaspersky Anti-Virus suite.
DarkTortilla can check for internet connectivity by issuing HTTP GET requests.
DarkTortilla can retrieve its primary payload from public sites such as Pastebin and Textbin.
DarkTortilla's payload has been renamed `PowerShellInfo.exe`.
DarkTortilla can use WMI queries to obtain system information.
DarkTortilla has used HTTP and HTTPS for C2.
DarkTortilla can use a variety of API calls for persistence and defense evasion.
DarkTortilla can enumerate a list of running processes on a compromised system.
DarkTortilla has relied on a user to open a malicious document or archived file delivered via email for initial execution.
DarkTortilla can download a keylogging module.
DarkTortilla can detect profilers by verifying the `COR_ENABLE_PROFILING` environment variable is present and active.
DarkTortilla can detect debuggers by using functions such as `DebuggerIsAttached` and `DebuggerIsLogging`. DarkTortilla can also detect profilers by verifying the `COR_ENABLE_PROFILING` environment variable is present and active.
DarkTortilla can search a compromised system's running processes and services to detect Hyper-V, QEMU, Virtual PC, Virtual Box, and VMware, as well as Sandboxie.
DarkTortilla can implement the `kernel32.dll` Sleep function to delay execution for up to 300 seconds before implementing persistence or processing an addon package.
DarkTortilla has been obfuscated with the DeepSea .NET and ConfuserEx code obfuscators.
DarkTortilla has been distributed via spearphishing emails containing archive attachments, with file types such as .iso, .zip, .img, .dmg, and .tar, as well as through malicious documents.
DarkTortilla can use a .NET-based DLL named `RunPe6` for process injection.
DarkTortilla can obtain system information by querying the `Win32_ComputerSystem`, `Win32_BIOS`, `Win32_MotherboardDevice`, `Win32_PnPEntity`, and `Win32_DiskDrive` WMI objects.
DarkTortilla has used the `WshShortcut` COM object to create a .lnk shortcut file in the Windows startup folder.
DarkTortilla has established persistence via the `Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Run` registry key and by creating a .lnk shortcut file in the Windows startup folder.
DarkTortilla can use `cmd.exe` to add registry keys for persistence.
DarkTortilla has established persistence via the `Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon` registry key.
DarkTortilla can download additional packages for keylogging, cryptocurrency mining, and other capabilities; it can also retrieve malicious payloads such as Agent Tesla, AsyncRat, NanoCore, RedLine, Cobalt Strike, and Metasploit.
title: Secureworks Counter Threat Unit Research Team. (2022, August 17). DarkTortilla Malware Analysis. Retrieved November 3, 2022.

text:
ROKRAT has the ability to gather a list of files and directories on the infected system.
ROKRAT can request to delete files.
title: Pantazopoulos, N.. (2018, November 8). RokRat Analysis. Retrieved May 21, 2020.

text:
SPAWNCHIMERA has decoded a XOR encoded private key.
SPAWNCHIMERA has fixed a buffer overflow vulnerability (CVE-2025-0282) by hooking the strncpy function and limiting the size to 256 to prevent other actors from leveraging the exploit. SPAWNCHIMERA has converted its process name to hexadecimal and verifies an added value which is triggered when the first byte of the source copied to the fixed strncpy function matches `0x04050203`.
SPAWNCHIMERA has executed only in memory and hooked itself into existing processes on the victim device to include the web process.
SPAWNCHIMERA has leveraged IPC using a UNIX domain socket between the dsmdm process and the web process.
SPAWNCHIMERA has encoded a private key with XOR. SPAWNCHIMERA has also encrypted data to be extracted using AES encryption.
SPAWNCHIMERA has the ability to bind on a localhost and listen on port 8300.
title: Yuma Masubuchi. (2025, February 20). SPAWNCHIMERA Malware: The Chimera Spawning from Ivanti Connect Secure Vulnerability. Retrieved April 17, 2026.

text:
Mini Shai-Hulud has examined commit messages for a keyword followed by base64 encoded segments to validate communications and to execute subsequent actions to include exfiltration.
Mini Shai-Hulud has utilized execution guardrails in order to prevent operating in restricted geolocations to include Russia by checking the devices language and terminating when a forbidden value is detected. Mini Shai-Hulud has also utilized designated instructions that execute when victim hosts match geolocations to include wiping victim devices when the device is determined to be located within Iran or Israel.
Mini Shai-Hulud has suppressed output so that nothing is printed to terminal and has utilized silent exiting when environmental variables match restricted values.
Mini Shai-Hulud has enumerated home directories, file paths and files associated with storing or containing credentials and other secrets.
Mini Shai-Hulud has discovered the compromised systems location through a query of the system timezone configuration and the locale settings.
Mini Shai-Hulud has utilized the Docker command-line tool to gather details of the victim environment and collect credentials.
Mini Shai-Hulud has evaded sandbox detection by applying a 1-in-6 probability gate that generates a random number which will only trigger the wiper functionality when the set number outcome is met even in environments that match parameters of a geopolitical target.
Mini Shai-Hulud has collected victim client certificates to assist in signed authentication assertion with Azure environments.
Mini Shai-Hulud has enumerated cloud accounts and subscriptions accessible to the targeted identity.
Mini Shai-Hulud has gathered system information of victim hosts through the use of common discovery commands to include `hostname`, `uname-a` and `printenv`. Mini Shai-Hulud has also conducted system checks of the victim device to include enumerating the system type and the number of CPUs operating on victim host.
Mini Shai-Hulud has established Fallback Channels to exfiltrate data to Github when other configured infrastructure is found to be unreachable.
Mini Shai-Hulud has exfiltrated encrypted archives over C2 domains.
Mini Shai-Hulud has leveraged a user-agent string that mimics a standard git client to avoid detection within network logs.
Mini Shai-Hulud has the ability to download additional payloads from adversary controlled or compromised infrastructure.
Mini Shai-Hulud has queried the system timezone configuration and timezone data files to include `/etc/localtime`, and locale settings to determine the geolocation of the compromised host.
Mini Shai-Hulud has used base64 encoding to obfuscate URLs used for C2.
Mini Shai-Hulud has gathered credentials stored in password managers to include password vaults.
Mini Shai-Hulud has evaded execution in virtual environments and sandboxes through checking system information to include the number of CPUs and exiting at times when there were less than four and other times when there were less than two CPUs.
Mini Shai-Hulud has compressed collected credentials to reduce transmission size and to make string content harder to detect in memory forensics captures.
Mini Shai-Hulud has gathered unsecured API keys stored in container orchestrators.
Mini Shai-Hulud has executed via the use of `subprocess.run` and fed input through standard input `stdin` which acted as a pipe to send data from the parent process and the child process `sys.executable` within memory.
title: Hunt.io. (2026, May 14). How TeamPCP's Python Toolkit Survives a C2 Takedown: FIRESCALE, GitHub, and the Victim's Own Account. Retrieved July 16, 2026.

text:
zwShell can obtain the name of the logged-in user on the victim.
zwShell can browse the file system.
zwShell can modify the Registry.
zwShell can obtain the victim PC name and OS version.
zwShell has used RDP for lateral movement.
zwShell can obtain the victim IP address.
zwShell has deleted itself after creating a service as well as deleted a temporary file when the system reboots.
zwShell has established persistence by adding itself as a new service.
zwShell has been copied over network shares to move laterally.
zwShell can launch command-line shells.
zwShell has used SchTasks for execution.

To establish persistence, Truvasys adds a Registry Run key with a value "TaskMgr" in an attempt to masquerade as the legitimate Windows Task Manager.
Truvasys adds a Registry Run key to establish persistence.

Some variants of Cherry Picker use AppInit_DLLs to achieve persistence by creating the following Registry key: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows "AppInit_DLLs"="pserver32.dll" Recent versions of Cherry Picker delete files and registry keys created by the malware.

text:
XCSSET has used `mdfind` to enumerate a list of apps known to grant screen sharing permissions and leverages a module to run the command `ls -la ~/Desktop`.
XCSSET has dropped a malicious applet into an app's `.../Contents/MacOS/` folder of a previously launched app to bypass Gatekeeper's security checks on first launch apps (prior to macOS 13).
title: Brandon Dalton. (2022, August 9). A bundle of nerves: Tweaking macOS security controls to thwart application bundle manipulation. Retrieved September 27, 2022.

text:
JSS Loader can download and execute JavaScript files.
JSS Loader can download and execute VBScript files.
JSS Loader has the ability to download and execute PowerShell scripts.
JSS Loader has the ability to download malicious executables to a compromised host.
JSS Loader has the ability to launch scheduled tasks to establish persistence.
title: Loui, E. and Reynolds, J. (2021, August 30). CARBON SPIDER Embraces Big Game Hunting, Part 1. Retrieved September 20, 2021.

title: Kennelly, J., Goody, K., Shilko, J. (2020, May 7). Navigating the MAZE: Tactics, Techniques and Procedures Associated With MAZE Ransomware Incidents. Retrieved May 18, 2020.

text: SMOKEDHAM has used net.exe user and net.exe users to enumerate local accounts on a compromised host. SMOKEDHAM has modified the Registry to hide created user accounts from the Windows logon screen. SMOKEDHAM has used whoami commands to identify system owners. SMOKEDHAM has encoded its C2 traffic with Base64. The SMOKEDHAM source code is embedded in the dropper as an encrypted string. SMOKEDHAM has used a fronted domain to obfuscate its hard-coded C2 server domain. SMOKEDHAM has added user accounts to local Admin groups. SMOKEDHAM has exfiltrated data to its C2 server. SMOKEDHAM has created user accounts. SMOKEDHAM has used reg.exe to create a Registry Run key. SMOKEDHAM can execute Powershell commands sent from its C2 server. SMOKEDHAM has used Powershell to download UltraVNC and ngrok from third-party file sharing sites. SMOKEDHAM has encrypted its C2 traffic with RC4. SMOKEDHAM has used the systeminfo command on a compromised host. SMOKEDHAM has communicated with its C2 servers via HTTPS and HTTP POST requests. SMOKEDHAM has modified registry keys for persistence, to enable credential caching for credential access, and to facilitate lateral movement via RDP.
title: FireEye. (2021, June 16). Smoking Out a DARKSIDE Affiliate’s Supply Chain Software Compromise. Retrieved September 22, 2021.

text:
MirageFox has a function for decrypting data containing C2 configuration information.
MirageFox can gather the username from the victim’s machine.
MirageFox can collect CPU and architecture information from the victim’s machine.
MirageFox is likely loaded via DLL hijacking into a legitimate McAfee binary.
MirageFox has the capability to execute commands using cmd.exe.
title: Rosenberg, J. (2018, June 14). MirageFox: APT15 Resurfaces With New Tools Based On Old Ones. Retrieved September 21, 2018.

text: COATHANGER hooks or replaces multiple legitimate processes and other functions on victim devices. COATHANGER will set the GID of `httpsd` to 90 when infected. COATHANGER is installed following exploitation of a vulnerable FortiGate device. COATHANGER will create a daemon for timed check-ins with command and control infrastructure. COATHANGER will remove and write malicious shared objects associated with legitimate system functions such as `read(2)`. COATHANGER can store obfuscated configuration information in the last 56 bytes of the file `/date/.bd.key/preload.so`. COATHANGER includes a binary labeled `authd` that can inject a library into a running process and then hook an existing function within that process with a new function from that library. COATHANGER creates and installs itself to a hidden installation directory. COATHANGER connects to command and control infrastructure using SSL. COATHANGER provides a BusyBox reverse shell for command and control. COATHANGER will query running process information to determine subsequent program execution flow. COATHANGER decodes configuration items from a bundled file for command and control activity. COATHANGER uses ICMP for transmitting configuration information to and from its command and control server. COATHANGER will survey the contents of system files during installation. COATHANGER uses an HTTP GET request to initialize a follow-on TLS tunnel for command and control. COATHANGER removes files from victim environments following use in multiple instances. COATHANGER copies the malicious file /data2/.bd.key/preload.so to /lib/preload.so, then launches a child process that executes the malicious file /data2/.bd.key/authd as /bin/authd with the arguments /lib/preload.so reboot newreboot 1. This injects the malicious preload.so file into the process with PID 1, and replaces its reboot function with the malicious newreboot function for persistence. The first stage of COATHANGER is delivered as a packed file.
title: Dutch Military Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD) & Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD). (2024, February 6). Ministry of Defense of the Netherlands uncovers COATHANGER, a stealthy Chinese FortiGate RAT. Retrieved February 7, 2024.

text:
STEADYPULSE can transmit URL encoded data over C2.
PULSECHECK can use Unix shell script for command execution.
SLIGHTPULSE can base64 encode all incoming and outgoing C2 messages.
STEADYPULSE can URL decode key/value pairs sent over C2.
PACEMAKER has the ability to extract credentials from OS memory.
SLIGHTPULSE has the ability to process HTTP GET requests as a normal web server and to insert logic that will read or write files or execute commands in response to HTTP POST requests.
PACEMAKER can parse `/proc/"process_name"/cmdline` to look for the string `dswsd` within the command line.
SLIGHTPULSE contains functionality to execute arbitrary commands passed to it.
SLOWPULSE can write logged ACE credentials to `/home/perl/PAUS.pm` in append mode, using the format string `%s:%s\n`.
PULSECHECK is a web shell that can enable command execution on compromised servers.
PACEMAKER can use a simple bash script for execution.
PULSECHECK can check HTTP request headers for a specific backdoor key and if found will output the result of the command in the variable `HTTP_X_CMD.`
STEADYPULSE is a web shell that can enable the execution of arbitrary commands on compromised web servers.
SLIGHTPULSE has piped the output from executed commands to `/tmp/1`.
PACEMAKER can enter a loop to read `/proc/` entries every 2 seconds in order to read a target application's memory.
PULSECHECK can base-64 encode encrypted data sent through C2.
SLOWPULSE can insert malicious logic to bypass RADIUS and ACE two factor authentication (2FA) flows if a designated attacker-supplied password is provided.
SLIGHTPULSE can RC4 encrypt all incoming and outgoing C2 messages.
STEADYPULSE can parse web requests made to a targeted server to determine the next stage of execution.
PACEMAKER can use PTRACE to attach to a targeted process to read process memory.
SLOWPULSE can log credentials on compromised Pulse Secure VPNs during the `DSAuth::AceAuthServer::checkUsernamePassword`ACE-2FA authentication procedure.
SLOWPULSE can hide malicious code in the padding regions between legitimate functions in the Pulse Secure `libdsplibs.so` file.
STEADYPULSE can add lines to a Perl script on a targeted server to import additional Perl modules.
SLOWPULSE can modify LDAP and two factor authentication flows by inspecting login credentials and forcing successful authentication if the provided password matches a chosen backdoor password.
SLIGHTPULSE is a web shell that can read, write, and execute files on compromised servers.
SLIGHTPULSE can read files specified on the local system.
PACEMAKER has written extracted data to `tmp/dsserver-check.statementcounters`.
SLIGHTPULSE can deobfuscate base64 encoded and RC4 encrypted C2 messages.
title: Perez, D. et al. (2021, April 20). Check Your Pulse: Suspected APT Actors Leverage Authentication Bypass Techniques and Pulse Secure Zero-Day. Retrieved February 5, 2024.

text: One variant of BlackEnergy creates a new service using either a hard-coded or randomly generated name. BlackEnergy has gathered information about local network connections using netstat. BlackEnergy has gathered information about network IP configurations using ipconfig.exe and about routing tables using route.exe. BlackEnergy attempts to bypass default User Access Control (UAC) settings by exploiting a backward-compatibility setting found in Windows 7 and later. One variant of BlackEnergy locates existing driver services that have been disabled and drops its driver component into one of those service's paths, replacing the legitimate executable. The malware then sets the hijacked service to start automatically to establish persistence. BlackEnergy has used a plug-in to gather credentials from web browsers including FireFox, Google Chrome, and Internet Explorer. BlackEnergy communicates with its C2 server over HTTP. BlackEnergy injects its DLL component into svchost.exe. BlackEnergy has used a plug-in to gather credentials stored in files on the host by various software programs, including The Bat! email client, Outlook, and Windows Credential Store. BlackEnergy has gathered a process list by using Tasklist.exe. BlackEnergy gathers a list of installed apps from the uninstall program Registry. It also gathers registered mail, browser, and instant messaging clients from the Registry. BlackEnergy has searched for given file types. BlackEnergy has enabled the TESTSIGNING boot configuration option to facilitate loading of a driver component. The BlackEnergy 3 variant drops its main DLL component and then creates a .lnk shortcut to that file in the startup folder. BlackEnergy has removed the watermark associated with enabling the TESTSIGNING boot configuration option by removing the relevant strings in the user32.dll.mui of the system. BlackEnergy has used Systeminfo to gather the OS version, as well as information on the system configuration, BIOS, the motherboard, and the processor.
title: F-Secure Labs. (2014). BlackEnergy & Quedagh: The convergence of crimeware and APT attacks. Retrieved March 24, 2016.

text:
TrickBot collects the users of the system.
TrickBot obtains the IP address, location, and other relevant network information from the victim’s machine.
TrickBot establishes persistence by creating an autostart service that allows it to run whenever the machine boots.
TrickBot can disable Windows Defender.
TrickBot searches the system for all of the following file extensions: .avi, .mov, .mkv, .mpeg, .mpeg4, .mp4, .mp3, .wav, .ogg, .jpeg, .jpg, .png, .bmp, .gif, .tiff, .ico, .xlsx, and .zip. It can also obtain browsing history, cookies, and plug-in information.
TrickBot uses web injects and browser redirection to trick the user into providing their login credentials on a fake or modified web page.
TrickBot can modify registry entries.
TrickBot can obtain passwords stored in files from web browsers such as Chrome, Firefox, Internet Explorer, and Microsoft Edge, sometimes using esentutl.
TrickBot collects email addresses from Outlook.
title: Anthony, N., Pascual, C.. (2018, November 1). Trickbot Shows Off New Trick: Password Grabber Module. Retrieved November 16, 2018.

text:
Backdoor.Oldrea can download additional modules from C2.
Backdoor.Oldrea can use rundll32 for execution on compromised hosts.
Backdoor.Oldrea can enumerate and map ICS-specific systems in victim environments.
Backdoor.Oldrea can use a network scanning module to identify ICS-related ports.
title: Slowik, J. (2021, October). THE BAFFLING BERSERK BEAR: A DECADE’S ACTIVITY TARGETING CRITICAL INFRASTRUCTURE. Retrieved December 6, 2021.

text:
HIUPAN has lured victims into executing malicious files from USBs including the use of files such as USBconfig.exe.
PUBLOAD has collected the machine’s tick count through the use of `GetTickCount`.
CLAIMLOADER has imitated legitimate software directories through the creation and storage of the EXE and DLL in `C:\ProgramData\` and the use of legitimate looking names of software.
TONESHELL has encoded a payload with a random 32-byte key using XOR. TONESHELL has also encoded payloads with a 256-byte key using XOR.
TONESHELL has generated unique GUIDs to identify victim devices. TONESHELL has leveraged environmental keying in payload delivery using the victim computer name and other configuration values. TONESHELL has also tracked IDs associated with reverse shell subprocesses to manage interactions and terminations from C2.
HIUPAN has added Registry Run keys to achieve persistence using `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run`.
CLAIMLOADER has leveraged Component Object Model (COM) objects to create a scheduled task using `ITaskService` interface.
HIUPAN has periodically checked for removable and hot-plugged drives connected to the infected machine, should one be found HIUPAN will propagate to the removeable drives by copying itself and accompanying malware components to a directory to the new drive in a hidden subdirectory `<Drive_Letter>:\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\` and hides any other existing files to ensure UsbConfig.exe is the only visible file on the device.
CLAIMLOADER has used tailored decoy documents as part of the installation routine to entice users to open attachments.
HIUPAN has used a config file “$.ini” to store a sleep multiplier to execute at a set interval value prior to initiating a watcher function that checks for a specific running process, that checks for removable drives and installs itself and supporting files if one is available.
HIUPAN has abused legitimate executables to side-load malicious DLLs to include the legitimate exe UsbConfig.exe.
HIUPAN has modified registry keys to ensure hidden files and extensions are not visible through the modification of `HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\Advanced`.
HIUPAN has checked periodically for removable drives and installs itself when a drive is detected.
PUBLOAD has utilized environmental keying in the payload to include the victim volume serial number, computer name, username, and machine’s tick count.
TONESHELL has created a mutex to avoid duplicate execution.
TONESHELL used FakeTLS headers in network packets to impersonate various versions of TLS protocols to blend in with legitimate network traffic. TONESHELL variants have utilized FakeTLS headers with the bytes `0x17 0x03 0x03` to represent TLSv1.2 and `0x17 0x03 0x04` for TLSv1.3.
TONESHELL has created a reverse shell using `cmd.exe`.
CLAIMLOADER has modified file attributes to remain hidden to a standard user.
TONESHELL has the ability to retrieve the name of the infected machine.
CLAIMLOADER has created scheduled tasks that execute the loader every five(5) minutes using `schtasks /F /Create /TN \"<fake_software_name>\" /SC minute /MO 5 /TR \"C:\\ProgramData\\<path_to_exe> <hardcoded_argument>\`.
title: Golo Muhr, Joshua Chung. (2025, May 15). Hive0154 targeting US, Philippines, Pakistan and Taiwan in suspected espionage campaign. Retrieved August 4, 2025.

text: LookBack can kill processes and delete services. LookBack has a C2 proxy tool that masquerades as GUP.exe, which is software used by Notepad++. LookBack uses a custom binary protocol over sockets for C2 communications. LookBack uses a modified version of RC4 for data transfer. LookBack can list running processes. LookBack has used VBA macros in Microsoft Word attachments to drop additional files to the host. LookBack can take desktop screenshots. LookBack can shutdown and reboot the victim machine. LookBack sets up a Registry Run key to establish a persistence mechanism. LookBack can retrieve file listings from the victim machine. LookBack side loads its communications module as a DLL into the libcurl.dll loader. LookBack executes the cmd.exe command. LookBack can enumerate services on the victim machine. LookBack’s C2 proxy tool sends data to a C2 server over HTTP. LookBack has a function that decrypts malicious data. LookBack removes itself after execution and can delete files on the system.
title: Raggi, M. Schwarz, D.. (2019, August 1). LookBack Malware Targets the United States Utilities Sector with Phishing Attacks Impersonating Engineering Licensing Boards. Retrieved February 25, 2021.

text:
Avaddon has been executed through a malicious JScript downloader.
Avaddon can collect the external IP address of the victim.
title: Gahlot, A. (n.d.). Threat Hunting for Avaddon Ransomware. Retrieved August 19, 2021.

text:
Line Runner is a persistent Lua-based web shell.
Line Dancer shellcode payloads are base64 encoded when transmitted to compromised devices.
title: Canadian Centre for Cyber Security. (2024, April 24). Cyber Activity Impacting CISCO ASA VPNs. Retrieved January 6, 2025.

text: DLL side-loading has been used to execute BBSRAT through a legitimate Citrix executable, ssonsvr.exe. The Citrix executable was dropped along with BBSRAT by the dropper. BBSRAT can query service configuration information. BBSRAT can start, stop, or delete services. BBSRAT can list running processes. BBSRAT uses Expand to decompress a CAB file into executable content. BBSRAT has been seen persisting via COM hijacking through replacement of the COM object for MruPidlList {42aedc87-2188-41fd-b9a3-0c966feabec1} or Microsoft WBEM New Event Subsystem {F3130CDB-AA52-4C3A-AB32-85FFC23AF9C1} depending on the system's CPU architecture. BBSRAT can delete files and directories. BBSRAT uses GET and POST requests over HTTP or HTTPS for command and control to obtain commands and send ZLIB compressed data back to the C2 server. BBSRAT can compress data with ZLIB prior to sending it back to the C2 server. BBSRAT uses a custom encryption algorithm on data sent back to the C2 server over HTTP. BBSRAT can modify service configurations. BBSRAT can list file and directory information. BBSRAT has been seen loaded into msiexec.exe through process hollowing to hide its execution.
title: Lee, B. Grunzweig, J. (2015, December 22). BBSRAT Attacks Targeting Russian Organizations Linked to Roaming Tiger. Retrieved August 19, 2016.

text:
SPAWNCHIMERA has searched the contents of two Python files scanner.py and scanner_legacy.py by searching for specific lines and replacing them with values that reduce their ability to track mismatches or new files.
SPAWNCHIMERA has created web shells that facilitate actions on the victim host.
SPAWNCHIMERA has updated the timestamp using the `touch` command.
SPAWNCHIMERA has modified the Ivanti Integrity Checker Tool to evade detection.
SPAWNCHIMERA has modified the boot process files within `/tmp/coreboot_fs/bin/init` to establish persistence.
SPAWNCHIMERA has deleted generated files and folders from victim devices.
SPAWNCHIMERA has used delayed execution to pause for a defined interval before performing environment discovery, repeatedly checking for specific processes, such as the `dslogserver` process, prior to continuing execution.
title: DHS/CISA. (2026, February 26). MAR-25993211-r1.v2 Ivanti Connect Secure (RESURGE): AR25-087A. Retrieved April 17, 2026.

text:
Emotet has been observed leveraging a module that retrieves passwords stored on a system for the current logged-on user.
Emotet has been observed leveraging a module that scrapes email data from Outlook.
title: CIS. (2018, December 12). MS-ISAC Security Primer- Emotet. Retrieved March 25, 2019.

text:
BACKUPOSINT v9.0 APEX PREDATOR has enumerated the ports on victim systems within the victim environment.
BACKUPOSINT v9.0 APEX PREDATOR has gathered credentials stored in configuration files.
BACKUPOSINT v9.0 APEX PREDATOR has created a skills file titled `AI LATERAL_SUGGESTIONS.md` that included tables mapped with harvested credentials with potential victim internal servers.
BACKUPOSINT v9.0 APEX PREDATOR has leveraged OpenAI’s GPT-4.1 API to analyze extracted data.
BACKUPOSINT v9.0 APEX PREDATOR has discovered system configurations on victim devices.
BACKUPOSINT v9.0 APEX PREDATOR has connected to compromised servers within the victim environment via SOCKS proxies.
BACKUPOSINT v9.0 APEX PREDATOR has the ability to enumerate the processes running within the victim environment.
BACKUPOSINT v9.0 APEX PREDATOR has performed remote system discovery mapping harvested credentials to systems within the target environment.
BACKUPOSINT v9.0 APEX PREDATOR has extracted system data to include histories.
BACKUPOSINT v9.0 APEX PREDATOR has exfiltrated data using OpenAI’s GPT-4.1 API.
title: Eyal Sela. (2026, April). The AI-Assisted Breach of Mexico's Government Infrastructure. Retrieved September 2, 2026.

text: RobbinHood deletes shadow copies to ensure that all the data cannot be restored easily. RobbinHood disconnects all network shares from the computer with the command net use * /DELETE /Y. RobbinHood will search for Windows services that are associated with antivirus software on the system and kill the process. RobbinHood uses cmd.exe on the victim's computer. RobbinHood will search for an RSA encryption key and then perform its encryption process on the system files. RobbinHood stops 181 Windows services on the system before beginning the encryption process.
title: Lee, S. (2019, May 17). CB TAU Threat Intelligence Notification: RobbinHood Ransomware Stops 181 Windows Services Before Encryption. Retrieved July 29, 2019.

text: GoldenSpy can execute remote commands via the command-line interface. GoldenSpy has established persistence by running in the background as an autostart service. GoldenSpy can execute remote commands in the Windows command shell using the WinExec() API. GoldenSpy has used HTTP over ports 9005 and 9006 for network traffic, 9002 for C2 requests, 33666 as a WebSocket, and 8090 to download files. GoldenSpy has been packaged with a legitimate tax preparation software. GoldenSpy has exfiltrated host environment information to an external C2 domain via port 9006. GoldenSpy's installer has delayed installation of GoldenSpy for two hours after it reaches a victim system. GoldenSpy has used the Ryeol HTTP Client to facilitate HTTP internet communication. GoldenSpy can create new users on an infected system. GoldenSpy has gathered operating system information. GoldenSpy's setup file installs initial executables under the folder %WinDir%\System32\PluginManager. GoldenSpy constantly attempts to download and execute files from the remote C2, including GoldenSpy itself if not found on the system. GoldenSpy has included a program "ExeProtector", which monitors for the existence of GoldenSpy on the infected system and redownloads if necessary.
title: Trustwave SpiderLabs. (2020, June 25). The Golden Tax Department and Emergence of GoldenSpy Malware. Retrieved July 23, 2020.

text:
BADHATCH can inject itself into a new `svchost.exe -k netsvcs` process using the asynchronous procedure call (APC) queue.
BADHATCH can utilize `powershell.exe` to execute commands on a compromised host.
BADHATCH can inject itself into an existing explorer.exe process by using `RtlCreateUserThread`.
BADHATCH can utilize Native API functions such as, `ToolHelp32` and `Rt1AdjustPrivilege` to enable `SeDebugPrivilege` on a compromised machine.
BADHATCH has the ability to load a second stage malicious DLL file onto a compromised machine.
BADHATCH has an embedded second stage DLL payload within the first stage of the malware.
BADHATCH has the ability to delete PowerShell scripts from a compromised machine.
BADHATCH has the ability to execute a malicious DLL by injecting into `explorer.exe` on a compromised machine.
BADHATCH can utilize WMI to collect system information, create new processes, and run malicious PowerShell scripts on a compromised machine.
BADHATCH can obtain current system information from a compromised machine such as the `SHELL PID`, `PSVERSION`, `HOSTNAME`, `LOGONSERVER`, `LASTBOOTUP`, OS type/version, bitness, and hostname.
BADHATCH can use HTTP and HTTPS over port 443 to communicate with actor-controlled C2 servers.
BADHATCH can beacon to a hardcoded C2 IP address using TLS encryption every 5 minutes.
BADHATCH can copy a large byte array of 64-bit shellcode into process memory and execute it with a call to `CreateThread`.
BADHATCH can use `cmd.exe` to execute commands on a compromised host.
BADHATCH can exfiltrate data over the C2 channel.
title: Savelesky, K., et al. (2019, July 23). ABADBABE 8BADFOOD: Discovering BADHATCH and a Detailed Look at FIN8's Tooling. Retrieved September 8, 2021.

text:
NanoCore creates a RunOnce key in the Registry to execute its VBS scripts each time the user logs on to the machine.
NanoCore uses VBS files.
title: Patel, K. (2018, March 02). The NanoCore RAT Has Resurfaced From the Sewers. Retrieved September 25, 2024.

text: Mosquito leverages the CreateProcess() and LoadLibrary() calls to execute files with the .dll and .exe extensions. Mosquito can launch PowerShell Scripts. Mosquito's installer uses WMI to search for antivirus display names. Mosquito’s installer is obfuscated with a custom crypter to obfuscate the installer. Mosquito executes cmd.exe and uses a pipe to read the results and send back the output to the C2 server. Mosquito can modify Registry keys under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\[dllname] to store configuration values. Mosquito also modifies Registry keys under HKCR\CLSID\...\InprocServer32 with a path to the launcher. Mosquito's installer searches the Registry and system to see if specific antivirus tools are installed on the system. Mosquito stores configuration values under the Registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\[dllname]. Mosquito uses a custom encryption algorithm, which consists of XOR and a stream that is similar to the Blum Blum Shub algorithm. Mosquito uses COM hijacking as a method of persistence. Mosquito deletes files using DeleteFileW API call. Mosquito's launcher uses rundll32.exe in a Registry Key value to start the main backdoor capability. Mosquito can upload and download files to the victim. Mosquito runs whoami on the victim’s machine. Mosquito uses the ipconfig command. Mosquito establishes persistence under the Registry key HKCU\Software\Run auto_update. Mosquito runs tasklist to obtain running processes.
title: ESET, et al. (2018, January). Diplomats in Eastern Europe bitten by a Turla mosquito. Retrieved July 3, 2018.

text:
HiddenFace can alter timestamps for directory content on targeted machines.
HiddenFace can store its configuration file in the Registry.
HiddenFace can inject code directly into legitimate applications.
HiddenFace can enumerate the hostname and username of the compromised system.
HiddenFace can download files from the C2 to victim systems.
HiddenFace has the ability to decrypt its payload prior to execution.
NOOPLDR can hide services used to aid execution.
NOOPLDR can use control flow flattening to help hide malicious code.
HiddenFace can use a custom TCP protocol over Port 443 for C2.
NOOPLDR can be executed via sideloading.
NOOPLDR can insert junk code to obfuscate malicious payloads.
NOOPLDR can be executed via MSBuild.
HiddenFace's passive mode listens on TCP 47000.
HiddenFace has used dynamic domain generation algorithms in C2.
HiddenFace has encrypted its payload with AES.
HiddenFace can upload files from the victim machine to C2 nodes.
title: Tomonaga, S. (2024, July 16). MirrorFace Attack against Japanese Organisations. Retrieved April 17, 2026.

text:
Egregor has used tools to gather information about users.
Egregor has used BITSadmin to download and execute malicious DLLs.
Egregor has used an encoded PowerShell command by a service created by Cobalt Strike for lateral movement.
Egregor can conduct Active Directory reconnaissance using tools such as Sharphound or AdFind.
Egregor has communicated with its C2 servers via HTTPS protocol.
Egregor has masqueraded the svchost.exe process to exfiltrate data.
Egregor has disabled Windows Defender to evade protections.
title: Bichet, J. (2020, November 12). Egregor – Prolock: Fraternal Twins ?. Retrieved January 6, 2021.

text: Maze has inserted large blocks of junk code, including some components to decrypt strings and other important information for later in the encryption process. Maze has used the “Wow64RevertWow64FsRedirection” function following attempts to delete the shadow volumes, in order to leave the system in the same state as it was prior to redirection. Maze has gathered all of the running system processes. Maze has used several Windows API functions throughout the encryption process including IsDebuggerPresent, TerminateProcess, Process32FirstW, among others. Maze has decrypted strings and other important information during the encryption process. Maze also calls certain functions dynamically to hinder analysis. Maze has used the "WNetOpenEnumW", "WNetEnumResourceW”, “WNetCloseEnum” and “WNetAddConnection2W” functions to enumerate the network resources on the infected machine. Maze has checked the language of the machine with function GetUserDefaultUILanguage and terminated execution if the language matches with an entry in the predefined list. Maze has forged POST strings with a random choice from a list of possibilities including "forum", "php", "view", etc. while making connection with the C2, hindering detection efforts. Maze has communicated to hard-coded IP addresses via HTTP. Maze has checked the language of the infected system using the "GetUSerDefaultUILanguage" function.
title: Mundo, A. (2020, March 26). Ransomware Maze. Retrieved May 18, 2020.

text: Royal ransomware uses `esxcli` to gather a list of running VMs and terminate them.
title: Morales, N. et al. (2023, February 20). Royal Ransomware Expands Attacks by Targeting Linux ESXi Servers. Retrieved March 30, 2023.

text:
MacMa installs a `com.apple.softwareupdate.plist` file in the `/LaunchAgents` folder with the `RunAtLoad` value set to `true`. Upon user login, MacMa is executed from `/var/root/.local/softwareupdate` with root privileges. Some variations also include the `LimitLoadToSessionType` key with the value `Aqua`, ensuring the MacMa only runs when there is a logged in GUI user.
MacMa can use Core Graphics Event Taps to intercept user keystrokes from any text input field and saves them to text files. Text input fields include Spotlight, Finder, Safari, Mail, Messages, and other apps that have text fields for passwords.
MacMa has used macOS API functions to perform tasks.
MacMa has downloaded additional files, including an exploit for used privilege escalation.
MacMa can execute supplied shell commands and uses bash scripts to perform additional actions.
MacMa has stored collected files locally before exfiltration.
MacMa has the ability to record audio.
MacMa has used Apple’s Core Graphic APIs, such as `CGWindowListCreateImageFromArray`, to capture the user's screen and open windows.
title: Wardle, P. (2021, November 11). OSX.CDDS (OSX.MacMa). Retrieved June 30, 2022.

text: InvisiMole has installed legitimate but vulnerable Total Video Player software and wdigest.dll library drivers on compromised hosts to exploit stack overflow and input validation vulnerabilities for code execution. InvisiMole has exploited CVE-2007-5633 vulnerability in the speedfan.sys driver to obtain kernel mode privileges. InvisiMole can register itself for execution and persistence via the Control Panel. InvisiMole can use a JavaScript file as part of its execution chain. InvisiMole has used scheduled tasks named MSST and \Microsoft\Windows\Autochk\Scheduled to establish persistence. InvisiMole has used TCP to download additional modules. InvisiMole can spread within a network via the BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) and EternalBlue (CVE-2017-0144) vulnerabilities in RDP and SMB respectively. InvisiMole can inject itself into another process to avoid detection including use of a technique called ListPlanting that customizes the sorting algorithm in a ListView structure. InvisiMole can use winapiexec tool for indirect execution of ShellExecuteW and CreateProcessA. InvisiMole has attempted to disguise itself by registering under a seemingly legitimate service name. InvisiMole has used rundll32.exe for execution. InvisiMole can replace legitimate software or documents in the compromised network with their trojanized versions, in an attempt to propagate itself within the network. InvisiMole can scan the network for open ports and vulnerable instances of RDP and SMB protocols. InvisiMole can check for the presence of network sniffers, AV, and BitDefender firewall. InvisiMole has used a custom implementation of DNS tunneling to embed C2 communications in DNS requests and replies. InvisiMole can use a .lnk shortcut for the Control Panel to establish persistence. InvisiMole can inject its code into a trusted process via the APC queue. InvisiMole can use the ITaskService, ITaskDefinition and ITaskSettings COM interfaces to schedule a task. InvisiMole has executed legitimate tools in hidden windows. InvisiMole can check for artifacts of VirtualBox, Virtual PC and VMware environment, and terminate itself if they are detected. InvisiMole can create hidden system directories. InvisiMole can use Data Protection API to encrypt its components on the victim’s computer, to evade detection, and to make sure the payload can only be decrypted and loaded on one specific compromised computer. InvisiMole has used ListPlanting to inject code into a trusted process. InvisiMole has undergone regular technical improvements in an attempt to evade detection. InvisiMole can inject its backdoor as a portable executable into a target process. InvisiMole can register a Windows service named CsPower as part of its execution chain, and a Windows service named clr_optimization_v2.0.51527_X86 to achieve persistence. InvisiMole can capture keystrokes on a compromised host. InvisiMole can use a modified base32 encoding to encode data within the subdomain of C2 requests. InvisiMole has used Windows services as a way to execute its malicious payload. InvisiMole can deliver trojanized versions of software and documents, relying on user execution. InvisiMole can collect jpeg files from connected MTP devices. InvisiMole can place a lnk file in the Startup Folder to achieve persistence.
title: Hromcova, Z. and Cherpanov, A. (2020, June). INVISIMOLE: THE HIDDEN PART OF THE STORY. Retrieved July 16, 2020.

text:
Agent Tesla can steal data from the victim’s clipboard.
Agent Tesla can access the victim’s webcam and record video.
Agent Tesla can capture screenshots of the victim’s desktop.
Agent Tesla can download additional files for execution on the victim’s machine.
Agent Tesla can log keystrokes on the victim’s machine.
Agent Tesla has routines for exfiltration over SMTP, FTP, and HTTP.
Agent Tesla can encrypt data with 3DES before sending it over to a C2 server.
title: Brumaghin, E., et al. (2018, October 15). Old dog, new tricks - Analysing new RTF-based campaign distributing Agent Tesla, Loki with PyREbox. Retrieved November 5, 2018.

text:
Hancitor has decoded Base64 encoded URLs to insert a recipient’s name into the filename of the Word document. Hancitor has also extracted executables from ZIP files.
Hancitor has the ability to download additional files from C2.
Hancitor has relied upon users clicking on a malicious link delivered through phishing.
Hancitor has used Base64 to encode malicious links.
Hancitor has been delivered via phishing emails which contained malicious links.
title: Tom Spring. (2017, January 11). Spammers Revive Hancitor Downloader Campaigns. Retrieved August 13, 2020.

text:
Mongall has been packed with Themida.
Heyoka Backdoor can gather process information.
Mongall can identify drives on compromised hosts.
Heyoka Backdoor can decrypt its payload prior to execution.
Mongall can retrieve the hostname via `gethostbyname`.
Heyoka Backdoor has been spread through malicious document lures.
Mongall has the ability to RC4 encrypt C2 communications.
Heyoka Backdoor can enumerate drives on a compromised host.
Heyoka Backdoor can check if it is running as a service on a compromised host.
Heyoka Backdoor has the ability to search the compromised host for files.
Mongall can use HTTP for C2 communication.
Heyoka Backdoor can use spoofed DNS requests to create a bidirectional tunnel between a compromised host and its C2 servers.
Mongall can download files to targeted systems.
Mongall can establish persistence with the auto start function including using the value `EverNoteTrayUService`.
Heyoka Backdoor can inject a DLL into rundll32.exe for execution.
Mongall can use `rundll32.exe` for execution.
Heyoka Backdoor can use DNS tunneling for C2 communications.
Heyoka Backdoor can use rundll32.exe to gain execution.
Mongall has the ability to decrypt its payload prior to execution.
Mongall can upload files and information from a compromised host to its C2 server.
Heyoka Backdoor has the ability to delete folders and files from a targeted system.
Mongall has the ability to upload files from victim's machines.
Heyoka Backdoor can encrypt its payload.
Mongall can use Base64 to encode information sent to its C2.
Mongall can identify removable media attached to compromised hosts.
Heyoka Backdoor can identify removable media attached to victim's machines.
Mongall can inject a DLL into `rundll32.exe` for execution.
Mongall has relied on a user opening a malicious document for execution.
Heyoka Backdoor has been named `srvdll.dll` to appear as a legitimate service.
Heyoka Backdoor can establish persistence with the auto start function including using the value `EverNoteTrayUService`.
title: Chen, Joey. (2022, June 9). Aoqin Dragon | Newly-Discovered Chinese-linked APT Has Been Quietly Spying On Organizations For 10 Years. Retrieved July 14, 2022.

text:
CosmicDuke steals user files from local hard drives with file extensions that match a predefined list.
CosmicDuke uses scheduled tasks typically named "Watchmon Service" for persistence.
CosmicDuke exfiltrates collected files automatically over FTP to remote servers.
CosmicDuke copies and exfiltrates the clipboard contents every 30 seconds.
CosmicDuke exfiltrates collected files over FTP or WebDAV. Exfiltration servers can be separately configured from C2 servers.
CosmicDuke uses Windows services typically named "javamtsup" for persistence.
CosmicDuke steals user files from network shared drives with file extensions and keywords that match a predefined list.
CosmicDuke takes periodic screenshots and exfiltrates them.
CosmicDuke steals user files from removable media with file extensions and keywords that match a predefined list.
CosmicDuke searches attached and mounted drives for file extensions and keywords that match a predefined list.
CosmicDuke searches for Microsoft Outlook data files with extensions .pst and .ost for collection and exfiltration.
CosmicDuke can use HTTP or HTTPS for command and control to hard-coded C2 servers.
CosmicDuke contains a custom version of the RC4 algorithm that includes a programming error.
title: F-Secure Labs. (2014, July). COSMICDUKE Cosmu with a twist of MiniDuke. Retrieved July 3, 2014.

text:
MESSAGETAP has XOR-encrypted and stored contents of SMS messages that matched its target list.
After checking for the existence of two files, keyword_parm.txt and parm.txt, MESSAGETAP XOR decodes and read the contents of the files.
MESSAGETAP stored targeted SMS messages that matched its target list in CSV files on the compromised system.
After loading the keyword and phone data files, MESSAGETAP begins monitoring all network connections to and from the victim server.
Once loaded into memory, MESSAGETAP deletes the keyword_parm.txt and parm.txt configuration files from disk.
MESSAGETAP checks two files, keyword_parm.txt and parm.txt, for instructions on how to target and save data parsed and extracted from SMS message data from the network traffic. If an SMS message contained either a phone number, IMSI number, or keyword that matched the predefined list, it is saved to a CSV file for later theft by the threat actor.
MESSAGETAP uses the libpcap library to listen to all traffic and parses network protocols starting with Ethernet and IP layers. It continues parsing protocol layers including SCTP, SCCP, and TCAP and finally extracts SMS message data and routing metadata.
MESSAGETAP checks for the existence of two configuration files (keyword_parm.txt and parm.txt) and attempts to read the files every 30 seconds.
title: Leong, R., Perez, D., Dean, T. (2019, October 31). MESSAGETAP: Who’s Reading Your Text Messages?. Retrieved May 11, 2020.

text:
RedLine Stealer has used both valid certificates and self-signed digital certificates to appear legitimate.
RedLine Stealer has collected data stored locally including chat logs and files associated with chat services such as Steam, Discord, and Telegram.
RedLine Stealer has used obfuscation tools such as DNGuard and Boxed App to pack their code.
title: Alexandre Cote Cyr. (2024, November 8). Life on a crooked RedLine: Analyzing the infamous infostealer’s backend. Retrieved September 17, 2025.

text:
Flame contains modules to infect USB sticks and spread laterally to other Windows systems the stick is plugged into using Autorun functionality.
Flame can take regular screenshots when certain applications are open that are sent to the command and control server.
title: Gostev, A. (2012, May 28). The Flame: Questions and Answers. Retrieved March 1, 2017.

text:
UPSTYLE restores timestamps to original values following modification.
UPSTYLE removes `bootstrap.min.css` after parsing command and control instructions, restoring the file to its original state.
UPSTYLE retrieves a non-existent webpage from the command and control server then parses commands from the resulting error logs to decode commands to the web shell.
UPSTYLE creates a `.pth` file beginning with the text `import` so that any time another process or script attempts to reference the modified item the malicious code will also run.
UPSTYLE attempts to retrieve a non-existent webpage from the command and control server resulting in hidden commands sent via resulting error messages.
UPSTYLE has masqueraded filenames using examples such as `update.py`.
UPSTYLE parses encoded commands from error logs after attempting to resolve a non-existing webpage from the command and control server.
UPSTYLE clears error logs after reading embedded commands for execution.
title: Volexity Threat Research. (2024, April 12). Zero-Day Exploitation of Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution Vulnerability in GlobalProtect (CVE-2024-3400). Retrieved November 20, 2024.

text: Trojan.Karagany can use netstat to collect a list of network connections. Trojan.Karagany can secure C2 communications with SSL and TLS. Trojan.Karagany can inject a suspended thread of its own process into a new process and initiate via the ResumeThread API. Trojan.Karagany can capture keystrokes on a compromised host. Trojan.Karagany can perform reconnaissance commands on a victim machine via a cmd.exe process. Trojan.Karagany can steal data and credentials from browsers. Trojan.Karagany has used plugins with a self-delete capability. Trojan.Karagany can detect commonly used and generic virtualization platforms based primarily on drivers and file paths. Trojan.Karagany can base64 encode and AES-128-CBC encrypt data prior to transmission. Trojan.Karagany can enumerate files and directories on a compromised host. Trojan.Karagany can communicate with C2 via HTTP POST requests. Trojan.Karagany can gather information on the network configuration of a compromised host. Trojan.Karagany can gather information about the user on a compromised host. Trojan.Karagany can monitor the titles of open windows to identify specific keywords. Trojan.Karagany can capture information regarding the victim's OS, security, and hardware configuration.
title: Secureworks. (2019, July 24). Updated Karagany Malware Targets Energy Sector. Retrieved August 12, 2020.

text:
If Shamoon cannot access shares using current privileges, it attempts access using hard coded, domain-specific credentials gathered earlier in the intrusion.
Shamoon decrypts ciphertext using an XOR cipher and a base64-encoded string.
Shamoon will reboot the infected system once the wiping functionality has been completed.
title: Falcone, R. (2018, December 13). Shamoon 3 Targets Oil and Gas Organization. Retrieved March 14, 2019.

text:
UPSTYLE stores primary content as base64-encoded objects.
UPSTYLE has the ability to read `/proc/self/cmdline` to see if it is running as a monitored process.
UPSTYLE encodes its main content prior to loading via Python as base64-encoded blobs.
UPSTYLE is a Python-based application.
title: Unit 42. (2024, April 12). Threat Brief: Operation MidnightEclipse, Post-Exploitation Activity Related to CVE-2024-3400 . Retrieved January 15, 2025.

text:
AppleSeed has automatically collected data from USB drives, keystrokes, and screen images before exfiltration.
AppleSeed has exfiltrated files using web services.
AppleSeed has compressed collected data before exfiltration.
AppleSeed has divided files if the size is 0x1000000 bytes or more.
title: KISA. (2021). Phishing Target Reconnaissance and Attack Resource Analysis Operation Muzabi. Retrieved March 8, 2024.

text: RGDoor encrypts files with XOR before sending them back to the C2 server. RGDoor uses HTTP for C2 communications. RGDoor decodes Base64 strings and decrypts strings using a custom XOR algorithm. RGDoor uploads and downloads files to and from the victim’s machine. RGDoor executes the whoami on the victim’s machine. RGDoor uses cmd.exe to execute commands on the victim’s machine.
title: Falcone, R. (2018, January 25). OilRig uses RGDoor IIS Backdoor on Targets in the Middle East. Retrieved July 6, 2018.

text:
Machete has used pyobfuscate, zlib compression, and base64 encoding for obfuscation. Machete has also used some visual obfuscation techniques by naming variables as combinations of letters to hinder analysis.
Machete has used TLS-encrypted FTP to exfiltrate data.
Machete stores files and logs in a folder on the local drive.
Machete can find, encrypt, and upload files from fixed and removable drives.
title: The Cylance Threat Research Team. (2017, March 22). El Machete's Malware Attacks Cut Through LATAM. Retrieved September 13, 2019.

text: Bisonal can check the system time set on the infected host.
title: Zykov, K. (2020, August 13). CactusPete APT group’s updated Bisonal backdoor. Retrieved May 5, 2021.

text:
A FinFisher variant uses a custom packer.
FinFisher probes the system to check for antimalware processes.
title: Kaspersky Lab's Global Research & Analysis Team. (2017, October 16). BlackOasis APT and new targeted attacks leveraging zero-day exploit. Retrieved February 15, 2018.

text:
CCBkdr can use a DGA for Fallback Channels if communications with the primary command and control server are lost.
CCBkdr was added to a legitimate, signed version 5.33 of the CCleaner software and distributed on CCleaner's distribution site.
title: Brumaghin, E. et al. (2017, September 18). CCleanup: A Vast Number of Machines at Risk. Retrieved March 9, 2018.

text:
AshTag can download malicious payloads from file sharing services.
AshTag can use HTTP to send and receive data from C2.
AshTag can use `volumeserialnumber` to enumerate volumes.
AshTag has been executed through victims downloading and opening malicious RAR archive files.
AshTag has enabled execution via DLL sideloading using a legitimate executable paired with a malicious DLL named wtsapi32.
The AshTag AshenOrchestrator component payload as been Base64 encoded and embedded with HTML content from the C2 server.
AshTag can check geolocation on targeted systems.
AshTag can set persistence using scheduled tasks.
The AshTag stager compoment can decode and decrypt Base64 and XOR-encrypted payloads.
The AshTag AshenOrchestrator component can enumerate files on victim hosts.
AshTag has exfiltrated reconnaissance data on targeted systems to C2 servers.
The AshTag loader and AshenOrchestrator components can collect reconnaissance data from victim machines.
AshTag has masqueraded as a legitimate VisualServer utility.
AshTag can use JSON files to deliver payloads and configuration files.
The AshTag AshenOrchestrator component has the ability to take screenshots.
AshTag can use a .NET program to execute WMI queries and send unique victim IDs to C2.
AshTag can use a set sleep time to delay C2 beaconing.
The AshTag stager component can retrieve and execute the main payload.
The AshTag AshenOrchestrator component has process management functionality.
title: Unit 42. (2025, December 11). Hamas-Affiliated Ashen Lepus Targets Middle Eastern Diplomatic Entities With New AshTag Malware Suite. Retrieved April 20, 2026.

text:
Royal can delete shadow copy backups with vssadmin.exe using the command `delete shadows /all /quiet`.
Royal has been spread through the use of phishing campaigns including "call back phishing" where victims are lured into calling a number provided through email.
title: CISA. (2023, March 2). #StopRansomware: Royal Ransomware. Retrieved March 31, 2023.

text: macOS.OSAMiner has used `curl` to download a Stripped Payloads from a public facing adversary-controlled webpage.
title: MITRE ATT&CK software S1048

text: RATANKBA uses HTTP/HTTPS for command and control communication. There is a variant of RATANKBA that uses a PowerShell script instead of the traditional PE form. RATANKBA uses cmd.exe to execute commands. RATANKBA uses WMI to perform process monitoring. RATANKBA gathers the victim’s IP address via the ipconfig -all command. RATANKBA gathers information about the OS architecture, OS name, and OS version/Service pack. RATANKBA lists the system’s processes. RATANKBA uploads and downloads information. RATANKBA performs a reflective DLL injection using a given pid.
title: Lei, C., et al. (2018, January 24). Lazarus Campaign Targeting Cryptocurrencies Reveals Remote Controller Tool, an Evolved RATANKBA, and More. Retrieved May 22, 2018.

text: KeyBoy uses VBS scripts for installing files and performing execution. KeyBoy issues the command reg add “HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon” to achieve persistence. KeyBoy uses Python scripts for installing files and performing execution. In one version of KeyBoy, string obfuscation routines were used to hide many of the critical values referenced in the malware.
title: Hulcoop, A., et al. (2016, November 17). It’s Parliamentary KeyBoy and the targeting of the Tibetan Community. Retrieved June 13, 2019.

text:
LockBit 3.0 has the ability to discover external storage devices.
LockBit 3.0 can use PowerShell to apply Group Policy changes.
LockBit 3.0 can use a compromised local account for lateral movement.
LockBit 3.0 can delete itself from disk.
LockBit 3.0 can delete log files on targeted systems.
LockBit 3.0 can change the Registry values for Group Policy refresh time, to disable SmartScreen, and to disable Windows Defender.
LockBit 3.0 can disable security tools to evade detection including Windows Defender.
LockBit 3.0 can encrypt targeted data using the AES-256, ChaCha20, or RSA-2048 algorithms.
LockBit 3.0 can enumerate local drive configuration.
LockBit 3.0 can identify network shares on compromised systems.
LockBit 3.0 can make execution dependent on specific parameters including a unique passphrase and the system language of the targeted host not being found on a set exclusion list.
LockBit 3.0 can create and check for a mutex containing a hash of the `MachineGUID` value at execution to prevent running more than one instance.
LockBit 3.0 can enumerate system hostname and domain.
LockBit 3.0 can enable options for propogation through Group Policy Objects.
LockBit 3.0 can bypass UAC to execute code with elevated privileges through an elevated Component Object Model (COM) interface.
LockBit 3.0 can encrypt C2 communications with AES.
LockBit 3.0 can terminate targeted processes and services related to security, backup, database management, and other applications that could stop or interfere with encryption.
LockBit 3.0 can Base64-encode C2 communication.
LockBit 3.0 can enable automatic logon through the `SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon` Registry key.
LockBit 3.0 can reboot the infected host into Safe Mode.
LockBit 3.0 can use SMB for lateral movement.
The LockBit 3.0 payload is decrypted at runtime.
LockBit 3.0 can exclude files associated with core system functions from encryption.
The LockBit 3.0 payload includes an encrypted main component.
LockBit 3.0 will not affect machines with language settings matching a defined exlusion list of mainly Eastern European languages.
LockBit 3.0 can delete volume shadow copies.
LockBit 3.0 can use HTTP to send victim host information to C2.
title: FBI et al. (2023, March 16). #StopRansomware: LockBit 3.0. Retrieved February 5, 2025.

text:
Bad Rabbit enumerates open SMB shares on internal victim networks.
Bad Rabbit has used Mimikatz to harvest credentials from the victim's machine.
Bad Rabbit has used various Windows API calls.
title: M.Léveille, M-E.. (2017, October 24). Bad Rabbit: Not‑Petya is back with improved ransomware. Retrieved January 28, 2021.

text:
PowGoop can use a modified Base64 encoding mechanism to send data to and from the C2 server.
PowGoop can send HTTP GET requests to malicious servers.
title: Cyber National Mission Force. (2022, January 12). Iranian intel cyber suite of malware uses open source tools. Retrieved September 30, 2022.

text:
JPIN can list running services.
Dipsind encrypts C2 data with AES256 in ECB mode.
A JPIN uses a encrypted and compressed payload that is disguised as a bitmap within the resource section of the installer.
Dipsind uses HTTP for C2.
JPIN's installer/uninstaller component deletes itself if it encounters a version of Windows earlier than Windows XP or identifies security-related processes running.
JPIN checks for the presence of certain security-related processes and deletes its installer/uninstaller component if it identifies any of them.
adbupd can use a WMI script to achieve persistence.
Dipsind can download remote files.
JPIN can enumerate drives and their types. It can also change file permissions using cacls.exe.
JPIN can inject content into lsass.exe to load a module.
JPIN can obtain system information such as OS version and disk space.
JPIN can obtain network information, including DNS, IP, and proxies.
JPIN contains a custom keylogger.
JPIN can obtain the victim user name.
adbupd can run a copy of cmd.exe.
A Dipsind variant registers as a Winlogon Event Notify DLL to establish persistence.
Dipsind can be configured to only run during normal working hours, which would make its communications harder to distinguish from normal traffic.
Dipsind can spawn remote shells.
JPIN can lower security settings by changing Registry keys.
JPIN can communicate over FTP.
JPIN can enumerate Registry keys.
JPIN can obtain the permissions of the victim user.
adbupd contains a copy of the OpenSSL library to encrypt C2 traffic.
JPIN can use the command-line utility cacls.exe to change file permissions.
A JPIN variant downloads the backdoor payload via the BITS service.
JPIN can list running processes.
Dipsind encodes C2 traffic with base64.
JPIN can send email over SMTP.
JPIN can download files and upgrade itself.
title: Windows Defender Advanced Threat Hunting Team. (2016, April 29). PLATINUM: Targeted attacks in South and Southeast Asia. Retrieved February 15, 2018.

text: SLOTHFULMEDIA has sent system information to a C2 server via HTTP and HTTPS POST requests. SLOTHFULMEDIA has collected disk information from a victim machine. SLOTHFULMEDIA can add, modify, and/or delete registry keys. It has changed the proxy configuration of a victim system by modifying the HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Internet Settings\ZoneMap registry. SLOTHFULMEDIA can enumerate open ports on a victim machine. SLOTHFULMEDIA has collected the username from a victim machine. SLOTHFULMEDIA has a keylogging capability. SLOTHFULMEDIA has the capability to start services. SLOTHFULMEDIA can enumerate files and directories. SLOTHFULMEDIA has enumerated processes by ID, name, or privileges. SLOTHFULMEDIA has taken a screenshot of a victim's desktop, named it "Filter3.jpg", and stored it in the local directory. SLOTHFULMEDIA has named a service it establishes on victim machines as "TaskFrame" to hide its malicious purpose. SLOTHFULMEDIA has the capability to stop processes and services. SLOTHFULMEDIA has downloaded files onto a victim machine. SLOTHFULMEDIA has deleted itself and the 'index.dat' file on a compromised machine to remove recent Internet history from the system. SLOTHFULMEDIA has the capability to enumerate services. SLOTHFULMEDIA has hashed a string containing system information prior to exfiltration via POST requests. SLOTHFULMEDIA has been created with a hidden attribute to insure it's not visible to the victim. SLOTHFULMEDIA has mimicked the names of known executables, such as mediaplayer.exe. SLOTHFULMEDIA has collected system name, OS version, adapter information, and memory usage from a victim machine. SLOTHFULMEDIA can inject into running processes on a compromised host.
