SLOTHFULMEDIA has uploaded files and information from victim machines. SLOTHFULMEDIA has used HTTP and HTTPS for C2 communications. SLOTHFULMEDIA can open a command line to execute commands. SLOTHFULMEDIA has created a service on victim machines named "TaskFrame" to establish persistence.
title: DHS/CISA, Cyber National Mission Force. (2020, October 1). Malware Analysis Report (MAR) MAR-10303705-1.v1 – Remote Access Trojan: SLOTHFULMEDIA. Retrieved October 2, 2020.

text: VPNFilter has the capability to wipe a portion of an infected device's firmware.
title: Tung, Liam. (2018, May 29). FBI to all router users: Reboot now to neuter Russia's VPNFilter malware. Retrieved March 7, 2024.

text: Ebury has obfuscated its strings with a simple XOR encryption with a static key. Ebury has used a DGA to generate a domain name for C2. Ebury has installed a self-signed RPM package mimicking the original system package on RPM based systems. Ebury has used DNS requests over UDP port 53 for C2. Ebury has encrypted C2 traffic using the client IP address, then encoded it as a hexadecimal string. Ebury can intercept private keys using a trojanized ssh-add function. Ebury has encoded C2 traffic in hexadecimal format. Ebury has intercepted unencrypted private keys as well as private key pass-phrases.
title: M.Léveillé, M.. (2014, February 21). An In-depth Analysis of Linux/Ebury. Retrieved April 19, 2019.

text:
Remsec is capable of listing contents of folders on the victim. Remsec also searches for custom network encryption software on victims.
Remsec is capable of using HTTP and HTTPS for C2.
Remsec is capable of using DNS for C2.
Remsec is capable of deleting files on the victim. It also securely removes itself after collecting and exfiltrating data.
Remsec contains a network loader to receive executable modules from remote attackers and run them on the local victim. It can also upload and download files over HTTP and HTTPS.
Remsec contains a keylogger component.
Remsec is capable of using ICMP, TCP, and UDP for C2.
Some data in Remsec is encrypted using RC5 in CBC mode, AES-CBC with a hardcoded key, RC4, or Salsa20. Some data is also base64-encoded.
Remsec is capable of using SMTP for C2.
title: Symantec Security Response. (2016, August 8). Backdoor.Remsec indicators of compromise. Retrieved August 17, 2016.

text:
SUPERNOVA had to receive an HTTP GET request containing a specific set of parameters in order to execute.
SUPERNOVA is a Web shell.
SUPERNOVA has masqueraded as a legitimate SolarWinds DLL.
title: Tennis, M. (2020, December 17). SUPERNOVA: A Novel .NET Webshell. Retrieved February 22, 2021.

text: KillDisk has a ransomware component that encrypts files with an AES key that is also RSA-1028 encrypted.
title: Catalin Cimpanu. (2016, December 29). KillDisk Disk-Wiping Malware Adds Ransomware Component. Retrieved January 12, 2021.

text:
ADVSTORESHELL connects to port 80 of a C2 server using Wininet API. Data is exchanged via HTTP POSTs.
C2 traffic from ADVSTORESHELL is encrypted, then encoded with Base64 encoding.
title: Kaspersky Lab's Global Research and Analysis Team. (2015, December 4). Sofacy APT hits high profile targets with updated toolset. Retrieved December 10, 2015.

text:
DownPaper collects the victim username and sends it to the C2 server.
DownPaper searches and reads the value of the Windows Update Registry Run key.
DownPaper uses the command line.
DownPaper uses PowerShell to add a Registry Run key in order to establish persistence.
DownPaper uses PowerShell for execution.
DownPaper collects the victim host name and serial number, and then sends the information to the C2 server.
DownPaper communicates to its C2 server over HTTP.
title: ClearSky Cyber Security. (2017, December). Charming Kitten. Retrieved December 27, 2017.

text:
Woody RAT can make `Ping` GET HTTP requests to its C2 server at regular intervals for network connectivity checks.
Woody RAT has used Base64 encoded strings and scripts.
Woody RAT has the ability to take a screenshot of the infected host desktop using Windows GDI+.
Woody RAT can use AES-CBC to encrypt data sent to its C2 server.
Woody RAT has relied on CVE-2022-30190 (Follina) for execution during delivery.
Woody RAT can identify administrator accounts on an infected machine.
Woody RAT has relied on users opening a malicious email attachment for execution.
Woody RAT can exfiltrate files from an infected machine to its C2 server.
Woody RAT can inject code into a targeted process by writing to the remote memory of an infected system and then create a remote thread.
Woody RAT can retrieve information about storage drives from an infected machine.
Woody RAT can execute PowerShell commands and scripts with the use of .NET DLL, `WoodyPowerSession`.
Woody RAT can deobfuscate Base64-encoded strings and scripts.
Woody RAT can communicate with its C2 server using HTTP requests.
Woody RAT can download files from its C2 server, including the .NET DLLs, `WoodySharpExecutor` and `WoodyPowerSession`.
Woody RAT can collect information from a compromised host.
Woody RAT can call `NtQuerySystemProcessInformation` with `SystemProcessInformation` to enumerate all running processes, including associated information such as PID, parent PID, image name, and owner.
Woody RAT has suppressed all error reporting by calling `SetErrorMode` with 0x8007 as a parameter.
Woody RAT can detect Avast Software, Doctor Web, Kaspersky, AVG, ESET, and Sophos antivirus programs.
Woody RAT can use RSA-4096 to encrypt data sent to its C2 server.
Woody RAT can retrieve network interface and proxy information.
Woody RAT can collect .NET, PowerShell, and Python information from an infected host.
Woody RAT has the ability to delete itself from disk by creating a suspended notepad process and writing shellcode to delete a file into the suspended process using `NtWriteVirtualMemory`.
Woody RAT can use multiple native APIs, including `WriteProcessMemory`, `CreateProcess`, and `CreateRemoteThread` for process injection.
Woody RAT can retrieve the following information from an infected machine: OS, architecture, computer name, OS build version, and environment variables.
Woody RAT can list all files and their associated attributes, including filename, type, owner, creation time, last access time, last write time, size, and permissions.
Woody RAT can search registry keys to identify antivirus programs on an compromised host.
Woody RAT can retrieve a list of user accounts and usernames from an infected machine.
Woody RAT has been delivered via malicious Word documents and archive files.
Woody RAT can create a suspended notepad process and write shellcode to delete a file into the suspended process using `NtWriteVirtualMemory`.
Woody RAT can execute commands using `cmd.exe`.
title: MalwareBytes Threat Intelligence Team. (2022, August 3). Woody RAT: A new feature-rich malware spotted in the wild. Retrieved December 6, 2022.

text:
IceApple can collect files, passwords, and other data from a compromised host.
The IceApple OWA credential logger can monitor for OWA authentication requests and log the credentials.
IceApple can use reflective code loading to load .NET assemblies into `MSExchangeOWAAppPool` on targeted Exchange servers.
The IceApple ifconfig module can iterate over all network interfaces on the host and retrieve the name, description, MAC address, DNS suffix, DNS servers, gateways, IPv4 addresses, and subnet masks.
The IceApple Active Directory Querier module can perform authenticated requests against an Active Directory server.
IceApple can harvest credentials from local and remote host registries.
IceApple can use a Base64-encoded AES key to decrypt tasking.
IceApple's Credential Dumper module can dump encrypted password hashes from SAM registry keys, including `HKLM\SAM\SAM\Domains\Account\F` and `HKLM\SAM\SAM\Domains\Account\Users\*\V`.
IceApple is an IIS post-exploitation framework, consisting of 18 modules that provide several functionalities.
The IceApple Result Retriever module can AES encrypt C2 responses.
IceApple can use Base64 and "junk" JavaScript code to obfuscate information.
The IceApple Directory Lister module can list information about files and directories including creation time, last write time, name, and size.
IceApple can encrypt and compress files using Gzip prior to exfiltration.
IceApple's Multi File Exfiltrator module can exfiltrate multiple files from a compromised host as an HTTP response over C2.
IceApple .NET assemblies have used `App_Web_` in their file names to appear legitimate.
The IceApple Server Variable Dumper module iterates over all server variables present for the current request and returns them to the adversary.
IceApple can delete files and directories from targeted systems.
IceApple can use HTTP GET to request and pull information from C2.
IceApple's Credential Dumper module can dump LSA secrets from registry keys, including: `HKLM\SECURITY\Policy\PolEKList\default`, `HKLM\SECURITY\Policy\Secrets\*\CurrVal`, and `HKLM\SECURITY\Policy\Secrets\*\OldVal`.
title: CrowdStrike. (2022, May). ICEAPPLE: A NOVEL INTERNET INFORMATION SERVICES (IIS) POST-EXPLOITATION FRAMEWORK. Retrieved June 27, 2022.

text:
SYNful Knock has the capability to add its own custom backdoor password when it modifies the operating system of the affected network device.
SYNful Knock can be sent instructions via special packets to change its functionality. Code for new functionality can be included in these messages.
title: Bill Hau, Tony Lee, Josh Homan. (2015, September 15). SYNful Knock - A Cisco router implant - Part I. Retrieved November 17, 2024.

text:
Janicab used a valid AppleDeveloperID to sign the code to get past security restrictions.
Janicab captured screenshots and sent them out to a C2 server.
Janicab used a cron job for persistence on Mac devices.
Janicab captured audio and sent it out to a C2 server.
title: Thomas. (2013, July 15). New signed malware called Janicab. Retrieved July 17, 2017.

text: UPPERCUT has been sideloaded through a legitimately signed application from the JustSystems Corporation.
title: Dominik Breitenbacher. (2025, March 18). Operation AkaiRyū: MirrorFace invites Europe to Expo 2025 and revives ANEL backdoor. Retrieved May 22, 2025.

text: Maze has attempted to delete the shadow volumes of infected machines, once before and once after the encryption process. Maze has disabled dynamic analysis and other security tools including IDA debugger, x32dbg, and OllyDbg. It has also disabled Windows Defender's Real-Time Monitoring feature and attempted to disable endpoint protection services. The Maze encryption process has used batch scripts with various commands. Maze has issued a shutdown command on a victim machine that, upon reboot, will run the ransomware within a VM. Maze has used WMI to attempt to delete the shadow volumes on a machine, and to connect a virtual machine to the network domain of the victim organization's network. Maze has created a file named "startup_vrun.bat" in the Startup folder of a virtual machine to establish persistence. Maze operators have used VirtualBox and a Windows 7 virtual machine to run the ransomware; the virtual machine's configuration file mapped the shared network drives of the target company, presumably so Maze can encrypt files on the shared drives as well as the local machine. Maze operators have created scheduled tasks masquerading as "Windows Update Security", "Windows Update Security Patches", and "Google Chrome Security Update" designed to launch the ransomware. Maze has stopped SQL services to ensure it can encrypt any database. Maze has delivered components for its ransomware attacks using MSI files, some of which have been executed from the command-line using msiexec. Maze has injected the malware DLL into a target process. Maze has created scheduled tasks using name variants such as "Windows Update Security", "Windows Update Security Patches", and "Google Chrome Security Update", to launch Maze at a specific time.
title: Brandt, A., Mackenzie, P.. (2020, September 17). Maze Attackers Adopt Ragnar Locker Virtual Machine Technique. Retrieved October 9, 2020.

text: Kazuar can sleep for a specific time and be set to communicate at specific intervals. If running in a Windows environment, Kazuar saves a DLL to disk that is injected into the explorer.exe process to execute the payload. Kazuar can also be configured to inject and execute within specific processes. Kazuar captures screenshots of the victim’s screen. Kazuar stages command output and collected data in files before exfiltration. Kazuar finds a specified directory, lists the files and metadata about those files. Kazuar obtains a list of running processes through WMI querying and the ps command. Kazuar can delete files. Kazuar gathers information on local drives. Kazuar uses cmd.exe to execute commands on the victim’s machine. Kazuar gathers information about local groups and members. Kazuar uses FTP and FTPS to communicate with the C2 server. Kazuar gathers information about network adapters. Kazuar can install itself as a new service. Kazuar obtains a list of running processes through WMI querying. Kazuar uses /bin/bash to execute commands on the victim’s machine. Kazuar adds a .lnk file to the Windows startup folder. Kazuar gathers information on users. Kazuar downloads additional plug-ins to load on the victim’s machine, including the ability to upgrade and replace its own binary. Kazuar adds a sub-key under several Registry run keys. Kazuar gathers information on local groups and members on the victim’s machine. Kazuar captures images from the webcam. Kazuar has used compromised WordPress blogs as C2 servers. Kazuar gathers information about opened windows. Kazuar is obfuscated using the open source ConfuserEx protector. Kazuar also obfuscates the name of created files/folders/mutexes and encrypts debug messages written to log files using the Rijndael cipher. Kazuar encodes communications to the C2 server in Base64. Kazuar gathers information on the system. Kazuar uses HTTP and HTTPS to communicate with the C2 server. Kazuar can also act as a webserver and listen for inbound HTTP requests through an exposed API. Kazuar uploads files from a specified directory to the C2 server. Kazuar can accept multiple URLs for C2 servers. Kazuar can overwrite files with random data before deleting them.
title: Levene, B, et al. (2017, May 03). Kazuar: Multiplatform Espionage Backdoor with API Access. Retrieved July 17, 2018.

text: Metamorfo has side-loaded its malicious DLL file. Metamorfo has used cmd.exe /c to execute files. Metamorfo has injected a malicious DLL into the Windows Media Player process (wmplayer.exe). Metamorfo uses JavaScript to get the system time. Metamorfo has embedded a "vmdetect.exe" executable to identify virtual machines at the beginning of execution. Metamorfo has encrypted payloads and strings. Metamorfo includes payloads written in JavaScript. Metamorfo has digitally signed executables using AVAST Software certificates. Metamorfo has searched the Program Files directories for specific folders and has searched for strings related to its mutexes. Metamorfo has configured persistence to the Registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, Spotify =% APPDATA%\Spotify\Spotify.exe and used .LNK files in the startup folder to achieve persistence. Metamorfo's C2 communication has been encrypted using OpenSSL. Metamorfo has performed process name checks and has monitored applications. Metamorfo has used HTTP for C2. Metamorfo has hidden its GUI using the ShowWindow() WINAPI call. Metamorfo has written process names to the Registry, disabled IE browser features, deleted Registry keys, and changed the ExtendedUIHoverTime key. Metamorfo has a function to kill processes associated with defenses and can prevent certain processes from launching. Metamorfo has used native WINAPI calls. Metamorfo has deleted itself from the system after execution. Metamorfo has downloaded a zip file for execution on the system. Metamorfo has disguised an MSI file as the Adobe Acrobat Reader Installer and has masqueraded payloads as OneDrive, WhatsApp, or Spotify, for example. Metamorfo has used MSI files to download additional files to execute. Upon execution, Metamorfo has unzipped itself after being downloaded to the system and has performed string decryption.
title: Erlich, C. (2020, April 3). The Avast Abuser: Metamorfo Banking Malware Hides By Abusing Avast Executable. Retrieved May 26, 2020.

text: ECCENTRICBANDWAGON has stored keystrokes and screenshots within the %temp%\GoogleChrome, %temp%\Downloads, and %temp%\TrendMicroUpdate directories. ECCENTRICBANDWAGON can delete log files generated from the malware stored at C:\windows\temp\tmp0207. ECCENTRICBANDWAGON can use cmd to execute commands on a victim’s machine. ECCENTRICBANDWAGON has encrypted strings with RC4. ECCENTRICBANDWAGON can capture screenshots and store them locally. ECCENTRICBANDWAGON can capture and store keystrokes.
title: Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. (2020, August 26). MAR-10301706-1.v1 - North Korean Remote Access Tool: ECCENTRICBANDWAGON. Retrieved March 18, 2021.

text:
Agent Tesla can list the current running processes on the system.
Agent Tesla has the capability to kill any running analysis processes and AV software.
title: Zhang, X. (2017, June 28). In-Depth Analysis of A New Variant of .NET Malware AgentTesla. Retrieved November 5, 2018.

text:
PUBLOAD has used RC4 encryption in C2 communications.
PUBLOAD has created scheduled tasks to maintain persistence with the command `schtasks.exe /F /Create /TN Microsoft_Licensing /sc minute /MO 1 /TR C:\\Users\\Public\\Libraries\...`
PUBLOAD has obtained the username from an infected host.
PUBLOAD has collected and sent system information including volume serial number, computer name, and system uptime to designated C2. PUBLOAD has also used several commands executed in sequence via `cmd` in a short interval to gather system information about the infected host including `systeminfo`. PUBLOAD has decrypted shellcode that collects the computer name.
PUBLOAD has decoded its payload prior to execution.
PUBLOAD has abused legitimate executables to side-load malicious DLLs.
PUBLOAD has added Registry Run keys to achieve persistence using `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run`.
PUBLOAD has obfuscated DLL names using the ror13AddHash32 algorithm.
PUBLOAD has embedded debug strings with messages to distract analysts. PUBLOAD has leveraged `OutputDebugStringW` and `OutputDebugStringA` functions.
title: Asheer Malhotra, Jungsoo An, Kendall Mc. (2022, May 5). Mustang Panda deploys a new wave of malware targeting Europe. Retrieved August 4, 2025.

text:
BOLDMOVE is capable of spawning a remote command shell.
BOLDMOVE uses web services for command and control communication.
BOLDMOVE performs system survey actions following initial execution.
BOLDMOVE can free all resources and terminate itself on victim machines.
BOLDMOVE can disable the Fortinet daemons `moglogd` and `syslogd` to evade detection and logging.
BOLDMOVE contains a watchdog-like feature that monitors a particular file for modification. If modification is detected, the legitimate file is backed up and replaced with a trojanized file to allow for persistence through likely system upgrades.
BOLDMOVE is capable of relaying traffic from command and control servers to follow-on systems.
BOLDMOVE can remove files on victim systems.
BOLDMOVE enumerates network interfaces on the infected host.
BOLDMOVE calls the signal function to ignore the signals SIGCHLD, SIGHIP, and SIGPIPE prior to starting primary logic.
BOLDMOVE can list information of all files in the system recursively from the root directory or from a specified directory.
BOLDMOVE is associated with exploitation of CVE-2022-49475 in FortiOS.
BOLDMOVE uses the WolfSSL library to implement SSL encryption for command and control communication.
BOLDMOVE verifies it is executing from a specific path during execution.
title: Scott Henderson, Cristiana Kittner, Sarah Hawley & Mark Lechtik, Google Cloud. (2023, January 19). Suspected Chinese Threat Actors Exploiting FortiOS Vulnerability (CVE-2022-42475). Retrieved December 31, 2024.

text: DCSrv has encrypted drives using the core encryption mechanism from DiskCryptor. DCSrv has masqueraded its service as a legitimate svchost.exe process. PyDCrypt has attempted to execute with PowerShell. PyDCrypt has used netsh to find RPC connections on remote machines. PyDCrypt has used `cmd.exe` for execution. PyDCrypt has decrypted and dropped the DCSrv payload to disk. PyDCrypt has dropped DCSrv under the `svchost.exe` name to disk. DCSrv has created new services for persistence by modifying the Registry. PyDCrypt has modified firewall rules to allow incoming SMB, NetBIOS, and RPC connections using `netsh.exe` on remote machines. PyDCrypt will remove all created artifacts such as dropped executables. DCSrv has a function to sleep for two hours before rebooting the system. PyDCrypt has been compiled and encrypted with PyInstaller, specifically using the --key flag during the build phase. PyDCrypt has probed victim machines with whoami and has collected the username from the machine. DCSrv has used various Windows API functions, including `DeviceIoControl`, as part of its encryption process. PyDCrypt, along with its functions, is written in Python. PyDCrypt has attempted to execute with WMIC. DCSrv's configuration is encrypted. DCSrv has created Registry keys for persistence. DCSrv can compare the current time on an infected host with a configuration value to determine when to start the encryption process.
title: Checkpoint Research. (2021, November 15). Uncovering MosesStaff techniques: Ideology over Money. Retrieved August 11, 2022.

text:
BlackCat has the ability modify access tokens.
BlackCat has the ability to stop VM services on compromised networks.
BlackCat can change the desktop wallpaper on compromised hosts.
BlackCat has the ability to wipe VM snapshots on compromised networks.
BlackCat has the ability to discover network shares on compromised networks.
title: Brandt, Andrew. (2022, July 14). BlackCat ransomware attacks not merely a byproduct of bad luck. Retrieved December 20, 2022.

text: QakBot can use a variety of commands, including esentutl.exe to steal sensitive data from Internet Explorer and Microsoft Edge, to acquire information that is subsequently exfiltrated. QakBot can modify the Registry to store its configuration information in a randomly named subkey under HKCU\Software\Microsoft. QakBot can store its configuration information in a randomly named subkey under HKCU\Software\Microsoft.
title: Rainey, K. (n.d.). Qbot. Retrieved September 27, 2021.

text: Penquin can report the IP of the compromised host to attacker controlled infrastructure. Penquin can report the file system type of a compromised host to C2. Penquin has mimicked the Cron binary to hide itself on compromised systems. Penquin has encrypted strings in the binary for obfuscation. Penquin can execute the command code do_download to retrieve remote files from C2. Penquin can add the executable flag to a downloaded file. Penquin can encrypt communications using the BlowFish algorithm and a symmetric key exchanged with Diffie Hellman. Penquin can remove strings from binaries. Penquin can delete downloaded executables after running them. Penquin can execute remote commands using bash scripts. Penquin can use Cron to create periodic and pre-scheduled background jobs. Penquin can report the disk space of a compromised host to C2. Penquin can execute the command code do_upload to send files to C2. Penquin installs a `TCP` and `UDP` filter on the `eth0` interface. Penquin can use the command code do_vslist to send file names, size, and status to C2.
title: Leonardo. (2020, May 29). MALWARE TECHNICAL INSIGHT TURLA “Penquin_x64”. Retrieved March 11, 2021.

text: DarkWatchman has used Base64 to encode PowerShell commands. DarkWatchman can use `cmd.exe` to execute commands. DarkWatchman can track key presses with a keylogger module. DarkWatchman has been observed deleting its original launcher after installation. DarkWatchman can execute PowerShell commands and has used PowerShell to execute a keylogger. DarkWatchman has collected the username from a victim machine. DarkWatchman can modify Registry values to store configuration strings, keylogger, and output of components. DarkWatchman reports window names along with keylogger information to provide application context. DarkWatchman can query the Registry to determine if it has already been installed on the system. DarkWatchman can retrieve browser history. DarkWatchman encodes data using hexadecimal representation before sending it to the C2 server. DarkWatchman can collect files from a compromised host. DarkWatchman has been delivered as compressed RAR payloads in ZIP files to victims. DarkWatchman can delete shadow volumes using vssadmin.exe. DarkWatchman has been delivered via spearphishing emails that contain a malicious zip file. DarkWatchman can collect time zone information and system `UPTIME`. DarkWatchman can use TLS to encrypt its C2 channel. DarkWatchman can store configuration strings, keylogger, and output of components in the Registry. DarkWatchman uses JavaScript to perform its core functionalities. DarkWatchman has used a DGA to generate a domain name for C2. DarkWatchman has created a scheduled task for persistence. DarkWatchman can identity the OS locale of a compromised host. DarkWatchman can stage local data in the Windows Registry. DarkWatchman can search for anti-virus products on the system. DarkWatchman can uninstall malicious components from the Registry, stop processes, and clear the browser history. DarkWatchman can list signed PnP drivers for smartcard readers. DarkWatchman has used the csc.exe tool to compile a C# executable. DarkWatchman can use WMI to execute commands. DarkWatchman has the ability to enumerate file and folder names. DarkWatchman can collect the OS version, system architecture, and computer name. DarkWatchman has used an icon mimicking a text file to mask a malicious executable. DarkWatchman can load DLLs. DarkWatchman has the ability to self-extract as a RAR archive. DarkWatchman uses HTTPS for command and control.
title: Smith, S., Stafford, M. (2021, December 14). DarkWatchman: A new evolution in fileless techniques. Retrieved January 10, 2022.

text:
BadPatch searches for files with specific file extensions.
BadPatch uses WMI to enumerate installed security products in the victim’s environment.
BadPatch uses SMTP for C2.
BadPatch collects the OS system, OS version, MAC address, and the computer name from the victim’s machine.
BadPatch uses HTTP for C2.
BadPatch stores collected data in log files before exfiltration.
BadPatch collects files from the local system that have the following extensions, then prepares them for exfiltration: .xls, .xlsx, .pdf, .mdb, .rar, .zip, .doc, .docx.
BadPatch attempts to detect if it is being run in a Virtual Machine (VM) using a WMI query for disk drive name, BIOS, and motherboard information.
BadPatch establishes a foothold by adding a link to the malware executable in the startup folder.
BadPatch has a keylogging capability.
BadPatch can download and execute or update malware.
BadPatch captures screenshots in .jpg format and then exfiltrates them.
title: Bar, T., Conant, S. (2017, October 20). BadPatch. Retrieved November 13, 2018.

text:
MoonWind can obtain the victim hostname, Windows version, RAM amount, and screen resolution.
MoonWind encrypts C2 traffic using RC4 with a static key.
MoonWind has a command to return a list of running processes.
MoonWind saves information from its keylogging routine as a .zip file in the present working directory.
MoonWind communicates over ports 80, 443, 53, and 8080 via raw sockets instead of the protocols usually associated with the ports.
MoonWind installs itself as a new service with automatic startup to establish persistence. The service checks every 60 seconds to determine if the malware is running; if not, it will spawn a new instance.
MoonWind can execute commands via an interactive command shell. MoonWind uses batch scripts for various purposes, including to restart and uninstall itself.
MoonWind completes network communication via raw sockets.
MoonWind has a command to return a directory listing for a specified directory.
MoonWind has a keylogger.
MoonWind obtains the number of removable drives from the victim.
MoonWind can obtain the number of drives on the victim machine.
MoonWind obtains the victim's current time.
MoonWind obtains the victim IP address.
MoonWind can delete itself or specified files.
MoonWind obtains the victim username.
title: Miller-Osborn, J. and Grunzweig, J.. (2017, March 30). Trochilus and New MoonWind RATs Used In Attack Against Thai Organizations. Retrieved March 30, 2017.

text: WhisperGate's downloader can reverse its third stage file bytes and reflectively load the file as a .NET assembly.
title: Insikt Group. (2020, January 28). WhisperGate Malware Corrupts Computers in Ukraine. Retrieved September 16, 2024.

text:
Vidar has used the `EnumSystemLocalesW` function to enumerate installed or supported locales on the victim machine. Vidar has also used a GET request to ip-api[.]com, resolving the victim's public IP address and country.
Vidar has masqueraded as a Microsoft Edge DLL. Vidar has masqueraded as MicrosoftUpdate.exe in the %TEMP% folder. Vidar has masqueraded as a Notepad++ installer named npp.Installer.x64.zip. Vidar has masqueraded as an executable named Setup.exe that mimics the legitimate Yahtzee application.
Vidar has packaged collected data into a zip file before exfiltration.
Vidar has gathered information about files on the victim machine. Specifically, Vidar has used `FindFirstFileExW` and `FindNextFileW`. Vidar has attempted to read hidden system directories, such as `$Recycle.Bin`, `$Windows.~BT`, and `$SysReset`, and the `C:\Windows\System32\config\SOFTWARE` directory using the `ReadFile` function. Vidar has also accessed internal streams, such as `$SDH`, and has read Jump Lists, which include recently opened files, programs and tasks.
Vidar has collected the victim's public IP address.
Vidar has exfiltrated sensitive data, such as credentials and cryptocurrency wallets, over the C2 server at 136.243.203[.]109. Vidar has exfiltrated collected data through its C2 channel.
Vidar has gathered credentials and data, including history, credit cards and auto-filled information, from decrypted browser files from Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Opera, Vivaldi, Waterfox and Palemoon.
Vidar has gathered hardware IDs (HWIDs) regarding the victim machine. Vidar has used `GetEnvironmentStringsW` and `GetModuleHandleExW` to gather information about the victim machine. Vidar has collected OS data from the victim machine.
Vidar has obfuscated and/or AES-encrypted its core code to avoid debugger and/or analysis tools. Vidar has used XOR to obfuscate the DLL name and the function name with key 0x05 to evade static string scanning. Vidar has Base64-encoded information relating to cryptocurrency wallet extensions.
Vidar has modified Windows Defender’s list of excluded file extensions, ensuring that .exe, .dll and .bat files are ignored during scans. Vidar has loaded amsi.dll, which resolves the `AmsiScanBuffer` variable to return `E_INVALIDARG`, which may disable Windows Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI).
Vidar has collected credentials and cryptocurrency wallets stored internally. Vidar has also decrypted local file stores, such as key4.db for Firefox, to find credentials.
title: Nannaka, B., Chhaparwal, P. (2026, July 7). Vidar Stealer Unmasked: Code Signing Abuse, Go Loaders and File Inflation. Retrieved July 8, 2026.

text: SUNBURST C2 data attempted to appear as benign XML related to .NET assemblies or as a faux JSON blob.
title: Symantec Threat Hunter Team. (2021, January 22). SolarWinds: How Sunburst Sends Data Back to the Attackers. Retrieved January 22, 2021.

text:
Shamoon accesses network share(s), enables share access to the target device, copies an executable payload to the target system, and uses a Scheduled Task/Job to execute the malware.
Shamoon scans the C-class subnet of the IPs on the victim's interfaces.
title: FireEye. (2016, November 30). FireEye Responds to Wave of Destructive Cyber Attacks in Gulf Region. Retrieved November 17, 2024.

text: OceanSalt can collect the computer name from the system. Seasalt has the capability to identify the drive type on a victim. OceanSalt can create a reverse shell on the infected endpoint using cmd.exe. OceanSalt has been executed via malicious macros. OceanSalt can collect the victim’s IP address. Seasalt creates a Registry entry to ensure infection after reboot under HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\currentVersion\Run. OceanSalt can delete files from the system. OceanSalt has been delivered via spearphishing emails with Microsoft Office attachments. OceanSalt can encode data with a NOT operation before sending the data to the control server. OceanSalt can collect the name and ID for every process running on the system. OceanSalt can extract drive information from the endpoint and search files on the system.
title: Sherstobitoff, R., Malhotra, A. (2018, October 18). ‘Operation Oceansalt’ Attacks South Korea, U.S., and Canada With Source Code From Chinese Hacker Group. Retrieved November 30, 2018.

text: OSX/Shlayer has used a resource fork to hide a compressed binary file of itself from the terminal, Finder, and potentially evade traditional scanners.
title: Erika Noerenberg. (2020, June 29). TAU Threat Analysis: Bundlore (macOS) mm-install-macos. Retrieved October 12, 2021.

text:
PUNCHBUGGY can load a DLL using the LoadLibrary API.
PUNCHTRACK aggregates collected data in a tmp file.
PUNCHBUGGY can load a DLL using Rundll32.
PUNCHBUGGY can establish using a AppCertDLLs Registry key.
title: Elovitz, S. & Ahl, I. (2016, August 18). Know Your Enemy:  New Financially-Motivated & Spear-Phishing Group. Retrieved February 26, 2018.

text: GoldMax can spawn a command shell, and execute native commands. GoldMax has used HTTPS and HTTP GET requests with custom HTTP cookies for C2. GoldMax has decoded and decrypted the configuration file when executed. GoldMax has been packed for obfuscation. GoldMax has written AES-encrypted and Base64-encoded configuration files to disk. GoldMax can check the current date-time value of the compromised system, comparing it to the hardcoded execution trigger and can send the current timestamp to the C2 server. GoldMax can exfiltrate files over the existing C2 channel. GoldMax can download and execute additional files. GoldMax will check if it is being run in a virtualized environment by comparing the collected MAC address to c8:27:cc:c2:37:5a.
title: Smith, L., Leathery, J., Read, B. (2021, March 4). New SUNSHUTTLE Second-Stage Backdoor Uncovered Targeting U.S.-Based Entity; Possible Connection to UNC2452. Retrieved March 12, 2021.

text: The Black Basta binary can use `chmod` to gain full permissions to targeted files.
title: Sharma, S. and Hegde, N. (2022, June 7). Black basta Ransomware Goes Cross-Platform, Now Targets ESXi Systems. Retrieved March 8, 2023.

text:
Prestige can use PowerShell for payload execution on targeted systems.
Prestige can traverse the file system to discover files to encrypt by identifying specific extensions defined in a hardcoded list.
Prestige has used the `Wow64DisableWow64FsRedirection()` and `Wow64RevertWow64FsRedirection()` functions to disable and restore file system redirection.
Prestige has the ability to register new registry keys for a new extension handler via `HKCR\.enc` and `HKCR\enc\shell\open\command`.
Prestige can delete the backup catalog from the target system using: `c:\Windows\System32\wbadmin.exe delete catalog -quiet` and can also delete volume shadow copies using: `\Windows\System32\vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet`.
Prestige has leveraged the CryptoPP C++ library to encrypt files on target systems using AES and appended filenames with `.enc`.
Prestige has attempted to stop the MSSQL Windows service to ensure successful encryption using `C:\Windows\System32\net.exe stop MSSQLSERVER`.
Prestige has been deployed using the Default Domain Group Policy Object from an Active Directory Domain Controller.
Prestige has been executed on a target system through a scheduled task created by Sandworm Team using Impacket.
title: MSTIC. (2022, October 14). New “Prestige” ransomware impacts organizations in Ukraine and Poland. Retrieved January 19, 2023.

text:
MiniFast has collected the username on targeted systems.
MiniFast has decoded Base64-encoded tasks from the C2.
MiniFast has the ability to upload files over C2 communications.
MiniFast has blended into network traffic by mimicking a Chrome browser using the following User-Agent string: `Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/146.0.0.0 Safari/537.36`.
MiniFast has encoded C2 instructions with Base64.
MiniFast has the ability to delete files and directories.
MiniFast has leveraged valid digital signatures from SSL[.]com to appear legitimate.
MiniFast has collected the victim's username, hostname and domain information.
MiniFast has listed files and folders within a specified directory.
MiniFast has enumerated logical drives on impacted devices.
MiniFast has the ability to terminate a process using its PID.
MiniFast has executed commands using `cmd.exe`.
MiniFast has collected data from local files and directories on the victim device.
MiniFast has created scheduled tasks using the name “WindowsSecurityUpdate.”
MiniFast has the ability to move data within the victim machine.
MiniFast has utilized HTTP POST, GET and PUT requests for communications with the C2.
MiniFast has been delivered within a malicious zip file.
MiniFast has the ability to archive files and directories using ZIP.
MiniFast has the ability to download additional files from C2.
MiniFast has the ability to check running processes and has returned process names and their PIDs. MiniFast has also checked its relative parent process.
MiniFast has the ability to execute a process with elevated privileges using `runas`.
title: Check Point. (2026, May 22). Fast and Furious – Nimbus Manticore Operations During the Iranian Conflict. Retrieved September 23, 2026.

text:
LockBit 3.0 can use code packing to hinder analysis.
LockBit 3.0 has the ability to directly call native Windows API items during execution.
title: INCIBE-CERT. (2024, March 14). LockBit: response and recovery actions. Retrieved February 5, 2025.

text:
The Gentlemen Ransomware has utilized the domain’s NETLOGON share to distribute the malicious payload to all domain-joined systems.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has leveraged Base64-encoded PowerShell scripts.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has gathered Active Directory domain details utilizing the PowerShell cmdlet `Get-ADDomain`.
The Gentlemen Ransomware has enabled Remote Desktop Protocol within victim environments.
title: Santos, J., et al. (2025, September 9). Unmasking The Gentlemen Ransomware: Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures Revealed . Retrieved September 18, 2026.

text: SeaDuke uses an event filter in WMI code to execute a previously dropped executable shortly after system startup.
title: Ballenthin, W., et al. (2015). Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) Offense, Defense, and Forensics. Retrieved March 30, 2016.

text:
HermeticWizard can use a list of hardcoded credentials in attempt to authenticate to SMB shares.
HermeticWizard has the ability to scan ports on a compromised network.
HermeticWizard has been named `exec_32.dll` to mimic a legitimate MS Outlook .dll.
HermeticWizard has used `regsvr32.exe /s /i` to execute malicious payloads.
HermeticWiper can overwrite the `C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs` file on a targeted system.
HermeticWizard can use a list of hardcoded credentials to to authenticate via NTLMSSP to the SMB shares on remote systems.
HermeticWizard can use `OpenRemoteServiceManager` to create a service.
HermeticWizard has the ability to use `wevtutil cl system` to clear event logs.
HermeticWizard can connect to remote shares using `WNetAddConnection2W`.
HermeticWiper can use `cmd.exe /Q/c move CSIDL_SYSTEM_DRIVE\temp\sys.tmp1 CSIDL_WINDOWS\policydefinitions\postgresql.exe 1> \\127.0.0.1\ADMIN$\_1636727589.6007507 2>&1` to deploy on an infected system.
HermeticWizard has been signed by valid certificates assigned to Hermetica Digital.
HermeticWizard can use WMI to create a new process on a remote machine via `C:\windows\system32\cmd.exe /c start C:\windows\system32\\regsvr32.exe /s /iC:\windows\<filename>.dll`.
HermeticWiper has used the name `postgressql.exe` to mask a malicious payload.
HermeticWiper has the ability to deploy through an infected system's default domain policy.
HermeticWiper can recursively wipe folders and files in `Windows`, `Program Files`, `Program Files(x86)`, `PerfLogs`, `Boot, System`, `Volume Information`, and `AppData` folders using `FSCTL_MOVE_FILE`. HermeticWiper can also overwrite symbolic links and big files in `My Documents` and on the Desktop with random bytes.
HermeticWizard can execute files on remote machines using DCOM.
HermeticWizard has the ability to create a new process using `rundll32`.
HermeticWizard can find machines on the local network by gathering known local IP addresses through `DNSGetCacheDataTable`, `GetIpNetTable`,`WNetOpenEnumW(RESOURCE_GLOBALNET, RESOURCETYPE_ANY)`,`NetServerEnum`,`GetTcpTable`, and `GetAdaptersAddresses.`
HermeticWizard can copy files to other machines on a compromised network.
HermeticWizard can use `cmd.exe` for execution on compromised hosts.
HermeticWizard has the ability to encrypt PE files with a reverse XOR loop.
title: ESET. (2022, March 1). IsaacWiper and HermeticWizard: New wiper and worm targetingUkraine. Retrieved April 10, 2022.

text: USBferry can execute various Windows commands. USBferry can detect the infected machine's network topology using ipconfig and arp. USBferry can use tasklist to gather information about the process running on the infected system. USBferry can use net view to gather information about remote systems. USBferry can use net user to gather information about local accounts. USBferry can use netstat and nbtstat to detect active network connections. USBferry can execute rundll32.exe in memory to avoid detection. USBferry can check for connected USB devices. USBferry can collect information from an air-gapped host machine. USBferry can copy its installer to attached USB storage devices. USBferry can detect the victim's file or folder list.
title: Chen, J.. (2020, May 12). Tropic Trooper’s Back: USBferry Attack Targets Air gapped Environments. Retrieved May 20, 2020.

text:
Netwalker's PowerShell script can decode and decrypt multiple layers of obfuscation, leading to the Netwalker DLL being loaded into memory.
Operators deploying Netwalker have used psexec and certutil to retrieve the Netwalker payload.
Operators deploying Netwalker have used batch scripts to retrieve the Netwalker payload.
Operators deploying Netwalker have used psexec to copy the Netwalker payload across accessible systems.
title: Szappanos, G., Brandt, A.. (2020, May 27). Netwalker ransomware tools give insight into threat actor. Retrieved May 27, 2020.

text: CHOPSTICK may modify Registry keys to store RC4 encrypted configuration information.
title: FireEye. (2015). APT28: A WINDOW INTO RUSSIA’S CYBER ESPIONAGE OPERATIONS?. Retrieved August 19, 2015.

text:
Bankshot creates processes using the Windows API calls: CreateProcessA() and CreateProcessAsUserA().
Bankshot collects files from the local system.
Bankshot can terminate a specific process by its process id.
Bankshot marks files to be deleted upon the next system reboot and uninstalls and removes itself from the system.
Bankshot identifies processes and collects the process ids.
Bankshot recursively generates a list of files within a directory and sends them back to the control server.
Bankshot exfiltrates data over its C2 channel.
Bankshot encodes commands from the control server using a range of characters and gzip.
Bankshot uses HTTP for command and control communication.
Bankshot leverages a known zero-day vulnerability in Adobe Flash to execute the implant into the victims’ machines.
Bankshot gathers domain and account names/information through process monitoring.
Bankshot uses the command-line interface to execute arbitrary commands.
Bankshot modifies the time of a file as specified by the control server.
Bankshot gathers system information, network addresses, and the operation system version.
Bankshot grabs a user token using WTSQueryUserToken and then creates a process by impersonating a logged-on user.
Bankshot gathers disk type and disk free space.
title: Sherstobitoff, R. (2018, March 08). Hidden Cobra Targets Turkish Financial Sector With New Bankshot Implant. Retrieved May 18, 2018.

text:
Embargo has modified the Windows Registry to start a custom service named irnagentd in Safe Mode.
Embargo has modified and deleted Registry keys to add services, and to disable Security Solutions such as Windows Defender.
Embargo has created persistence through the DLL variant of the MDeployer toolkit by creating a service called irnagentd that launches after the system is rebooted in Safe Mode.
Embargo has utilized a BAT script to disable security solutions.
Embargo has obtained persistence of the loader MDeployer by creating a scheduled task named “Perf_sys.”
Embargo has leveraged MS4Killer to deliver a vulnerable driver to the victim device, sometimes referred to as Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD). Embargo has utilized the vulnerable driver probmon.sys version 3.0.0.4 which had a revoked certificated from “ITM System Co.,LTD.”
Embargo has encrypted both MDeployer and MS4 Killer payloads with RC4.
Embargo has used a DLL variant of MDeployer to disable security solutions through Safe Mode.

Embargo has leveraged MDeployer to terminate the MS4Killer process, delete the decrypted payload files and a driver file dropped by MS4killer, and reboot the system.

Carbon can collect the IP address of the victims and other computers on the network using the commands: ipconfig -all nbtstat -n, and nbtstat -s. Carbon uses the net group command. Carbon uses the command net time \\127.0.0.1 to get information the system’s time.

Taidoor has the ability to modify the Registry on compromised hosts using RegDeleteValueA and RegCreateKeyExA. Taidoor can copy cmd.exe into the system temp folder. Taidoor can query the Registry on compromised hosts using RegQueryValueExA. Taidoor can use GetCurrentProcessId for process discovery. Taidoor can use DeleteFileA to remove files from infected hosts.

Wiarp creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can inject files into running processes.
Wiarp creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can create a service.
Wiarp creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can open a command line interface.
Wiarp creates a backdoor through which remote attackers can download files.

text: Emissary is capable of configuring itself as a service. Emissary has the capability to execute ver and systeminfo commands. Variants of Emissary have used rundll32.exe in Registry values added to establish persistence. Emissary has the capability to execute the command net localgroup administrators. Emissary has the capability to execute the command ipconfig /all. A variant of Emissary appends junk data to the end of its DLL file to create a large file that may exceed the maximum size that anti-virus programs can scan. Emissary has the capability to execute the command net start to interact with services. Emissary has the capability to execute gpresult. Variants of Emissary have added Run Registry keys to establish persistence.

text:
Squirrelwaffle has gathered victim computer information and configurations.
Squirrelwaffle has encrypted collected data using a XOR-based algorithm.
Squirrelwaffle has collected the victim’s external IP address.
Squirrelwaffle has relied on victims to click on a malicious link send via phishing campaigns.
Squirrelwaffle has encoded its communications to C2 servers using Base64.
Squirrelwaffle has used HTTP POST requests for C2 communications.
Squirrelwaffle can collect the user name from a compromised host.
Squirrelwaffle has exfiltrated victim data using HTTP POST requests to its C2 servers.
Squirrelwaffle has been distributed through phishing emails containing a malicious URL.
Squirrelwaffle has been executed using `regsvr32.exe`.

SHOTPUT uses netstat to list TCP connection status.
SHOTPUT has a command to obtain a process listing.
SHOTPUT has a command to retrieve information about connected users.
SHOTPUT is obscured using XOR encoding and appended to a valid GIF file.
SHOTPUT has a command to list all servers in the domain, as well as one to locate domain controllers on a domain.
SHOTPUT has a command to obtain a directory listing.

text: CookieMiner has checked for the presence of "Little Snitch", macOS network monitoring and application firewall software, stopping and exiting if it is found. CookieMiner has installed multiple new Launch Agents in order to maintain persistence for cryptocurrency mining software. CookieMiner has used base64 encoding to obfuscate scripts on the system. CookieMiner has used python scripts on the user’s system, as well as the Python variant of the Empire agent, EmPyre. CookieMiner has looked for files in the user's home directory with "wallet" in their name using find. CookieMiner can download additional scripts from a web server. CookieMiner has used the curl --upload-file command to exfiltrate data over HTTP. CookieMiner can steal Google Chrome and Apple Safari browser cookies from the victim’s machine. CookieMiner has retrieved iPhone text messages from iTunes phone backup files. CookieMiner has used a Unix shell script to run a series of commands targeting macOS. CookieMiner has used Google Chrome's decryption and extraction operations. CookieMiner can steal saved usernames and passwords in Chrome as well as credit card credentials. CookieMiner has loaded coinmining software onto systems to mine for Koto cryptocurrency.
title: Chen, y., et al. (2019, January 31). Mac Malware Steals Cryptocurrency Exchanges’ Cookies. Retrieved July 22, 2020.

text:
SDBbot has the ability to record video on a compromised host.
SDBbot has the ability to add a value to the Registry Run key to establish persistence if it detects it is running with regular user privilege.
SDBbot has the ability to decrypt and decompress its payload to enable code execution.
SDBbot has used a packed installer file.
title: Frydrych, M. (2020, April 14). TA505 Continues to Infect Networks With SDBbot RAT. Retrieved May 29, 2020.

text: Zebrocy uses the tasklist and wmic process get Capture, ExecutablePath commands to gather the processes running on the system. Cannon can gather the username from the system. Cannon can gather drive information from the victim's machine. Cannon can collect the current time zone information from the victim’s machine. Cannon can take a screenshot of the desktop. Cannon exfiltrates collected data over email via SMTP/S and POP3/S C2 channels. Cannon can obtain victim drive information as well as a list of folders in C:\Program Files. A variant of Zebrocy captures screenshots of the victim’s machine in JPEG and BMP format. Zebrocy enumerates information about connected storage devices. Cannon can obtain a list of processes running on the system. Cannon can gather system information from the victim’s machine such as the OS version, and machine name. Zebrocy decodes its secondary payload and writes it to the victim’s machine. Zebrocy also uses AES and XOR to decrypt strings and payloads. Cannon adds the Registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon to establish persistence. Cannon can download a payload for execution. Cannon uses SMTP/S and POP3/S for C2 communications by sending and receiving emails.
title: Falcone, R., Lee, B. (2018, November 20). Sofacy Continues Global Attacks and Wheels Out New ‘Cannon’ Trojan. Retrieved November 26, 2018.

text:
gh0st RAT can load DLLs into memory.
gh0st RAT can execute its service if the Service key exists. If the key does not exist, gh0st RAT will create and run the service.
gh0st RAT has added a Registry Run key to establish persistence.
gh0st RAT operators have used dynamic DNS to mask the true location of their C2 behind rapidly changing IP addresses.
gh0st RAT has the capability to to delete files.
gh0st RAT has altered the InstallTime subkey.
gh0st RAT has used the `InterlockedExchange`, `SeShutdownPrivilege`, and `ExitWindowsEx` Windows API functions.
gh0st RAT can download files to the victim’s machine.
gh0st RAT has gathered system architecture, processor, OS configuration, and installed hardware information.
gh0st RAT has encrypted TCP communications to evade detection.
gh0st RAT can create a new service to establish persistence.
gh0st RAT has decrypted and loaded the gh0st RAT DLL into memory, once the initial dropper executable is launched.
gh0st RAT has used Zlib to compress C2 communications data before encrypting it.
gh0st RAT can inject malicious code into process created by the “Command_Create&Inject” function.
gh0st RAT has used an encrypted protocol within TCP segments to communicate with the C2.
gh0st RAT has checked for the existence of a Service key to determine if it has already been installed on the system.
gh0st RAT is able to wipe event logs.
title: Quinn, J. (2019, March 25). The odd case of a Gh0stRAT variant. Retrieved July 15, 2020.

text: Babuk can use “WNetOpenEnumW” and “WNetEnumResourceW” to enumerate files in network resources for encryption. Babuk can enumerate all services running on a compromised host. Babuk has the ability to check running processes on a targeted system. Babuk has the ability to use the command line to control execution on compromised hosts. Babuk has the ability to enumerate files on a targeted system. Babuk can stop specific services related to backups. Babuk has the ability to delete shadow volumes using vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet. Babuk can enumerate disk volumes, get disk information, and query service status.
title: Mundo, A. et al. (2021, February). Technical Analysis of Babuk Ransomware. Retrieved August 11, 2021.

text:
LunarMail can capture screenshots from compromised hosts.
LunarWeb can capture information on group policy settings
LunarLoader can use reflective loading to decrypt and run malicious executables in a new thread.
LunarMail can parse IDAT chunks from .png files to look for zlib-compressed and AES encrypted C2 commands.
LunarWeb can create a ZIP archive with specified files and directories.
LunarWeb can retrieve output from arbitrary processes and shell commands via a pipe.
LunarWeb has the ability to retrieve directory listings.
LunarMail can create an arbitrary process with a specified command line and redirect its output to a staging directory.
LunarWeb can zlib-compress data prior to exfiltration.
LunarWeb can use WMI queries and shell commands such as systeminfo.exe to collect the operating system, BIOS version, and domain name of the targeted system.
LunarMail can decrypt strings to retrieve configuration settings.
LunarMail can search its staging directory for output files it has produced.
LunarWeb has run shell commands to obtain a list of installed security products.
LunarWeb can run a custom binary protocol under HTTPS for C2.
LunarWeb can enumerate system network connections.
LunarMail can capture environmental variables on compromised hosts.
LunarMail can communicates with C2 using email messages via the Outlook Messaging API (MAPI).
LunarWeb can collect user information from the targeted host.
LunarWeb can send AES encrypted C2 commands.
LunarMail has been installed through a malicious macro in a Microsoft Word document.
LunarWeb has used shell commands to list running processes.
LunarWeb has the ability to run shell commands via PowerShell.
LunarMail can create a directory in `%TEMP%\` to stage data prior to exfilration.
LunarWeb can self-delete from a compromised host if safety checks of C2 connectivity fail.
LunarMail has been installed using a VBA macro.
LunarMail can capture the recipients of sent email messages from compromised accounts.
LunarMail has used RC4 and AES to encrypt strings and its exfiltration configuration respectively.
LunarLoader can use the DNS domain name of a compromised host to create a decryption key to ensure a malicious payload can only execute against the intended targets.
LunarWeb can decrypt strings related to communication configuration using RC4 with a static key.
LunarWeb can use Base64 encoding to obfuscate C2 commands.
LunarWeb can split exfiltrated data that exceeds 1.33 MB in size into multiple random sized parts between 384 and 512 KB.
LunarWeb can discover local group memberships.
LunarLoader has the ability to use Microsoft Outlook add-ins to establish persistence.
LunarWeb can use `POST` to send victim identification to C2 and `GET` to retrieve commands.
LunarWeb has the ability to use a HTTP proxy server for C&C communications.
LunarMail can delete the previously used staging directory and files on subsequent rounds of exfiltration and replace it with a new one.
LunarLoader can verify the targeted host's DNS name which is then used in the creation of a decyrption key.
LunarMail can use email image attachments with embedded data for receiving C2 commands and data exfiltration.
LunarMail can ping a specific C2 URL with the ID of a victim machine in the subdomain.
LunarLoader can deobfuscate files containing the next stages in the infection chain.
LunarWeb can receive C2 commands hidden in the structure of .jpg and .gif images.
LunarWeb can send short C2 commands, up to 512 bytes, encrypted with RSA-4096.
LunarWeb can use WMI queries for discovery on the victim host.
LunarWeb can identify shared resources in compromised environments.
LunarWeb can run shell commands using a BAT file with a name matching `%TEMP%\<⁠random_9_alnum_chars>.batfile` or through cmd.exe with the `/c` and `/U` option for Unicode output.
LunarMail can set the `PR_DELETE_AFTER_SUBMIT` flag to delete messages sent for data exfiltration.
LunarWeb can pause for a number of hours before entering its C2 communication loop.
LunarWeb can use shell commands to discover network adapters and configuration.
LunarWeb can use one C2 URL for first contact and to upload information about the host computer and two additional C2 URLs for getting commands.
The LunarWeb install files have been encrypted with AES-256.
LunarMail has the ability to use Outlook add-ins for persistence.
LunarWeb can list installed software on compromised systems.

text:
PureCrypter can insert junk code to avoid detection.
PureCrypter code contains an ExclusionRegionNames option where it can compare the results of `kernel32!GetGeoInfo` with a list of regions.
PureCrypter has the ability to delay for a specified number of seconds before execution.
PureCrypter can set multiple Registry Run keys to establish persistence.
PureCrypter can use Telegram or Discord to send infection status messages.
PureCrypter can identify virtual machines by querying the WMI object Win32_ComputerSystem for manufacturer and model and check it against the regular expression Microsoft|VMWare|Virtual.
PureCrypter has used a .NET downloader named 63342221.BAT and has used .jpg, .png, and .log as false extensions for malicious files.
PureCrypter has used multiple file names to appear legitimate such as firefox\firefox.exe, Google\chrome.exe, and Taskmgr.exe.
PureCrypter has the ability to call `CheckRemoteDebuggerPresent`.
PureCrypter can inject its final stage into another process on the targeted system.
PureCrypter can send a TLS 1.2 encrypted infection message via Discord webhook.
PureCrypter can execute a PowerShell command to self-delete.
PureCrypter can use `kernel32!GetGeoInfo` to determine system location.
PureCrypter code contains a global mutex.
PureCrypter has executed `Set-MpPreference -ExclusionPath` to exclude files or folders from Windows Defender scans.

text:
CANONSTAGER uses the Thread Local Storage (TLS) array data structure to store function addresses resolved by its custom API hashing algorithm. The function addresses are later called throughout the binary from offsets into the TLS array.
STATICPLUGIN has utilized Windows COM Installer Object to download an MSI package containing files masqueraded as a BMP file.
STATICPLUGIN has masqueraded as a BMP file to hide its true MSI file extension.
CANONSTAGER has leveraged naming conventions of its malicious DLL to match legitimate services to include cnmpaui.dll which matches the legitimate executable cnmpaui.exe that is aligned with a Canon Ink Jet Printer Assistant Tool.
STATICPLUGIN has required user execution to load subsequent malicious payloads.
CANONSTAGER has created a new window with a height and width of zero to remain hidden on the screen.
STATICPLUGIN has been signed with a valid Certificate Authority(CA) to circumvent endpoint defenses.
CANONSTAGER has utilized custom API hashing to obfuscate the Windows APIs being used.
STATICPLUGIN has leveraged naming conventions that match legitimate services to include AdobePlugins.exe.
CANONSTAGER has abused legitimate executables to side-load malicious DLLs.
CANONSTAGER has leveraged Native API calls to execute code within the victim’s system including `GetCurrentDirectoryW`, `RegisterClassW` and `CreateWindowExW`. CANONSTAGER also created a new overlapped window that initiates callback functions to a windows procedure that processes Windows messages until a designated message type of 0x0018 WM_SHOWWINDOW is observed which then initiates the deployment of a subsequent malicious payload.
title: Patrick Whitsell. (2025, August 25). Deception in Depth: PRC-Nexus Espionage Campaign Hijacks Web Traffic to Target Diplomats. Retrieved September 9, 2025.

SYSCON has the ability to execute commands through cmd on a compromised host.
SYSCON has the ability to use Systeminfo to identify system information.
SYSCON has the ability to use FTP in C2 communications.
CARROTBAT has the ability to determine the operating system of the compromised host and whether Windows is being run with x86 or x64 architecture.
SYSCON has the ability to use Tasklist to list running processes.
CARROTBAT has the ability to execute command line arguments on a compromised host.

Flame can create backdoor accounts with login `HelpAssistant` on domain connected systems if appropriate rights are available.
Flame can record audio using any existing hardware recording devices.
Flame can create backdoor accounts with login “HelpAssistant” on domain connected systems if appropriate rights are available.
Flame can use MS10-061 to exploit a print spooler vulnerability in a remote system with a shared printer in order to move laterally.
Flame identifies security software such as antivirus through the Security module.

text:
RedLine Stealer has obfuscated scripts within text files used in execution.
RedLine Stealer has used Base64 to encode command and control traffic.
RedLine Stealer has achieved persistence via scheduled tasks.
RedLine Stealer has utilized HTTP for C2 communications. RedLine Stealer has also conducted C2 communications to hardcoded C2 servers over HTTPS. RedLine Stealer has leveraged SOAP protocol for C2 communications.
RedLine Stealer malware has leveraged Lua bytecode to perform malicious behavior.
RedLine Stealer can query the Windows Registry.
RedLine Stealer has executed windows cmd using `ErrorHandler.cmd` to create scheduled tasks.
RedLine Stealer has been installed via MSI Installer.
RedLine Stealer can capture screenshots on a compromised host.

text: Lokibot has utilized multiple techniques to bypass UAC. Lokibot has used process hollowing to inject itself into legitimate Windows process. Lokibot downloaded several staged items onto the victim's machine. Lokibot has decoded and decrypted its stages multiple times using hard-coded keys to deliver the final payload, and has decoded its server response hex string using XOR. Lokibot's second stage DLL has set a timer using “timeSetEvent” to schedule its next execution. Lokibot has used cmd /c commands embedded within batch scripts. Lokibot has used LoadLibrary(), GetProcAddress() and CreateRemoteThread() API functions to execute its shellcode. Lokibot embedded the commands schtasks /Run /TN \Microsoft\Windows\DiskCleanup\SilentCleanup /I inside a batch script. Lokibot has tricked recipients into enabling malicious macros by getting victims to click "enable content" in email attachments. Lokibot is delivered via a malicious XLS attachment contained within a spearhpishing email. Lokibot has reflectively loaded the decoded DLL into memory. Lokibot has used HTTP for C2 communications. Lokibot has used PowerShell commands embedded inside batch scripts. Lokibot can search for specific files on an infected host. Lokibot has modified the Registry as part of its UAC bypass process. Lokibot has used VBS scripts and XLS macros for execution. Lokibot will delete its dropped files after bypassing UAC. Lokibot has performed a time-based anti-debug check before downloading its third stage.
title: Muhammad, I., Unterbrink, H.. (2021, January 6). A Deep Dive into Lokibot Infection Chain. Retrieved August 31, 2021.

KEYPLUG can use a hardcoded one-byte XOR encoded configuration file.
DEADEYE can use `msiexec.exe` for execution of malicious DLL.
The KEYPLUG Windows variant has retrieved C2 addresses from encoded data in posts on tech community forums.
DEADEYE has used `schtasks /change` to modify scheduled tasks including `\Microsoft\Windows\PLA\Server Manager Performance Monitor`, `\Microsoft\Windows\Ras\ManagerMobility, \Microsoft\Windows\WDI\SrvSetupResults`, and `\Microsoft\Windows\WDI\USOShared`.
KEYPLUG has the ability to communicate over HTTP and WebSocket Protocol (WSS) for C2.
KEYPLUG can obtain the current tick count of an infected computer.
DEADEYE has encrypted its payload.
DEADEYE can discover the DNS domain name of a targeted system.
KEYPLUG can use TCP and KCP (KERN Communications Protocol) over UDP for C2 communication.
DEADEYE can ensure it executes only on intended systems by identifying the victim's volume serial number, hostname, and/or DNS domain.
DEADEYE can use `rundll32.exe` for execution of living off the land binaries (lolbin) such as `SHELL32.DLL`.
DEADEYE can enumerate a victim computer's volume serial number and host name.
DEADEYE can execute the `GetComputerNameA` and `GetComputerNameExA` WinAPI functions.
KEYPLUG has used Cloudflare CDN associated infrastructure to redirect C2 communications to malicious domains.
KEYPLUG can use TLS-encrypted WebSocket Protocol (WSS) for C2.
KEYPLUG can decode its configuration file to determine C2 protocols.
The DEADEYE.EMBED variant of DEADEYE can embed its payload in an alternate data stream of a local file.
DEADEYE has the ability to combine multiple sections of a binary which were broken up to evade detection into a single .dll prior to execution.
The DEADEYE.EMBED variant of DEADEYE has the ability to embed payloads inside of a compiled binary.
title: Rufus Brown, Van Ta, Douglas Bienstock, Geoff Ackerman, John Wolfram. (2022, March 8). Does This Look Infected? A Summary of APT41 Targeting U.S. State Governments. Retrieved July 8, 2022.

WannaCry contains a thread that will attempt to scan for new attached drives every few seconds. If one is identified, it will encrypt the files on the attached device.
WannaCry attempts to kill processes associated with Exchange, Microsoft SQL Server, and MySQL to make it possible to encrypt their data stores.

title: MITRE ATT&CK software S0244

text:
UBoatRAT can upload and download files to the victim’s machine.
UBoatRAT has used GitHub and a public blog service in Hong Kong for C2 communications.
UBoatRAT encrypts instructions in its C2 network payloads using a simple XOR cipher.
UBoatRAT can start a command shell.
UBoatRAT checks for virtualization software such as VMWare, VirtualBox, or QEmu on the compromised machine.
UBoatRAT has used HTTP for C2 communications.

UBoatRAT can list running processes on the system.

text:
JHUHUGIT has exploited CVE-2015-1701 and CVE-2015-2387 to escalate privileges.
JHUHUGIT has registered itself as a scheduled task to run each time the current user logs in.

jRAT can query and kill system processes.
