text:
ShrinkLocker disables protectors used to secure the BitLocker encryption key on victim systems.
ShrinkLocker is a VisualBasic script (VBS) object that calls multiple other operating system functions during execution.
ShrinkLocker calls Wevtutil to clear the Windows PowerShell and Microsoft-Windows-Powershell/Operational logs.
ShrinkLocker renames disk labels on victim hosts to the threat actor's email address to enable the victim to contact the threat actor for ransom negotiation.
ShrinkLocker modifies various registry keys associated with system logon and BitLocker functionality to effectively lock-out users following disk encryption.
ShrinkLocker will exfiltrate victim system information along with the encryption key via an HTTP POST.
ShrinkLocker captures the IP address of the victim system and sends this to the attacker following encryption.
ShrinkLocker uses the legitimate BitLocker application to encrypt victim files for ransom.
ShrinkLocker can delete itself depending on various checks performed during execution.
ShrinkLocker uses WMI queries to gather various information about the victim machine and operating system.
ShrinkLocker can restart the victim system if it encounters an error during execution, and will forcibly shutdown the system following encryption to lock out victim users.
ShrinkLocker uses a subdomain on the legitimate Cloudflare resource "trycloudflare[.]com" to obfuscate the threat actor's actual address and to tunnel information sent from victim systems.
ShrinkLocker uses HTTP POST requests to communicate victim information back to the threat actor.
ShrinkLocker turns on the system firewall and deletes all of its rules during execution.
ShrinkLocker uses WMI to query information about the victim operating system.
ShrinkLocker uses PowerShell to disable protectors used to secure the BitLocker encryption key on victim machines and then delete the key from the system.
title: Cristian Souza, Eduardo Ovalle, Ashley Muñoz, & Christopher Zachor. (2024, May 23). ShrinkLocker: Turning BitLocker into ransomware. Retrieved December 7, 2024.

text:
StoneDrill can wipe the master boot record of an infected computer.
StoneDrill can wipe the accessible physical or logical drives of the infected machine.
title: Security Response attack Investigation Team. (2019, March 27). Elfin: Relentless Espionage Group Targets Multiple Organizations in Saudi Arabia and U.S.. Retrieved April 10, 2019.

text: Gazer creates a mutex using the hard-coded value `{531511FA-190D-5D85-8A4A-279F2F592CC7}` to ensure that only one instance of itself is running. For early Gazer versions, the compilation timestamp was faked. Gazer communicates with its C2 servers over HTTP. Gazer can establish persistence through the system screensaver by configuring it to execute the malware. Gazer stores configuration items in alternate data streams (ADSs) if the Registry is not accessible. Gazer can establish persistence by setting the value “Shell” with “explorer.exe, %malware_pathfile%” under the Registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon.
title: ESET. (2017, August). Gazing at Gazer: Turla’s new second stage backdoor. Retrieved September 14, 2017.

text:
NativeZone has used rundll32 to execute a malicious DLL.
NativeZone has, upon execution, displayed a message box that appears to be related to a Ukrainian electronic document management system.
NativeZone can check for the presence of KM.EkeyAlmaz1C.dll and will halt execution unless it is in the same directory as the rest of the malware's components.
title: Guerrero-Saade, J. (2021, June 1). NobleBaron | New Poisoned Installers Could Be Used In Supply Chain Attacks. Retrieved August 4, 2021.

text:
ZxxZ can search a compromised host to determine if it is running Windows Defender or Kasperky antivirus.
ZxxZ has relied on victims to open a malicious attachment delivered via email.
ZxxZ has used scheduled tasks for persistence and execution.
ZxxZ has been encoded to avoid detection from static analysis tools.
ZxxZ can download and execute additional files.
ZxxZ has used a XOR key to decrypt strings.
ZxxZ can search the registry of a compromised host.
ZxxZ has been distributed via spearphishing emails, usually containing a malicious RTF or Excel attachment.
ZxxZ can collect the username from a compromised host.
ZxxZ has been disguised as a Windows security update service.
ZxxZ has created a snapshot of running processes using `CreateToolhelp32Snapshot`.
ZxxZ has collected the host name and operating system product name from a compromised machine.
ZxxZ can collect data from a compromised host.
ZxxZ has used API functions such as `Process32First`, `Process32Next`, and `ShellExecuteA`.
title: Raghuprasad, C . (2022, May 11). Bitter APT adds Bangladesh to their targets. Retrieved June 1, 2022.

text:
Line Runner used CVE-2024-20353 to trigger victim devices to reboot, in the process unzipping and installing the Line Dancer payload.
Line Dancer can gather system configuration information by running the native `show configuration` command.
Line Runner intercepts HTTP requests to the victim Cisco ASA, looking for a request with a 32-character, victim dependent parameter. If that parameter matches a value in the malware, a contained payload is then written to a Lua script and executed.
Line Dancer can execute native commands in networking device command line interfaces.
Line Dancer can hook both the crash dump process and the Autehntication, Authorization, and Accounting (AAA) functions on compromised machines to evade forensic analysis and authentication mechanisms.
Line Dancer exfiltrates collected data via command and control channels.
Line Runner utilizes HTTP to retrieve and exfiltrate information staged using Line Dancer.
Line Runner utilizes an HTTP-based Lua backdoor on victim machines.
Line Dancer can modify the crash dump process on infected machines to skip crash dump generation and proceed directly to device reboot for both persistence and forensic evasion purposes.
Line Dancer uses HTTP POST requests to interact with compromised devices.
Line Runner utilizes Lua scripts for command execution.
Line Dancer can create and exfiltrate packet captures from compromised environments.
Line Runner removes its initial ZIP delivery archive after processing the enclosed LUA script.
Line Dancer can disable syslog on compromised devices.
Line Runner uses a ZIP payload that is automatically extracted with its contents, a LUA script, executed for initial execution via CVE-2024-20359.
title: Cisco Talos. (2024, April 24). ArcaneDoor - New espionage-focused campaign found targeting perimeter network devices. Retrieved January 6, 2025.

text:
Smoke Loader uses a simple one-byte XOR method to obfuscate values in the malware.
Smoke Loader spawns a new copy of c:\windows\syswow64\explorer.exe and then replaces the executable code in memory with malware.
Smoke Loader downloads a new version of itself once it has installed. It also downloads additional plugins.
Smoke Loader adds a Registry Run key for persistence and adds a script in the Startup folder to deploy the payload.
Smoke Loader adds a Visual Basic script in the Startup folder to deploy the payload.
Smoke Loader uses HTTP for C2.
title: Hasherezade. (2016, September 12). Smoke Loader – downloader with a smokescreen still alive. Retrieved March 20, 2018.

text:
A PingPull variant can communicate with its C2 servers by using HTTPS.
PingPull can use `cmd.exe` to run various commands as a reverse shell.
PingPull can encode C2 traffic with Base64.
PingPull has the ability to timestomp a file.
PingPull has the ability to exfiltrate stolen victim data through its C2 channel.
PingPull can retrieve the IP address of a compromised host.
PingPull can use HTTPS over port 8080 for C2.
PingPull can retrieve the hostname of a compromised host.
PingPull can decrypt received data from its C2 server by using AES.
PingPull can enumerate storage volumes and folder contents of a compromised host.
PingPull variants have the ability to communicate with C2 servers using ICMP or TCP.
PingPull can mimic the names and descriptions of legitimate services such as `iphlpsvc`, `IP Helper`, and `Onedrive` to evade detection.
PingPull can collect data from a compromised host.
PingPull can use AES, in cipher block chaining (CBC) mode padded with PKCS5, to encrypt C2 server communications.
PingPull has the ability to install itself as a service.
title: Unit 42. (2022, June 13). GALLIUM Expands Targeting Across Telecommunications, Government and Finance Sectors With New PingPull Tool. Retrieved August 7, 2022.

text:
Sykipot uses SSL for encrypting C2 communications.
Sykipot has been known to establish persistence by adding programs to the Run Registry key.
title: Blasco, J. (2013, March 21). New Sykipot developments [Blog]. Retrieved November 12, 2014.

text:
Ursnif has gathered information about running processes.
Ursnif has used hooked APIs to take screenshots.
Ursnif has injected code into target processes via thread local storage callbacks.
Ursnif has used tmp files to stage gathered information.
Ursnif has used strings from legitimate system files and existing folders for its file, folder, and Registry entry names.
Ursnif has used HTTP POSTs to exfil gathered information.
Ursnif has used Reg to query the Registry for installed programs.
Ursnif has used Systeminfo to gather system information.
Ursnif has gathered information about running services.
Ursnif has hooked APIs to perform a wide variety of information theft, such as monitoring traffic from browsers.
Ursnif has deleted data staged in tmp files after exfiltration.
Ursnif has used HTTPS for C2.
title: Caragay, R. (2015, March 26). URSNIF: The Multifaceted Malware. Retrieved June 5, 2019.

text:
PowerExchange can exfiltrate files via its email C2 channel.
PowerExchange can use PowerShell to execute commands received from C2.
PowerExchange can receive and send back the results of executed C2 commands through email.
PowerExchange can decode Base64-encoded files and call `WriteAllBytes` to write the files to compromised hosts.
PowerExchange can decode and decrypt C2 commands received via email.
title: Symantec Threat Hunter Team. (2023, October 19). Crambus: New Campaign Targets Middle Eastern Government. Retrieved November 27, 2024.

text: Pikabot, following payload decryption, creates a process hard-coded into the dropped (e.g., WerFault.exe) and injects the decrypted core modules into it. Pikabot gathers victim network information through commands such as ipconfig and ipconfig /all. Pikabot loads a set of PNG images stored in the malware's resources section (RCDATA), each with an encrypted section containing portions of the core Pikabot core module. These sections are loaded and decrypted using a bitwise XOR operation with a hardcoded 32 bit key. Pikabot can execute Windows shell commands via cmd.exe. Pikabot maintains persistence following system checks through the Run key in the registry.
title: Brett Stone-Gross & Nikolaos Pantazopoulos. (2023, May 24). Technical Analysis of Pikabot. Retrieved July 12, 2024.

text: Pteranodon exfiltrates screenshot files to its C2 server. Pteranodon can delete files that may interfere with it executing. It also can delete temporary files and itself after the initial script executes. Pteranodon can capture screenshots at a configurable interval. Pteranodon copies itself to the Startup folder to establish persistence. Pteranodon can use `cmd.exe` for execution on victim systems. Pteranodon can download and execute additional files. Pteranodon identifies files matching certain file extension and copies them to subdirectories it created. Pteranodon executes functions using rundll32.exe. Pteranodon can use HTTP for C2. Pteranodon schedules tasks to invoke its components in order to establish persistence. Pteranodon creates various subdirectories under %Temp%\reports\% and copies files to those subdirectories. It also creates a folder at C:\Users\\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\store to store screenshot JPEG files.
title: Kasza, A. and Reichel, D. (2017, February 27). The Gamaredon Group Toolset Evolution. Retrieved March 1, 2017.

text:
Manjusaka data exfiltration takes place over HTTP channels.
Manjusaka can gather information about specific files on the victim system.
Manjusaka performs basic system profiling actions to fingerprint and register the victim system with the C2 controller.
Manjusaka extracts credentials from the Windows Registry associated with Premiumsoft Navicat, a utility used to facilitate access to various database types.
Manjusaka has used HTTP for command and control communication.
Manjusaka gathers credentials from Chromium-based browsers.
Manjusaka gathers information about current network connections, local and remote addresses associated with them, and associated processes.
Manjusaka communication includes a client-created session cookie with base64-encoded information representing information from the victim system.
Manjusaka can execute arbitrary commands passed to it from the C2 controller via `cmd.exe /c`.
Manjusaka can take screenshots of the victim desktop.
title: Asheer Malhotra & Vitor Ventura. (2022, August 2). Manjusaka: A Chinese sibling of Sliver and Cobalt Strike. Retrieved September 4, 2024.

text: BBSRAT has been loaded through DLL side-loading of a legitimate Citrix executable that is set to persist through the Registry Run key location HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\ssonsvr.exe.
title: MITRE ATT&CK software S0127

text:
Hikit can upload files from compromised machines.
Hikit performs XOR encryption.
Hikit has been spread through spear phishing.
Zox has the ability to list processes.
Zox can enumerate attached drives.
Zox has the ability to use SMB for communication.
Zox has used the .PNG file format for C2 communications.
Zox has the ability to upload files from a targeted system.
Hikit has the ability to download files to a compromised host.
Zox has been encoded with Base64.
Zox can download files to a compromised machine.
Zox can enumerate files on a compromised host.
Zox has the ability to leverage local and remote exploits to escalate privileges.
Hikit supports peer connections.
title: Novetta. (n.d.). Operation SMN: Axiom Threat Actor Group Report. Retrieved November 12, 2014.

text:
BOOKWORM has decoded its Base64 encoded payload prior to execution. BOOKWORM has also encrypted files with RC4 and has decrypted its payload prior to execution.
BOOKWORM has created a hidden window when conducting key logging and clipboard theft through its KBLogger.dll module.
BOOKWORM has created services that attempt to resemble legitimate services to include a service named `Microsoft Windows DeviceSync Service`.
BOOKWORM has obtained the username from an infected host.
BOOKWORM has modified Registry key values as part of its created service `DeviceSync`.
BOOKWORM has used its KBLogger.dll module to capture keystrokes and stored them in a folder.
BOOKWORM has communicated with its C2 via HTTP POST requests.
BOOKWORM has used encryption and compression algorithms to obfuscate the traffic between the system and C2 server, methods observed included RC4, AES, XOR with 0x5a, and LZO.
BOOKWORM has used valid legitimate digital signatures and certificates to evade detection.
BOOKWORM has created a service named `Microsoft Windows DeviceSync Service` at `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\DeviceSync\` to trigger execution when the system starts and to maintain persistence.
BOOKWORM has used DLL side-loading to execute the malicious payload. BOOKWORM has also side-loaded DLL components into a legitimate process, including Microsoft Malware Protection `MsMpEng.exe` and Kaspersky Anti-Virus `ushata.exe`.
BOOKWORM has been delivered using self-extracting RAR archives.
BOOKWORM has used its KBLogger.dll module to steal data saved to the clipboard.
title: Robert Falcone, Mike Scott, Juan Cortes. (2015, November 10). Bookworm Trojan: A Model of Modular Architecture. Retrieved July 21, 2025.

text: Mispadu contains a copy of the OpenSSL library to encrypt C2 traffic.
title: Pedro Tavares (Segurança Informática). (2020, September 15). Threat analysis: The emergent URSA trojan impacts many countries using a sophisticated loader. Retrieved March 13, 2024.

text:
Cadelspy has the ability to record audio from the compromised host.
Cadelspy has the ability to steal data from the clipboard.
Cadelspy has the ability to steal information about printers and the documents sent to printers.
Cadelspy has the ability to capture screenshots and webcam photos.
Cadelspy has the ability to identify open windows on the compromised host.
Cadelspy has the ability to log keystrokes on the compromised host.
Cadelspy has the ability to compress stolen data into a .cab file.
Cadelspy has the ability to discover information about the compromised host.
title: Symantec Security Response. (2015, December 7). Iran-based attackers use back door threats to spy on Middle Eastern targets. Retrieved April 17, 2019.

text:
Keydnap uses HTTPS for command and control.
Keydnap uses the keychaindump project to read securityd memory.
Keydnap uses a Launch Agent to persist.
Keydnap uses Python for scripting to execute additional commands.
Keydnap puts a space after a false .jpg extension so that execution actually goes through the Terminal.app program.
Keydnap uses a copy of tor2web proxy for HTTPS communications.
Keydnap prompts the users for credentials.
title: Patrick Wardle. (2017, January 1). Mac Malware of 2016. Retrieved September 21, 2018.

text: Peppy can identify specific files for exfiltration. Crimson can determine when it has been installed on a host for at least 15 days before downloading the final payload. Peppy can download and execute remote files. Crimson can decode its encoded PE file prior to execution. Peppy can log keystrokes on compromised hosts. Crimson contains a command to collect and exfiltrate emails from Outlook. Peppy can take screenshots on targeted systems. Crimson can check the Registry for the presence of HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\last_edate to determine how long it has been installed on a host. Crimson can set a Registry key to determine how long it has been installed and possibly to indicate the version number. Peppy has the ability to automatically exfiltrate files and keylogs. Peppy can use HTTP to communicate with C2. Peppy has the ability to execute shell commands. Crimson can use a HTTP GET request to download its final payload.
title: Huss, D. (2016, March 1). Operation Transparent Tribe. Retrieved June 8, 2016.

text:
KillDisk has the ability to quit and delete itself.
KillDisk registers as a service under the Plug-And-Play Support name.
title: Cherepanov, A.. (2016, December 13). The rise of TeleBots: Analyzing disruptive KillDisk attacks. Retrieved June 10, 2020.

text:
Derusbi binds to a raw socket on a random source port between 31800 and 31900 for C2.
Derusbi has used unencrypted HTTP on port 443 for C2.
Derusbi gathers the name of the local host, version of GNU Compiler Collection (GCC), and the system information about the CPU, machine, and operating system.
Derusbi is capable of obtaining directory, file, and drive listings.
Derusbi is capable of creating a remote Bash shell and executing commands.
The Derusbi malware supports timestomping.
Derusbi is capable of deleting files. It has been observed loading a Linux Kernel Module (LKM) and then deleting it from the hard disk as well as overwriting the data with null bytes.
A Linux version of Derusbi checks if the victim user ID is anything other than zero (normally used for root), and the malware will not execute if it does not have root privileges. Derusbi also gathers the username of the victim.
Derusbi collects current and parent process IDs.
Derusbi obfuscates C2 traffic with variable 4-byte XOR keys.
Derusbi uses a backup communication method with an HTTP beacon.
title: Fidelis Cybersecurity. (2016, February 29). The Turbo Campaign, Featuring Derusbi for 64-bit Linux. Retrieved March 2, 2016.

text:
RedLine Stealer can get a list of programs on the victim device.
RedLine Stealer has an anti-sandbox technique that requires the malware to consistently check with the C2 server, if the communication fails RedLine Stealer will not continue execution.
RedLine Stealer has encrypted and encoded configuration data with Base64 and XOR functions.
RedLine Stealer can collect information from browsers and browser extensions.
RedLine Stealer can retrieve system default language and time zone.
RedLine Stealer can disable security software and update services.
RedLine Stealer has decoded its payload prior to execution.
title: Splunk Threat Research Team. (2023, June 1). Do Not Cross The 'RedLine' Stealer: Detections and Analysis. Retrieved September 17, 2025.

text: DarkGate initial installation involves dropping several files to a hidden directory named after the victim machine name. Additionally, DarkGate uses attrib to hide a directory in the following command: ` C:\Windows\system32\attrib.exe” +h C:/rjtu/`.
title: Divya. (2024, April 30). Darkgate Malware Leveraging Autohotkey Following Teams. Retrieved November 22, 2024.

text:
IMAPLoader is executed via the AppDomainManager injection technique.
IMAPLoader is a loader used to retrieve follow-on payload encoded in email messages for execution on victim systems.
IMAPLoader imports native Windows APIs such as `GetConsoleWindow` and `ShowWindow`.
IMAPLoader creates scheduled tasks for persistence based on the operating system version of the victim machine.
IMAPLoader uses WMI queries to gather information about the victim machine.
IMAPLoader hides the Windows Console window created by its execution by directly importing the `kernel32.dll` and `user32.dll` libraries `GetConsoleWindow` and `ShowWindow` APIs.
IMAPLoader uses the IMAP email protocol for command and control purposes.
IMAPLoader modifies Windows tasks on the victim machine to reference a retrieved PE file through a path modification.
IMAPLoader uses WMI queries to query system information on victim hosts.
title: PwC Threat Intelligence. (2023, October 25). Yellow Liderc ships its scripts and delivers IMAPLoader malware. Retrieved August 14, 2024.

text: PowerStallion uses Microsoft OneDrive as a C2 server via a network drive mapped with net use. PowerStallion uses PowerShell loops to iteratively check for available commands in its OneDrive C2 server. PowerStallion uses a XOR cipher to encrypt command output written to its OneDrive C2 server. PowerStallion has been used to monitor process lists. PowerStallion modifies the MAC times of its local log files to match that of the victim's desktop.ini file.
title: Faou, M. and Dumont R.. (2019, May 29). A dive into Turla PowerShell usage. Retrieved June 14, 2019.

text:
Bumblebee can use asynchronous procedure call (APC) injection to execute commands received from C2.
Bumblebee has the ability to base64 encode C2 server responses.
Bumblebee can use a COM object to execute queries to gather system information.
Bumblebee can encrypt C2 requests and responses with RC4
Bumblebee has the ability to perform anti-virtualization checks.
Bumblebee has the ability to set a hardcoded and randomized sleep interval.
Bumblebee can uninstall its loader through the use of a `Sdl` command.
Bumblebee can use backup C2 servers if the primary server fails.
Bumblebee has been downloaded to victim's machines from OneDrive.
title: Merriman, K. and Trouerbach, P. (2022, April 28). This isn't Optimus Prime's Bumblebee but it's Still Transforming. Retrieved August 22, 2022.

text: Remexi uses AutoIt and VBS scripts throughout its execution process. Remexi utilizes scheduled tasks as a persistence mechanism. Remexi decrypts the configuration data using XOR with 25-character keys. Remexi searches for files on the system. Remexi silently executes received commands with cmd.exe. Remexi uses BITSAdmin to communicate with the C2 server over HTTP. Remexi performs exfiltration over BITSAdmin, which is also used for the C2 channel. Remexi utilizes Run Registry keys in the HKLM hive as a persistence mechanism. Remexi has a command to capture active windows on the machine and retrieve window titles. Remexi achieves persistence using Userinit by adding the Registry key HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\Userinit. Remexi takes screenshots of windows of interest. Remexi gathers and exfiltrates keystrokes from the machine. Remexi collects text from the clipboard. Remexi obfuscates its configuration data with XOR. Remexi encrypts and adds all gathered browser data into files for upload to C2. Remexi executes received commands with wmic.exe (for WMI commands).
title: Legezo, D. (2019, January 30). Chafer used Remexi malware to spy on Iran-based foreign diplomatic entities. Retrieved April 17, 2019.

text:
Ninja can store its final payload in the Registry under `$HKLM\SOFTWARE\Classes\Interface\` encrypted with a dynamically generated key based on the drive’s serial number.
Samurai can encrypt the names of requested APIs.
Samurai can encrypt API name strings with an XOR-based algorithm.
The Samurai loader component can create multiple Registry keys to force the svchost.exe process to load the final backdoor.
Ninja has the ability to use a proxy chain with up to 255 hops when using TCP.
Samurai can deliver its final payload as a compressed, encrypted and base64-encoded blob.
Ninja can change or create the last access or write times.
Samurai can check for the presence and version of the .NET framework.
Ninja can create the services `httpsvc` and `w3esvc` for persistence .
Samurai can leverage an exfiltration module to download arbitrary files from compromised machines.
Samurai can compile and execute downloaded modules at runtime.
Ninja has gained execution through victims opening malicious executable files embedded in zip archives.
China Chopper's server component can download remote files.
Samurai has the ability to call Windows APIs.
Ninja has been distributed to victims via the messaging app Telegram.
Samurai can base64 encode data sent in C2 communications prior to its encryption.
Samurai can use a remote command module for execution via the Windows command line.
Samurai has the ability to proxy connections to specified remote IPs and ports through a a proxy module.
Samurai can encrypt C2 communications with AES.
Ninja can configure its agent to work only in specific time frames.
Ninja has the ability to modify headers and URL paths to hide malicious traffic in HTTP requests.
Samurai can use a proxy module to forward TCP packets to external hosts.
Ninja can XOR and AES encrypt C2 messages.
Samurai can use a .NET HTTPListener class to receive and handle HTTP POST requests.
Samurai can create a service at `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\SvcHost` to trigger execution and maintain persistence.
Samurai has been used to deploy other malware including Ninja.
Ninja can encode C2 communications with a base64 algorithm using a custom alphabet.
Ninja has the ability to mimic legitimate services with customized HTTP URL paths and headers to hide malicious traffic.
Samurai can query `SOFTWARE\Microsoft\.NETFramework\policy\v2.0` for discovery.
Samurai has created the directory `%COMMONPROGRAMFILES%\Microsoft Shared\wmi\` to contain DLLs for loading successive stages.
Ninja can use HTTP for C2 communications.
Samurai can use a specific module for file enumeration.
Ninja can enumerate the IP address on compromised systems.
Ninja can use pipes to redirect the standard input and the standard output.
title: Dedola, G. (2022, June 21). APT ToddyCat. Retrieved January 3, 2024.

text:
Caminho can use junk code for obfuscation.
Caminho has the ability to download files onto compromised hosts.
Caminho can deobfuscate downloaded files prior to execution.
Caminho has launched and hollowed out MSBuild.exe to host malicious code.
Caminho can use code flattening for payload obfuscation.
Caminho can use `System.Net.WebClient.downloadString()` for file download.
title: Pellegrino, G. (2025, December 16). BlindEagle Targets Colombian Government Agency with Caminho and DCRAT. Retrieved April 16, 2026.

text:
TEXTMATE uses DNS TXT records for C2.
POWERSOURCE has been observed being used to download TEXTMATE and the Cobalt Strike Beacon payload onto victims.
title: Miller, S., et al. (2017, March 7). FIN7 Spear Phishing Campaign Targets Personnel Involved in SEC Filings. Retrieved March 8, 2017.

text: Machete has scanned and looked for cryptographic keys and certificate file extensions. Machete can download additional files for execution on the victim’s machine. Machete sends stolen data to the C2 server every 10 minutes. Machete’s downloaded data is decrypted using AES. Machete retrieves the user profile data (e.g., browsers) from Chrome and Firefox browsers. Machete's collected data is encrypted with AES before exfiltration. Machete has a component to check for running processes to look for web browsers. Machete detects the insertion of new devices by listening for the WM_DEVICECHANGE window message. Machete renamed task names to masquerade as legitimate Google Chrome, Java, Dropbox, Adobe Reader and Python tasks. Machete uses the netsh wlan show networks mode=bssid and netsh wlan show interfaces commands to list all nearby WiFi networks and connected interfaces. Machete's collected data is exfiltrated over the same channel used for C2. Machete has used AES to exfiltrate documents. Machete has sent data over HTTP if FTP failed, and has also used a fallback server. Machete’s collected files are exfiltrated automatically to remote servers. Once a file is uploaded, Machete will delete it from the machine. Machete collects stored credentials from several web browsers. Machete has the capability to exfiltrate stolen data to a hidden folder on a removable drive. Machete searches the File system for files of interest. Machete has been packed with NSIS. Machete saves the window names. Machete stores zipped files with profile data from installed web browsers. Machete collects the hostname of the target computer.
title: ESET. (2019, July). MACHETE JUST GOT SHARPER Venezuelan government institutions under attack. Retrieved September 13, 2019.

text: BISCUIT has a command to download a file from the C2 server. Variants of WEBC2 achieve persistence by using DLL search order hijacking, usually by copying the DLL file to %SYSTEMROOT% (C:\WINDOWS\ntshrui.dll). BISCUIT has a command to launch a command shell on the system. GLOOXMAIL communicates to servers operated by Google using the Jabber/XMPP protocol for C2. Seasalt is capable of installing itself as a service. Seasalt obfuscates configuration data. Seasalt has a command to delete a specified file. Seasalt has masqueraded as a service called "SaSaut" with a display name of "System Authorization Service" in an apparent attempt to masquerade as a legitimate service. BISCUIT has a command to enumerate running processes and identify their owners. BISCUIT uses SSL for encrypting C2 communications. Seasalt uses cmd.exe to create a reverse shell on the infected endpoint. Seasalt uses HTTP for C2 communications. BISCUIT has a command to gather the username from the system. BISCUIT has a command to periodically take screenshots of the system. Seasalt has a command to download additional files. CALENDAR has a command to run cmd.exe to execute commands. Seasalt has a command to perform a process listing. BISCUIT can capture keystrokes.
title: Mandiant. (n.d.). Appendix C (Digital) - The Malware Arsenal. Retrieved July 18, 2016.

text:
FlawedAmmyy leverages WMI to enumerate anti-virus on the victim.
FlawedAmmyy has used SEAL encryption during the initial C2 handshake.
FlawedAmmyy will attempt to detect anti-virus products during the initial infection.
FlawedAmmyy can collect the victim's operating system and computer name during the initial infection.
FlawedAmmyy may obfuscate portions of the initial C2 handshake.
FlawedAmmyy has used HTTP for C2.
FlawedAmmyy will attempt to detect if a usable smart card is current inserted into a card reader.
title: Proofpoint Staff. (2018, March 7). Leaked Ammyy Admin Source Code Turned into Malware. Retrieved May 28, 2019.

text: AppleSeed can find and collect data from removable media devices. AppleSeed can call regsvr32.exe for execution. AppleSeed can identify the OS version of a targeted system. AppleSeed can use a second channel for C2 when the primary channel is in upload mode. AppleSeed has the ability to execute its payload via PowerShell. AppleSeed can pull a timestamp from the victim's machine. AppleSeed can exfiltrate files via the C2 channel. AppleSeed has the ability to communicate with C2 over HTTP. AppleSeed can enumerate the current process on a compromised host. AppleSeed can stage files in a central location prior to exfiltration. AppleSeed has the ability to use JavaScript to execute PowerShell. AppleSeed can delete files from a compromised host after they are exfiltrated. AppleSeed can gain system level privilege by passing SeDebugPrivilege to the AdjustTokenPrivilege API. AppleSeed can zip and encrypt data collected on a target system. AppleSeed can use GetKeyState and GetKeyboardState to capture keystrokes on the victim’s machine. AppleSeed has been distributed to victims through malicious e-mail attachments. AppleSeed has the ability to create the Registry key name EstsoftAutoUpdate at HKCU\Software\Microsoft/Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce to establish persistence. AppleSeed can take screenshots on a compromised host by calling a series of APIs. AppleSeed can disguise JavaScript files as PDFs. AppleSeed has the ability to search for .txt, .ppt, .hwp, .pdf, and .doc files in specified directories. AppleSeed has used UPX packers for its payload DLL. AppleSeed can achieve execution through users running malicious file attachments distributed via email. AppleSeed has the ability to Base64 encode its payload and custom encrypt API calls. AppleSeed has the ability to rename its payload to ESTCommon.dll to masquerade as a DLL belonging to ESTsecurity. AppleSeed can identify the IP of a targeted system. AppleSeed can decode its payload prior to execution. AppleSeed has the ability to use multiple dynamically resolved API calls. AppleSeed can collect data on a compromised host.
title: Jazi, H. (2021, June 1). Kimsuky APT continues to target South Korean government using AppleSeed backdoor. Retrieved June 10, 2021.

text:
Octopus has been delivered via spearsphishing emails.
Octopus has exfiltrated data to file sharing sites.
Octopus can exfiltrate files from the system using a documents collector tool.
Octopus has compressed data before exfiltrating it using a tool called Abbrevia.
Octopus has relied upon users clicking on a malicious attachment delivered through spearphishing.
title: Cherepanov, A. (2018, October 4). Nomadic Octopus Cyber espionage in Central Asia. Retrieved October 13, 2021.

text: SpeakUp can perform brute forcing using a pre-defined list of usernames and passwords in an attempt to log in to administrative panels. SpeakUp uses the arp -a command. SpeakUp uses Python scripts. SpeakUp uses cron tasks to ensure persistence. SpeakUp uses POST and GET requests over HTTP to communicate with its main C&C server. SpeakUp encodes C&C communication using Base64. SpeakUp encodes its second-stage payload with Base64. SpeakUp uses Perl scripts. SpeakUp attempts to exploit the following vulnerabilities in order to execute its malicious script: CVE-2012-0874, CVE-2010-1871, CVE-2017-10271, CVE-2018-2894, CVE-2016-3088, JBoss AS 3/4/5/6, and the Hadoop YARN ResourceManager. SpeakUp uses the ifconfig -a command. SpeakUp deletes files to remove evidence on the machine. SpeakUp uses the whoami command. SpeakUp checks for availability of specific ports on servers. SpeakUp uses the cat /proc/cpuinfo | grep -c “cpu family” 2>&1 command to gather system information. SpeakUp downloads and executes additional files from a remote server.
title: Check Point Research. (2019, February 4). SpeakUp: A New Undetected Backdoor Linux Trojan. Retrieved April 17, 2019.

text:
jRAT can capture clipboard data.
jRAT has the capability to log keystrokes from the victim’s machine, both offline and online.
jRAT can list local services.
jRAT payloads have been packed.
jRAT can capture microphone recordings.
jRAT can list network connections.

text:

INC Ransomware can use the Microsoft Win32 Restart Manager to kill processes with a specific handle or that are accessing resources it wants to encrypt.
INC Ransomware can receive command line arguments to encrypt specific files and directories.

TONESHELL has created a malicious service DISMsrv to maintain persistence.
TONESHELL has added Registry Run keys to achieve persistence.
TONESHELL has capabilities to conduct keylogging.

text: Siloscape searches for the Kubernetes config file and other related files using a regular expression. Siloscape can run cmd through an IRC channel. Siloscape searches for the kubectl binary. Siloscape has decrypted the password of the C2 server with a simple byte by byte XOR. Siloscape also writes both an archive of Tor and the unzip binary to disk from data embedded within the payload using Visual Studio’s Resource Manager. Siloscape uses Tor to communicate with C2. Siloscape checks for Kubernetes node permissions. Siloscape can send kubectl commands to victim clusters through an IRC channel and can run kubectl locally to spread once within a victim cluster. Siloscape has leveraged a vulnerability in Windows containers to perform an Escape to Host. Siloscape is executed after the attacker gains initial access to a Windows container using a known vulnerability. Siloscape impersonates the main thread of CExecSvc.exe by calling NtImpersonateThread. Siloscape maps the host’s C drive to the container by creating a global symbolic link to the host through the calling of NtSetInformationSymbolicLink. Siloscape makes various native API calls. Siloscape itself is obfuscated and uses obfuscated API calls. Siloscape connects to an IRC server for C2.
title: Prizmant, D. (2021, June 7). Siloscape: First Known Malware Targeting Windows Containers to Compromise Cloud Environments. Retrieved June 9, 2021.

text:
Playcrypt can avoid encrypting files with a .PLAY, .exe, .msi, .dll, .lnk, or .sys file extension.
Playcrypt can use AlphaVSS to delete shadow copies.
title: Trend Micro Research. (2023, July 21). Ransomware Spotlight: Play. Retrieved September 24, 2024.

text:
RansomHub has created an autorun Registry key through the `-safeboot-instance -pass` command line argument.

RansomHub has an encrypted configuration file.

RansomHub can delete events from the Security, System, and Application logs.
RansomHub can use PowerShell to delete volume shadow copies.

text: BendyBear can load and execute modules and Windows Application Programming (API) calls using standard shellcode API hashing. BendyBear can query the host's Registry key at HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Console\QuickEdit to retrieve data. BendyBear can check for analysis environments and signs of debugging using the Windows API kernel32!GetTickCountKernel32 call. BendyBear has used byte randomization to obscure its behavior. BendyBear changes its runtime footprint during code execution to evade signature-based defenses. BendyBear communicates to a C2 server over port 443 using modified RC4 and XOR-encrypted chunks. BendyBear has the ability to determine local time on a compromised host. BendyBear has used a custom RC4 and XOR encrypted protocol over port 443 for C2. BendyBear has encrypted payloads using RC4 and XOR. BendyBear has decrypted function blocks using a XOR key during runtime to evade detection. BendyBear is designed to download an implant from a C2 server.
title: Harbison, M. (2021, February 9). BendyBear: Novel Chinese Shellcode Linked With Cyber Espionage Group BlackTech. Retrieved February 16, 2021.

KONNI has used AES to encrypt C2 traffic.
KONNI has been packed for obfuscation.

Egregor can perform a language check of the infected system and can query the CPU information (cupid).
Egregor has been decrypted before execution.
Egregor can enumerate all connected drives.

Egregor can encrypt all non-system files using a hybrid AES-RSA algorithm prior to displaying a ransom note.

text: Qilin can set the wallpaper on compromised hosts to display a ransom message in each encrypted folder. Qilin can enumerate domain-connected hosts during its discovery phase. Qilin can terminate specific services on compromised hosts. Qilin has named its payload file TeamViewer_Host_Setup to disguise itself as a legitimate TeamViewer file. Cobalt Strike's Beacon payload is capable of running shell commands without cmd.exe and PowerShell commands without powershell.exe Cobalt Strike can also use `CreateThreadpoolWait`, `SetThreadpoolWait`, and `MessageBoxA` for sandbox evasion and execution of embedded payloads in memory. Qilin can define specific processes to be terminated or left alone at execution. Qilin has used PsExec to distribute a second encryptor, named encryptor_1.exe, across the targeted environment. The Cobalt Strike loader can use the `MessageBoxA` API to prompt for user interaction as an anti-sandbox measure. Qilin can use symbolic links to redirect file paths for remote and local objects and can use `chmod +x` to make its payload binary executable. Qilin can run PowerShell cmdlets to discover domain groups. Cobalt Strike can deobfuscate shellcode using a rolling XOR and decrypt metadata from Beacon sessions. The Cobalt Strike loader component can also decrypt the .bss section of the Beacon binary prior to execution. Qilin can identify specific services for termination or to be left running at execution. Qilin can execute `vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet` to remove volume shadow copies and can disable High Availability (HA) and Distributed Resource Scheduler (DRS) in vCenter clusters. Qilin can make Registry modifications to share networked drives between elevated and non-elevated processes and to increase the number of outstanding network requests per client. Qilin can also modify `HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Control Panel\Desktop\Wallpaper` to enable posting of ransom messages. Qilin can detect virtual machine environments including ESXi hosts, datacenters, and clusters within vCenter environments. Qilin has run `cmd /C [PsExec] -accepteula \\IP Address -c -f -h -d -i C:\Users\xxx\.exe --password [PASSWORD] --spread --spread-process` to execute its encryptor to target multiple network shares. Qilin has created a RunOnce autostart entry at `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce*aster = %Public%\enc.exe` pointing to a dropped copy of itself in the Public folder. Qilin can use WMIC to change the Volume Shadow Copy Service (VSS) startup type to manual. Qilin can enable SSH access on ESXi hosts. Cobalt Strike can leverage the HTTP protocol for C2 communication, while hiding the actual data in either an HTTP header, URI parameter, the transaction body, or appending it to the URI. Cobalt Strike has also added Host: ocsp.verisign.com to HTTP headers to mimic Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) traffic. Qilin has created a scheduled task named TVInstallRestore to mimic TeamViewer. Qilin can use PowerShell cmdlets to enumerate domain users. Qilin can embed a copy of PsExec within its payload and place it in the %Temp% directory under a randomly generated filename.
title: Takeda, T. et al. (2025, October 26). Uncovering Qilin attack methods exposed through multiple cases. Retrieved March 26, 2026.

text:
The Carbanak malware communicates to its command server using HTTP with an encrypted payload.
Carbanak encodes the message body of HTTP traffic with Base64.
Carbanak encrypts the message body of HTTP traffic with RC2 (in CBC mode). Carbanak also uses XOR with random keys for its communications.
Carbanak logs key strokes for configured processes and sends them back to the C2 server.
title: Kaspersky Lab's Global Research and Analysis Team. (2015, February). CARBANAK APT THE GREAT BANK ROBBERY. Retrieved August 23, 2018.

Moneybird contains a configuration blob embedded in the malware itself.

DustySky collects information about running processes from victims.

text:
MacMa can enumerate running processes.
MacMa decrypts a downloaded file using AES-128-EBC with a custom delta.
MacMa has used TLS encryption to initialize a custom protocol for C2 communications.
MacMa can manage remote screen sessions.
MacMa can delete itself from the compromised computer.
MacMa has the capability to create and modify file timestamps.
MacMa can collect IP addresses from a compromised host.
MacMa can collect information about a compromised computer's disk sizes.
MacMa can collect information about a compromised computer, including: Hardware UUID, Mac serial number, and macOS version.

MacMa has used TCP port 5633 for C2 Communication.
MacMa has removed the `com.apple.quarantineattribute` from the dropped file, `$TMPDIR/airportpaird`.
MacMa can clear possible malware traces such as application logs.
MacMa can collect the username from the compromised machine.
MacMa can dump credentials from the macOS keychain.
MacMa has used a custom JSON-based protocol for its C&C communications.
MacMa can collect then exfiltrate files from the compromised system.
MacMa exfiltrates data from a supplied path over its C2 channel.

text: Gold Dragon collects endpoint information using the systeminfo command. RunningRAT captures keystrokes and sends them back to the C2 server. RunningRAT contains code to compress files. Gold Dragon collects the endpoint victim's username and uses it as a basis for downloading additional components from the C2 server. Brave Prince gathers file and directory information from the victim’s machine. Gold Dragon stores information gathered from the endpoint in a file named 1.hwp. Gold Dragon can download additional components from the C2 server. Some Brave Prince variants have used South Korea's Daum email service to exfiltrate information, and later variants have posted the data to a web server via an HTTP post command. Brave Prince lists the running processes. RunningRAT kills antimalware running process. Gold Dragon encrypts data using Base64 before being sent to the command and control server. Gold Dragon checks for anti-malware products and processes. RunningRAT contains code to delete files from the victim’s machine. Gold Dragon establishes persistence in the Startup folder. Brave Prince terminates antimalware processes. RunningRAT contains code to open and copy data from the clipboard. Gold Dragon uses cmd.exe to execute commands for discovery. RunningRAT contains code to clear event logs. RunningRAT gathers logical drives information and volume information. Gold Dragon enumerates registry keys with the command regkeyenum and obtains information for the Registry key HKEY_CURRENT_USER\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run. Gold Dragon terminates anti-malware processes if they’re found running on the system. RunningRAT uses a batch file to kill a security program task and then attempts to remove itself. Brave Prince collects hard drive content and system configuration information. RunningRAT gathers the OS version and processor information. Gold Dragon uses HTTP for communication to the control servers. Gold Dragon lists the directories for Desktop, program files, and the user’s recently accessed files. Brave Prince gathers network configuration information as well as the ARP cache. RunningRAT adds itself to the Registry key Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run to establish persistence upon reboot. Gold Dragon checks the running processes on the victim’s machine. Brave Prince gathers information about the Registry. Gold Dragon deletes one of its files, 2.hwp, from the endpoint after establishing persistence.
title: Sherstobitoff, R., Saavedra-Morales, J. (2018, February 02). Gold Dragon Widens Olympics Malware Attacks, Gains Permanent Presence on Victims’ Systems. Retrieved June 6, 2018.

text:
PUNCHBUGGY has been observed using a Registry Run key.
PUNCHBUGGY has Gzipped information and saved it to a random temp file before exfil.
PUNCHBUGGY can gather user names.
PUNCHBUGGY has used PowerShell to decode base64-encoded assembly.
PUNCHBUGGY can gather system information such as computer names.
PUNCHBUGGY has used python scripts.
PUNCHBUGGY has saved information to a random temp file before exfil.
PUNCHBUGGY has hashed most its code's functions and encrypted payloads with base64 and XOR.
PUNCHBUGGY can gather AVs registered in the system.
PUNCHBUGGY mimics filenames from %SYSTEM%\System32 to hide DLLs in %WINDIR% and/or %TEMP%.
PUNCHBUGGY enables remote interaction and can obtain additional code over HTTPS GET and POST requests.
PUNCHBUGGY can download additional files and payloads to compromised hosts.
PUNCHBUGGY has used PowerShell scripts.
PUNCHBUGGY can delete files written to disk.

text:
GLASSTOKEN can use PowerShell for command execution.
GLASSTOKEN has hexadecimal and Base64 encoded C2 content.
GLASSTOKEN has the ability to decode hexadecimal and Base64 C2 requests.
GLASSTOKEN is a web shell capable of tunneling C2 connections and code execution on compromised Ivanti Secure Connect VPNs.
title: Meltzer, M. et al. (2024, January 10). Active Exploitation of Two Zero-Day Vulnerabilities in Ivanti Connect Secure VPN. Retrieved February 27, 2024.

text:
SpicyOmelette can identify the IP of a compromised system.

SpicyOmelette has collected data and other information from a compromised host.

SpicyOmelette has been distributed via emails containing a malicious link that appears to be a PDF document.

SpicyOmelette can enumerate running software on a targeted system.

text:

ZIPLINE can use `/bin/sh` to create a reverse shell and execute commands.
WARPWIRE can capture credentials submitted during the web logon process in order to access layer seven applications such as RDP.
WIREFIRE can AES encrypt process output sent from compromised devices to C2.

WARPWIRE can embed itself into a legitimate file on compromised Ivanti Connect Secure VPNs.
ZIPLINE can find and append specific files on Ivanti Connect Secure VPNs based upon received commands.

WIREFIRE is a web shell that can download files to and execute arbitrary commands from compromised Ivanti Connect Secure VPNs.

Hikit has used HTTP for C2.
Hikit has the ability to create a remote shell and run given commands.

text: Saint Bot will use the malicious file slideshow.mp4 if present to load the core API provided by ntdll.dll to avoid any hooks placed on calls to the original ntdll.dll file by endpoint detection and response or antimalware software. Saint Bot has been distributed through malicious links contained within spearphishing emails. OutSteel can automatically scan for and collect files with specific extensions. Saint Bot has relied on users to click on a malicious link delivered via a spearphishing. OutSteel attempts to download and execute Saint Bot to a statically-defined location attempting to mimic svchost: %TEMP%\\svjhost.exe. Saint Bot has attempted to bypass UAC using `fodhelper.exe` to escalate privileges. OutSteel has been distributed as a malicious attachment within a spearphishing email. OutSteel can download files from its C2 server. OutSteel can upload files from a compromised host over its C2 channel. OutSteel has used `cmd.exe` to scan a compromised host for specific file extensions. The Saint Bot loader has used API calls to spawn `MSBuild.exe` in a suspended state before injecting the decrypted Saint Bot binary into it. Saint Bot has used the command `timeout 20` to pause the execution of its initial loader. Saint Bot can run a batch script named `del.bat` to remove any Saint Bot payload-linked files from a compromise system if anti-analysis or locale checks fail. OutSteel can collect information from a compromised host. Saint Bot has run several virtual machine and sandbox checks, including checking if `Sbiedll.dll` is present in a list of loaded modules, comparing the machine name to `HAL9TH` and the user name to `JohnDoe`, and checking the BIOS version for known virtual machine identifiers. Saint Bot can download additional files onto a compromised host. OutSteel has been distributed through malicious links contained within spearphishing emails. Saint Bot can search a compromised host for specific files. OutSteel can identify running processes on a compromised host. Saint Bot has used `.vbs` scripts for execution. OutSteel has relied on a user to execute a malicious attachment delivered via spearphishing. Saint Bot has used `cmd.exe` and `.bat` scripts for execution. OutSteel was developed using the AutoIT scripting language. OutSteel can search for specific file extensions, including zipped files. Saint Bot has used PowerShell for execution. Saint Bot has enumerated running processes on a compromised host to determine if it is running under the process name `dfrgui.exe`. Saint Bot has been obfuscated to help avoid detection. OutSteel can download the Saint Bot malware for follow-on execution. OutSteel can delete itself following the successful execution of a follow-on payload. OutSteel can automatically upload collected files to its C2 server. OutSteel has relied on a user to click a malicious link within a spearphishing email. OutSteel has used HTTP for C2 communications.
title: Unit 42. (2022, February 25). Spear Phishing Attacks Target Organizations in Ukraine, Payloads Include the Document Stealer OutSteel and the Downloader SaintBot. Retrieved June 9, 2022.

text: PipeMon can decrypt password-protected executables. PipeMon can check for the presence of ESET and Kaspersky security software. PipeMon communications are RC4 encrypted. PipeMon can iterate over the running processes to find a suitable injection target. PipeMon can send time zone information from a compromised host to C2. PipeMon can inject its modules into various processes using reflective DLL loading. PipeMon can establish persistence by registering a malicious DLL as an alternative Print Processor which is loaded when the print spooler service starts. PipeMon has used call to LoadLibrary to load its installer. PipeMon loads its modules using reflective loading or custom shellcode. PipeMon's first stage has been executed by a call to CreateProcess with the decryption password in an argument. PipeMon has used a call to LoadLibrary to load its installer. PipeMon modules are stored on disk with seemingly benign names including use of a file extension associated with a popular word processor. PipeMon installer can use UAC bypass techniques to install the payload. PipeMon can install additional modules via C2 commands. PipeMon can collect and send OS version and computer name as a part of its C2 beacon. PipeMon can attempt to gain administrative privileges using token impersonation. The PipeMon installer has modified the Registry key HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Environments\Windows x64\Print Processors to install PipeMon as a Print Processor. PipeMon has stored its encrypted payload in the Registry under `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Print\Components\`. PipeMon has modified the Registry to store its encrypted payload. PipeMon can switch to an alternate C2 domain when a particular date has been reached. PipeMon, its installer, and tools are signed with stolen code-signing certificates. The PipeMon communication module can use a custom protocol based on TLS over TCP. PipeMon modules are stored encrypted on disk. PipeMon can collect and send the local IP address, RDP information, and the network adapter physical address as a part of its C2 beacon. PipeMon can use parent PID spoofing to elevate privileges.
title: Tartare, M. et al. (2020, May 21). No “Game over” for the Winnti Group. Retrieved August 24, 2020.

text:
RedLeaves is launched through use of DLL search order hijacking to load a malicious dll.
SNUGRIDE communicates with its C2 server over HTTP.
ChChes collects the victim's %TEMP% directory path and version of Internet Explorer.
RedLeaves can receive and execute commands with cmd.exe. It can also provide a reverse shell.
SNUGRIDE encrypts C2 traffic using AES with a static key.
SNUGRIDE establishes persistence through a Registry Run key.
SNUGRIDE is capable of executing commands and spawning a reverse shell.
In one instance, menuPass added PlugX as a service with a display name of "Corel Writing Tools Utility."
RedLeaves can enumerate and search for files and directories.

Megazord can ignore specified directories for encryption.
Megazord has the ability to terminate a list of services and processes.
Megazord has the ability to print the trace, debug, error, info, and warning logs.
Megazord can execute multiple commands post infection via `cmd.exe`.
Megazord can terminate a list of specified services and processes.

text:
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can query the Kubernetes API for credentials.
CanisterWorm has checked if the target system’s time zone is “Asia/Tehran” or “Iran.”
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has used .pth files to establish persistence on compromised hosts due to the Python interpreter's automatic processing of .pth files at startup.
CanisterWorm has performed environment fingerprinting to identify Kubernetes clusters. CanisterWorm has also searched for Kubernetes pods using the command ` os.path.exists("/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount") or "KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST" in os.environ `.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has the ability to download additional payloads to targeted systems.
CanisterWorm has targeted wiper components that can delete entire clusters and execute recursive file deletions on non-containerized hosts.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has abused the shell script files entrypoint.sh (in trivy-action) and setup.sh (in ast-github-action/2.3.28) for discovery and credential harvesting.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has infected victims through malicious pre and post-install scripts within the package.json file.
CanisterWorm can deploy privileged DaemonSets in Kubernetes clusters for data wiping using kubectl.
CanisterWorm has masqueraded itself as systemd or as a PostgreSQL utility named pgmon.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer can inject malicious pre or post-install scripts within package.json for payload execution.
CanisterWorm has checked the target system's timezone `(/etc/timezone, timedatectl)` for `Asia/Tehran` or `Iran` and the `LANG` environment variable for `fa_IR` to identify systems matching an Iranian locale prior to deploying its destructive wiper component.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has leveraged Python scripts to download additional payloads, engage in discovery, and to establish persistence.
CanisterWorm can periodically poll a decentralized Internet Computer Protocol (ICP) canister to retrieve a dynamic URL for payload delivery.
TeamPCP Cloud Stealer has used `curl` to upload stolen data to attacker controlled domains.
title: Unit 42. (2026, March 31). Weaponizing the Protectors: TeamPCP’s Multi-Stage Supply Chain Attack on Security Infrastructure. Retrieved July 1, 2026.

text:
LAMEHUG can save collected data and files of interest in `C:\ProgramData\info\` to consolidate for exfiltration.
LAMEHUG has the ability to collect system information and files of interest from compromised systems.
LAMEHUG has the ability to execute Windows commands returned from C2 to gather system information.
LAMEHUG can gather service information on targeted systems.
LAMEHUG can gather Active Directory domain information.
LAMEHUG payloads have been disguised with legitimate looking filenames including AI_generator_uncensored_Canvas_PRO_v0.9.exe and AI_image_generator_v0.95.exe.
LAMEHUG can gather process information on targeted systems.
LAMEHUG can use Python scripts for execution.
LAMEHUG can recursively copy files from targeted directories on victim hosts.
LAMEHUG can target directories on victim machines for file collection.
LAMEHUG has used the Hugging Face API to query the Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct LLM to generate one-line Windows commands for the collection of system information and documents in specific folders on compromised hosts. LAMEHUG subsequently executed the returned commands and exfiltrated the collected files and information to adversary-controlled C2 servers.
LAMEHUG can enumerate network information on compromised hosts.
LAMEHUG can exfiltrate collected system information and documents to C2.
title: Google Threat Intelligence Group. (2025, November 5). GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Advances in Threat Actor Usage of AI Tools. Retrieved March 31, 2026.

text:
Black Basta can reboot victim machines in safe mode with networking via `bcdedit /set safeboot network`.
Black Basta can enumerate volumes.
Black Basta has established persistence by creating a new service named `FAX` after deleting the legitimate service by the same name.
Black Basta can delete shadow copies using vssadmin.exe.
Black Basta has the ability to use native APIs for numerous functions including discovery and defense evasion.
Black Basta can collect system boot configuration and CPU information.
Black Basta has modified the Registry to enable itself to run in safe mode, to change the icons and file extensions for encrypted files, and to add the malware path for persistence.
Black Basta can create a new service to establish persistence.
title: Zargarov, N. (2022, May 2). New Black Basta Ransomware Hijacks Windows Fax Service. Retrieved March 7, 2023.

text:
A module in CozyCar allows arbitrary commands to be executed by invoking C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe. The CozyCar dropper copies the system file rundll32.exe to the install location for the malware, then uses the copy of rundll32.exe to load and execute the main CozyCar component. One persistence mechanism used by CozyCar is to register itself as a Windows service. CozyCar's main method of communicating with its C2 servers is using HTTP or HTTPS. The payload of CozyCar is encrypted with simple XOR with a rotating key. The CozyCar configuration file has been encrypted with RC4 keys. One persistence mechanism used by CozyCar is to set itself to be executed at system startup by adding a Registry value under one of the following Registry keys:
HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\
HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\
HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\Explorer\Run
HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\Explorer\Run A system info module in CozyCar gathers information on the victim host’s configuration. One persistence mechanism used by CozyCar is to register itself as a scheduled task. Password stealer and NTLM stealer modules in CozyCar harvest stored credentials from the victim, including credentials used as part of Windows NTLM user authentication. The main CozyCar dropper checks whether the victim has an anti-virus product installed. If the installed product is on a predetermined list, the dropper will exit. Some versions of CozyCar will check to ensure it is not being executed inside a virtual machine or a known malware analysis sandbox environment. If it detects that it is, it will exit. CozyCar has executed Mimikatz to harvest stored credentials from the victim and further victim penetration. CozyCar uses Twitter as a backup C2 channel to Twitter accounts specified in its configuration file. The CozyCar dropper has masqueraded a copy of the infected system's rundll32.exe executable that was moved to the malware's install directory and renamed according to a predefined configuration file.
title: F-Secure Labs. (2015, April 22). CozyDuke: Malware Analysis. Retrieved December 10, 2015.

text:
PoetRAT has used FTP for C2 communications.
PoetRAT has exfiltrated data over the C2 channel.
PoetRAT has `pyminifier` to obfuscate scripts.
PoetRAT has used HTTP and HTTPs for C2 communications.
PoetRAT has used LZMA and base64 libraries to decode obfuscated scripts.
PoetRAT has called cmd through a Word document macro.
PoetRAT has executed a Lua script through a Lua interpreter for Windows.
title: Mercer, W. Rascagneres, P. Ventura, V. (2020, October 6). PoetRAT: Malware targeting public and private sector in Azerbaijan evolves . Retrieved April 9, 2021.

text:
ShadowPad has decrypted a binary blob to start execution.
ShadowPad has used FTP for C2 communications.
ShadowPad maintains a configuration block and virtual file system in the Registry.
ShadowPad has collected the current date and time of the victim system.
ShadowPad has collected the PID of a malicious process.
ShadowPad uses a DGA that is based on the day of the month for C2 servers.
ShadowPad can modify the Registry to store and maintain a configuration block and virtual file system.
ShadowPad has collected the username of the victim system.
ShadowPad has discovered system information including memory status, CPU frequency, and OS versions.
ShadowPad has used UDP for C2 communications.
ShadowPad has collected the domain name of the victim system.
ShadowPad has injected an install module into a newly created process.
ShadowPad has injected a DLL into svchost.exe.
ShadowPad communicates over HTTP to retrieve a string that is decoded into a C2 server URL.
ShadowPad has deleted arbitrary Registry values.
ShadowPad has used DNS tunneling for C2 communications.
ShadowPad has discovered system information including volume serial numbers.
title: Kaspersky Lab. (2017, August). ShadowPad: popular server management software hit in supply chain attack. Retrieved March 22, 2021.

REvil can connect to and disable the Symantec server on the victim's network.

Shai-Hulud has delayed execution of its larger payloads by forking itself into background process.
Shai-Hulud has used POST to exfiltrate secrets from the victim environment to an attacker-controlled URL.
Shai-Hulud has leveraged compromised accounts to log into cloud services to access cloud hosted repositories.

text:
Ebury is executed through hooking the keyutils.so file used by legitimate versions of `OpenSSH` and `libcurl`.
If credentials are not collected for two weeks, Ebury encrypts the credentials using a public key and sends them via UDP to an IP address located in the DNS TXT record.
Ebury disables OpenSSH, system (`systemd`), and audit logs (`/sbin/auditd`) when the backdoor is active.
When Ebury is running as an OpenSSH server, it uses LD_PRELOAD to inject its malicious shared module in to programs launched by SSH sessions. Ebury hooks the following functions from `libc` to inject into subprocesses; `system`, `popen`, `execve`, `execvpe`, `execv`, `execvp`, and `execl`.
Ebury exfiltrates a list of outbound and inbound SSH sessions using OpenSSH's `known_host` files and `wtmp` records. Ebury can exfiltrate SSH credentials through custom DNS queries or use the command `Xcat` to send the process's ssh session's credentials to the C2 server.
Ebury modifies the `keyutils` library to add malicious behavior to the OpenSSH client and the curl library.
Ebury acts as a user land rootkit using the SSH service.
Ebury can use the commands `Xcsh` or `Xcls` to open a shell with Ebury level permissions and `Xxsh` to open a shell with root level.
title: Marc-Etienne M.Léveillé. (2024, May 1). Ebury is alive but unseen. Retrieved May 21, 2024.

Ursnif has used Tor for C2.
Ursnif has used a peer-to-peer (P2P) network for C2.
title: NJCCIC. (2016, September 27). Ursnif. Retrieved September 12, 2024.

text:
Explosive has commonly set file and path attributes to hidden.
Explosive has leveraged its keylogging capabilities to gain access to administrator accounts on target servers.
Explosive has collected the computer name from the infected host.
Explosive has collected the MAC address from the victim's machine.
Explosive has a function to call the OpenClipboard wrapper.
Explosive has a function to download a file to the infected system.
Explosive can scan all .exe files located in the USB drive.
Explosive has a function to use the OpenClipboard wrapper.
Explosive has used HTTP for communication.
Explosive has a function to write itself to Registry values.
Explosive has collected the username from the infected host.
