text: Cobalt Strike includes a capability to modify the Beacon payload to eliminate known signatures or unpacking methods. Cobalt Strike can enumerate services on compromised hosts. Cobalt Strike can explore files on a compromised system. Cobalt Strike can exploit vulnerabilities such as MS14-058. Cobalt Strike's Beacon payload is capable of capturing screenshots. Cobalt Strike can use Base64, URL-safe Base64, or NetBIOS encoding in its C2 traffic. Cobalt Strike can spawn a job to inject into LSASS memory and dump password hashes. Cobalt Strike uses a custom command and control protocol that is encapsulated in HTTP, HTTPS, or DNS. In addition, it conducts peer-to-peer communication over Windows named pipes encapsulated in the SMB protocol. All protocols use their standard assigned ports. Cobalt Strike can collect data from a local system. Cobalt Strike can use WinRM to execute a payload on a remote host. Cobalt Strike can track key presses with a keylogger module. Cobalt Strike can timestomp any files or payloads placed on a target machine to help them blend in. The Cobalt Strike System Profiler can discover applications through the browser and identify the version of Java the target has. Cobalt Strike can determine the NetBios name and the IP addresses of targets machines including domain controllers. Cobalt Strike's execute-assembly command can run a .NET executable within the memory of a sacrificial process by loading the CLR. Cobalt Strike can use process hollowing for execution. Cobalt Strike can use a number of known techniques to bypass Windows UAC. Cobalt Strike can identify targets by querying account groups on a domain contoller. Cobalt Strike can use spoof arguments in spawned processes that execute beacon commands. Cobalt Strike can use PsExec to execute a payload on a remote host. It can also use Service Control Manager to start new services. Cobalt Strike can be configured to have commands relayed over a peer-to-peer network of infected hosts. This can be used to limit the number of egress points, or provide access to a host without direct internet access. Cobalt Strike can perform browser pivoting and inject into a user's browser to inherit cookies, authenticated HTTP sessions, and client SSL certificates. Cobalt Strike has the ability to accept a value for HTTP Host Header to enable domain fronting. Cobalt Strike can steal access tokens from exiting processes. Cobalt Strike can SSH to a remote service. Cobalt Strike can use net localgroup to list local groups on a system. Cobalt Strike can use sudo to run a command.
title: Strategic Cyber LLC. (2020, November 5). Cobalt Strike: Advanced Threat Tactics for Penetration Testers. Retrieved April 13, 2021.

text:
SocGholish has used Amazon Web Services to host second-stage servers.
SocGholish has single or double Base-64 encoded references to its second-stage server URLs.
title: Milenkoski, A. (2022, November 7). SocGholish Diversifies and Expands Its Malware Staging Infrastructure to Counter Defenders. Retrieved March 22, 2024.

text:
RogueRobin uses regsvr32.exe to run a .sct file for execution.
RogueRobin decodes an embedded executable using base64 and decompresses it.
RogueRobin has used Google Drive as a Command and Control channel.
title: Lee, B., Falcone, R. (2019, January 18). DarkHydrus delivers new Trojan that can use Google Drive for C2 communications. Retrieved April 17, 2019.

text: Trojan.Karagany can upload, download, and execute files on the victim. Trojan.Karagany can take a desktop screenshot and save the file into \ProgramData\Mail\MailAg\shot.png. Trojan.Karagany can create a link to itself in the Startup folder to automatically start itself upon system restart. Backdoor.Oldrea collects information about available drives, default browser, desktop file list, My Documents, Internet history, program files, and root of available drives. It also searches for ICS-related software files. Trojan.Karagany can use Tasklist to collect a list of running tasks. Backdoor.Oldrea collects information about the OS and computer name. Some Backdoor.Oldrea samples contain a publicly available Web browser password recovery tool. Some Backdoor.Oldrea samples use standard Base64 + bzip2, and some use standard Base64 + reverse XOR + RSA-2048 to decrypt data received from C2 servers. Backdoor.Oldrea injects itself into explorer.exe. Backdoor.Oldrea collects information about running processes. Backdoor.Oldrea adds Registry Run keys to achieve persistence. Backdoor.Oldrea writes collected data to a temporary file in an encrypted form before exfiltration to a C2 server. Backdoor.Oldrea contains a cleanup module that removes traces of itself from the victim. Trojan.Karagany samples sometimes use common binary packers such as UPX and Aspack on top of a custom Delphi binary packer. Trojan.Karagany can create directories to store plugin output and stage data for exfiltration. Backdoor.Oldrea collects address book information from Outlook. Trojan.Karagany can dump passwords and save them into \ProgramData\Mail\MailAg\pwds.txt. Backdoor.Oldrea collects information about the Internet adapter configuration. Backdoor.Oldrea collects the current username from the victim.
title: Symantec Security Response. (2014, June 30). Dragonfly: Cyberespionage Attacks Against Energy Suppliers. Retrieved April 8, 2016.

text:
DUSTTRAP can retrieve and load additional payloads.
DUSTTRAP can enumerate Registry items.
DUSTPAN decrypts and executes an embedded payload.
DUSTTRAP can enumerate domain accounts.
DUSTTRAP can identify infected system log information.
DUSTTRAP can use `ping` to identify remote hosts within the victim network.
DUSTTRAP can enumerate local user accounts.
DUSTTRAP can execute commands via `cmd.exe`.
DUSTPAN decodes and decrypts embedded payloads.
DUSTTRAP can capture screenshots.
DUSTTRAP can remove network shares from infected systems.
DUSTTRAP can enumerate infected system network information.
DUSTPAN can inject its decrypted payload into another process.
DUSTPAN decrypts an embedded payload.
DUSTTRAP can identify and enumerate victim system network shares.
DUSTTRAP contains additional embedded DLLs and configuration files that are loaded into memory during execution.
DUSTTRAP can enumerate running processes.
DUSTTRAP reads the infected system's current time and writes it to a log file during execution.
DUSTTRAP can enumerate running application windows.
DUSTPAN is often disguised as a legitimate Windows binary such as `w3wp.exe` or `conn.exe`.
DUSTTRAP begins with an initial launcher that decrypts an AES-128-CFB encrypted file on disk and executes it in memory.
DUSTTRAP can gather data from infected systems.
DUSTTRAP compromises the `.text` section of a legitimate system DLL in `%windir%` to hold the contents of retrieved plug-ins.
DUSTTRAP restores the `.text` section of compromised DLLs after malicious code is loaded into memory and before the file is closed.
DUSTTRAP can identify victim environment Group Policy information.
DUSTTRAP can enumerate files and directories.
DUSTTRAP can delete infected system log information.
DUSTPAN can persist as a Windows Service in operations.
DUSTTRAP can perform keylogging operations.
DUSTTRAP can exfiltrate collected data over C2 channels.
DUSTTRAP can identify Active Directory information and related items.
DUSTTRAP deobfuscates embedded payloads.
DUSTTRAP decryption relies on the infected machine's `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Cryptography\MachineGUID` value.
DUSTTRAP can identify security software.
DUSTTRAP reads the value of the infected system's `HKLM\SYSTEM\Microsoft\Cryptography\MachineGUID` value.
title: Mike Stokkel et al. (2024, July 18). APT41 Has Arisen From the DUST. Retrieved September 16, 2024.

text:
CLAIMLOADER has utilized XOR-encrypted API names and native APIs of `LdrLoadDll()` and `LderGetProcedureAddress()` to resolve imports dynamically.
CLAIMLOADER has used various Windows API calls during execution, when establishing persistence and defense evasion. CLAIMLOADER has also leveraged the legitimate API functions to run its shellcode through the callback function, including `GetDC()` and `EnumFontsW()`. CLAIMLOADER established persistence by utilizing the API `SHSetValue()`. CLAIMLOADER has utilized APIs with callback functions such as `EnumpropsExW`, `EnumSystemLanguageGroupsA`, and `EnumCalendarInfoExW`.
CLAIMLOADER has added Registry Run keys to achieve persistence using `HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run`.
CLAIMLOADER has created hardcoded mutex to ensure only a single instance of the malware is running.
CLAIMLOADER has used a legitimately signed executable to execute a malicious payload within a DLL file.
CLAIMLOADER has decoded its payload prior to execution.
title: Golo Muhr, Joshua Chung. (2025, June 23). Hive0154 aka Mustang Panda shifts focus on Tibetan community to deploy Pubload backdoor. Retrieved August 4, 2025.

text: Akira will leverage COM objects accessed through WMI during execution to evade detection. Akira executes native Windows functions such as GetFileAttributesW and `GetSystemInfo`. Akira verifies the deletion of volume shadow copies by checking for the existence of the process ID related to the process created to delete these items. Akira can identify remote file shares for encryption. Akira executes from the Windows command line and can take various arguments for execution. Akira uses the GetSystemInfo Windows function to determine the number of processors on a victim machine.
title: Max Kersten & Alexandre Mundo. (2023, November 29). Akira Ransomware. Retrieved April 4, 2024.

text: A variant of Elise executes dir C:\progra~1 when initially run. Elise enumerates processes via the tasklist command. Elise is capable of launching a remote shell on the host to delete itself. Elise can download additional files from the C2 server for execution. If establishing persistence by installation as a new service fails, one variant of Elise establishes persistence for the created .exe file by setting the following Registry key: HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\svchost : %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Network\svchost.exe. Other variants have set the following Registry keys for persistence: HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\imejp : [self] and HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\IAStorD. Elise executes ipconfig /all after initial communication is made to the remote server. Elise creates a file in AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\Explorer and stores all harvested data in that file. Elise injects DLL files into iexplore.exe.
title: Accenture Security. (2018, January 27). DRAGONFISH DELIVERS NEW FORM OF ELISE MALWARE TARGETING ASEAN DEFENCE MINISTERS’ MEETING AND ASSOCIATES. Retrieved November 17, 2024.

text:
Bumblebee can deobfuscate C2 server responses and unpack its code on targeted hosts.
Bumblebee can identify processes associated with analytical tools.
Bumblebee has the ability to search for designated file paths and Registry keys that indicate a virtualized environment from multiple products.
Bumblebee has relied upon a user opening an ISO file to enable execution of malicious shortcut files and DLLs.
Bumblebee can search for tools used in static analysis.
Bumblebee has been delivered as password-protected zipped ISO files and used control-flow-flattening to obfuscate the flow of functions.
Bumblebee can use `LoadLibrary` to attempt to execute GdiPlus.dll.
Bumblebee can check the Registry for specific keys.
Bumblebee has gained execution through luring users into opening malicious attachments.
Bumblebee can use multiple Native APIs.
Bumblebee can use PowerShell for execution.
Bumblebee can identify specific analytical tools based on running processes.
Bumblebee has named component DLLs "RapportGP.dll" to match those used by the security company Trusteer.
title: Salem, A. (2022, April 27). The chronicles of Bumblebee: The Hook, the Bee, and the Trickbot connection. Retrieved September 2, 2022.

text:
Dridex can abuse legitimate Windows executables to side-load malicious DLL files.
Dridex can use `regsvr32.exe` to initiate malicious code.
Dridex can maintain persistence via the creation of scheduled tasks within system directories such as `windows\system32\`, `windows\syswow64,` `winnt\system32`, and `winnt\syswow64`.
title: Red Canary. (2021, February 9). Dridex - Red Canary Threat Detection Report. Retrieved August 3, 2023.

text:
CanisterWorm has spread through an automated process that infects and publishes npm packages.
CanisterWorm has used embedded second stage Base64-encoded payloads.
CanisterWorm has leveraged stolen npm tokens to automate compromise by enumerating all publishable packages in a namespace, bumping versions, and publishing itself across the entire scope.
CanisterWorm has registered itself as a systemd service for persistence on targeted Kubernetes nodes.
CanisterWorm has leveraged a Sleep setting of five minutes before executing tasks to evade sandbox environments.
CanisterWorm has used shell commands to enable and start the malicious systemd service for execution and persistence.
CanisterWorm can establish persistence in CI/CD environments by launching a background process (deploy.js) with stolen tokens.
CanisterWorm has leveraged stolen tokens from Trivy users to publish itself across over 46 npm packages.
CanisterWorm has discovered npm pathways and directories that frequently store .npmrc files to check for _authToken values.
CanisterWorm has decoded a long Base64 string to obtain a Python script for its second-stage payload.
CanisterWorm has used a Python script as a second-stage backdoor.
CanisterWorm has mimicked legitimate PostgreSQL components (pgmon, pglog, and .pg_state) to masquerade malicious files.
CanisterWorm has downloaded and executed binaries from dead drop URLs retrieved from ICP canister C2 nodes. CanisterWorm has also downloaded kubectl to compromised environments if it was not already installed.
CanisterWorm can leverage stolen tokens to execute Javascsript (deploy.js) for self-propagation.
CanisterWorm has used executed `systemctl --user daemon-reload` to reload systemd, then enables and starts the malicious service.
title: Eriksen, C. (2026, March 20). TeamPCP deploys CanisterWorm on NPM following Trivy compromise. Retrieved July 27, 2026.

text:
BlackCat can clear Windows event logs using `wevtutil.exe`.
BlackCat can use `wmic.exe` to delete shadow copies on compromised networks.
BlackCat can enumerate files for encryption.
BlackCat can utilize `net use` commands to identify domain users.
BlackCat can use Windows commands such as `fsutil behavior set SymLinkEvaluation R2L:1` to redirect file system access to a different location after gaining access into compromised networks.
BlackCat has the ability to add the following registry key on compromised networks to maintain persistence: `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services \LanmanServer\Paramenters`
BlackCat can utilize `net use` commands to discover the user name on a compromised host.
BlackCat can broadcasts NetBIOS Name Service (NBNC) messages to search for servers connected to compromised networks.
BlackCat can enumerate local drives.
BlackCat can obtain the computer name and UUID.
BlackCat can replicate itself across connected servers via `psexec`.
BlackCat can delete shadow copies using `vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet` and `wmic.exe Shadowcopy Delete`; it can also modify the boot loader using `bcdedit /set {default} recoveryenabled No`.
BlackCat can determine if a user on a compromised host has domain admin privileges.
BlackCat can execute commands on a compromised network with the use of `cmd.exe`.
BlackCat has the ability to encrypt Windows devices, Linux devices, and VMWare instances.
BlackCat can bypass UAC to escalate privileges.
title: Microsoft Defender Threat Intelligence. (2022, June 13). The many lives of BlackCat ransomware. Retrieved December 20, 2022.

text:
A BlackEnergy 2 plug-in uses WMI to gather victim host details.
BlackEnergy 2 contains a "Destroy" plug-in that destroys data stored on victim hard drives by overwriting file contents.
title: Baumgartner, K. and Garnaeva, M.. (2015, February 17). BE2 extraordinary plugins, Siemens targeting, dev fails. Retrieved March 24, 2016.

text:
DOWNIISSA can delete files after download.
DOWNIISSA can create an instance of msiexec.exe and inject LODEINFO shellcode into the memory of the process.
DOWNIISSA can decode strings prior to execution.
LODEINFO can use legitimate EXE files to sideload malicious DLLs.
LODEINFO components have been compressed with zip for delivery.
DOWNIISSA code is base64 encoded and XOR encrypted.
DOWNIISSA can use the `URLDownloadToFileA()` API to download from remote resources.
LODEINFO can enumerate the MAC address of the compromised host.
DOWNIISSA can download files to the compromised host.
DOWNIISSA can inject shellcode directly into process memory including WINWORD.exe and msiexec.exe.
title: Ishimaru, S. (2022, October 31). APT10: Tracking down LODEINFO 2022, part I. Retrieved April 17, 2026.

text: MacSpy uses Tor for command and control. Proton persists via Launch Agent. FruitFly has the ability to list processes on the system. FruitFly executes and stores obfuscated Perl scripts. FruitFly saves itself with a leading "." to make it a hidden file. Proton prompts users for their credentials. MacSpy uses HTTP for command and control. iKitten saves itself with a leading "." so that it's hidden from users by default. Proton uses VNC to connect into systems. FruitFly persists via a Launch Agent. Proton removes logs from /var/logs and /Library/logs. FruitFly takes screenshots of the user's desktop. MacSpy persists via a Launch Agent. Proton gathers credentials in files for keychains. Proton gathers credentials for Google Chrome. FruitFly will delete files on the system. Proton uses macOS' .command file type to script actions. iKitten will zip up the /Library/Keychains directory before exfiltrating it. MacSpy can capture screenshots of the desktop over multiple monitors. Dok prompts the user for credentials. Proton captures the content of the desktop with the screencapture binary. MacSpy captures keystrokes. FruitFly looks for specific files and file types. Proton uses an encrypted file to store commands and configuration values. iKitten lists the current processes running. iKitten adds an entry to the rc.common file for persistence. iKitten collects the keychains on the system. Proton zips up files before exfiltrating them. Proton uses a keylogger to capture keystrokes. Proton removes all files in the /tmp directory. Proton kills security tools like Wireshark that are running. Dok installs a root certificate to aid in Adversary-in-the-Middle actions using the command add-trusted-cert -d -r trustRoot -k /Library/Keychains/System.keychain /tmp/filename. Proton modifies the tty_tickets line in the sudoers file. iKitten will look for the current IP address. MacSpy can steal clipboard contents. Dok uses AppleScript to create a login item for persistence. iKitten prompts the user for their credentials. MacSpy can record the sounds from microphones on a computer. Proton gathers credentials in files for 1password. Dok downloads and installs Tor via homebrew.
title: Patrick Wardle. (n.d.). Mac Malware of 2017. Retrieved September 21, 2018.

text: Cardinal RAT checks its current working directory upon execution and also contains watchdog functionality that ensures its executable is located in the correct path (else it will rewrite the payload). Cardinal RAT can download and execute additional payloads. Cardinal RAT contains watchdog functionality that periodically ensures HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows\Load is set to point to its executable. Cardinal RAT and its watchdog component are compiled and executed after being delivered to victims as embedded, uncompiled source code. Cardinal RAT is downloaded using HTTP over port 443. Cardinal RAT establishes Persistence by setting the HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows\Load Registry key to point to its executable. Cardinal RAT can log keystrokes. Cardinal RAT can execute commands. Cardinal RAT can uninstall itself, including deleting its executable. Cardinal RAT contains watchdog functionality that ensures its process is always running, else spawns a new instance. Cardinal RAT sets HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows\Load to point to its executable. Cardinal RAT can capture screenshots. Cardinal RAT encodes many of its artifacts and is encrypted (AES-128) when downloaded. Cardinal RAT can act as a reverse proxy. Cardinal RAT can communicate over multiple C2 host and port combinations. Cardinal RAT injects into a newly spawned process created from a native Windows executable. Cardinal RAT lures victims into executing malicious macros embedded within Microsoft Excel documents. Cardinal RAT decodes many of its artifacts and is decrypted (AES-128) after being downloaded. Cardinal RAT can collect the username from a victim machine. Cardinal RAT applies compression to C2 traffic using the ZLIB library. Cardinal RAT can collect the hostname, Microsoft Windows version, and processor architecture from a victim machine. Cardinal RAT uses a secret key with a series of XOR and addition operations to encrypt C2 traffic.
title: Grunzweig, J.. (2017, April 20). Cardinal RAT Active for Over Two Years. Retrieved December 8, 2018.

text:
Micropsia uses HTTP and HTTPS for C2 network communications.
Micropsia gathers the hostname and OS version from the victim’s machine.
Micropsia collects the username from the victim’s machine.
Micropsia creates a shortcut to maintain persistence.
Micropsia obfuscates the configuration with a custom Base64 and XOR.
Micropsia can download and execute an executable from the C2 server.
Micropsia searches for anti-virus software and firewall products installed on the victim’s machine using WMI.
title: Rascagneres, P., Mercer, W. (2017, June 19). Delphi Used To Score Against Palestine. Retrieved November 13, 2018.

text:
DRATzarus can enumerate and examine running processes to determine if a debugger is present.
DRATzarus has been named `Flash.exe`, and its dropper has been named `IExplorer`.
DRATzarus's dropper can be packed with UPX.
DRATzarus can use HTTP or HTTPS for C2 communications.
DRATzarus can use the `GetTickCount` and `GetSystemTimeAsFileTime` API calls to measure function timing. DRATzarus can also remotely shut down into sleep mode under specific conditions to evade detection.
DRATzarus can use various API calls to see if it is running in a sandbox.
DRATzarus can deploy additional tools onto an infected machine.
DRATzarus can collect information from a compromised host.
DRATzarus can obtain a list of users from an infected machine.
DRATzarus can use `IsDebuggerPresent` to detect whether a debugger is present on a victim.
DRATzarus can search for other machines connected to compromised host and attempt to map the network.
DRATzarus can use the `GetTickCount` and `GetSystemTimeAsFileTime` API calls to inspect system time.
DRATzarus can be partly encrypted with XOR.
title: ClearSky Research Team. (2020, August 13). Operation 'Dream Job' Widespread North Korean Espionage Campaign. Retrieved December 20, 2021.

text:
Sardonic can use WMI to execute PowerShell commands on a compromised machine.
Sardonic has the ability to call Win32 API functions to determine if `powershell.exe` is running.
Sardonic can encode client ID data in 32 uppercase hex characters and transfer to the actor-controlled C2 server.
Sardonic has the ability to collect the computer name, and CPU manufacturer name from a compromised machine. Sardonic also has the ability to execute the `ver` and `systeminfo` commands.
Sardonic has the ability to delete created WMI objects to evade detections.
Sardonic has the ability to execute PowerShell commands on a compromised machine.
Sardonic can use a WMI event filter to invoke a command-line event consumer to gain persistence.
Sardonic has the ability to send a random 64-byte RC4 key to communicate with actor-controlled C2 servers by using an RSA public key.
Sardonic has the ability to execute the `net start` command.
Sardonic has the ability to execute the `net view` command.
Sardonic has the ability to use an RC4 key to encrypt communications to and from actor-controlled C2 servers.
Sardonic can communicate with actor-controlled C2 servers by using a custom little-endian binary protocol.
Sardonic has the ability to execute the `netstat` command.
Sardonic PowerShell scripts can be encrypted with RC4 and compressed using Gzip.
Sardonic has the ability to collect the C:\ drive serial number from a compromised machine.
Sardonic has the ability to connect with actor-controlled C2 servers using a custom binary protocol over port 443.
Sardonic has the ability to execute the `ipconfig` command.
Sardonic has the ability to upload additional malicious files to a compromised machine.
Sardonic has the ability to execute the `tasklist` command.
title: Budaca, E., et al. (2021, August 25). FIN8 Threat Actor Goes Agile with New Sardonic Backdoor. Retrieved August 9, 2023.

text:
Emotet has been observed dropping browser password grabber modules.
Emotet has exfiltrated data over its C2 channel.
Emotet has used Powershell to retrieve the malicious payload and download additional resources like Mimikatz.
Emotet is known to use RSA keys for encrypting C2 traffic.
Emotet has used custom packers to protect its payloads.
Emotet has been observed dropping and executing password grabber modules including Mimikatz.
title: Trend Micro. (2019, January 16). Exploring Emotet's Activities . Retrieved March 25, 2019.

text:
PLEAD has the ability to upload and download files to and from an infected host.
TSCookie has the ability to upload and download files to and from the infected host.
TSCookie has the ability to identify the IP of the infected host.
TSCookie has the ability to list processes on the infected host.
TSCookie has the ability to steal saved passwords from the Internet Explorer, Edge, Firefox, and Chrome browsers.
PLEAD has the ability to execute shell commands on the compromised host.
TSCookie has been executed via malicious links embedded in e-mails spoofing the Ministries of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology of Japan.
PLEAD has the ability to proxy network communications.
TSCookie has the ability to decrypt, load, and execute a DLL and its resources.
PLEAD has used RC4 encryption to download modules.
TSCookie has encrypted network communications with RC4.
TSCookie has the ability to execute shell commands on the infected host.
TSCookie can multiple protocols including HTTP and HTTPS in communication with command and control (C2) servers.
TSCookie has the ability to discover drive information on the infected host.
title: Tomonaga, S. (2018, June 8). PLEAD Downloader Used by BlackTech. Retrieved May 6, 2020.

text:
Astaroth has used malicious VBS e-mail attachments for execution.
Javali can use DLL side-loading to load malicious DLLs into legitimate executables.
Melcoz has been packed with VMProtect and Themida.
Melcoz can use VBS scripts to execute malicious DLLs.
Grandoreiro can obtain C2 information from Google Docs.
Javali can read C2 information from Google Documents and YouTube.
Javali has been delivered as malicious e-mail attachments.
Melcoz has been distributed through an AutoIt loader script.
Grandoreiro can monitor browser activity for online banking actions and display full-screen overlay images to block user access to the intended site or present additional data fields.
Astaroth has used an XOR-based algorithm to encrypt payloads twice with different keys.
Melcoz has the ability to download additional files to a compromised host.
Astaroth can launch itself via DLL Search Order Hijacking.
Astaroth uses JavaScript to perform its core functionalities.
Melcoz has been spread through malicious links embedded in e-mails.
Melcoz can monitor content saved to the clipboard.
Astaroth can create a new process in a suspended state from a targeted legitimate process in order to unmap its memory and replace it with malicious code.
Javali has achieved execution through victims clicking links to malicious websites.
Grandoreiro has used compromised websites and Google Ads to bait victims into downloading its installer.
Javali can download payloads from remote C2 servers.
The Grandoreiro payload has been delivered encrypted with a custom XOR-based algorithm and also as a base64-encoded ZIP file.
Melcoz has the ability to steal credentials from web browsers.
Grandoreiro can use VBScript to execute malicious code.
Melcoz can use DLL hijacking to bypass security controls.
Astaroth has been delivered via malicious e-mail attachments.
Melcoz can monitor the victim's browser for online banking sessions and display an overlay window to manipulate the session in the background.
Astaroth can store C2 information on cloud hosting services such as AWS and CloudFlare and websites like YouTube and Facebook.
Melcoz can monitor the clipboard for cryptocurrency addresses and change the intended address to one controlled by the adversary.
Javali can use large obfuscated libraries to hinder detection and analysis.
Melcoz can use MSI files with embedded VBScript for execution.
Grandoreiro can use a DGA for hiding C2 addresses, including use of an algorithm with a user-specific key that changes daily.
Javali has used embedded VBScript to download malicious payloads from C2.
Javali has achieved execution through victims opening malicious attachments, including MSI files with embedded VBScript.
Astaroth can abuse alternate data streams (ADS) to store content for malicious payloads.
Javali has been delivered via malicious links embedded in e-mails.
Javali can monitor processes for open browsers and custom banking applications.
Grandoreiro can use MSI files to execute DLLs.
Astaroth uses a fromCharCode() deobfuscation method to avoid explicitly writing execution commands and to hide its code.
Melcoz has gained execution through victims opening malicious links.
Astaroth has used malicious files including VBS, LNK, and HTML for execution.
Javali can capture login credentials from open browsers including Firefox, Chrome, Internet Explorer, and Edge.
Astaroth uses certutil and BITSAdmin to download additional malware.
Javali has used the MSI installer to download and execute malicious payloads.
Astaroth can check for Windows product ID's used by sandboxes and usernames and disk serial numbers associated with analyst environments.
title: GReAT. (2020, July 14). The Tetrade: Brazilian banking malware goes global. Retrieved November 9, 2020.

text:
STARWHALE has the ability to create the following Windows service to establish persistence on an infected host: `sc create Windowscarpstss binpath= "cmd.exe /c cscript.exe c:\\windows\\system32\\w7_1.wsf humpback_whale" start= "auto" obj= "LocalSystem"`.
STARWHALE has stored collected data in a file called `stari.txt`.
STARWHALE has the ability to execute commands via `cmd.exe`.
STARWHALE can use the VBScript function `GetRef` as part of its persistence mechanism.
title: Tomcik, R. et al. (2022, February 24). Left On Read: Telegram Malware Spotted in Latest Iranian Cyber Espionage Activity. Retrieved August 18, 2022.

text:
Exbyte performs various checks to determine if it is running in a sandboxed environment to prevent analysis.
Exbyte enumerates all document files on an infected machine, then creates a summary of these items including filename and directory location prior to exfiltration to cloud hosting services.
Exbyte checks for the presence of various security software products during execution.
title: Symantec Threat Hunter Team. (2022, October 21). Exbyte: BlackByte Ransomware Attackers Deploy New Exfiltration Tool. Retrieved December 16, 2024.

text:
Snip3 can create a VBS file in startup to persist after system restarts.
Snip3 has been delivered to targets via downloads from malicious domains.
Snip3 has been delivered to victims through malicious e-mail attachments.
Snip3 has been delivered to victims through e-mail links to malicious files.
Snip3 has been executed through luring victims into clicking malicious links.
title: Jornet, A. (2021, December 23). Snip3, an investigation into malware. Retrieved September 19, 2023.

text:
Qilin has been executed by luring victims into clicking links in spearphishing emails.
Qilin has the ability to clear Windows Event Logs.
Qilin can delete itself from infected hosts after execution.
Qilin has been delivered via malicious links in spearphishing emails.
title: Bradshaw, A. et al. (2025, April 1). Qilin affiliates spear-phish MSP ScreenConnect admin, targeting customers downstream. Retrieved September 26, 2025.

text:
Machete is written in Python and is used in conjunction with additional Python scripts.
Machete collects the MAC address of the target computer and other network configuration information.
Machete captures screenshots.
Machete captures audio from the computer’s microphone.
Machete uses HTTP for Command & Control.
Machete takes photos from the computer’s web camera.
Machete logs keystrokes from the victim’s machine.
Machete uses FTP for Command & Control.
Machete produces file listings in order to search for files to be exfiltrated.
title: kate. (2020, September 25). APT-C-43 steals Venezuelan military secrets to provide intelligence support for the reactionaries — HpReact campaign. Retrieved November 20, 2020.

text:
USBStealer automatically exfiltrates collected files via removable media when an infected device connects to an air-gapped victim machine after initially being connected to an internet-enabled victim machine.
USBStealer drops commands for a second victim onto a removable media drive inserted into the first victim, and commands are executed when the drive is inserted into the second victim.
USBStealer registers itself under a Registry Run key with the name "USB Disk Security."
USBStealer mimics a legitimate Russian program called USB Disk Security.
Once a removable media device is inserted back into the first victim, USBStealer collects data from it that was exfiltrated from a second victim.
USBStealer has several commands to delete files associated with the malware from the victim.
USBStealer sets the timestamps of its dropper files to the last-access and last-write timestamps of a standard Windows library chosen on the system.
USBStealer collects files matching certain criteria from the victim and stores them in a local directory for later exfiltration.
USBStealer monitors victims for insertion of removable drives. When dropped onto a second victim, it also enumerates drives connected to the system.
USBStealer searches victim drives for files matching certain extensions (“.skr”,“.pkr” or “.key”) or names.
Most strings in USBStealer are encrypted using 3DES and XOR and reversed.
USBStealer drops itself onto removable media and relies on Autorun to execute the malicious file when a user opens the removable media on another system.
USBStealer exfiltrates collected files via removable media from air-gapped victims.
For all non-removable drives on a victim, USBStealer executes automated collection of certain files for later exfiltration.
title: Calvet, J. (2014, November 11). Sednit Espionage Group Attacking Air-Gapped Networks. Retrieved January 4, 2017.

text:
TONESHELL has the ability to pause operations for a specified duration prior to follow-on execution of activities.
StarProxy has decrypted network packets using a custom algorithm.
StarProxy has used native windows API calls such as `GetLocalTime()` to retrieve system data.
TONESHELL included functionality to create sub-processes with a specific user’s token.
TONESHELL included functionality to retrieve a list of user accounts.
TONESHELL has used DLL injection to execute payloads received from the C2 server.
StarProxy has leveraged two 256-byte XOR keys to encrypt and decrypt network packets using a custom algorithm.
StarProxy has utilized TLS record headers in network packets to impersonate various versions of TLS protocols to blend in with legitimate network traffic. StarProxy used FakeTLS to communicate with its C2 server.
TONESHELL has utilized a modified DJB2 algorithm to resolve APIs.
StarProxy has used TCP for C2 communications to target IPs or domains. StarProxy contained code to support both UDP and TCP connections.
StarProxy has been side-loaded by the legitimate, signed executable, IsoBurner.exe.
StarProxy has used the command line for execution of commands.
StarProxy has proxied traffic between infected devices and their C2 servers.
TONESHELL has deleted payload files received from the C2 server.
StarProxy has utilized the windows API call `GetLocalTime()` to retrieve a SystemTime structure to generate a seed value.
title: Sudeep Singh. (2025, April 16). Latest Mustang Panda Arsenal: ToneShell and StarProxy | P1. Retrieved July 21, 2025.

text:
SnappyTCP spawns a reverse TCP shell following an HTTP-based negotiation.
SnappyTCP creates the reverse shell using a pthread spawning a bash shell.
SnappyTCP can use OpenSSL and TLS certificates to encrypt traffic.
SnappyTCP connects to the command and control server via a TCP socket using HTTP.
SnappyTCP is a reverse TCP shell with command and control capabilities used for persistence purposes.
title: PwC Threat Intelligence. (2023, December 5). The Tortoise and The Malware. Retrieved November 20, 2024.
